notes.html:
1. Complex Numbers

Real numbers cannot satisfy $x^2 = -1$. We introduce the imaginary unit to solve this.

The Imaginary Unit

The imaginary unit, denoted by $i$, is the number whose square is $-1$. $$i^2 = -1$$

Complex Numbers

Complex numbers are numbers of the form: $$a + bi$$ where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.

  • $a$ is the real part.
  • $b$ is the imaginary part.

Standard Form

Written as $a + bi$:

  • $3 + (-2)i$ is written as $3 - 2i$.
  • $a + 0i$ is written as $a$ (Real numbers $\subset$ Complex numbers).
  • $0 + bi$ is written as $bi$ (pure imaginary number).
Example 1: Complex Numbers

Examples of complex numbers $a + bi$:

Complex Number Real Part Imaginary Part
$3 + 4i$ $3$ $4$
$\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{3}i$ $\frac{1}{2}$ $-\frac{2}{3}$
$6i$ $0$ $6$
$-7$ $-7$ $0$

Note: Pure imaginary numbers have real part 0; real numbers have imaginary part 0.

1 Add, Subtract, Multiply, and Divide Complex Numbers

Complex numbers follow the familiar rules of algebra for real numbers.

Equality of Complex Numbers

$$a + bi = c + di \quad \text{if and only if } a = c \text{ and } b = d \tag{1}$$

Sum of Complex Numbers

$$(a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i \tag{2}$$

Difference of Complex Numbers

$$(a + bi) - (c + di) = (a - c) + (b - d)i \tag{3}$$

EXAMPLE 1 Adding and Subtracting Complex Numbers

(a) $(3 + 5i) + (-2 + 3i) = [3 + (-2)] + (5 + 3)i = 1 + 8i$

(b) $(6 + 4i) - (3 + 6i) = (6 - 3) + (4 - 6)i = 3 + (-2)i = 3 - 2i$

Product of Complex Numbers

$$(a + bi) \cdot (c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i \tag{4}$$

EXAMPLE 2 Multiplying Complex Numbers

$$(5 + 3i) \cdot (2 + 7i) = 5 \cdot (2 + 7i) + 3i(2 + 7i) = 10 + 35i + 6i + 21i^2$$

Using the Distributive Property and $i^2 = -1$: $$\begin{aligned} &= 10 + 41i + 21(-1) \\ &= -11 + 41i \end{aligned}$$

Examples:

  • $(2i)(2i) = 4i^2 = -4$
  • $(2 + i)(1 - i) = 2 - 2i + i - i^2 = 3 - i$

Conjugate

Definition: Conjugate

If $z = a + bi$ is a complex number, then its conjugate, denoted by $\overline{z}$, is defined as $$\overline{z} = \overline{a + bi} = a - bi$$

Examples: $\overline{2 + 3i} = 2 - 3i$ and $\overline{-6 - 2i} = -6 + 2i$

EXAMPLE 3 Multiplying a Complex Number by Its Conjugate

Find the product of $z = 3 + 4i$ and its conjugate $\overline{z}$.

Since $\overline{z} = 3 - 4i$: $$z\overline{z} = (3 + 4i)(3 - 4i) = 9 - 12i + 12i - 16i^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$$

Dividing Complex Numbers

To simplify $\frac{a + bi}{c + di}$, multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator: $c - di$.

$$ \frac{a + bi}{c + di} = \frac{(a + bi)(c - di)}{(c + di)(c - di)} = \frac{(ac + bd) + (bc - ad)i}{c^2 + d^2} $$

Don’t memorize the full formula — just remember:

Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator, then expand normally.

Example 3: Dividing Complex Numbers

Express in form $a + bi$:
(a) $\frac{3 + 5i}{1 - 2i}$
(b) $\frac{7 + 3i}{4i}$

Solution

(a) Conjugate of $1 - 2i$ is $1 + 2i$:

$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{3 + 5i}{1 - 2i} &= \frac{(3 + 5i)(1 + 2i)}{(1 - 2i)(1 + 2i)} \\ &= \frac{3(1) + 3(2i) + 5i(1) + 5i(2i)}{1^2 + (-2)^2} \\ &= \frac{3 + 6i + 5i + 10i^2}{5} \\ &= \frac{3 + 11i - 10}{5} \quad \leftarrow i^2 = -1 \\ &= \frac{-7 + 11i}{5} = -\frac{7}{5} + \frac{11}{5}i \end{aligned} $$

(b) Conjugate of $4i = 0 + 4i$ is $-4i$:

$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{7 + 3i}{4i} &= \frac{(7 + 3i)(-4i)}{(4i)(-4i)} \\ &= \frac{-28i -12i^2}{-16i^2} \\ &= \frac{-28i + 12}{16} \quad \leftarrow i^2 = -1 \\ &= \frac{12 - 28i}{16} = \frac{3}{4} - \frac{7}{4}i \end{aligned} $$

Theorem

The product of a complex number and its conjugate is a nonnegative real number. If $z = a + bi$, then $$z\overline{z} = a^2 + b^2 \tag{5}$$

Proof: If $z = a + bi$, then $$z\overline{z} = (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 - (bi)^2 = a^2 - b^2i^2 = a^2 + b^2 \quad \blacksquare$$

Reciprocal of a Complex Number

Note

To express $\frac{1}{z}$ in standard form, multiply numerator and denominator by $\overline{z}$:

$$\frac{1}{a + bi} = \frac{1}{z} \cdot \frac{\overline{z}}{\overline{z}} = \frac{\overline{z}}{z\overline{z}} = \frac{a - bi}{a^2 + b^2} = \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2} - \frac{b}{a^2 + b^2}i$$

EXAMPLE 4 Writing the Reciprocal of a Complex Number in Standard Form

Write $\frac{1}{3+4i}$ in standard form $a+bi$; that is, find the reciprocal of $3+4i$.

Solution Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of $3+4i$, which is $3-4i$.

$$ \frac{1}{3+4i} = \frac{1}{3+4i} \cdot \frac{3-4i}{3-4i} = \frac{3-4i}{9+16} = \frac{3}{25} - \frac{4}{25}i $$

To express the quotient of two complex numbers in standard form, multiply the numerator and denominator of the quotient by the conjugate of the denominator.

EXAMPLE 5 Writing the Quotient of Two Complex Numbers in Standard Form

Write each of the following in standard form. (a) $\dfrac{1+4i}{5-12i}$ (b) $\dfrac{2-3i}{4-3i}$

Solution

(a) $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{1+4i}{5-12i} &= \frac{1+4i}{5-12i} \cdot \frac{5+12i}{5+12i} = \frac{5+12i+20i+48i^2}{25+144} \\ &= \frac{-43+32i}{169} = -\frac{43}{169} + \frac{32}{169}i \end{aligned} $$

(b) $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{2-3i}{4-3i} &= \frac{2-3i}{4-3i} \cdot \frac{4+3i}{4+3i} = \frac{8+6i-12i-9i^2}{16+9} \\ &= \frac{17-6i}{25} = \frac{17}{25} - \frac{6}{25}i \end{aligned} $$

Properties of Conjugates

The conjugate of a complex number has general properties useful for simplification.

Theorem: Conjugate of a Real Number

For a real number $a = a + 0i$, the conjugate is the real number itself. $$\overline{a} = a$$

Theorem: Properties of Conjugates

Let $z$ and $w$ be complex numbers.

  1. Double Conjugate: The conjugate of the conjugate is the number itself. $$\overline{(\overline{z})} = z \tag{6}$$

  2. Conjugate of a Sum: The conjugate of the sum equals the sum of the conjugates. $$\overline{z + w} = \overline{z} + \overline{w} \tag{7}$$

  3. Conjugate of a Product: The conjugate of the product equals the product of the conjugates. $$\overline{z \cdot w} = \overline{z} \cdot \overline{w} \tag{8}$$

EXAMPLE 6 Verifying Properties of Conjugates

Let $z = 2 - 3i$, $w = 1 + 4i$, and $a = 5$. Verify the properties of conjugates.

Property 1 (Real Number): $$\overline{a} = \overline{5} = 5$$

Property 2 (Double Conjugate): $$\overline{(\overline{z})} = \overline{(2 + 3i)} = 2 - 3i=z $$

Property 3 (Sum): $$ \begin{aligned} \text{LHS: } \overline{z + w} &= \overline{(2 - 3i) + (1 + 4i)} = \overline{3 + i} = 3 - i \\ \text{RHS: } \overline{z} + \overline{w} &= (2 + 3i) + (1 - 4i) = 3 - i \end{aligned} $$ $\text{LHS} = \text{RHS} \checkmark$

Property 4 (Product): $$ \begin{aligned} \text{LHS: } \overline{z \cdot w} &= \overline{(2 - 3i)(1 + 4i)} = \overline{2 + 8i - 3i - 12i^2} = \overline{14 + 5i} = 14 - 5i \\ \text{RHS: } \overline{z} \cdot \overline{w} &= (2 + 3i)(1 - 4i) = 2 - 8i + 3i - 12i^2 = 14 - 5i \end{aligned} $$ $\text{LHS} = \text{RHS} \checkmark$

Powers of $i$

The powers of $i$ repeat in a cycle of 4:

$$ \begin{aligned} i^1 &= i & i^5 &= i \\ i^2 &= -1 & i^6 &= -1 \\ i^3 &= -i & i^7 &= -i \\ i^4 &= 1 & i^8 &= 1 \end{aligned} $$

EXAMPLE 7 Evaluating Powers of $i$

(a) $i^{27} = i^{24} \cdot i^3 = (i^4)^6 \cdot i^3 = 1^6 \cdot (-i) = -i$

(b) $i^{101} = i^{100} \cdot i = (i^4)^{25} \cdot i = 1^{25} \cdot i = i$

EXAMPLE 8 Writing the Power of a Complex Number in Standard Form

Write $(2 + i)^3$ in standard form.

Using the binomial formula $(x + a)^3 = x^3 + 3ax^2 + 3a^2x + a^3$:

$$ \begin{aligned} (2 + i)^3 &= 2^3 + 3 \cdot i \cdot 2^2 + 3 \cdot i^2 \cdot 2 + i^3 \\ &= 8 + 12i + 6(-1) + (-i) \\ &= 2 + 11i \end{aligned} $$

2. Solve Quadratic Equations in the Complex Number System

Quadratic equations with negative discriminants have no real solutions ($\mathbb{R}$) but always have solutions in the complex number ($\mathbb{C}$) system.

Definition: Principal Square Root of $-N$

If $N$ is a positive real number, the principal square root of $-N$ is: $$ \sqrt{-N} = \sqrt{N}i $$ where $i$ is the imaginary unit and $i^2 = -1$.

Warning

In writing $\sqrt{-N} = \sqrt{N}i$, be sure to place $i$ outside the $\sqrt{}$ symbol.

EXAMPLE 9 Evaluating the Square Root of a Negative Number

(a) $\sqrt{-1} = \sqrt{1}i = i$ (b) $\sqrt{-4} = \sqrt{4}i = 2i$ (c) $\sqrt{-8} = \sqrt{8}i = 2\sqrt{2}i$

EXAMPLE 10 Solving Equations

Solve each equation in the complex number system. (a) $x^2 = 4$ (b) $x^2 = -9$

Solution

(a) $$ x = \pm\sqrt{4} = \pm 2 $$ Solution set: $\{-2, 2\}$

(b) $$ x = \pm\sqrt{-9} = \pm\sqrt{9}i = \pm 3i $$ Solution set: $\{-3i, 3i\}$

Warning

When working with square roots of negative numbers, do not set the square root of a product equal to the product of the square roots. $$\sqrt{100} = \sqrt{(-25)(-4)} \neq \sqrt{-25}\sqrt{-4} = (5i)(2i) = 10i^2 = -10$$

Theorem: Quadratic Formula

In the complex number system, the solutions of $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, where $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$ and $a \neq 0$, are given by: $$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \tag{9}$$

EXAMPLE 11 Solving Quadratic Equations in the Complex Number System

Solve $x^2 - 4x + 8 = 0$ in the complex number system.

Here $a = 1, b = -4, c = 8$, and $b^2 - 4ac = 16 - 4(1)(8) = -16$.

$$ x = \frac{-(-4) \pm \sqrt{-16}}{2(1)} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16}i}{2} = \frac{4 \pm 4i}{2} = 2 \pm 2i $$

Solution set: $\{2 - 2i, 2 + 2i\}$

Check:

  • $2 + 2i$: $(2 + 2i)^2 - 4(2 + 2i) + 8 = 4 + 8i + 4i^2 - 8 - 8i + 8 = 4 - 4 = 0 \checkmark$
  • $2 - 2i$: $(2 - 2i)^2 - 4(2 - 2i) + 8 = 4 - 8i + 4i^2 - 8 + 8i + 8 = 4 - 4 = 0 \checkmark$
Character of the Solutions of a Quadratic Equation

For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ with real coefficients:

  1. If $b^2 - 4ac > 0$: two unequal real solutions
  2. If $b^2 - 4ac = 0$: repeated real solution (double root)
  3. If $b^2 - 4ac < 0$: two complex solutions that are conjugates of each other

When $b^2 - 4ac = -N < 0$: $$ > x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{-N}}{2a} = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{N}i}{2a} = \frac{-b}{2a} \pm \frac{\sqrt{N}}{2a}i > $$ These solutions are conjugates of each other.

EXAMPLE 12 Determining the Character of Solutions

Without solving, determine the character of the solutions:

(a) $3x^2 + 4x + 5 = 0$

$a = 3, b = 4, c = 5$ $b^2 - 4ac = 16 - 4(3)(5) = -44 < 0$

Two complex conjugates (not real).

(b) $2x^2 + 4x + 1 = 0$

$a = 2, b = 4, c = 1$ $b^2 - 4ac = 16 - 8 = 8 > 0$

Two unequal real numbers.

(c) $9x^2 - 6x + 1 = 0$

$a = 9, b = -6, c = 1$ $b^2 - 4ac = 36 - 4(9)(1) = 0$

Repeated real number (double root).

References

  • Precalculus, 9th Edition (Michael Sullivan) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf, (p. A54 - A58)

notes.html:
Polar Form of Complex Numbers; De Moivre's Theorem

Graphing Complex Numbers

Complex numbers $z = a + bi$ are graphed in the complex plane:

  • Real axis (Re): Horizontal axis ($a$).
  • Imaginary axis (Im): Vertical axis ($b$).
  • Plot $z$ as the point $(a, b)$.
Example 2: Graphing Sets of Complex Numbers

(a) $S = \{a + bi \mid a \ge 0\}$: Right half-plane (including imaginary axis). (b) $T = \{a + bi \mid a < 1, b \ge 0\}$: Region to the left of $x=1$ and above x-axis (Quadrant II and part of QI).

Modulus of a Complex Number

The modulus (or absolute value) $|z|$ is the distance from the origin to $z=a+bi$.

Definition

$$ |z| = |a + bi| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} $$

Example 3: Calculating Modulus
  • $|3 + 4i| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$
  • $|8 - 5i| = \sqrt{8^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{89}$
Example 4: Graphing Sets Defined by Modulus

(a) $C = \{z \mid |z| = 1\}$: Circle of radius 1 centered at origin (Unit Circle). (b) $D = \{z \mid |z| \le 1\}$: Unit disk (interior and boundary of unit circle).

Polar Form of Complex Numbers

Any complex number $z = a + bi$ can be written in polar (trigonometric) form using $r = |z|$ and angle $\theta$.

Polar Form

$$ z = r(\cos \theta + i \sin \theta) $$ where:

  • $r = |z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ (modulus)
  • $\tan \theta = \frac{b}{a}$ ($\theta$ is the argument)

Note: The argument $\theta$ is not unique; any $\theta + 2n\pi$ works. Choose $\theta$ based on the quadrant of $(a,b)$.

Example 5: Writing Complex Numbers in Polar Form

(a) $1 + i$

  • $r = \sqrt{1^2+1^2} = \sqrt{2}$
  • $\tan \theta = 1/1 = 1 \implies \theta = \pi/4$ (QI)
  • Result: $\sqrt{2}(\cos \frac{\pi}{4} + i \sin \frac{\pi}{4})$

(b) $-1 + \sqrt{3}i$

  • $r = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2} = 2$
  • $\tan \theta = -\sqrt{3} \implies \theta = 2\pi/3$ (QII)
  • Result: $2(\cos \frac{2\pi}{3} + i \sin \frac{2\pi}{3})$

(c) $-4\sqrt{3} - 4i$

  • $r = \sqrt{48 + 16} = 8$
  • $\tan \theta = \frac{-4}{-4\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \implies \theta = 7\pi/6$ (QIII)
  • Result: $8(\cos \frac{7\pi}{6} + i \sin \frac{7\pi}{6})$

(d) $3 + 4i$

  • $r = \sqrt{3^2+4^2} = 5$
  • $\theta = \tan^{-1}(4/3) \approx 0.93$ rad (QI, not a standard angle)
  • Result: $5[\cos(\tan^{-1}\frac{4}{3}) + i \sin(\tan^{-1}\frac{4}{3})] \approx 5(\cos 0.93 + i \sin 0.93)$

Multiplication, Division, and Powers of Complex Numbers

Multiplication and Division in Polar Form

Let $z_1 = r_1(\cos \theta_1 + i \sin \theta_1)$ and $z_2 = r_2(\cos \theta_2 + i \sin \theta_2)$.

Multiplication: Multiply moduli, add arguments. $$ z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2 [\cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2) + i \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)] $$

Division: Divide moduli, subtract arguments. $$ \frac{z_1}{z_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2} [\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2) + i \sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2)] \quad (z_2 \neq 0) $$

Example 6: Multiplying and Dividing

Let $z_1 = 2(\cos \frac{\pi}{4} + i \sin \frac{\pi}{4})$ and $z_2 = 5(\cos \frac{\pi}{3} + i \sin \frac{\pi}{3})$.

(a) Product: $$ > \begin{aligned} > z_1 z_2 &= (2)(5) \left[ \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\pi}{3}\right) + i \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\pi}{3}\right) \right] \\ > &= 10 \left( \cos \frac{7\pi}{12} + i \sin \frac{7\pi}{12} \right) \approx -2.588 + 9.659i > \end{aligned} > $$

(b) Quotient: $$ > \begin{aligned} > \frac{z_1}{z_2} &= \frac{2}{5} \left[ \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi}{3}\right) + i \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi}{3}\right) \right] \\ > &= \frac{2}{5} \left[ \cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{12}\right) + i \sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{12}\right) \right] \approx 0.3864 - 0.1035i > \end{aligned} > $$

De Moivre's Theorem

De Moivre's Theorem

If $z = r(\cos \theta + i \sin \theta)$, then for any integer $n$ (negative, positive and zero): $$ z^n = r^n (\cos n\theta + i \sin n\theta) $$ To take the $n$th power, take the $n$th power of the modulus and multiply the argument by $n$.

Example 7: Finding a Power Using De Moivre's Theorem

Find $\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}i\right)^{10}$.

Solution First, write in polar form. Since $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}i = \frac{1}{2}(1+i)$, and $1+i = \sqrt{2}(\cos \frac{\pi}{4} + i \sin \frac{\pi}{4})$: $$ z = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \left( \cos \frac{\pi}{4} + i \sin \frac{\pi}{4} \right) $$ Apply De Moivre's Theorem: $$ > \begin{aligned} > z^{10} &= \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^{10} \left[ \cos\left(10 \cdot \frac{\pi}{4}\right) + i \sin\left(10 \cdot \frac{\pi}{4}\right) \right] \\ > &= \frac{2^5}{2^{10}} \left( \cos \frac{5\pi}{2} + i \sin \frac{5\pi}{2} \right) \\ > &= \frac{1}{32} (0 + i(1)) = \frac{1}{32}i > \end{aligned} > $$

nth Roots of Complex Numbers

Formula for nth Roots

If $z = r(\cos \theta + i \sin \theta)$ and $n$ is a positive integer, $z$ has $n$ distinct $n$th roots $w_k$: $$ w_k = r^{1/n} \left[ \cos\left(\frac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}\right) + i \sin\left(\frac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}\right) \right] $$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, n-1$.

Guidelines for Finding nth Roots
  1. Modulus: The modulus of each $n$th root is $r^{1/n}$.
  2. Argument: The argument of the first root ($k=0$) is $\theta/n$.
  3. Roots: Repeatedly add $2\pi/n$ to get the argument of each successive root.

Geometric property: The $n$th roots are spaced equally on a circle of radius $r^{1/n}$.

Example 8: Finding Roots of a Complex Number

Find the six sixth roots of $z = -64$.

Solution In polar form, $z = 64(\cos \pi + i \sin \pi)$. Here $r=64, \theta=\pi, n=6$. Modulus of roots: $64^{1/6} = 2$. Arguments: $\frac{\pi + 2k\pi}{6}$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4,5$.

$$ > \begin{aligned} > w_0 &= 2\left(\cos \frac{\pi}{6} + i \sin \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \sqrt{3} + i & (k=0) \\ > w_1 &= 2\left(\cos \frac{\pi}{2} + i \sin \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2i & (k=1) \\ > w_2 &= 2\left(\cos \frac{5\pi}{6} + i \sin \frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\sqrt{3} + i & (k=2) \\ > w_3 &= 2\left(\cos \frac{7\pi}{6} + i \sin \frac{7\pi}{6}\right) = -\sqrt{3} - i & (k=3) \\ > w_4 &= 2\left(\cos \frac{3\pi}{2} + i \sin \frac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -2i & (k=4) \\ > w_5 &= 2\left(\cos \frac{11\pi}{6} + i \sin \frac{11\pi}{6}\right) = \sqrt{3} - i & (k=5) > \end{aligned} > $$

Example 9: Finding Cube Roots (using degrees)

Find the three cube roots of $z = 2 + 2i$.

Solution Convert to polar form using degrees: $r = \sqrt{2^2+2^2} = 2\sqrt{2}$, $\theta = 45^\circ$. $$ z = 2\sqrt{2}(\cos 45^\circ + i \sin 45^\circ) $$ Modulus of roots: $(2\sqrt{2})^{1/3} = (2^{3/2})^{1/3} = 2^{1/2} = \sqrt{2}$. Arguments: $\frac{45^\circ + 360^\circ k}{3} = 15^\circ + 120^\circ k$.

$$ > \begin{aligned} > w_0 &= \sqrt{2}(\cos 15^\circ + i \sin 15^\circ) \approx 1.366 + 0.366i & (k=0) \\ > w_1 &= \sqrt{2}(\cos 135^\circ + i \sin 135^\circ) = -1 + i & (k=1) \\ > w_2 &= \sqrt{2}(\cos 255^\circ + i \sin 255^\circ) \approx -0.366 - 1.366i & (k=2) > \end{aligned} > $$

Example 10: Solving an Equation Using the nth Roots Formula

Solve the equation $z^6 + 64 = 0$.

Solution Rewrite as $z^6 = -64$. The solutions are the six sixth roots of $-64$, which were found in Example 8.

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 618)

notes.html:
Chapter 4 Review: Properties and Formulas

Exponential Functions

The exponential function $f$ with base $a$ ($a > 0, a \ne 1$) is defined for all real numbers $x$ by:

$$f(x) = a^x$$

  • Domain: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Range: $(0, \infty)$

The Natural Exponential Function

The natural exponential function is the exponential function with base $e$:

$$f(x) = e^x$$

The number $e$ is defined as the value that $\left(1 + 1/n\right)^n$ approaches as $n \to \infty$ ($e \approx 2.7182818284590\dots$).

Compound Interest

  • Compounded $n$ times per year:

    $$A(t) = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}$$

    where $P = \text{principal}$, $r = \text{annual interest rate}$, $t = \text{years}$, $A(t) = \text{amount}$.

  • Compounded continuously:

    $$A(t) = Pe^{rt}$$

Logarithmic Functions

The logarithmic function $\log_a$ with base $a$ ($a > 0, a \ne 1$) is defined for $x > 0$ by:

$$\log_a x = y \iff a^y = x$$

  • Domain: $(0, \infty)$

  • Range: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Common Logarithm: $\log x = \log_{10} x$

  • Natural Logarithm: $\ln x = \log_e x$

Properties of Logarithms

  1. $\log_a 1 = 0$

  2. $\log_a a = 1$

  3. $\log_a a^x = x$

  4. $a^{\log_a x} = x$

Laws of Logarithms

Let $a$ be a logarithm base ($a > 0, a \ne 1$), and let $A, B$, and $C$ be real numbers or algebraic expressions representing real numbers, with $A > 0$ and $B > 0$:

  1. $\log_a(AB) = \log_a A + \log_a B$

  2. $\log_a(A/B) = \log_a A - \log_a B$

  3. $\log_a(A^C) = C\log_a A$

Change of Base Formula

$$\log_b x = \frac{\log_a x}{\log_a b}$$

Equation Solving Guidelines

Guidelines for Solving Exponential Equations

  1. Isolate the exponential term on one side of the equation.

  2. Take the logarithm of each side, and use the Laws of Logarithms to “bring down the exponent”.

  3. Solve for the variable.

Guidelines for Solving Logarithmic Equations

  1. Isolate the logarithmic term(s) on one side of the equation, and use the Laws of Logarithms to combine logarithmic terms if necessary.

  2. Rewrite the equation in exponential form.

  3. Solve for the variable.

Modeling with Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

Exponential Growth Model

$$n(t) = n_0 e^{rt}$$

where $n_0 = \text{initial population (at } t = 0)$, and $r = \text{relative growth rate}$.

Logistic Growth Model

$$n(t) = \frac{M}{1 + Ae^{-rt}}$$

where $M = \text{carrying capacity}$ and $A = (M - n_0)/n_0$.

Radioactive Decay Model

$$m(t) = m_0 e^{-rt}$$

where the relative decay rate is $\boxed{r = \frac{\ln 2}{h}}$ given half-life $h$.

Newton's Law of Cooling

$$T(t) = T_s + D_0 e^{-kt}$$

where $T_s = \text{surrounding temperature}$, $D_0 = \text{initial temperature difference}$, and $k > 0$.

Logarithmic Scales

  • The pH Scale:

    $$pH = -\log[H^+]$$

  • The Richter Scale:

    $$M = \log\frac{I}{S}$$

  • The Decibel Scale:

    $$B = 10 \log\frac{I}{I_0}$$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 397)

notes.html:
Exponential Equations

An exponential equation is an equation in which the variable occurs in the exponent. One-to-one properties of exponential functions allow for direct solving:

$$a^x = a^y \implies x = y$$

Example 1: Exponential Equations

Solve each exponential equation.

(a)

$$\begin{aligned} 5^x &= 125 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ 5^x &= 5^3 \qquad &\leftarrow 125 = 5^3 \\ x &= 3 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{one-to-one property} \end{aligned}$$

(b)

$$\begin{aligned} 5^{2x} &= 5^{x+1} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ 2x &= x + 1 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{one-to-one property} \\ x &= 1 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{solve for } x \end{aligned}$$

Guidelines for Solving Exponential Equations

  1. Isolate the exponential expression on one side of the equation.

  2. Take the logarithm of each side, then use the Laws of Logarithms to “bring down the exponent.”

  3. Solve for the variable.

Example 2: Solving an Exponential Equation

Consider the exponential equation $3^{x+2} = 7$.

(a) Find the exact solution of the equation expressed in terms of logarithms.

(b) Use a calculator to find an approximation to the solution rounded to six decimal places.

(a)

$$\begin{aligned} 3^{x+2} &= 7 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ \log(3^{x+2}) &= \log 7 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{take log of each side} \\ (x + 2)\log 3 &= \log 7 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 3 (bring down exponent)} \\ x + 2 &= \frac{\log 7}{\log 3} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{divide by } \log 3 \\ x &= \frac{\log 7}{\log 3} - 2 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{subtract 2} \end{aligned}$$

Exact solution: $x = \frac{\log 7}{\log 3} - 2$

(b)

Approximation: $x \approx -0.228756$

Example 4: Solving an Exponential Equation Algebraically and Graphically

Solve the equation $e^{3-2x} = 4$ algebraically.

Solution: Algebraic

$$\begin{aligned} e^{3-2x} &= 4 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ \ln(e^{3-2x}) &= \ln 4 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{take } \ln \text{ of each side} \\ 3 - 2x &= \ln 4 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{property of } \ln \\ -2x &= -3 + \ln 4 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{subtract 3} \\ x &= \frac{1}{2}(3 - \ln 4) \approx 0.807 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{multiply by } -\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Example 5: An Exponential Equation of Quadratic Type

Solve the equation $e^{2x} - e^x - 6 = 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} e^{2x} - e^x - 6 &= 0 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ (e^x)^2 - e^x - 6 &= 0 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law of Exponents} \\ (e^x - 3)(e^x + 2) &= 0 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{factor (quadratic in } e^x) \end{aligned}$$

Inline substitution check: Let $w = e^x \implies w^2 - w - 6 = 0 \implies (w - 3)(w + 2) = 0$

$$\begin{aligned} e^x - 3 &= 0 \qquad &\text{or} \qquad e^x + 2 &= 0 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Zero-Product Property} \\ e^x &= 3 & e^x &= -2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} e^x &= 3 \implies x = \ln 3 \approx 1.0986 \\ e^x &= -2 \implies \emptyset \qquad &\leftarrow e^x > 0 \ \forall x \end{aligned}$$

Solution: $x = \ln 3$

Example 6: An Equation Involving Exponential Functions

Solve the equation $3xe^x + x^2e^x = 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3xe^x + x^2e^x &= 0 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ x(3 + x)e^x &= 0 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{factor out common factors} \\ x(3 + x) &= 0 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{divide by } e^x \ \ (\text{valid since } e^x \ne 0) \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} x = 0 \qquad &\text{or} \qquad 3 + x = 0 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Zero-Product Property} \\ & \qquad \qquad \ \ \ \ x = -3 \end{aligned}$$

Solutions: $x = 0, \ x = -3$

Check:

$$\begin{aligned} x = 0: \quad & 3(0)e^0 + 0^2e^0 = 0 \quad \checkmark \\ x = -3: \quad & 3(-3)e^{-3} + (-3)^2e^{-3} = -9e^{-3} + 9e^{-3} = 0 \quad \checkmark \end{aligned}$$

Logarithmic Equations

A logarithmic equation is an equation in which a logarithm of the variable occurs. One-to-one properties of logarithmic functions allow for direct solving:

$$\log_a x = \log_a y \implies x = y$$

Example 7: Solving a Logarithmic Equation

Solve the equation $\log_5(x^2 + 1) = \log_5(x - 2) + \log_5(x + 3)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \log_5(x^2 + 1) &= \log_5(x - 2) + \log_5(x + 3) \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ \log_5(x^2 + 1) &= \log_5[(x - 2)(x + 3)] \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 1: } \log_a AB = \log_a A + \log_a B \\ \log_5(x^2 + 1) &= \log_5(x^2 + x - 6) \qquad &\leftarrow \text{expand} \\ x^2 + 1 &= x^2 + x - 6 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{log is one-to-one (or raise 5 to each side)} \\ 1 &= x - 6 \\ x &= 7 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{solve for } x \end{aligned}$$

Solution: $x = 7$

Check: Verify that $x = 7$ satisfies the original equation (arguments must remain positive). $\checkmark$

Example 8: Solving Logarithmic Equations

Solve each equation for $x$.

(a)

$$\begin{aligned} \ln x &= 8 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ x &= e^8 \approx 2981 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{exponential form} \end{aligned}$$

Alternative Method:

$$\begin{aligned} \ln x &= 8 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ e^{\ln x} &= e^8 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{raise } e \text{ to each side} \\ x &= e^8 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{property of } \ln \end{aligned}$$

(b)

$$\begin{aligned} \log_2(25 - x) &= 3 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ 25 - x &= 2^3 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{exponential form (or raise 2 to each side)} \\ 25 - x &= 8 \\ x &= 25 - 8 = 17 \end{aligned}$$

Example 9: Solving a Logarithmic Equation

Solve the equation $4 + 3 \log(2x) = 16$.

$$\begin{aligned} 4 + 3 \log(2x) &= 16 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given equation} \\ 3 \log(2x) &= 12 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{subtract 4} \\ \log(2x) &= 4 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{divide by 3} \\ 2x &= 10^4 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{exponential form (or raise 10 to each side)} \\ 2x &= 10000 \\ x &= 5000 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{divide by 2} \end{aligned}$$

Solution: $x = 5000$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 369)

notes.html:
Exponential Functions

Exponential functions get their name from the fact that the variable is in the exponent.

$$\begin{aligned} f(3) &= 2^3 = 8 \\ f(10) &= 2^{10} = 1024 \\ f(30) &= 2^{30} = 1,073,741,824 \end{aligned} \quad \longleftrightarrow \quad \begin{aligned} g(x) &= x^2 \\ g(30) &= 30^2 = 900 \end{aligned}$$

To define $a^x$ when $x$ is an irrational number, approximate $x$ by rational numbers.

$$\text{Since } \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73205\dots \implies a^{\sqrt{3}} \text{ is approximated by } a^{1.7}, a^{1.73}, a^{1.732}, a^{1.7320}, a^{1.73205}, \dots$$

$$5^{\sqrt{3}} \approx 5^{1.732} \approx 16.2411\dots$$

The Laws of Exponents are still true when the exponents are real numbers.

see: Laws of Exponents

Info

Exponential Functions

The exponential function with base $a$ is defined for all real numbers $x$ by

$$f(x) = a^x$$

where $a > 0$ and $a \ne 1$.

If $a = 1$, then $f(x) = 1^x = 1$, which is a constant function.

Examples of Exponential Functions

$$f(x) = 2^x \quad \leftarrow \text{Base 2} \qquad g(x) = 3^x \quad \leftarrow \text{Base 3} \qquad h(x) = 10^x \quad \leftarrow \text{Base 10}$$

Graphs of Exponential Functions

Example

Example 2: Graphing Exponential Functions by Ploting Points

Draw the graph of each function.

(a) $f(x) = 3^x \qquad$ (b) $g(x) = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^x$

x f(x)=3x g(x)=(31​)x
$-3$ $\frac{1}{27}$ $27$
$-2$ $\frac{1}{9}$ $9$
$-1$ $\frac{1}{3}$ $3$
$0$ $1$ $1$
$1$ $3$ $\frac{1}{3}$
$2$ $9$ $\frac{1}{9}$
$3$ $27$ $\frac{1}{27}$

The graph of $g(x) = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^x$ is the reflection of the graph of $f(x) = 3^x$ about the $y$-axis.

In general, the graph of $g(x) = \left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^x$ is the reflection of the graph of $f(x) = a^x$ about the $y$-axis:

$$g(x) = \left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^x = \frac{1}{a^x} = a^{-x} = f(-x)$$

see: Reflecting Graphs

Families of Exponential Functions

All graphs of the family $f(x) = a^x$ have $y$-intercept 1 because $f(0) = a^0 = 1$ for $a \ne 0$.

There are two kinds of exponential functions:

  • Exponential Growth ($a > 1$): The function increases rapidly.

  • Exponential Decay ($0 < a < 1$): The function decreases rapidly.

The $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote for $f(x) = a^x$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{When } a > 1: \quad a^x \to 0 &\text{ as } x \to -\infty \\ \text{When } 0 < a < 1: \quad a^x \to 0 &\text{ as } x \to \infty \end{aligned}$$

Additionally, $a^x > 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Info

Graphs of Exponential Functions

The exponential function

$$f(x) = a^x \qquad (a > 0, \ a \ne 1)$$

  • Domain: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Range: $(0, \infty)$

  • $y$-intercept: $1$

  • Horizontal Asymptote: Line $y = 0$ ($x$-axis)

Example

Example 4: Transformations of Exponential Functions

Use the graph of $f(x) = 2^x$ to sketch the graph of each function. State the $y$-intercept, domain, range, and horizontal asymptote.

(a) $g(x) = 1 + 2^x$

Transformation: Shift upward 1 unit.

  • $y$-intercept: $g(0) = 1 + 2^0 = 2$

  • Domain: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Range: $(1, \infty)$

  • Horizontal Asymptote: $y = 1$

(b) $h(x) = -2^x$

Transformation: Reflect about the $x$-axis.

  • $y$-intercept: $h(0) = -2^0 = -1$

  • Domain: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Range: $(-\infty, 0)$

  • Horizontal Asymptote: $y = 0$

D

(c) $k(x) = 2^{x-1}$

Transformation: Shift 1 unit right.

  • $y$-intercept: $k(0) = 2^{0-1} = \frac{1}{2}$

  • Domain: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Range: $(0, \infty)$

  • Horizontal Asymptote: $y = 0$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 238)

notes.html:
Laws of Logarithms

Let $a$ be a positive number with $a \ne 1$. Let $A, B$, and $C$ be real numbers with $A > 0$ and $B > 0$.

Laws of Logarithms

  1. $\log_a(AB) = \log_a A + \log_a B$

  2. $\log_a\left(\frac{A}{B}\right) = \log_a A - \log_a B$

  3. $\log_a(A^C) = C\log_a A$

Proofs

Law 1

$$\begin{aligned} \log_a(AB) &= \log_a(a^u a^v) \qquad &\leftarrow \text{let } \log_a A = u \implies a^u = A \text{ and } \log_a B = v \implies a^v = B \\ &= \log_a(a^{u+v}) \\ &= u + v \\ &= \log_a A + \log_a B \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned}$$

Law 2

$$\begin{aligned} \log_a A &= \log_a\left[\left(\frac{A}{B}\right)B\right] \\ &= \log_a\left(\frac{A}{B}\right) + \log_a B \qquad &\leftarrow \text{by Law 1} \\ \log_a\left(\frac{A}{B}\right) &= \log_a A - \log_a B \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned}$$

Law 3

$$\begin{aligned} \log_a(A^C) &= \log_a((a^u)^C) \qquad &\leftarrow \text{let } \log_a A = u \implies a^u = A \\ &= \log_a(a^{uC}) \\ &= uC \\ &= C\log_a A \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned}$$

Example 1: Using the Laws of Logarithms to Evaluate Expressions

Evaluate each expression.

(a)

$$\begin{aligned} \log_4 2 + \log_4 32 &= \log_4(2 \cdot 32) \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 1} \\ &= \log_4 64 \\ &= 3 \qquad &\leftarrow 64 = 4^3 \end{aligned}$$

(b)

$$\begin{aligned} \log_2 80 - \log_2 5 &= \log_2\left(\frac{80}{5}\right) \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 2} \\ &= \log_2 16 \\ &= 4 \qquad &\leftarrow 16 = 2^4 \end{aligned}$$

(c)

$$\begin{aligned} -\frac{1}{3} \log 1000 &= \log 1000^{-1/3} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 3} \\ &= \log \frac{1}{10} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{property of negative exponents} \\ &= -1 \qquad &\leftarrow \frac{1}{10} = 10^{-1} \end{aligned}$$

Example 3: Combining Logarithmic Expressions

Use the Laws of Logarithms to combine each expression into a single logarithm.

(a)

$$\begin{aligned} 3 \log x + \frac{1}{2} \log(x + 1) &= \log x^3 + \log(x + 1)^{1/2} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 3} \\ &= \log(x^3(x + 1)^{1/2}) \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 1} \end{aligned}$$

(b)

$$\begin{aligned} 3 \ln s + \frac{1}{2} \ln t - 4 \ln(t^2 + 1) &= \ln s^3 + \ln t^{1/2} - \ln(t^2 + 1)^4 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 3} \\ &= \ln(s^3 t^{1/2}) - \ln(t^2 + 1)^4 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 1} \\ &= \ln \frac{s^3 \sqrt{t}}{(t^2 + 1)^4} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 2} \end{aligned}$$

Change of Base Formula

Change of Base Formula

$$\log_b x = \frac{\log_a x}{\log_a b} \qquad a > 0, \ b > 0$$

Alternative formulation shows $\log_b x$ is a constant multiple of $\log_a x$:

$$\log_b x = \frac{1}{\log_a b} \cdot \log_a x$$

Proof

$$\begin{aligned} y &= \log_b x \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Given} \\ b^y &= x \qquad &\leftarrow \text{exponential form} \\ \log_a b^y &= \log_a x \qquad &\leftarrow \text{take } \log_a \text{ of each side} \\ y \log_a b &= \log_a x \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 3} \\ y &= \frac{\log_a x}{\log_a b} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{divide by } \log_a b \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned}$$

Setting $x = a$ yields the specific case:

$$\log_b a = \frac{1}{\log_a b}$$

Example 5: Evaluating Logarithms with the Change of Base Formula

Use the Change of Base Formula to express each logarithm in terms of common or natural logarithms, then evaluate to five decimal places.

(a) $\log_8 5$

$$\log_8 5 = \frac{\log_{10} 5}{\log_{10} 8} \approx 0.77398$$

(b) $\log_9 20$

$$\log_9 20 = \frac{\ln 20}{\ln 9} \approx 1.36342$$

Example 6: Using the Change of Base Formula

Let $f(x) = \log_6 x$ and $g(x) = (\ln x)/(\ln 6)$. Explain why $f(x) = g(x)$.

$$f(x) = \log_6 x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln 6} = g(x) \qquad \leftarrow \text{by Change of Base formula}$$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 362)

notes.html:
Logarithmic Functions

Every exponential function $f(x) = a^x$ ($a > 0, a \ne 1$) is a one-to-one function by the Horizontal Line Test and therefore has an inverse function $f^{-1}$, called the logarithmic function with base $a$ (denoted by $\log_a$).

$$f^{-1}(x) = y \iff f(y) = x$$

see: One-to-One Functions and Their Inverses

Info

Definition of Logarithmic Functions

For $a > 0$ and $a \ne 1$, the logarithmic function with base $a$, denoted by $\log_a$, is defined by

$$\log_a x = y \iff a^y = x$$

$\log_a x$ is the exponent to which the base $a$ must be raised to give $x$.

  • We read $\log_a x = y$ as "log base $a$ of $x$ is $y$."

  • Parentheses are usually omitted: $\log_a(x) = \log_a x$.

Switching Forms

When switching between the logarithmic form $\log_a x = y$ and the exponential form $a^y = x$, the base remains the same.

Example

Example 1: Logarithmic and Exponential Forms

The logarithmic and exponential forms are equivalent equations: If one is true, then so is the other.

Logarithmic Form Exponential Form
$\log_{10} 100,000 = 5$ $10^5 = 100,000$
$\log_2 8 = 3$ $2^3 = 8$
$\log_2\left(\frac{1}{8}\right) = -3$ $2^{-3} = \frac{1}{8}$
$\log_{1/3} 9 = -2$ $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{-2} = 9$

It is important to understand that $\log_a x$ is an exponent.

x log10​x
$10^4$ $4$
$10^3$ $3$
$10^2$ $2$
$10$ $1$
$1$ $0$
$10^{-1}$ $-1$
$10^{-2}$ $-2$
$10^{-3}$ $-3$
$10^{-4}$ $-4$
Example

Example 2: Evaluating Logarithms

(a) $\log_{10} 1000 = 3 \qquad$ because $\quad 10^3 = 1000$

(b) $\log_2 32 = 5 \qquad\quad$ because $\quad 2^5 = 32$

(c) $\log_{10} 0.1 = -1 \qquad$ because $\quad 10^{-1} = 0.1$

(d) $\log_{16} 4 = \frac{1}{2} \qquad\quad$ because $\quad 16^{1/2} = 4$

(e) $\log_{1/2} 16 = -4 \qquad$ because $\quad \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-4} = 16$

Applying the cancellation equations of the Inverse Function Property to $f(x) = a^x$ and $f^{-1}(x) = \log_a x$ yields:

$$\begin{aligned} \log_a(a^x) &= x \qquad (x \in \mathbb{R}) \\ a^{\log_a x} &= x \qquad (x > 0) \end{aligned}$$

see: Inverse Function Property

Info

Properties of Logarithms

Property Reason
1. $\log_a 1 = 0$ We must raise $a$ to the power $0$ to get $1$.
2. $\log_a a = 1$ We must raise $a$ to the power $1$ to get $a$.
3. $\log_a a^x = x$ We must raise $a$ to the power $x$ to get $a^x$.
4. $a^{\log_a x} = x$ $\log_a x$ is the power to which $a$ must be raised to get $x$.
Example

Example 3: Applying Properties of Logarithms

We illustrate the properties of logarithms when the base is $5$.

  • $$\log_5 1 = 0 \qquad \text{Property 1}$$

  • $$\log_5 5 = 1 \qquad \text{Property 2}$$

  • $$\log_5 5^8 = 8 \qquad \text{Property 3}$$

  • $$5^{\log_5 12} = 12 \qquad \text{Property 4}$$

Example

Example 4: Graphing a Logarithmic Function by Plotting Points

Sketch the graph of $f(x) = \log_2 x$.

To make a table of values, choose $x$-values to be powers of 2 so that their logarithms are easily evaluated:

x log2​x
$2^3 = 8$ $3$
$2^2 = 4$ $2$
$2^1 = 2$ $1$
$1$ $0$
$2^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}$ $-1$
$2^{-2} = \frac{1}{4}$ $-2$
$2^{-3} = \frac{1}{8}$ $-3$
$2^{-4} = \frac{1}{16}$ $-4$

Families of Logarithmic Functions

Figure 3 shows graphs of the family of logarithmic functions $y = \log_a x$ for various values of the base $a$.

  • When $a > 1$: The function increases. As the base $a$ gets larger, the graph grows more slowly for $x > 1$.

  • When $0 < a < 1$: The function decreases.

All these graphs pass through the $x$-intercept $1$ because $\log_a 1 = 0$ for any valid base $a$. The $y$-axis ($x = 0$) serves as a vertical asymptote for the entire family.

Graphs of Logarithmic Functions ($a > 1$)

Since $y = \log_a x$ is the inverse function of $y = a^x$, its graph is a geometric reflection about the line $y = x$ of the corresponding exponential graph.

Because $f(x) = a^x$ has domain $\mathbb{R}$ and range $(0, \infty)$, its inverse function swapping inputs and outputs means that $y = \log_a x$ has:

  • Domain: $(0, \infty)$

  • Range: $\mathbb{R}$

Info

Graphs of Logarithmic Functions ($a > 1$)

The logarithmic function

$$f(x) = \log_a x \qquad (a > 1)$$

  • Domain: $(0, \infty)$

  • Range: $\mathbb{R}$

  • $x$-intercept: $1$

  • Vertical Asymptote: The line $x = 0$ (the $y$-axis)

As $x \to 0^{+}$, $\log_a x \to -\infty$.

For $a > 1$, the fact that the exponential counterpart $y = a^x$ increases extremely rapidly for $x > 0$ dictates that its inverse $y = \log_a x$ is a very slowly increasing function for $x > 1$.

Example

Example 5: Reflecting Graphs of Logarithms

Sketch the graph of each function. State the $x$-intercept, domain, range, and vertical asymptote.

(a) $g(x) = -\log_2 x$

Transformation: Start with the graph of $f(x) = \log_2 x$ and reflect it across the $x$-axis.

  • $x$-intercept: $1$ (unchanged by $x$-axis reflection)

  • Domain: $(0, \infty)$

  • Range: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Vertical Asymptote: $x = 0$

(b) $h(x) = \log_2(-x)$

Transformation: Start with the graph of $f(x) = \log_2 x$ and reflect it across the $y$-axis.

  • $x$-intercept: $-1$ (the point $(1,0)$ reflects to $(-1,0)$)

  • Domain: $(-\infty, 0)$

  • Range: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Vertical Asymptote: $x = 0$

Example

Example 6: Shifting Graphs of Logarithmic Functions

Sketch the graph of each function. State the domain, range, and vertical asymptote.

(a) $g(x) = 2 + \log_5 x$

Transformation: Start with the graph of $f(x) = \log_5 x$ and shift it upward 2 units.

  • Point shift: The point $(1,0)$ on the graph of $f$ shifts to $(1,2)$ on the graph of $g$.

  • Domain: $(0, \infty)$

  • Range: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Vertical Asymptote: $x = 0$

(b) $h(x) = \log_{10}(x - 3)$

Transformation: Start with the graph of $f(x) = \log_{10} x$ and shift it to the right 3 units.

  • Point shift: The point $(1,0)$ on the graph of $f$ shifts to $(4,0)$ on the graph of $h$.

  • Domain: $(3, \infty)$

  • Range: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Vertical Asymptote: $x = 3$

Common Logarithms

Logarithms with base 10 are referred to as common logarithms.

Info

Common Logarithm

The logarithm with base 10 is called the common logarithm and is denoted by omitting the base:

$$\log x = \log_{10} x$$

From the fundamental definition of logarithms:

$$\log 10 = 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \log 100 = 2$$

To evaluate a value that is not an exact integer power of 10, such as $\log 50$:

  • Find the exponent $y$ such that $10^y = 50$.

  • Since $10^1 = 10$ and $10^2 = 100$, it is clear that:

    $$1 < \log 50 < 2$$

Example

Example 7: Evaluating Common Logarithms

Use a calculator to find appropriate values of $f(x) = \log x$, and use these values to sketch the graph.

By evaluating points that are not standard powers of 10:

x logx
$0.01$ $-2$
$0.1$ $-1$
$0.5$ $-0.301$
$1$ $0$
$4$ $0.602$
$5$ $0.699$
$10$ $1$

Natural Logarithms

Info

The logarithm with base $e$ is called the natural logarithm and is denoted by $\ln$: $$\ln x = \log_e x$$

The natural logarithmic function $y = \ln x$ is the inverse function of the natural exponential function $y = e^x$.

$$\ln x = y \iff e^y = x$$

Properties of Natural Logarithms

Property Reason
1. $\ln 1 = 0$ We must raise $e$ to the power $0$ to get $1$.
2. $\ln e = 1$ We must raise $e$ to the power $1$ to get $e$.
3. $\ln e^x = x$ We must raise $e$ to the power $x$ to get $e^x$.
4. $e^{\ln x} = x$ $\ln x$ is the power to which $e$ must be raised to get $x$.
Example 10: Finding the Domain of a Logarithmic Function

Find the domain of the function $f(x) = \ln(4 - x^2)$.

$$\begin{aligned} 4 - x^2 &> 0 \qquad \leftarrow \text{argument must be positive} \\ x^2 &< 4 \\ |x| &< 2 \\ -2 < x &< 2 \end{aligned}$$

Domain: $\{x \mid -2 < x < 2\} = (-2, 2)$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 352)

notes.html:
Logarithmic Scales

When a physical quantity varies over an extremely large range, taking its logarithm maps the values onto a manageable scale. On a logarithmic scale, numbers are represented by their logarithms.

The pH Scale

Used by chemists to measure the acidity of a solution by compressing the wide variance of hydrogen ion concentrations $[H^+]$.

Info

$$pH = -\log[H^+]$$

$[H^+] = \text{concentration of hydrogen ions in moles per liter (M)}$

  • Neutral: $pH = 7$

  • Acidic: $pH < 7$

  • Basic: $pH > 7$

Inverse rule to extract concentration:

$$\text{Reverse the Rule} \quad \boxed{[H^+] = 10^{-pH}}$$

Each single-unit increase in pH corresponds to a **10-fold decrease** in $[H^+]$.
Example

(a) Find the pH of human blood where $[H^+] = 3.16 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}$.

$$\begin{aligned} pH &= -\log(3.16 \times 10^{-8}) \\ &\approx 7.5 \qquad \leftarrow \text{basic } (pH > 7) \end{aligned}$$

(b) Find $[H^+]$ of rain with a $pH = 2.4$.

$$\begin{aligned} \log[H^+] &= -2.4 \\ [H^+] &= 10^{-2.4} \approx 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M} \end{aligned}$$

The Richter Scale

Measures the magnitude $M$ of an earthquake relative to a reference benchmark.

Info

$$M = \log\frac{I}{S}$$

$I = \text{intensity (seismograph amplitude at 100 km)}$ $S = \text{standard earthquake intensity } (10^{-4}\text{ cm})$

An increase of 1 unit on the Richter scale indicates a **10-fold increase** in earthquake intensity $I$.
Example

(a) Find the magnitude if $I = 3.75\text{ cm}$.

$$M = \log\frac{3.75}{10^{-4}} = \log 37500 \approx 4.6$$

(b) Find the intensity $I$ if $M = 5.1$.

$$\begin{aligned} 10^{5.1} &= \frac{I}{10^{-4}} \\ I &= 10^{5.1} \cdot 10^{-4} = 10^{1.1} \approx 12.6\text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

(c) Compare 1906 earthquake ($M_1 = 8.3$) and 1989 earthquake ($M_2 = 7.1$).

$$\begin{aligned} \log\frac{I_1}{I_2} &= \log\frac{I_1/S}{I_2/S} = \log\frac{I_1}{S} - \log\frac{I_2}{S} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{Law 2} \\ &= 8.3 - 7.1 = 1.2 \\ \frac{I_1}{I_2} &= 10^{1.2} \approx 16 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{16 times more intense} \end{aligned}$$

The Decibel Scale

Measures the perceived loudness level $B$ of sounds.

Info

$$B = 10 \log\frac{I}{I_0}$$

$I = \text{sound intensity in } W/m^2$ $I_0 = \text{threshold of hearing } (10^{-12}\text{ W/m}^2)$

Example

(a) Find $B$ for a jet takeoff with $I = 100\text{ W/m}^2$.

$$B = 10 \log\frac{10^2}{10^{-12}} = 10 \log 10^{14} = 10(14) = 140\text{ dB}$$

(b) Find $I$ for a motorcycle with $B = 90\text{ dB}$.

$$\begin{aligned} 90 &= 10 \log\frac{I}{10^{-12}} \\ 9 &= \log I - \log 10^{-12} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{divide by 10 and apply Law 2} \\ 9 &= \log I + 12 \\ \log I &= -3 \\ I &= 10^{-3}\text{ W/m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 391)

Fish environment with $M = 30,000$, $n_0 = 3000$, and initial rate $r = 0.1848$:
Polonium-210 with $h = 138$ days and initial mass $m_0 = 300$ mg. Find remaining mass after $t = 365$ days:
Coffee at $200^\circ\text{F}$ is placed in a $70^\circ\text{F}$ room ($T_s = 70 \implies D_0 = 200 - 70 = 130$). It cools to $150^\circ\text{F}$ at $t = 10$ minutes. Find constant $k$:

notes.excerpt: --- 1. Exponential Growth (Doubling Time) Used when growth is expressed via a baseline doubling period. [!info] $$n(t) n_0 2^{t/a}$$ $n_0 \text{initial population} \quad a \text{doubling time} \quad t
notes.html:
1. Exponential Growth (Doubling Time)

Used when growth is expressed via a baseline doubling period.

Info

$$n(t) = n_0 2^{t/a}$$

$n_0 = \text{initial population} \quad a = \text{doubling time} \quad t = \text{time}$

Initial rabbits $n_0 = 645$, doubles every $a = 3$ months. Find population at $t = 12$ months:

$$n(12) = 645 \cdot 2^{12/3} = 645 \cdot 2^4 = 10,320 \quad \text{rabbits}$$

2. Exponential Growth (Relative Growth Rate)

Used when growth is expressed via a continuous, instantaneous relative rate $r$.

Info

$$n(t) = n_0 e^{rt}$$

$n_0 = \text{initial population} \quad r = \text{relative growth rate} \quad t = \text{time}$

Initial bacteria $n_0 = 500$, growth rate $r = 40\% = 0.4$ per hour. Find time $t$ to reach $n(t) = 80,000$:

$$\begin{aligned} 80,000 &= 500 e^{0.4t} \\ 160 &= e^{0.4t} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{divide by 500} \\ \ln 160 &= 0.4t \qquad &\leftarrow \text{take } \ln \text{ of each side} \\ t &= \frac{\ln 160}{0.4} \approx 12.68 \quad \text{hours} \end{aligned}$$

Model Conversion Insight

To convert a generic exponential baseline model $y = C \cdot b^t$ into an intrinsic base-$e$ model $y = C \cdot e^{kt}$, map the growth constant via:

$$\boxed{k = \ln b} \implies y = C \cdot e^{(\ln b)t}$$

3. Logistic Growth

Accounts for environmental carrying capacities $M$ that restrict infinite exponential overgrowth.

Info

$$n(t) = \frac{M}{1 + Ae^{-rt}}$$

$M = \text{carrying capacity} \quad r = \text{initial relative growth rate} \quad A = \frac{M - n_0}{n_0}$

Fish environment with $M = 30,000$, $n_0 = 3000$, and initial rate $r = 0.1848$:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \frac{30,000 - 3000}{3000} = 9 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{calculate coefficient } A \\ n(t) &= \frac{30,000}{1 + 9e^{-0.1848t}} \end{aligned}$$

4. Radioactive Decay

Models mass minimization via a stabilizing half-life baseline period $h$.

Info

$$m(t) = m_0 2^{-t/h} = m_0 e^{-rt}$$

$m_0 = \text{initial mass} \quad h = \text{half-life} \quad \boxed{r = \frac{\ln 2}{h}} = \text{relative decay rate}$

Polonium-210 with $h = 138$ days and initial mass $m_0 = 300$ mg. Find remaining mass after $t = 365$ days:

$$\begin{aligned} r &= \frac{\ln 2}{138} \approx 0.00502 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{determine relative decay rate} \\ m(365) &= 300 e^{-0.00502(365)} \approx 48.01 \quad \text{mg} \end{aligned}$$

5. Newton's Law of Cooling

Models temperature equalization matching surrounding ambient conditions.

Info

$$T(t) = T_s + D_0 e^{-kt}$$

$T_s = \text{surrounding temperature} \quad D_0 = T_{\text{initial}} - T_s \quad k = \text{cooling constant } (k > 0)$

Coffee at $200^\circ\text{F}$ is placed in a $70^\circ\text{F}$ room ($T_s = 70 \implies D_0 = 200 - 70 = 130$). It cools to $150^\circ\text{F}$ at $t = 10$ minutes. Find constant $k$:

$$\begin{aligned} 70 + 130e^{-10k} &= 150 \\ 130e^{-10k} &= 80 \qquad &\leftarrow \text{subtract 70} \\ e^{-10k} &= \frac{8}{13} \qquad &\leftarrow \text{divide by 130} \\ -10k &= \ln\left(\frac{8}{13}\right) \qquad &\leftarrow \text{take } \ln \text{ of each side} \\ k &= -\frac{1}{10}\ln\left(\frac{8}{13}\right) \approx 0.04855 \end{aligned}$$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 379)

notes.html:
The Number $e$

The number $e$ is defined as the value that $\left(1 + 1/n\right)^n$ approaches as $n$ becomes large.

n (1+n1​)n
$1$ $2.00000$
$5$ $2.48832$
$10$ $2.59374$
$100$ $2.70481$
$1000$ $2.71692$
$10,000$ $2.71815$
$100,000$ $2.71827$
$1,000,000$ $2.71828$

Rounded to five decimal places, $e \approx 2.71828$.

Info

$$\boxed{e \approx 2.71828182845904523536}$$

The number $e$ is an irrational number; it cannot be written as an exact value in decimal form.

The Natural Exponential Function

The notation $e$ was chosen by Leonhard Euler, probably because it is the first letter of the word exponential.

Since $2 < e < 3$, the graph of the natural exponential function lies between the graphs of $y = 2^x$ and $y = 3^x$.

Info

The Natural Exponential Function

The natural exponential function is the exponential function

$$f(x) = e^x$$

with base $e$. It is often referred to as the exponential function.

Example

Example 2: Graphing Exponential Functions

Sketch the graph of each function. State the $y$-intercept, domain, range, and horizontal asymptote.

(a) $f(x) = 3e^{0.5x}$

Plotting points:

x f(x)=3e0.5x
$-3$ $0.67$
$-2$ $1.10$
$-1$ $1.82$
$0$ $3.00$
$1$ $4.95$
$2$ $8.15$
$3$ $13.45$

  • $y$-intercept: $f(0) = 3e^0 = 3$

  • Domain: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Range: $(0, \infty)$

  • Horizontal Asymptote: $y = 0$

(b) $g(x) = e^{-x} - 2$

Transformation: Start with $y = e^x$, reflect about the $y$-axis to get $y = e^{-x}$, then shift downward 2 units.

  • $y$-intercept: $g(0) = e^0 - 2 = -1$

  • Domain: $\mathbb{R}$

  • Range: $(-2, \infty)$

  • Horizontal Asymptote: $y = -2$

Example

Example 3: Combinations Involving Exponential Functions

Use a graphing device to graph each function. State the $y$-intercept and use the graph to find the horizontal asymptote and any local extrema.

(a) $g(x) = e^{-x^2}$

  • $y$-intercept: $g(0) = e^0 = 1$

  • Local Extrema: Local maximum value of $1$ at $x = 0$

  • Horizontal Asymptote: $y = 0$

    $$\text{As } |x| \to \infty, \quad e^{x^2} \to \infty \implies y = \frac{1}{e^{x^2}} \to 0$$

(b) $l(x) = \frac{5}{1 + e^{-x}}$

  • $y$-intercept: $l(0) = \frac{5}{1 + e^0} = \frac{5}{2}$

  • Local Extrema: None

  • Horizontal Asymptotes:

    $$\begin{aligned} \text{As } x \to \infty, \quad &e^{-x} \to 0 \implies y \to \frac{5}{1 + 0} = 5 \\ \text{As } x \to -\infty, \quad &e^{-x} \to \infty \implies y \to 0 \end{aligned}$$

    Horizontal asymptotes at $y = 5$ and $y = 0$

(c) $s(x) = 10xe^{-0.1x}$

  • $y$-intercept: $s(0) = 10(0)e^0 = 0$

  • Local Extrema: Local maximum value of approximately $36.8$ at $x \approx 10.0$

  • Horizontal Asymptote: $y = 0$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 346)

notes.html:
Date: 2026-09-28 Tags: Linear Algebra, Strang, Mathematics, Matrices, Linear Independence

Matrices

To this point, linear combinations have been written as scalars multiplying vectors. Introducing matrices provides a crucial change in viewpoint: we can rewrite combinations by placing the vectors into the columns of a matrix $A$.

Core Principle: Matrix Multiplication (Column View)

Multiplying a matrix $A$ by a vector $x$ produces a linear combination of the columns of $A$.

$$Ax = x_1(\text{column 1}) + x_2(\text{column 2}) + x_3(\text{column 3})$$

For example, combining three vectors $u, v, w$ with scalars $x_1, x_2, x_3$ looks like this in matrix form:

$$Ax = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 - x_1 \\ x_3 - x_2 \end{bmatrix}$$

In this new viewpoint, the matrix $A$ acts on the input vector $x$ to produce an output vector $b$.

Pitfall: Row vs. Column Perspectives

You may have previously learned to multiply $Ax$ a row at a time by taking the dot product of each row of $A$ with the vector $x$. While computing by rows is correct and yields the same result, working with $Ax$ as a combination of columns is the fundamental key to understanding linear algebra.

The Difference Matrix and Inverse Systems

The matrix $A$ shown above is called a "difference matrix" because its output vector $b$ contains the differences of the components of the input vector $x$. If we input the squares $x = (1, 4, 9)$, the matrix produces the odd numbers as differences:

$$Ax = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 0 \\ 4 - 1 \\ 9 - 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} = b$$

The Inverse Problem

Up to now, we computed the output $b$ from a known $x$. The inverse problem asks: Which combination of columns produces a particular vector $b$? This means treating $b$ as known and solving the linear system $Ax = b$ for the unknown $x$.

Definition: Invertible and Inverse Matrix

If we can recover $x$ perfectly from $b$, the matrix $A$ is invertible. We write the solution as $x = A^{-1}b$, where $A^{-1}$ is the inverse matrix.

For our difference matrix $A$, the inverse matrix $A^{-1}$ is a sum matrix. If $b$ contains the differences of $x$, then $x$ can be reconstructed by accumulating the sums of $b$:

$$x = A^{-1}b = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \\ b_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_1 + b_2 \\ b_1 + b_2 + b_3 \end{bmatrix}$$

Core Principle: The Calculus Analogy

Linear algebra shares a perfect analogy with the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

  • The forward difference operation $Ax = b$ is analogous to taking a derivative: $\frac{dx}{dt} = b(t)$.

  • The inverse sum operation $x = A^{-1}b$ is analogous to taking an integral: $x(t) = \int b(t) dt$.

Singular Matrices and Cyclic Differences

Not all matrices are invertible. If we change the third column of $A$ to create a "cyclic difference matrix" $C$, the system behaves completely differently:

$$Cx = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 - x_3 \\ x_2 - x_1 \\ x_3 - x_2 \end{bmatrix} = b$$

Solving $Cx = b$ is generally impossible because the left sides of the equations ($x_1 - x_3$, $x_2 - x_1$, $x_3 - x_2$) always add up to zero. Therefore, no solution exists unless the components of the target vector $b$ also add up to zero ($b_1 + b_2 + b_3 = 0$).

Furthermore, if we want to solve $Cx = 0$, there are infinitely many solutions: any constant vector $x = (c, c, c)$ produces zero differences. (This undetermined constant $c$ is exactly analogous to the $+C$ added to indefinite integrals).

Independence and Dependence

The algebraic failure of the cyclic matrix $C$ has a direct geometric explanation regarding how its columns combine.

*(Independent vectors $u, v, w$ fill the whole 3D space. Dependent vectors $u, v, w^*$ are constrained to a 2D plane.)*
Property Independent Columns (Matrix $A$) Dependent Columns (Matrix $C$)
Geometry Combinations of columns fill the whole three-dimensional space. Columns lie in the same plane. Combinations cannot reach vectors outside this plane.
Zero Solution $Ax = 0$ has only one solution: $x = (0,0,0)$. $Cx = 0$ has many solutions (other non-zero combinations give the zero vector, e.g., $u + v + w^* = 0$).
Matrix Status $A$ is an invertible matrix. $C$ is a singular matrix (no inverse exists).

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 22-27)

notes.html:
Date: 2026-09-22 Tags: Linear Algebra, Mathematics, Dot Product, Orthogonality

The Dot Product and Vector Length

While adding vectors and multiplying them by scalars are the foundational operations of linear spaces, the dot product (or inner product) introduces the geometry of lengths and angles. It involves multiplying corresponding components of two vectors and summing the results to produce a single scalar number.

Definition: The Dot Product

For vectors $v = (v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n)$ and $w = (w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n)$, the dot product is defined as:

$$> v \cdot w = v_1 w_1 + v_2 w_2 + \dots + v_n w_n >$$

This simple algebraic operation has powerful real-world interpretations. In economics, multiplying a price vector by a quantity vector yields total income. In mechanics, multiplying weights by distances gives moments to determine if a system balances.

Length of a Vector

The most important special case is the dot product of a vector with itself. Instead of finding the angle between two different vectors, $v \cdot v$ finds the length of $v$ squared.

Core Principle: Vector Length

The length (or norm) $\vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{}$ of a vector $v$ is the square root of its dot product with itself.

$$> \text{length} = \vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{} = \sqrt{v \cdot v} = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \dots + v_n^2} >$$

This is the direct $n$-dimensional extension of the Pythagorean theorem. In two dimensions, the components $v_1$ and $v_2$ form the sides of a right triangle, making the length of the vector the hypotenuse $\sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2}$.

(The length $\sqrt{v \cdot v}$ of two-dimensional and three-dimensional vectors computed via right triangles.)

Perpendicularity and Angles

In mathematics, zero is always a special number. For dot products, $v \cdot w = 0$ carries a specific geometric meaning: the vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal).

To understand why a zero dot product means an angle of $90^\circ$, we use the Pythagoras Law for the sides of a right triangle formed by vectors $v$, $w$, and their difference $v-w$.

Proof of Perpendicularity condition: If $v$ and $w$ are perpendicular, the triangle formed by $v$, $w$, and $v-w$ must satisfy Pythagoras:

$$\begin{aligned} \vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{}^2 + \vert{}\vert{}w\vert{}\vert{}^2 &= \vert{}\vert{}v - w\vert{}\vert{}^2 \\ (v_1^2 + v_2^2) + (w_1^2 + w_2^2) &= (v_1 - w_1)^2 + (v_2 - w_2)^2 \\ v_1^2 + v_2^2 + w_1^2 + w_2^2 &= v_1^2 - 2v_1w_1 + w_1^2 + v_2^2 - 2v_2w_2 + w_2^2 \end{aligned}$$

Subtracting the squared terms from both sides leaves:

$$0 = -2v_1w_1 - 2v_2w_2$$

Dividing by $-2$ yields the fundamental result:

$$v_1w_1 + v_2w_2 = 0 \implies v \cdot w = 0$$

The Cosine Formula

When $v \cdot w$ is not zero, its sign immediately reveals whether the angle $\theta$ between the vectors is acute or obtuse.

  • $v \cdot w > 0 \implies \theta < 90^\circ$

  • $v \cdot w < 0 \implies \theta > 90^\circ$

By dividing vectors by their lengths, we normalize them. The dot product of these normalized vectors gives the exact cosine of the angle between them.

Theorem: The Cosine Formula

If $v$ and $w$ are nonzero vectors, the angle $\theta$ between them is found by:

$$> \cos \theta = \frac{v \cdot w}{\vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{} \vert{}\vert{}w\vert{}\vert{}} >$$

(Perpendicular vectors have $v \cdot w = 0$. The borderline divides half-planes where the dot product is positive (acute angles) and negative (obtuse angles).)

Unit Vectors

A unit vector $u$ is a vector whose length equals one, meaning $u \cdot u = 1$. You can create a unit vector in the same direction as any nonzero vector $v$ by dividing it by its length:

$$u = \frac{v}{\vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{}}$$

In the $xy$-plane, standard unit vectors along the axes are written as $i = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $j = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Any unit vector making an angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis can be expressed simply as $u = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta \\ \sin \theta \end{bmatrix}$.

Fundamental Inequalities

Because the cosine of any angle can never exceed $1$ (or fall below $-1$), the cosine formula directly leads to one of the most important inequalities in mathematics.

Inequality Name Mathematical Statement Intuition
Schwarz Inequality $\vert{}v \cdot w\vert{} \le \vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{} \cdot \vert{}\vert{}w\vert{}\vert{}$ The absolute value of the dot product never exceeds the product of the lengths. Equality only holds if one vector is a multiple of the other (angle is $0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$).
Triangle Inequality $\vert{}\vert{}v + w\vert{}\vert{} \le \vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{} + \vert{}\vert{}w\vert{}\vert{}$ The length of the sum of two vectors cannot exceed the sum of their individual lengths (side 3 of a triangle is shorter than side 1 + side 2).
Pitfall

It is a common mistake to assume $\vert{}\vert{}v + w\vert{}\vert{}$ equals $\vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{} + \vert{}\vert{}w\vert{}\vert{}$. This is only true in the extremely rare "flat triangle" case where vector $w$ is a positive scalar multiple of vector $v$ (e.g., $w = cv$ where $c \ge 0$).

Computational Representation

When computing these operations algorithmically (in MATLAB, Python, or Julia), it is highly useful to frame the dot product as a matrix operation. The dot product $v \cdot w$ is structurally a row vector times a column vector.

If vectors are stored as columns by default, computing the inner product requires transposing the first vector.

$$v^T w = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 & v_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} = v_1 w_1 + v_2 w_2$$

(Note: In MATLAB, this is natively written as v' * w instead of $v \cdot w$).

Worked Example: Testing Inequalities

Problem: For the vectors $v = (3,4)$ and $w = (4,3)$, test the Schwarz inequality on $v \cdot w$ and the triangle inequality on $\vert{}\vert{}v + w\vert{}\vert{}$. Find $\cos \theta$.

Step-by-Step Solution:

  1. Compute lengths and dot product:

$$\begin{aligned} \vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{} &= \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \\ \vert{}\vert{}w\vert{}\vert{} &= \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \\ v \cdot w &= (3)(4) + (4)(3) = 12 + 12 = 24 \end{aligned}$$

  1. Test Schwarz Inequality ($\vert{}v \cdot w\vert{} \le \vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{} \cdot \vert{}\vert{}w\vert{}\vert{}$):

$$24 \le (5)(5) \implies 24 \le 25 \quad \text{(True)}$$

  1. Test Triangle Inequality ($\vert{}\vert{}v + w\vert{}\vert{} \le \vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{} + \vert{}\vert{}w\vert{}\vert{}$): First find the sum vector: $v + w = (7, 7)$

$$\vert{}\vert{}v + w\vert{}\vert{} = \sqrt{7^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{98} = 7\sqrt{2}$$

$$7\sqrt{2} \le 5 + 5 \implies \approx 9.89 \le 10 \quad \text{(True)}$$

  1. Find Cosine of the Angle:

$$\cos \theta = \frac{v \cdot w}{\vert{}\vert{}v\vert{}\vert{} \vert{}\vert{}w\vert{}\vert{}} = \frac{24}{25}$$

(Since $\cos \theta$ is very close to 1, the angle between $v$ and $w$ is quite small).

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 11-17)

notes.html:
Vectors and Core Operations

The heart of linear algebra lies in two fundamental operations: adding vectors and multiplying vectors by numbers (scalars). These operations build the foundation for moving into $n$-dimensional space.

Definition: Column Vector

A vector $v$ is standardly written as a column, not a row, to keep its components distinct.

$$v = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix}$$

Here, $v_1$ is the first component (movement along the $x$-axis) and $v_2$ is the second component (movement along the $y$-axis). To save space in text, a column vector is sometimes written in row form with parentheses and commas: $v = (v_1, v_2)$.

Pitfall: Row vs. Column Vectors

The row form $v = (1, 1, -1)$ is just a space-saving typographic convention. It is in actuality a column vector temporarily lying down. A true $1 \times 3$ row vector like $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ is geometrically the same but mathematically represents the "transpose" of the column vector.

Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication

Vector addition is performed component by component.

$$v + w = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 + w_1 \\ v_2 + w_2 \end{bmatrix}$$

Scalar multiplication involves multiplying each component of a vector by a constant number $c$.

$$cv = c \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} cv_1 \\ cv_2 \end{bmatrix}$$

(Vector addition $v + w = (3, 4)$ produces the diagonal of a parallelogram. Traveling along $v$ then $w$ gives the same endpoint as traveling along $w$ then $v$.)

Linear Combinations

Core Principle: Linear Combinations

Combining addition and scalar multiplication produces a linear combination of the vectors. By multiplying vector $v$ by scalar $c$, vector $w$ by scalar $d$, and adding the results, you obtain the linear combination $cv + dw$.

$$cv + dw = c \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix} + d \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} cv_1 + dw_1 \\ cv_2 + dw_2 \end{bmatrix}$$

Special cases of linear combinations include the sum ($1v + 1w$), the difference ($1v - 1w$), and the zero vector ($0v + 0w$). The zero vector is always a possible linear combination of any set of vectors.

The Geometry of Combinations (The Big Picture)

Understanding the geometry of linear combinations is the key to linear algebra. If you take all possible combinations of a set of vectors by allowing the scalars to be any real numbers, the resulting combinations will geometrically "fill" spaces of varying dimensions.

Vector Combinations Geometric Picture in 3D Space ($u, v, w \in \mathbb{R}^3$)
All multiples $cu$ Fills a line passing through the origin $(0,0,0)$.
All combinations $cu + dv$ Fills a plane passing through the origin $(0,0,0)$.
All combinations $cu + dv + ew$ Fills the entire three-dimensional space (if $w$ is not on the $u,v$ plane).
((a) A line through $u$ containing all multiples $cu$. (b) A plane containing all linear combinations $cu + dv$ of the vectors $u$ and $v$.)

Worked Examples

Example 1: Describing a Plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$

Describe the plane generated by the combinations of $v = (1, 1, 0)$ and $w = (0, 1, 1)$. Find a vector that is not a combination of $v$ and $w$.

Step-by-Step Derivation: The plane contains all combinations $cv + dw$.

$$cv + dw = c \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + d \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} c \\ c+d \\ d \end{bmatrix}$$

For any point in this plane, the second component ($c+d$) must always exactly equal the sum of the first component ($c$) and the third component ($d$).

Therefore, a vector like $\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$ is not on the plane because the components do not satisfy the required relationship: $2 \neq 1 + 3$.

Example 2: Solving for Linear Combination Coefficients

Find two equations for scalars $c$ and $d$ so that the linear combination $cv + dw$ equals a target vector $b$:

$$v = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad w = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad b = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Step-by-Step Derivation: Set up the vector equation:

$$c \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} + d \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Split the vector equation into two ordinary scalar equations by looking at the components separately:

$$\begin{aligned} 2c - d &= 1 \\ -c + 2d &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Solving this system (each equation represents a line, and their intersection is the solution) yields $c = \frac{2}{3}$ and $d = \frac{1}{3}$.

This fundamental setup can also be written natively as a matrix equation, which is the primary direction of the subject:

$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c \\ d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 1-7)

notes.html:
Date: 2026-10-05 Tags: Linear Algebra, Strang, Mathematics, LU Factorization, Computational Cost

Elimination = Factorization: $A = LU$

Many key ideas in linear algebra, when examined closely, are actually factorizations of a matrix. The most important factorization in practice comes directly from Gaussian elimination: the original matrix $A$ becomes the product of two triangular matrices, $L$ and $U$.

Core Principle: LU Factorization

The forward elimination process that reduces a matrix $A$ to an upper triangular matrix $U$ can be reversed. The matrix that reverses these steps is a lower triangular matrix $L$.

$$A = LU$$ > Where $L$ is lower triangular and $U$ is upper triangular. > >

The Mechanics of $L$

In a $3 \times 3$ system without row exchanges, forward elimination multiplies $A$ by elementary matrices $E_{ij}$ to produce $U$:

$$E_{32}E_{31}E_{21}A = U$$

To recover $A$ from $U$, we move the $E$ matrices to the other side by multiplying by their inverses:

$$A = (E_{21}^{-1}E_{31}^{-1}E_{32}^{-1})U = LU$$

Theorem: The Structure of $L$

Every inverse matrix $E_{ij}^{-1}$ is lower triangular, with $1$s on the main diagonal and the exact multiplier $\ell_{ij}$ in its off-diagonal position. The product of these inverses, $L$, simply collects all the multipliers $\ell_{ij}$ directly into their respective $(i, j)$ positions without mixing them up.

This is the primary reason for working with $L$ instead of the overall elimination matrix $E$. While multiplying forward elimination matrices mixes up the numbers, multiplying their inverses in reverse order keeps the multipliers perfectly separated and unchanged.

Better Balance: The $LDU$ Factorization

The factorization $A = LU$ is slightly "unsymmetric" because $U$ has the pivots on its diagonal, whereas $L$ has $1$s on its diagonal.

To balance this, we can divide $U$ by a diagonal matrix $D$ that contains the pivots. This leaves a new upper triangular matrix (still conventionally called $U$) that also has $1$s on its diagonal.

$$A = LDU$$

In this triangular factorization, $L$ is lower triangular with $1$s on the diagonal, $D$ is the diagonal matrix of pivots, and $U$ is upper triangular with $1$s on the diagonal.

Solving Systems Using $LU$

When a computer solves $Ax = b$, it separates the process into two stages. The factors $L$ and $U$ are completely decided by the left side matrix $A$. Once $A$ is factored, the right side $b$ is processed using two triangular systems.

Core Principle: Two Triangular Systems

The original system $Ax = b$ can be rewritten as $LUx = b$. This is solved in two fast steps:

  1. Forward Substitution: Solve $Lc = b$ for the intermediate vector $c$.

  2. Back Substitution: Solve $Ux = c$ for the final solution vector $x$.

By saving $L$ and $U$, the memory of the elimination process is preserved, allowing the system to rapidly solve for any new right-side vector $b$ without re-eliminating $A$.

The Cost of Elimination

A critical practical question in scientific computing is the computation time required for large systems (e.g., $n = 100,000$). The cost is measured in terms of multiplications and subtractions.

Operation Mathematical Task Operation Count (Dense Matrix) Operation Count (Band Matrix, width $w$)
Factor Reduce $A$ to $L$ and $U$ $\approx \frac{1}{3}n^3$
 $\approx nw^2$
Solve Solve $Lc = b$ and $Ux = c$ exactly $n^2$
 $\approx 2nw$
Pitfall: Dense vs. Sparse Matrices

The $\frac{1}{3}n^3$ rule means that a system with $100,000$ variables would take a million seconds (over 11 days) on a standard PC if the matrix is completely dense (full of non-zero entries). However, most massive matrices in practice are sparse or band matrices. For a band matrix with a small bandwidth $w$ (like a tridiagonal matrix where $w=1$), the factorization cost plummets from $\frac{1}{3}n^3$ to just $n$, allowing lightning-fast computations.

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 107-112)

notes.html:
Date: 2026-09-28 Tags: Linear Algebra, Strang, Mathematics, Matrices, Gaussian Elimination

Matrices times Vectors

A linear system is written compactly as $Ax = b$. The matrix $A$ acts on the vector $x$ to produce $b$.

There are two primary ways to compute $Ax$:

  • Row Form (Dot Products): The $i$-th component of $Ax$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with $x$.

$$(Ax)_i = (\text{row } i) \cdot x = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j$$

  • Column Form (Linear Combinations): $Ax$ is a linear combination of the columns of $A$, weighted by the components of $x$.

Elimination Matrices ($E_{ij}$)

Elimination steps are executed using matrix multiplication. We multiply the system by an elimination matrix $E$ to subtract multiples of one equation from another.

Definition: Elimination Matrix $E_{ij}$

The matrix $E_{ij}$ subtracts a multiple $\ell$ of row $j$ from row $i$. Form it by taking the identity matrix $I$ and replacing the zero in the $(i, j)$ position with $-\ell$.

Example: To subtract $2$ times row 1 from row 2 (multiplier $\ell = 2$), $E_{21}$ has a $-2$ in the $(2, 1)$ position:

$$E_{21} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Multiplying $E_{21}A$ applies this operation to the entire matrix.

Permutation Matrices ($P_{ij}$)

When a zero appears in a pivot position, we execute a row exchange using a permutation matrix.

Definition: Permutation Matrix $P_{ij}$

The matrix $P_{ij}$ exchanges row $i$ and row $j$. Form it by exchanging row $i$ and row $j$ of the identity matrix $I$.

Example: To exchange row 2 and row 3, use $P_{23}$:

$$P_{23} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

The Augmented Matrix

To solve $Ax = b$, row operations applied to $A$ must also apply to $b$.

Core Principle: The Augmented Matrix

Enlarge $A$ by attaching $b$ as an extra column: $[A \ b]$.

Elimination matrices act on whole rows of this augmented matrix simultaneously:

$$E [A \ b] = [EA \ Eb]$$

The forward elimination from $A$ to the upper triangular matrix $U$ is a sequence of multiplications:

$$E_{32}E_{31}E_{21}A = U$$

Rules of Matrix Multiplication

Matrix multiplication dictates how operations can be grouped.

Property Rule Status Explanation
Associative Law $A(BC) = (AB)C$ True You can group multiplications differently: $E(Ax) = (EA)x$.
Commutative Law $AB \neq BA$ False Order matters. Left multiplication acts on rows, right acts on columns.
Column-by-Column $AB = A[b_1 \ b_2]$ True $A$ multiplies each column of $B$ separately: $AB = [Ab_1 \ Ab_2]$.
Pitfall: Left vs. Right Multiplication
  • Multiplying on the left ($EA$) acts on the rows of $A$.
  • Multiplying on the right ($AE$) acts on the columns of $A$.

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 58-64)
