notes.excerpt: --- Date: 2026-10-05 Tags: Linear Algebra, Strang, Mathematics, Inverse Matrices, Gauss-Jordan Elimination --- Inverse Matrices The fundamental idea of an inverse matrix is that it completely reverses
notes.html:
Date: 2026-10-05 Tags: Linear Algebra, Strang, Mathematics, Inverse Matrices, Gauss-Jordan Elimination

Inverse Matrices

The fundamental idea of an inverse matrix is that it completely reverses or "undoes" the transformation applied by the original matrix.

Definition: Inverse Matrix

A square matrix $A$ is invertible if there exists a matrix $A^{-1}$ of the same size such that:

$$A^{-1}A = I \quad \text{and} \quad AA^{-1} = I$$ > Where $I$ is the identity matrix. If $A^{-1}$ exists, it is called a "two-sided inverse."

If a matrix has an inverse, we can algebraically solve the linear system $Ax = b$ by multiplying both sides by $A^{-1}$, yielding the single, unique solution $x = A^{-1}b$.

Properties of Invertibility

Not all matrices have inverses. A matrix without an inverse is called singular.

Condition Description
Pivot Test An inverse exists if and only if elimination produces a full set of $n$ non-zero pivots.
Uniqueness A matrix cannot have two different inverses. If $BA = I$ and $AC = I$, then $B = C$.
Determinant Test For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, the determinant $ad - bc$ must not be zero.
Diagonal Matrices A diagonal matrix is invertible provided no diagonal entries are zero. The inverse simply contains $1/d_i$ along the diagonal.
Pitfall: The $Ax = 0$ Test

If there is a nonzero vector $x$ such that $Ax = 0$, then $A$ cannot have an inverse. No matrix can bring the zero vector back to a nonzero vector $x$. If $A$ is invertible, $Ax = 0$ can only have the zero solution ($x = 0$).

The $2 \times 2$ Inverse Formula

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, the inverse can be computed directly using its determinant:

$$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc} \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$$

The Inverse of a Product

When multiplying two invertible matrices $A$ and $B$, their product $AB$ is also invertible. However, the inverse of the product is the product of the inverses in reverse order.

Core Principle: Reverse Order Law
$$(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$$ > **Intuition:** Think of operations in real life. If you put on your socks ($B$) and then your shoes ($A$), to reverse the process, you must first take off your shoes ($A^{-1}$) and then take off your socks ($B^{-1}$).

This rule extends to three or more matrices: $(ABC)^{-1} = C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}$.

Inverses of Elimination Matrices

The inverse of an elementary elimination matrix $E$ is remarkably simple. If $E$ subtracts $5$ times row 1 from row 2, its inverse $E^{-1}$ simply adds $5$ times row 1 back to row 2. You only need to flip the sign of the multiplier.

$$E = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \implies E^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Calculating $A^{-1}$ by Gauss-Jordan Elimination

While we can solve $Ax = b$ without explicitly finding $A^{-1}$, computing the inverse itself requires solving $AA^{-1} = I$. This means we are solving $n$ systems of equations simultaneously, one for each column of the identity matrix $I$.

Core Principle: Gauss-Jordan Method

To find $A^{-1}$, we augment the matrix $A$ with the identity matrix $I$ to form the block matrix $\begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix}$. We then perform row operations to reduce $A$ to $I$. Those same row operations automatically transform $I$ into $A^{-1}$.

$$\begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix} \xrightarrow{\text{row operations}} \begin{bmatrix} I & A^{-1} \end{bmatrix}$$

Step-by-Step Gauss-Jordan

Let's find the inverse of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$.

  1. Set up the augmented matrix $\begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix}$: $$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & | & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 7 & | & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

  2. Forward Elimination (Create zeros below pivots): Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2 to eliminate the 4. $$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & | & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & | & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{(This is } \begin{bmatrix} U & L^{-1} \end{bmatrix})$$

  3. Upward Elimination (Create zeros above pivots): Subtract 3 times row 2 from row 1 to eliminate the 3. $$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & | & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & | & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

  4. Normalize Pivots (Divide rows by their pivots): Divide row 1 by 2 to get $1$s on the diagonal. $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & | & 3.5 & -1.5 \\ 0 & 1 & | & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{(This is } \begin{bmatrix} I & A^{-1} \end{bmatrix})$$

The right half is the inverse matrix $A^{-1}$.

(Note: Gauss-Jordan is computationally expensive for large systems, requiring $n^3$ operations. If you only need to solve $Ax = b$, standard elimination is much faster).

Recognizing Invertible Matrices

Usually, deciding if a matrix is invertible requires doing the work to find a full set of pivots. However, some matrices can be immediately recognized as invertible by inspection.

Diagonally Dominant Matrices: A matrix is diagonally dominant if the absolute value of each diagonal entry $a_{ii}$ is strictly greater than the sum of the absolute values of all other entries in that row.

$$|a_{ii}| > \sum_{j \neq i} |a_{ij}|$$

Theorem: Diagonal Dominance

Every diagonally dominant matrix is invertible.

Proof Intuition: If $A$ is diagonally dominant and we assume $Ax = 0$ for a nonzero vector $x$, look at the largest component of $x$, say $x_i$. The row equation would require the diagonal term $a_{ii}x_i$ to be perfectly balanced by the sum of the off-diagonal terms. But because $a_{ii}$ is so strictly large (dominant), the off-diagonal terms physically cannot add up to cancel it out. Therefore, $Ax = 0$ is impossible for a nonzero $x$, meaning $A$ must be invertible.

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 71-77)

Date: 2026-10-05 Tags: Linear Algebra, Strang, Mathematics, Matrix Operations, Block Matrices

Matrix Operations Basics

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers.

  • Dimension: $m \times n$ denotes $m$ rows and $n$ columns.
  • Entry $a_{ij}$: The number located in the $i$-th row and $j$-th column.
  • Addition ($A + B$): Add corresponding entries. Valid only if matrices have the exact same shape.
  • Scalar Multiplication ($cA$): Multiply every entry in the matrix by the constant scalar $c$.

Matrix Multiplication

Rule for Matrix Multiplication

To multiply $AB$, the inner dimensions must match: the number of columns in $A$ must equal the number of rows in $B$.

$$(m \times n) \times (n \times p) = (m \times p)$$

There are four distinct ways to compute the product $AB = C$:

1. The Dot Product Way (Standard)

The entry $C_{ij}$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ and column $j$ of $B$.

$$(AB)_{ij} = (\text{row } i \text{ of } A) \cdot (\text{column } j \text{ of } B) = \sum_{k=1}^n a_{ik}b_{kj}$$

*(Row 2 of A and Column 3 of B combine to produce the entry in row 2, column 3 of AB)*

2. The Column Way

Matrix $A$ multiplies every column of $B$ individually. Each column of $AB$ is a linear combination of the columns of $A$.

$$A \begin{bmatrix} b_1 & \dots & b_p \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Ab_1 & \dots & Ab_p \end{bmatrix}$$

3. The Row Way

Every row of $A$ multiplies the entire matrix $B$. Each row of $AB$ is a linear combination of the rows of $B$.

$$\begin{bmatrix} \text{row } i \text{ of } A \end{bmatrix} B = \begin{bmatrix} \text{row } i \text{ of } AB \end{bmatrix}$$

4. Columns Multiply Rows

Multiply each column $k$ of $A$ by the corresponding row $k$ of $B$ (each producing an $m \times p$ matrix), and add the results.

$$AB = (\text{col 1})(\text{row 1}) + (\text{col 2})(\text{row 2}) + \dots + (\text{col } n)(\text{row } n)$$

Laws for Matrix Operations

Property Rule Status
Commutative (Addition) $A + B = B + A$ True
Associative (Addition) $A + (B + C) = (A + B) + C$ True
Distributive (Scalar) $c(A + B) = cA + cB$ True
Commutative (Multiplication) $AB = BA$ False
Distributive (Left) $A(B + C) = AB + AC$ True
Distributive (Right) $(A + B)C = AC + BC$ True
Associative (Multiplication) $A(BC) = (AB)C$ True
Pitfall: Commutativity

Matrix multiplication is rarely commutative. Even if $A$ and $B$ are square matrices of the same size, $AB$ will generally not equal $BA$. The identity matrix $I$ is a notable exception ($AI = IA = A$).

Matrix Powers

For square matrices, exponents follow standard algebraic rules (provided $A$ has an inverse for negative powers).

$$A^p = AAA \dots A \text{ (p factors)}$$

$$A^p A^q = A^{p+q}$$

$$(A^p)^q = A^{pq}$$

Block Matrices and Block Multiplication

Matrices can be partitioned into smaller sub-matrices called blocks.

Block Multiplication

If the blocks of $A$ can multiply the blocks of $B$ (i.e., cuts between columns of $A$ match cuts between rows of $B$), block multiplication is valid and follows the same rules as scalar entries. $$\begin{bmatrix} A_{11} & A_{12} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} B_{11} \\ B_{21} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} A_{11}B_{11} + A_{12}B_{21} \\ A_{21}B_{11} + A_{22}B_{21} \end{bmatrix}$$

Block Elimination (Schur Complement)

Elimination can be performed on whole blocks simultaneously using a block elimination matrix.

$$\begin{bmatrix} I & 0 \\ -CA^{-1} & I \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ 0 & D - CA^{-1}B \end{bmatrix}$$

The resulting bottom-right block, $D - CA^{-1}B$, is called the Schur complement.

Application: Graph Adjacency Matrices

A network graph of $n$ nodes can be represented by an $n \times n$ adjacency matrix $S$.

  • $S_{ij} = 1$ if an edge directly connects node $i$ to node $j$.
  • $S_{ij} = 0$ if there is no direct connection.
Theorem: Powers of Adjacency Matrices

The entry in row $i$, column $j$ of the matrix $S^N$ represents the exact total number of $N$-step paths between node $i$ and node $j$.

For example, computing $(S^2)_{ij}$ via the dot product formula:

$$(S^2)_{ij} = s_{i1}s_{1j} + s_{i2}s_{2j} + \dots + s_{in}s_{nj}$$

Each term $s_{ik}s_{kj}$ evaluates to $1$ only if a path exists from $i \to k$ and from $k \to j$, counting valid 2-step walks.

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 71-77)

Date: 2026-09-28 Tags: Linear Algebra, Strang, Mathematics, Gaussian Elimination

Gaussian Elimination

A systematic method to solve linear equations by transforming a full system $Ax=b$ into an upper triangular system $Ux=c$.

  • Goal: Eliminate variables below the main diagonal to enable back substitution.

  • Method: Subtract multiples of one equation from another.

Definition: Pivots and Multipliers

  • Pivot: The first nonzero entry in the row used for elimination. Pivots lie on the diagonal of $U$. Zero is never allowed as a pivot.

  • Multiplier ($\ell_{ij}$): The ratio used to eliminate a specific entry.

$$\ell_{ij} = \frac{\text{entry to eliminate in row } i}{\text{pivot in row } j}$$

Core Principle: Geometric Preservation

Row operations completely change the equations and the angles of the lines/planes, but they do not change the solution (the intersection point).

*(Eliminating $x$ makes the second line horizontal ($8y=8$), but the lines still intersect at $(3,1)$)*.

Breakdown of Elimination

Elimination fails if the algorithm is forced to divide by zero.

Breakdown Type Condition Row Picture Geometry Result
No Solution Reaches a false equation (e.g., $0y = 8$). Parallel lines. Inconsistent (Singular matrix).
Infinitely Many Reaches a trivial equation (e.g., $0y = 0$). Same line. Dependent (One variable is "free").
Temporary Failure Zero in pivot position, but non-zero entry below it. Normal intersecting lines Row Exchange produces valid pivots.

(Figure 2.6: No solution / Parallel lines. Figure 2.7: Infinitely many solutions / Same line).

Example: 3x3 Elimination & Back Substitution

System:

$$\begin{cases} 2x + 4y - 2z &= 2 \\ 4x + 9y - 3z &= 8 \\ -2x - 3y + 7z &= 10 \end{cases}$$

Forward Elimination ($A \to U$):

  • Column 1 (Pivot is $\mathbf{2}$):

  • Eliminate $4x$ (Eq 2): Multiplier $\ell_{21} = 4/2 = 2$. $\text{Eq 2} - 2(\text{Eq 1}) \implies 1y + 1z = 4$

  • Eliminate $-2x$ (Eq 3): Multiplier $\ell_{31} = -2/2 = -1$. $\text{Eq 3} - (-1)(\text{Eq 1}) \implies 1y + 5z = 12$

  • Column 2 (New Pivot is $\mathbf{1}$):

  • Eliminate $1y$ (New Eq 3): Multiplier $\ell_{32} = 1/1 = 1$. $\text{New Eq 3} - 1(\text{New Eq 2}) \implies 4z = 8$

Upper Triangular System ($Ux = c$): Pivots ($\mathbf{2, 1, 4}$) are now clearly visible on the diagonal.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{2}x + 4y - 2z &= 2 \\ \mathbf{1}y + 1z &= 4 \\ \mathbf{4}z &= 8 \end{aligned}$$

Back Substitution: Solve from bottom to top.

  1. From Eq 3: $4z = 8 \implies z = 2$

  2. From Eq 2: $y + 2 = 4 \implies y = 2$

  3. From Eq 1: $2x + 4(2) - 2(2) = 2 \implies 2x = -2 \implies x = -1$

Solution: $(-1, 2, 2)$.

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 46-51)

notes.html:
Definition: Transpose ($A^T$)

The transpose of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is an $n \times m$ matrix $A^T$ where the columns of $A^T$ are the rows of $A$.

$$(A^T)_{ij} = A_{ji}$$

Properties of Transposes

Operation Rule
Sum $(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T$
Product $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$
Inverse $(A^{-1})^T = (A^T)^{-1}$
  • The transpose of a product comes in reverse order (similar to the inverse of a product).

Inner and Outer Products

Using matrix transpose notation replaces the standard dot product notation:

  • Inner Product (Dot Product): $x^T y$ yields a $1 \times 1$ scalar.

  • Outer Product: $x y^T$ yields an $n \times n$ matrix.

Core Principle: Dot Product Identity

The inner product of $Ax$ with $y$ equals the inner product of $x$ with $A^T y$.

$$(Ax)^T y = x^T (A^T y)$$

Symmetric Matrices

Definition: Symmetric Matrix ($S$)

A symmetric matrix is a square matrix that equals its own transpose.

$$S^T = S \implies s_{ji} = s_{ij}$$

  • Symmetric Inverses: The inverse of a symmetric matrix is also symmetric: $(S^{-1})^T = S^{-1}$.

  • Symmetric Products: For any matrix $A$, the products $A^T A$ and $A A^T$ are always square, symmetric matrices.

The $LDL^T$ Factorization

When a matrix $S$ is symmetric, the standard $A = LDU$ factorization is simplified. The upper triangular matrix $U$ becomes the exact transpose of the lower triangular matrix $L$.

$$S = LDL^T$$

Permutation Matrices ($P$)

Definition: Permutation Matrix ($P$)

A permutation matrix $P$ has the rows of the identity matrix $I$ in any order. It is used to execute row exchanges.

  • There are exactly $n!$ permutation matrices of order $n$.

  • Inverse equals Transpose: For any permutation matrix, its inverse is its transpose.

$$P^{-1} = P^T \implies P^T P = I$$

The $PA = LU$ Factorization

When standard Gaussian elimination encounters a zero in the pivot position, row exchanges are required.

Core Principle: $PA = LU$

If $A$ is invertible, a permutation matrix $P$ can reorder its rows in advance so that standard elimination succeeds without any further exchanges.

$$PA = LU$$

  • $P$: Permutation matrix (reorders the rows of $A$).

  • $L$: Lower triangular matrix (contains the multipliers).

  • $U$: Upper triangular matrix (contains the pivots on the diagonal).

Process:

  1. Collect all necessary row exchanges into a single permutation matrix $P$.

  2. Multiply $PA$ to place the rows in the correct order.

  3. Factor $PA$ normally into $LU$.

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 109-115)

Vectors and Linear Equations

The central problem of linear algebra is to solve a system of linear equations. A standard system of two equations in two unknowns can be analyzed from two distinctly different visual and mathematical perspectives: the row picture and the column picture.

Given the linear system:

$$ \begin{cases} x - 2y &= 1 \\ 3x + 2y &= 11 \end{cases}$$

The Row Picture (Intersection of Planes/Lines)

We begin a row at a time. In two dimensions, each row represents a linear equation that produces a straight line in the $xy$-plane. The solution to the system is the single point where these lines intersect.

By finding points that satisfy each equation (e.g., $x=3, y=1$ solves both), we find the intersection point $(3, 1)$.

(Row picture: Two lines meeting at a single point $(3, 1)$, which is the solution to both equations.)

For a $3 \times 3$ system (three equations, three unknowns $x, y, z$), the row picture shows three planes in three-dimensional space. Two planes typically intersect in a line $L$, and the third plane cuts that line at a single intersection point, which is the solution.

(Row picture in 3D: Two planes meet at a line $L$. Three planes meet at a single point.)

The Column Picture (Linear Combination of Vectors)

Instead of looking at horizontal rows, we can separate the original system into its vertical columns to create a vector equation.

$$x \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} + y \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 11 \end{bmatrix}$$

Core Principle: The Column Picture

The column picture combines the column vectors on the left side to produce the vector $b$ on the right side. The problem is to find the correct scalar coefficients ($x$ and $y$) that multiply these columns so their vector sum equals the target vector.

Using the same solution from the row picture ($x=3, y=1$), we can verify that $3(\text{column 1}) + 1(\text{column 2}) = b$.

(Column picture: Combining column vectors with scalar weights to produce the right side $(1, 11)$.)

The column picture scales perfectly to higher dimensions. It is much easier to visualize a linear combination of four vectors in four-dimensional space than it is to imagine four hyperplanes intersecting at a single point.

The Matrix Form: $Ax = b$

We can combine the coefficients of the linear system into a single matrix $A$. The rows of $A$ give the row picture, and the columns give the column picture.

$$\text{Matrix equation } Ax = b \implies \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 11 \end{bmatrix}$$

There are two fundamental ways to compute the multiplication of a matrix $A$ and a vector $x$:

Method Mathematical Definition Intuition
Multiplication by Rows $Ax$ comes from dot products, each row of $A$ times the column vector $x$. Defines the $i$-th component of the output vector as $(\text{row } i) \cdot x$.
Multiplication by Columns $Ax$ is a linear combination of the column vectors of $A$, weighted by the components of $x$. Defines the output vector as $x_1(\text{column 1}) + x_2(\text{column 2}) + \dots$.

(Note: Strang's text strongly emphasizes understanding $Ax$ as a combination of the columns of $A$.)

Matrix Notation and The Identity Matrix

Matrix entries are denoted by their row and column index. The entry $a_{ij}$ (or $A(i,j)$) is located in row $i$ and column $j$. An $m$ by $n$ matrix has $m$ rows and $n$ columns, containing $mn$ total entries.

Definition: The Identity Matrix

The identity matrix $I$ has $1$'s on the "main diagonal" and $0$'s everywhere else. Multiplying any vector by $I$ leaves the vector unchanged.

$$I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad Ix = x$$

Worked Example: Solving by Inspection

Problem: Describe the column picture of these three equations $Ax = b$. Solve by careful inspection of the columns.

$$\begin{cases} x + 3y + 2z &= -3 \\ 2x + 2y + 2z &= -2 \\ 3x + 5y + 6z &= -5 \end{cases}$$

Step-by-Step Solution: First, rewrite the system as a matrix-vector equation $Ax = b$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -2 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix}$$

The column picture asks for a linear combination of the three columns of $A$ that produces the vector $b$.

By inspecting the columns, we can see that the target vector $b = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -2 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix}$ is exactly the negative of the second column $\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$.

Therefore, we need $0$ of the first column, $-1$ of the second column, and $0$ of the third column. The solution is:

$$x = 0, \quad y = -1, \quad z = 0$$

(If the right side changed to $b = (4, 4, 8)$, which is the sum of the first two columns, the solution would instead be $x=1, y=1, z=0$).

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 31-34, 40)

notes.html:
1. The Third Level of Understanding

The six organizing facts of Spaces of Vectors
  1. The standard $n$-dimensional space $\mathbb{R}^n$ contains all real column vectors with $n$ components.
  2. If $v$ and $w$ are in a vector space $S$, every combination $cv + dw$ must be in $S$.
  3. The "vectors" in $S$ can be matrices or functions of $x$. The 1-point space $Z$ consists of $x = 0$.
  4. A subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a vector space inside $\mathbb{R}^n$ (example: the line $y = 3x$ inside $\mathbb{R}^2$).
  5. The column space of $A$ contains all combinations of the columns of $A$: a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$.
  6. The column space contains all the vectors $Ax$. So $Ax = b$ is solvable when $b$ is in $C(A)$.

2. The Space $\mathbb{R}^n$ and the Eight Conditions

Definition : The space $\mathbb{R}^n$

The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ consists of all column vectors $v$ with $n$ components. The components are real numbers (hence $\mathbb{R}$); a vector with $n$ complex components lies in the space $\mathbb{C}^n$.

  • $\mathbb{R}^2$ = the usual $xy$-plane; $v = (x, y)$;
  • $\mathbb{R}^3$ = points $(x, y, z)$ in three-dimensional space;
  • $\mathbb{R}^1$ = a line (like the $x$-axis).

The greatness of linear algebra: it deals easily with five-dimensional space. We don't draw the vectors, we just need the $n$ numbers.

The two essential operations (they produce linear combinations, and the result stays inside the space):

$$ v + w \quad (\text{add component at a time}), \qquad c v \quad (\text{multiply every component by the scalar } c) $$

Définition / Théorème : The eight required conditions

A series of properties can be verified in $\mathbb{R}^n$; three of them are:

  • Commutative law: $v + w = w + v$;
  • Distributive law: $c(v + w) = cv + cw$;
  • Unique zero vector: $0 + v = v$.

These are three of the eight conditions required of every vector space (the full standard list):

  1. $v + w = w + v$; 2. $(v + w) + u = v + (w + u)$; 3. unique zero vector $0$; 4. unique $-v$ with $v + (-v) = 0$; 5. $c(v + w) = cv + cw$; 6. $(c + d)v = cv + dv$; 7. $c(dv) = (cd)v$; 8. $1v = v$.
Definition : Real vector space

A real vector space is a set of "vectors" together with rules for vector addition and for multiplication by real numbers. The addition and the multiplication must produce vectors that are in the space, and the eight conditions must be satisfied.

Example : Three vector spaces other than $\mathbb{R}^n$
  • $\mathbf{M}$: the vector space of all real $2 \times 2$ matrices;
  • $\mathbf{F}$: the vector space of all real functions $f(x)$ — infinite-dimensional;
  • $\mathbf{Z}$: the vector space that consists only of a zero vector — zero-dimensional, the smallest possible vector space.

In $M$ the "vectors" are matrices; in $F$ they are functions; in $Z$ the only addition is $0 + 0 = 0$. In each case we can add (matrices to matrices, functions to functions) and multiply by $4$, and the result is still in $M$, $F$, or $Z$. A smaller function space is $\mathbf{P}$ (or $\mathbf{P}_n$): all polynomials $a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n$ of degree $n$.

No space can do without its zero vector: each space has its own — the zero matrix, the zero function, the vector $(0,0,0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

3. Subspaces

Definition : Subspace

A subspace of a vector space is a set of vectors (including $0$) that satisfies two requirements: if $v$ and $w$ are vectors in the subspace and $c$ is any scalar, then $$ > \text{(i)} \quad v + w \text{ is in the subspace} \qquad \text{(ii)} \quad cv \text{ is in the subspace} > $$ In other words the set is closed under addition $v+w$ and multiplication $cv$ (and $dw$). We can also subtract, because $-w$ is in the subspace and $v + (-w) = v - w$. All linear combinations stay in the subspace.

Définition / Théorème : First fact — the zero vector

Every subspace contains the zero vector. The plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has to go through $(0,0,0)$. This follows directly from rule (ii): choose $c = 0$, and the rule requires $0v$ to be in the subspace.

Modélisation : The complete list of subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^3$
Label Subspace
$(L)$ Any line through $(0,0,0)$
$(P)$ Any plane through $(0,0,0)$
$(\mathbb{R}^3)$ The whole space
$(Z)$ The single vector $(0,0,0)$
Piège / Cas Particulier : Planes and sets that fail
  • Planes that don't contain the origin fail the tests: they are not subspaces (the zero vector is missing).
  • Example 1 (quarter-plane): keep only vectors $(x, y)$ with components positive or zero. $(2,3)$ is included but $(-2,-3)$ is not: rule (ii) is violated at $c = -1$. Not a subspace.
  • Example 2 (two quarter-planes): include also vectors with both components negative. Rule (ii) now holds (any $c$), but rule (i) fails: $v = (2,3)$ and $w = (-3,-2)$ give $v + w = (-1, 1)$, outside the set. Two quarter-planes don't make a subspace.
Définition / Théorème : The rule for subspaces (combined form)

Rules (i) and (ii) combine into a single requirement: $$ > \text{A subspace containing } v \text{ and } w \text{ must contain all} \textbf{ linear combinations } cv + dw. > $$

Example 3 : Subspaces inside the matrix space $M$

Inside $M$ (all $2 \times 2$ matrices), two subspaces:

  • $(U)$ all upper triangular matrices $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & d \end{bmatrix}$;
  • $(D)$ all diagonal matrices $\begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & d \end{bmatrix}$.

Add any two matrices in $U$: the sum is in $U$. Add diagonal matrices: the sum is diagonal. Here $D$ is also a subspace of $U$. The zero matrix is in both (when $a = b = d = 0$); $Z$ is always a subspace. Multiples of the identity $cI$ also form a subspace: $2I + 3I$ is in it, and so is $3(4I)$ — a "line of matrices" inside $M$, $U$, and $D$. Is $I$ a subspace by itself? Certainly not. Only the zero matrix is.

4. The Column Space of $A$

Definition : Column space $C(A)$

The column space consists of all linear combinations of the columns of $A$: $$ > C(A) = \{ Ax : x \in \mathbb{R}^n \} = \left\{ \sum_{j} x_j \, (\text{column } j) \right\} > $$ If $A$ is $m \times n$, its columns have $m$ components, so the columns belong to $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $C(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$ (not $\mathbb{R}^n$): adding combinations or multiplying by scalars still produces combinations of the columns.

Théorème : The solvability criterion

$$ > \text{The system } Ax = b \text{ is solvable } \iff b \in C(A). > $$ To solve $Ax = b$ is to express $b$ as a combination of the columns; the coefficients of that combination give the solution $x$. If $b$ is not in the column space produced by $A$: no solution.

Example 4 : A $3 \times 2$ matrix whose column space is a plane

Let $A$ be a $3 \times 2$ matrix with two independent columns $v_1, v_2 \in \mathbb{R}^3$: $$ > Ax = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 & v_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = x_1 v_1 + x_2 v_2 > $$ The column space of all combinations of the two columns fills a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Figure 3.2). With only 2 columns, $C(A)$ can't be all of $\mathbb{R}^3$. The plane has zero thickness, so most right sides $b$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are not in the column space: for most $b$ there is no solution to the 3 equations in 2 unknowns. Of course $(0,0,0)$ is in $C(A)$ — the plane passes through the origin, and $Ax = 0$ always has the solution $x = 0$. The attainable right sides $b$ are exactly the vectors in $C(A)$: the first column itself (take $x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0$), the second column (take $x_1 = 0, x_2 = 1$), and — the new level of understanding — all their combinations.

Definition : Span of a set $S$

Instead of columns in $\mathbb{R}^m$, start with any set $S$ of vectors in a vector space $V$. Taking all combinations produces a subspace: $$ > SS = \{ c_1 v_1 + \cdots + c_N v_N \} = \text{the subspace of } V \text{ "spanned" by } S > $$ $SS$ is always the smallest subspace containing $S$. When $S$ = the columns of $A$, $SS = C(A)$; when $S$ = one nonzero vector $v$, $SS$ = the line through $v$. The columns span the column space.

Example 5 : Comparing column spaces in $\mathbb{R}^2$
  • $I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: $C(I)$ is the whole space $\mathbb{R}^2$ — every vector is a combination of the columns.
  • $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$: $C(A)$ is only a line. The second column $(2,4)$ is a multiple of the first $(1,2)$; the column space contains $(1,2)$, $(2,4)$, and all $(c, 2c)$ along that line. $Ax = b$ is solvable only when $b$ is on the line.
  • $B$ (a $2 \times 3$ matrix whose second column is twice the first, with a third column completing the span): $C(B)$ is all of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Every $b$ is attainable — and attainable in several ways: for $b = (5,4)$, $x = (0,1,1)$ (column 2 + column 3) and $x = (2,0,1)$ ($2 \times$ column 1 + column 3) both work. Same column space as $I$, but more solutions because $x$ has extra components.
Bridge to your engineering track

The criterion "$Ax=b$ solvable $\iff b \in C(A)$" is exactly the membership test your pure-Python Matrix class must implement in solve(b): Gaussian elimination either produces $x$ (b in the span) or exposes a contradictory row $0 = \text{nonzero}$ (b outside the span). The column space is the set of reachable right-hand sides — the same logic you will meet again in MML as the image of a linear map.

5. Worked Examples (complete)

Worked Example 3.1A : Constructing $A$ with prescribed solvability

Given three different vectors $b_1, b_2, b_3$. Construct a matrix so that $Ax = b_1$ and $Ax = b_2$ are solvable, but $Ax = b_3$ is not. Solution. Make $b_1$ and $b_2$ the two columns of $A$: then the solutions are $x = (1, 0)$ and $x = (0, 1)$. To keep $Ax = b_3$ unsolvable, don't make the column space any larger — the question becomes: $$ > Ax = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 & b_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = b_3 \quad ? \quad \text{i.e., is } b_3 \text{ a combination of } b_1, b_2? > $$ If no: we have the desired matrix. If yes: construction is impossible, because any column space containing $b_1$ and $b_2$ must contain all their linear combinations, hence $b_3$, hence $Ax = b_3$ would necessarily be solvable.

Worked Example 3.1B : Subspace $S$ of $V$, then subspace $SS$ of $S$
Space $V$ As combinations As solutions A subspace $S$ A subspace $SS \subseteq S$
$V_1$ all combinations of $(1,1,0,0)$, $(1,1,1,0)$, $(1,1,1,1)$ all solutions of $v_1 - v_2 = 0$ combinations of the first two vectors multiples $(c, c, 0, 0)$ of the first
$V_2$ all combinations of $(1,0,-1)$, $(1,-1,1)$ all solutions of $u \cdot v = 0$, $u = (1,2,1)$ the line through $(1,-1,1)$ $Z$ (zero subspace)
$V_3$ all combinations of $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ all solutions $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ of $b = c$ (symmetric) the diagonal matrices multiples $cI$
$V_4$ all combinations of $1, x, x^2, x^3$ all solutions of $\frac{d^4 y}{dx^4} = 0$ quadratic polynomials linear polynomials (then constants as $SSS$)

In all four parts one could also take $S = V$ itself and $SS = Z$. Each $V$ admits two descriptions: "all combinations of…" and "all solutions of…".

6. Review of the Key Ideas

Ce qu'il faut retenir
  1. $\mathbb{R}^n$ contains all column vectors with $n$ real components.
  2. $M$ ($2 \times 2$ matrices), $F$ (functions), and $Z$ (zero vector alone) are vector spaces.
  3. A subspace containing $v$ and $w$ must contain all their combinations $cv + dw$.
  4. The combinations of the columns of $A$ form the column space $C(A)$; the column space is "spanned" by the columns.
  5. $Ax = b$ has a solution exactly when $b$ is in the column space of $A$: $$ > C(A) = \text{all combinations of the columns} = \text{all vectors } Ax > $$

References

Gilbert Strang — Introduction to Linear Algebra, Chapter 3: Vector Spaces and Subspaces, §3.1 "Spaces of Vectors" (p. 123–130)

notes.excerpt: --- The Nullspace of $A$ [!info] Definition: Nullspace $N(A)$ The nullspace $N(A)$ of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ consists of all solutions $x$ to the homogeneous equation $Ax 0$. $$ N(A) \{x \in \math
notes.html:
The Nullspace of $A$

Definition: Nullspace $N(A)$

The nullspace $N(A)$ of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ consists of all solutions $x$ to the homogeneous equation $Ax = 0$. $$ N(A) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid Ax = 0\} $$

Subspace Verification

The nullspace is always a vector subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$:

  1. Contains Zero: $A(0) = 0$, so $0 \in N(A)$.
  2. Closed under Addition: If $x, y \in N(A)$, then $A(x + y) = Ax + Ay = 0 + 0 = 0$.
  3. Closed under Scalar Multiplication: If $x \in N(A)$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, then $A(cx) = c(Ax) = c(0) = 0$.
Pitfall: Subspace Ambient Spaces

For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$:

  • The Nullspace $N(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ($x$ has $n$ components).
  • The Column Space $C(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$ ($Ax$ has $m$ components).

Computing the Nullspace: Elimination to $R$

Elementary row operations change the rows and column space of a matrix, but they never change the solutions to $Ax = 0$.

$$ N(A) = N(U) = N(R) $$

Definition: Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF)

The reduced row echelon form $R = \text{rref}(A)$ is reached by continuing elimination past $U$:

  1. Use pivot rows to eliminate upward, creating zeros above every pivot.
  2. Divide each pivot row by its pivot to make all pivots equal to $1$.
  3. Zero rows are collected at the bottom.

Pivot Variables, Free Variables, and Special Solutions

The columns of $A$ and $R$ split into two distinct categories:

Column Type Pivot Status Corresponding Variables Role in Elimination
Pivot Columns Contains a leading $1$ in $R$ Pivot variables Determined uniquely by back-substitution
Free Columns No pivot Free variables Assigned arbitrary scalar values (parameters)
  • Rank ($r$): The number of pivots (number of nonzero rows in $R$).
  • Number of Pivot Variables: $r$.
  • Number of Free Variables: $n - r$.
Core Principle: Special Solutions

To find the basis for $N(A)$, compute the $n - r$ special solutions:

  1. Set one free variable to $1$ and all other free variables to $0$.
  2. Solve $Rx = 0$ for the pivot variables.
  3. Repeat for each free variable.

The nullspace $N(A)$ is the set of all linear combinations of these special solutions: $$ x = c_1 s_1 + c_2 s_2 + \dots + c_{n-r} s_{n-r} $$

The Fundamental Existence Theorem

If a matrix has more columns than rows ($n > m$), the rank satisfies $r \le m < n$. There are at least $n - m > 0$ free variables, which guarantees that $Ax = 0$ has nonzero solutions in its nullspace.

The Block Form of $R$ and the Nullspace Matrix $N$

When pivot columns appear first, $R$ partitions cleanly into the $r \times r$ identity block $I$ and an $r \times (n - r)$ free block $F$:

$$ R = \begin{bmatrix} I & F \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} $$

The special solutions assemble into the columns of an $n \times (n - r)$ nullspace matrix $N$:

$$ N = \begin{bmatrix} -F \\ I \end{bmatrix} $$

Proof of Orthogonality/Kernel Condition: $$ RN = \begin{bmatrix} I & F \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -F \\ I \end{bmatrix} = -F + F = 0 $$

Rank One Matrices ($r = 1$)

A matrix has rank $r = 1$ when every row is a scalar multiple of a single pivot row.

  • Outer Product Form: Every rank-one matrix can be factored as a column times a row: $$ A = u v^T $$
  • Column Space: The 1-dimensional line along $u$.
  • Nullspace: The $(n - 1)$-dimensional hyperplane perpendicular to the vector $v$: $$ Ax = 0 \iff u(v^T x) = 0 \iff v^T x = 0 $$

Worked Examples

Example 1: Finding Special Solutions for a $2 \times 4$ Matrix

Find the reduced echelon form $R$, the rank $r$, and the special solutions for: $$ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 4 \\ 3 & 8 & 6 & 16 \end{bmatrix} $$

1. Elimination to Upper Triangular Form $U$: Subtract $3 \times (\text{row } 1)$ from row 2: $$ U = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} $$ Pivots are in column 1 ($a_{11} = 1$) and column 2 ($u_{22} = 2$). Columns 3 and 4 are free.

2. Elimination to Reduced Form $R$:

  • Divide row 2 by $2$: $$ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} $$
  • Subtract $2 \times (\text{row } 2)$ from row 1: $$ R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} $$ Rank $r = 2$. Pivot variables: $x_1, x_2$. Free variables: $x_3, x_4$.

3. Construct Special Solutions:

  • For $x_3 = 1, x_4 = 0$: $$ \begin{aligned} x_1 + 2(1) + 0(0) &= 0 \implies x_1 = -2 \\ x_2 + 0(1) + 2(0) &= 0 \implies x_2 = 0 \end{aligned} \implies s_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} $$

  • For $x_3 = 0, x_4 = 1$: $$ \begin{aligned} x_1 + 2(0) + 0(1) &= 0 \implies x_1 = 0 \\ x_2 + 0(0) + 2(1) &= 0 \implies x_2 = -2 \end{aligned} \implies s_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} $$

Complete Nullspace Solution: $$ x = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} $$

Example 2: Inverting from Special Solutions to $R$

Construct the reduced row echelon matrix $R$ whose special solutions to $Rx = 0$ are: $$ s_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad s_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ -6 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} $$

Derivation:

  • The free variables correspond to entries where $s_i$ contains $1$: variables $x_2$ and $x_4$.
  • The pivot variables are $x_1$ and $x_3$.
  • The components of $s_1$ and $s_2$ give the coefficients of the free columns with flipped signs: $$ R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} $$

References

Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th Ed), Gilbert Strang (p. 135-141)

notes.html:
The Dot Product

Definition of the Dot Product

If $\mathbf{u} = \langle a_1, a_2 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{v} = \langle b_1, b_2 \rangle$, their dot product is: $$ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 $$ Note: The result is a scalar (real number), not a vector.

Example 1: Calculating Dot Products

(a) If $\mathbf{u} = \langle 3, -2 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{v} = \langle 4, 5 \rangle$: $$ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = (3)(4) + (-2)(5) = 12 - 10 = 2 $$

(b) If $\mathbf{u} = 2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{v} = 5\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j}$: $$ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = (2)(5) + (1)(-6) = 10 - 6 = 4 $$

Properties of the Dot Product
  1. Commutative: $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}$
  2. Scalar Multiplication: $(c\mathbf{u}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u} \cdot (c\mathbf{v})$
  3. Distributive: $(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{w}$
  4. Magnitude: $|\mathbf{u}|^2 = \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}$
The Dot Product Theorem

If $\theta$ is the angle between two nonzero vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$: $$ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}| |\mathbf{v}| \cos \theta $$

Proof: Apply Law of Cosines to triangle formed by vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v},$ and $\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}$.

Finding the Angle: $$ \cos \theta = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}| |\mathbf{v}|} $$

Example 2: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors

Find angle between $\mathbf{u} = \langle 2, 5 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{v} = \langle 4, -3 \rangle$.

$$ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = (2)(4) + (5)(-3) = 8 - 15 = -7 $$ $$ |\mathbf{u}| = \sqrt{4+25} = \sqrt{29}, \quad |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{16+9} = 5 $$ $$ \cos \theta = \frac{-7}{5\sqrt{29}} \implies \theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{-7}{5\sqrt{29}}\right) \approx 105.1^\circ $$

Orthogonal Vectors

Two nonzero vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are perpendicular (orthogonal) if and only if: $$ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0 $$ (Because $\cos(\pi/2) = 0$)

Example 3: Checking for Perpendicular Vectors

(a) $\mathbf{u} = \langle 3, 5 \rangle, \mathbf{v} = \langle 2, -8 \rangle$: $$ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 6 - 40 = -34 \neq 0 \quad (\text{Not perpendicular}) $$

(b) $\mathbf{u} = \langle 2, 1 \rangle, \mathbf{v} = \langle -1, 2 \rangle$: $$ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = -2 + 2 = 0 \quad (\text{Perpendicular}) $$

Component, Projection, and Work

The Component of $\mathbf{u}$ Along $\mathbf{v}$

Also called the scalar projection. It represents the magnitude of the portion of $\mathbf{u}$ that points in the direction of $\mathbf{v}$. $$ \text{comp}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u} = |\mathbf{u}| \cos \theta = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|} $$ Note: This is a scalar, not a vector. It is negative if $\pi/2 < \theta \le \pi$.

Example 4: Resolving a Force into Components

A 3000 lb car is on a driveway inclined at $15^\circ$.

  • Force rolling car down (parallel to incline): $$ |\mathbf{u}| = 3000 \cos(75^\circ) \approx 776 \text{ lb} $$ (Angle between weight vector and incline is $90-15=75^\circ$)
  • Force on driveway (perpendicular): $$ |\mathbf{v}| = 3000 \cos(15^\circ) \approx 2898 \text{ lb} $$
Example 5: Finding Components

Let $\mathbf{u} = \langle 1, 4 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{v} = \langle -2, 1 \rangle$. $$ \text{comp}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u} = \frac{(1)(-2) + (4)(1)}{\sqrt{(-2)^2 + 1^2}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} $$

The Vector Projection of $\mathbf{u}$ Onto $\mathbf{v}$

Denoted $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u}$. It is a vector parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ with length equal to the component of $\mathbf{u}$ along $\mathbf{v}$. $$ \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u} = (\text{comp}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u}) \frac{\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|} = \left( \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2} \right) \mathbf{v} $$

Resolving Vectors: Any vector $\mathbf{u}$ can be written as $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}_1 + \mathbf{u}_2$ where:

  • $\mathbf{u}_1 = \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u}$ (parallel to $\mathbf{v}$)
  • $\mathbf{u}_2 = \mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u}$ (orthogonal to $\mathbf{v}$)
Example 6: Resolving a Vector into Orthogonal Vectors

Let $\mathbf{u} = \langle -2, 9 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{v} = \langle -1, 2 \rangle$.

(a) Find $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u}$: $$ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = (-2)(-1) + (9)(2) = 20 $$ $$ |\mathbf{v}|^2 = (-1)^2 + 2^2 = 5 $$ $$ \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u} = \frac{20}{5} \langle -1, 2 \rangle = 4\langle -1, 2 \rangle = \langle -4, 8 \rangle $$

(b) Resolve $\mathbf{u}$:

  • Parallel part: $\mathbf{u}_1 = \langle -4, 8 \rangle$
  • Orthogonal part: $\mathbf{u}_2 = \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_1 = \langle -2, 9 \rangle - \langle -4, 8 \rangle = \langle 2, 1 \rangle$

Work

Work Formula

If a constant force $\mathbf{F}$ moves an object along displacement vector $\mathbf{D}$, the work $W$ is: $$ W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{D} = |\mathbf{F}| |\mathbf{D}| \cos \theta $$ (Only the component of force in the direction of motion does work).

Example 7: Calculating Work

Force $\mathbf{F} = \langle 2, 3 \rangle$ moves object from $(1, 3)$ to $(5, 9)$.

  • Displacement $\mathbf{D} = \langle 5-1, 9-3 \rangle = \langle 4, 6 \rangle$.
  • Work $W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{D} = (2)(4) + (3)(6) = 8 + 18 = 26$ ft-lb.
Example 8: Calculating Work (Angle)

Child pulls wagon with 20 lb force at $60^\circ$ angle for 100 ft.

  • Displacement $\mathbf{D} = 100\mathbf{i}$.
  • Force $\mathbf{F} = 20(\cos 60^\circ \mathbf{i} + \sin 60^\circ \mathbf{j}) = 10\mathbf{i} + 10\sqrt{3}\mathbf{j}$.
  • Work $W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{D} = (10)(100) + (10\sqrt{3})(0) = 1000$ ft-lb.

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 647)

notes.excerpt: --- Vectors [!info] Geometric Description of Vectors A vector is a directed line segment representing a quantity with magnitude and direction (e.g., displacement, velocity, force). - Notation: $\vec{A
notes.html:
Vectors

Geometric Description of Vectors

A vector is a directed line segment representing a quantity with magnitude and direction (e.g., displacement, velocity, force).

  • Notation: $\vec{AB}$ or boldface $\mathbf{u}$. $A$ is initial point, $B$ is terminal point.
  • Magnitude (Length): Denoted $|\vec{AB}|$ or $|\mathbf{u}|$.
  • Equality: Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction (position doesn't matter).

Vector Operations (Geometric):

  • Addition ($\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$):
    • Triangle Rule: Place initial point of $\mathbf{v}$ at terminal point of $\mathbf{u}$. Sum is vector from start of $\mathbf{u}$ to end of $\mathbf{v}$.
    • Parallelogram Rule: Place initial points together. Sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$.
  • Scalar Multiplication ($c\mathbf{v}$):
    • Magnitude: $|c| |\mathbf{v}|$.
    • Direction: Same as $\mathbf{v}$ if $c > 0$; opposite if $c < 0$.
  • Subtraction ($\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$): Defined as $\mathbf{u} + (-\mathbf{v})$. Geometrically, it is the other diagonal of the parallelogram formed by $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$.
Vectors in the Coordinate Plane (Component Form)

A vector $\mathbf{v}$ can be represented analytically by its components $\langle a_1, a_2 \rangle$, where $a_1$ is horizontal change and $a_2$ is vertical change.

Component Form from Points: If vector $\mathbf{v}$ has initial point $P(x_1, y_1)$ and terminal point $Q(x_2, y_2)$: $$ \mathbf{v} = \langle x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1 \rangle $$

Magnitude: $$ |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2} $$

Example 1: Describing Vectors in Component Form

(a) Find component form of $\mathbf{u}$ with initial point $(-2, 5)$ and terminal point $(3, 7)$. $$ \mathbf{u} = \langle 3 - (-2), 7 - 5 \rangle = \langle 5, 2 \rangle $$

(b) If $\mathbf{v} = \langle 3, 7 \rangle$ starts at $(2, 4)$, find terminal point $(x, y)$. $$ \langle x - 2, y - 4 \rangle = \langle 3, 7 \rangle \implies x-2=3, y-4=7 \implies (5, 11) $$

(c) Sketch $\mathbf{w} = \langle 2, 3 \rangle$ at various initial points. (All arrows are parallel, length $\sqrt{13}$, pointing up-right).

Example 2: Magnitudes of Vectors

Find magnitude of each vector.

(a) $\mathbf{u} = \langle 2, -3 \rangle$ $$ |\mathbf{u}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{4+9} = \sqrt{13} $$

(b) $\mathbf{v} = \langle 5, 0 \rangle$ $$ |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 0^2} = 5 $$

(c) $\mathbf{w} = \langle \frac{3}{5}, \frac{4}{5} \rangle$ $$ |\mathbf{w}| = \sqrt{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{9}{25} + \frac{16}{25}} = \sqrt{1} = 1 $$ (Note: This is a unit vector).

Algebraic Operations on Vectors

Algebraic Operations on Vectors

If $\mathbf{u} = \langle a_1, a_2 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{v} = \langle b_1, b_2 \rangle$: $$ > \begin{aligned} > \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} &= \langle a_1 + b_1, a_2 + b_2 \rangle \\ > \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} &= \langle a_1 - b_1, a_2 - b_2 \rangle \\ > c\mathbf{u} &= \langle ca_1, ca_2 \rangle \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}) > \end{aligned} > $$

Example 3: Operations with Vectors

Given $\mathbf{u} = \langle 2, -3 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{v} = \langle -1, 2 \rangle$: $$ > \begin{aligned} > \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} &= \langle 2+(-1), -3+2 \rangle = \langle 1, -1 \rangle \\ > \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} &= \langle 2-(-1), -3-2 \rangle = \langle 3, -5 \rangle \\ > 2\mathbf{u} &= 2\langle 2, -3 \rangle = \langle 4, -6 \rangle \\ > -3\mathbf{v} &= -3\langle -1, 2 \rangle = \langle 3, -6 \rangle \\ > 2\mathbf{u} + 3\mathbf{v} &= \langle 4, -6 \rangle + \langle -3, 6 \rangle = \langle 1, 0 \rangle > \end{aligned} > $$

Properties of Vectors

Vector Addition:

  • Commutative: $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}$
  • Associative: $\mathbf{u} + (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}) = (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{w}$
  • Identity: $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{u}$
  • Inverse: $\mathbf{u} + (-\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0}$

Scalar Multiplication:

  • Distributive: $c(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = c\mathbf{u} + c\mathbf{v}$ and $(c+d)\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{u}$
  • Associative: $(cd)\mathbf{u} = c(d\mathbf{u})$
  • Identity: $1\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}$
  • Zero property: $0\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}, c\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$

Length: $|c\mathbf{u}| = |c| |\mathbf{u}|$

Unit Vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$

A unit vector has length 1. Two standard unit vectors are: $$ \mathbf{i} = \langle 1, 0 \rangle \quad \mathbf{j} = \langle 0, 1 \rangle $$

Vectors in Terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$

Any vector $\mathbf{v} = \langle a_1, a_2 \rangle$ can be written as: $$ \mathbf{v} = a_1 \mathbf{i} + a_2 \mathbf{j} $$

Example 4: Vectors in Terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$

(a) Write $\mathbf{u} = \langle 5, -8 \rangle$ in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$. $$ \mathbf{u} = 5\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j} $$

(b) If $\mathbf{u} = 3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j}$, find $2\mathbf{u} + 5\mathbf{v}$. $$ > \begin{aligned} > 2\mathbf{u} + 5\mathbf{v} &= 2(3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) + 5(-\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j}) \\ > &= (6\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}) + (-5\mathbf{i} + 30\mathbf{j}) \\ > &= \mathbf{i} + 34\mathbf{j} > \end{aligned} > $$

Horizontal and Vertical Components

If a vector $\mathbf{v}$ has magnitude $|\mathbf{v}|$ and direction angle $\theta$ (standard position):

Component Form from Magnitude and Direction

$$ \mathbf{v} = \langle |\mathbf{v}| \cos \theta, |\mathbf{v}| \sin \theta \rangle = |\mathbf{v}| \cos \theta \, \mathbf{i} + |\mathbf{v}| \sin \theta \, \mathbf{j} $$

Example 5: Components and Direction of a Vector

(a) Vector $\mathbf{v}$ has length 8 and direction $\pi/3$. $$ > \begin{aligned} > a_1 &= 8 \cos(\pi/3) = 4 \\ > a_2 &= 8 \sin(\pi/3) = 4\sqrt{3} \\ > \mathbf{v} &= 4\mathbf{i} + 4\sqrt{3}\mathbf{j} > \end{aligned} > $$

(b) Find direction of $\mathbf{u} = -\sqrt{3}\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$. $$ \tan \theta = \frac{1}{-\sqrt{3}} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} $$ Reference angle is $\pi/6$. Since terminal point is in Quadrant II (x negative, y positive): $$ \theta = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6} $$

Using Vectors to Model Velocity and Force

Velocity Vectors

The true velocity $\mathbf{w}$ of an object moving in a medium (like wind or water) is the sum of the object's velocity relative to the medium ($\mathbf{v}$) and the velocity of the medium ($\mathbf{u}$). $$ \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} $$

Example 6: The True Speed and Direction of an Airplane

Airplane heads due North at 300 mi/h. Wind flows N 30° E at 40 mi/h.

(a) Component Form:

  • Airplane relative to air ($\mathbf{v}$): Due North $\implies$ angle $90^\circ$. $$ \mathbf{v} = 0\mathbf{i} + 300\mathbf{j} = 300\mathbf{j} $$
  • Wind ($\mathbf{u}$): N 30° E $\implies$ angle $90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$ from positive x-axis. $$ \mathbf{u} = 40(\cos 60^\circ \mathbf{i} + \sin 60^\circ \mathbf{j}) = 20\mathbf{i} + 20\sqrt{3}\mathbf{j} \approx 20\mathbf{i} + 34.64\mathbf{j} $$

(b) True Velocity ($\mathbf{w}$): $$ \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = 20\mathbf{i} + (20\sqrt{3} + 300)\mathbf{j} \approx 20\mathbf{i} + 334.64\mathbf{j} $$

(c) True Speed and Direction:

  • Speed: $|\mathbf{w}| = \sqrt{20^2 + 334.64^2} \approx 335.2$ mi/h.
  • Direction: $\tan \theta = \frac{334.64}{20} \approx 16.732 \implies \theta \approx 86.6^\circ$. This is N $3.4^\circ$ E (since $90^\circ - 86.6^\circ = 3.4^\circ$).
Example 7: Calculating a Heading

Boat speed 10 mi/h. River flows East at 5 mi/h. Find heading to land directly opposite.

Solution:

  • River velocity: $\mathbf{u} = 5\mathbf{i}$.
  • Boat velocity relative to water: $\mathbf{v} = 10(\cos \theta \mathbf{i} + \sin \theta \mathbf{j})$.
  • True course: $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = (5 + 10\cos \theta)\mathbf{i} + (10\sin \theta)\mathbf{j}$.

To land directly across, the horizontal component must be 0: $$ 5 + 10\cos \theta = 0 \implies \cos \theta = -\frac{1}{2} $$ $$ \theta = 120^\circ \quad (\text{or N } 30^\circ \text{ W}) $$

Resultant Force

Force is a vector. The resultant force $\mathbf{F}$ acting on an object is the vector sum of all individual forces.

Example 8: Resultant Force

Two forces act at point $P$: $\mathbf{F}_1$ (10 lb at 45°) and $\mathbf{F}_2$ (20 lb at 150°).

Solution: Convert to component form: $$ \mathbf{F}_1 = 10(\cos 45^\circ \mathbf{i} + \sin 45^\circ \mathbf{j}) = 5\sqrt{2}\mathbf{i} + 5\sqrt{2}\mathbf{j} $$ $$ \mathbf{F}_2 = 20(\cos 150^\circ \mathbf{i} + \sin 150^\circ \mathbf{j}) = -10\sqrt{3}\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j} $$

Sum the vectors: $$ > \begin{aligned} > \mathbf{F} &= \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 \\ > &= (5\sqrt{2} - 10\sqrt{3})\mathbf{i} + (5\sqrt{2} + 10)\mathbf{j} \\ > &\approx -10\mathbf{i} + 17\mathbf{j} > \end{aligned} > $$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 637)

notes.html:
tags: [mathematics, linear-algebra, formal-sciences] source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra

Definition

The branch of mathematics concerned with linear equations, linear maps, and their representation in vector spaces via matrices. It underlies nearly every other branch of mathematics and most of quantitative science.

1. History

Period Development Key Figures
Ancient China Rod calculus method for solving simultaneous linear equations (The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, Ch. 8) — precursor to Gaussian elimination —
1637 Introduction of coordinates into geometry → systems of linear equations arise naturally from intersecting lines/planes René Descartes
1693 First systematic method for solving linear systems, via determinants Gottfried Leibniz
1750 Explicit closed-form solution of linear systems using determinants (Cramer's rule) Gabriel Cramer
~1800s Systematic elimination method (linked to geodesy) Carl Friedrich Gauss
1843 Discovery of quaternions — a 4D system generalizing complex numbers William R. Hamilton
1844 Theory of Extension — foundational concepts of what became linear algebra Hermann Grassmann
1848 Coined the term matrix (Latin for "womb") James Joseph Sylvester
1856 Matrix multiplication and the inverse matrix defined → enabled the general linear group Arthur Cayley
1872 Linear Associative Algebra Benjamin Peirce (extended by his son C.S. Peirce)
1888 First modern, precise definition of a vector space Giuseppe Peano
Early 1900s Linear algebra generalized into abstract algebra; theory of linear transformations of finite-dim. vector spaces matures —
Mid-1900s onward Rise of computers → efficient algorithms for Gaussian elimination and matrix decomposition become central to computing —

Framing shift: until the 19th century, linear algebra was taught through systems of equations and matrices. Modern treatments prefer the vector space framing — more general, more synthetic, conceptually cleaner (though more abstract).

2. Core Objects

Object Informal Meaning
Vector space $V$ over field $F$ Set closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication, satisfying 8 axioms (associativity, commutativity, identity, inverses, distributivity, compatibility)
Linear map $T: V \to W$ Function preserving vector addition and scalar multiplication: $T(au+bv) = aT(u)+bT(v)$
Linear subspace Subset of $V$ closed under the same two operations
Span Smallest subspace containing a given set of vectors (all their linear combinations)
Linear independence No vector in the set is a combination of the others
Basis Linearly independent spanning set — minimal generating, maximal independent
Dimension Cardinality of any basis (invariant — Dimension Theorem)
Matrix Concrete finite-dimensional representation of a linear map, once bases are chosen
Eigenvector / eigenvalue $f(v) = av$ — direction preserved (up to scaling) by the map
Determinant Scalar encoding invertibility & volume-scaling of a linear map
Dual space $V^*$ Space of linear forms $V \to F$
Inner product Bilinear form giving $V$ geometric structure: length, angle, orthogonality

Key structural fact: two finite-dim. vector spaces over the same field are isomorphic iff they have the same dimension — matrices and abstract vector spaces are "two languages for the same concepts."

3. Subfields & Extensions

Area What It Adds
Matrix theory Explicit computation: elimination, decomposition, normal forms (Jordan, Frobenius)
Multilinear algebra Maps linear in several variables at once; tensor products
Module theory Vector spaces generalized to a ring $R$ instead of a field — no guaranteed basis
Functional analysis Linear algebra + analysis on infinite-dim. function spaces (Banach, Hilbert spaces)
Numerical linear algebra Algorithmic/computational side — BLAS, LAPACK, complexity of solving large systems
Linear algebra & geometry Lines, planes, rotations, projective/affine space as linear-algebraic objects

4. How Central Is It?

Linear algebra sits near the root of the math dependency tree:

  • Geometry is now usually built from linear algebra (points/lines/planes/rotations as linear objects), inverting the classical (synthetic) order.
  • Functional analysis = linear algebra applied to (infinite-dimensional) function spaces.
  • Nonlinear systems, when not directly solvable, are handled by linearizing — the differential of a function at a point is the best linear approximation there. This is why linear algebra is the gateway to almost all applied math (optimization, ML, PDEs).
  • It's one of the few math subjects that is simultaneously deeply theoretical (abstract algebra, module theory) and maximally computational (it is what GPUs and supercomputers are optimized to do).
For your AI/ML track specifically

Linear algebra is the substrate under nearly everything downstream in your roadmap — least squares, PCA, backprop-as-Jacobian-chains, attention (all matrix multiplications), convex optimization, and probability-as-linear-operators (Markov chains) all reduce to objects on this page.

5. Where It's Used

Domain Application
Physics Quantum mechanics (wave functions as vectors in Hilbert space), electromagnetism (Lorentz transformations), classical mechanics
Engineering Fluid dynamics & CFD (linearizing Navier–Stokes), power systems (eigenvalue analysis for grid stability), robotics (rigid body transforms)
Computer science Computer graphics (rotations/projections as matrices), computer vision, graph algorithms
Machine learning / AI Every layer of a neural net is a linear map + nonlinearity; PCA, SVD, embeddings, attention mechanisms
Statistics Regression (least squares), multivariate analysis, covariance structure
Earth science Weather forecasting — atmosphere discretized into cells, evolved via large linear (or linearized) systems
Hardware GPUs are architected around matrix operations; specialized vector/array processors exist since the 1960s (Cray, ILLIAC IV) specifically for linear algebra throughput
Signal processing Fourier analysis = choice of orthogonal basis in a function space

6. Canonical References

(cross-referencing your existing roadmap)

  • Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right — abstract, basis-free approach (your queue)
  • Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra — applied/computational, MIT 18.06 companion
  • Roman, Advanced Linear Algebra — graduate-level, module-theoretic framing

See Also

  • Vector Spaces
  • Matrix Decompositions
  • Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
  • Convex Optimization

notes.html:
Determinants and Cramer's Rule

Determinant of a $2 \times 2$ Matrix

For a matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$, the determinant is: $$ \det(A) = |A| = ad - bc $$ Mnemonic: (Product of main diagonal) - (Product of anti-diagonal).

Example 1

Evaluate $\begin{vmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix}$. $$ 6(3) - (-3)(2) = 18 - (-6) = 24 $$

Minors and Cofactors

To find the determinant of larger matrices, we use minors and cofactors.

Definitions

Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix.

  1. Minor ($M_{ij}$): The determinant of the submatrix obtained by deleting the $i$-th row and $j$-th column of $A$.
  2. Cofactor ($A_{ij}$): The minor multiplied by a sign factor. $$ A_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij} $$

Checkerboard Sign Pattern: The sign $(-1)^{i+j}$ creates a checkerboard pattern of $+$ and $-$ starting with $+$ in the top-left: $$ \begin{bmatrix} + & - & + & \dots \\ - & + & - & \dots \\ + & - & + & \dots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{bmatrix} $$

Determinant of an $n \times n$ Matrix

Cofactor Expansion

The determinant of $A$ is the sum of the entries of any row (or column) multiplied by their respective cofactors.

Expanding by the First Row: $$ \det(A) = a_{11}A_{11} + a_{12}A_{12} + \dots + a_{1n}A_{1n} $$

Example 2: Determinant of a $3 \times 3$ Matrix

Evaluate $\det(A)$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ -2 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$.

Solution: Expand along the first row (signs: $+ - +$). $$ > \begin{aligned} > \det(A) &= 2 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 \end{vmatrix} - 3 \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ -2 & 6 \end{vmatrix} + (-1) \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{vmatrix} \\ > &= 2(12 - 20) - 3(0 - (-8)) - 1(0 - (-4)) \\ > &= 2(-8) - 3(8) - 4 \\ > &= -16 - 24 - 4 \\ > &= -44 > \end{aligned} > $$

Expansion by Any Row or Column

You can expand along any row or column to get the same result. This is useful if a row or column contains zeros.

Example 3: Expanding the matrix from Example 2 along the second row (signs: $- + -$). $$ > \begin{aligned} > \det(A) &= -0 \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 5 & 6 \end{vmatrix} + 2 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 6 \end{vmatrix} - 4 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -2 & 5 \end{vmatrix} \\ > &= 0 + 2(12 - 2) - 4(10 - (-6)) \\ > &= 2(10) - 4(16) \\ > &= 20 - 64 \\ > &= -44 > \end{aligned} > $$

Invertibility Criterion and Transformations

Invertibility Criterion

A square matrix $A$ has an inverse if and only if its determinant is non-zero. $$ A \text{ is invertible} \iff \det(A) \neq 0 $$

Example 4: Using the Determinant to Show That a Matrix Is Not Invertible

Show that $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 5 & 6 & 2 & 6 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 9 \end{bmatrix}$ has no inverse.

Solution: Calculate $\det(A)$. Expand by the second row (since it has three zeros). The only non-zero entry is $a_{24} = 3$. The sign for position $(2,4)$ is $(-1)^{2+4} = +1$. $$ > \begin{aligned} > \det(A) &= 3 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 5 & 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \end{vmatrix} > \end{aligned} > $$ Now expand this $3 \times 3$ minor by the third column (two zeros). The entry is 2 at position $(2,3)$. Sign is $(-1)^{2+3} = -1$. $$ > \begin{aligned} > \det(A) &= 3 \left[ -2 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{vmatrix} \right] \\ > &= 3(-2)(1(4) - 2(2)) \\ > &= -6(0) = 0 > \end{aligned} > $$ Since $\det(A) = 0$, $A$ has no inverse.

Row and Column Transformations

Property of Determinants

If matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by adding a multiple of one row (or column) to another row (or column), then: $$ \det(A) = \det(B) $$ This allows us to introduce zeros into a row or column to simplify the expansion.

Example 5: Using Transformations to Calculate a Determinant

Find $\det(A)$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 2 & -1 & -4 \\ 3 & 5 & -3 & 11 \\ 24 & 6 & 1 & -12 \\ 2 & 2 & 7 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Solution: Step 1: Create zeros in Row 3. Notice Row 3 is almost 3 times Row 1 ($24 \approx 3 \times 8$, $6 \approx 3 \times 2$, $-12 \approx 3 \times -4$). Operation: $R_3 - 3R_1 \to R_3$. $$ > \det(A) = \begin{vmatrix} 8 & 2 & -1 & -4 \\ 3 & 5 & -3 & 11 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 7 & -1 \end{vmatrix} > $$ Expand by Row 3. The only non-zero term is 4 at $(3,3)$. Sign is $+$. $$ \det(A) = 4 \begin{vmatrix} 8 & 2 & -4 \\ 3 & 5 & 11 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix} $$

Step 2: Simplify the $3 \times 3$ determinant. Add 2 times Column 3 to Column 1 to create zeros. Operation: $C_1 + 2C_3 \to C_1$. $$ > \det(A) = 4 \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 25 & 5 & 11 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix} > $$ Expand by Column 1. The only non-zero term is 25 at $(2,1)$. Sign is $-$. $$ > \begin{aligned} > \det(A) &= 4 \left[ -25 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix} \right] \\ > &= -100 [ (2)(-1) - (-4)(2) ] \\ > &= -100 [ -2 + 8 ] \\ > &= -100(6) = -600 > \end{aligned} > $$ Since $\det(A) \neq 0$, the matrix has an inverse.

Cramer's Rule

Derivation for Two Variables

Consider the system: $$ > \begin{cases} > ax + by = r \\ > cx + dy = s > \end{cases} > $$ Solving for $x$ and $y$ by elimination yields: $$ x = \frac{rd - bs}{ad - bc}, \quad y = \frac{as - cr}{ad - bc} $$ The numerators and denominators are determinants of $2 \times 2$ matrices.

Cramer's Rule for Systems in Two Variables

The system $\begin{cases} ax + by = r \\ cx + dy = s \end{cases}$ has the solution: $$ x = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} r & b \\ s & d \end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix}}, \quad y = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} a & r \\ c & s \end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix}} $$ Provided that $D = \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} \neq 0$.

Notation:

  • $D$: Determinant of the coefficient matrix.
  • $D_x$: Determinant formed by replacing the first column ($x$-coefficients) of $D$ with the constants ($r, s$).
  • $D_y$: Determinant formed by replacing the second column ($y$-coefficients) of $D$ with the constants ($r, s$).

$$ x = \frac{|D_x|}{|D|}, \quad y = \frac{|D_y|}{|D|} $$

Example 6: Using Cramer's Rule (Two Variables)

Solve $\begin{cases} 2x + 6y = -1 \\ x + 8y = 2 \end{cases}$.

Solution:

  1. Find $|D|$: $$ |D| = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 8 \end{vmatrix} = 2(8) - 6(1) = 10 $$
  2. Find $|D_x|$ (replace col 1 with constants): $$ |D_x| = \begin{vmatrix} -1 & 6 \\ 2 & 8 \end{vmatrix} = (-1)(8) - 6(2) = -20 $$
  3. Find $|D_y|$ (replace col 2 with constants): $$ |D_y| = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 2(2) - (-1)(1) = 5 $$
  4. Solve: $$ x = \frac{-20}{10} = -2, \quad y = \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2} $$
Cramer's Rule (General Case)

For a system of $n$ linear equations in $n$ variables $DX = B$: $$ x_1 = \frac{|D_{x_1}|}{|D|}, \quad x_2 = \frac{|D_{x_2}|}{|D|}, \quad \dots, \quad x_n = \frac{|D_{x_n}|}{|D|} $$ where $D_{x_i}$ is the matrix obtained by replacing the $i$-th column of the coefficient matrix $D$ with the constant matrix $B$. Condition: $|D| \neq 0$.

Example 7: Using Cramer's Rule (Three Variables)

Solve $\begin{cases} 2x - 3y + 4z = 1 \\ x + 0y + 6z = 0 \\ 3x - 2y + 0z = 5 \end{cases}$.

Solution: Calculate determinants (note the 0 coefficients for missing variables):

  • $|D|$: $\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 6 \\ 3 & -2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -38$
  • $|D_x|$ (replace col 1 with $1, 0, 5$): $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 5 & -2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -78$
  • $|D_y|$ (replace col 2 with $1, 0, 5$): $\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 6 \\ 3 & 5 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -22$
  • $|D_z|$ (replace col 3 with $1, 0, 5$): $\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = 13$

Final Values: $$ x = \frac{-78}{-38} = \frac{39}{19}, \quad y = \frac{-22}{-38} = \frac{11}{19}, \quad z = \frac{13}{-38} = -\frac{13}{38} $$

Areas of Triangles Using Determinants

Area of a Triangle Formula

If a triangle has vertices $(a_1, b_1)$, $(a_2, b_2)$, and $(a_3, b_3)$ in the coordinate plane, its area $\mathcal{A}$ is: $$ > \mathcal{A} = \pm \frac{1}{2} \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & 1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & 1 \\ a_3 & b_3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} > $$ Note: Choose the sign ($+$ or $-$) that results in a positive area.

Example 8: Area of a Triangle

Find the area of the triangle with vertices $(-1, 4)$, $(3, 6)$, and $(1, 2)$.

Solution Set up the determinant: $$ > \mathcal{A} = \pm \frac{1}{2} \begin{vmatrix} -1 & 4 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} > $$ Calculate the determinant (expanding along the first row): $$ > \begin{aligned} > \det &= -1(6 - 2) - 4(3 - 1) + 1(6 - 6) \\ > &= -1(4) - 4(2) + 0 \\ > &= -12 > \end{aligned} > $$ Apply the formula: $$ \mathcal{A} = \pm \frac{1}{2}(-12) $$ To make the area positive, choose the negative sign: $$ \mathcal{A} = -\frac{1}{2}(-12) = 6 $$

notes.excerpt: --- Inverses of Matrices and Matrix Equations [!info] Identity Matrix The identity matrix $I_n$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with 1s on the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere. It acts as the multiplicative
notes.html:
Inverses of Matrices and Matrix Equations

Identity Matrix

The identity matrix $I_n$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with 1s on the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere. It acts as the multiplicative identity (like the number 1). $$ A \cdot I_n = A \quad \text{and} \quad I_n \cdot B = B $$

Examples: $$ I_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad I_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $$

Inverse of a $2 \times 2$ Matrix

Formula for $2 \times 2$ Inverse

If $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$, then the inverse $A^{-1}$ is: $$ A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc} \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix} $$

Determinant: The quantity $ad - bc$ is the determinant.

  • If $ad - bc = 0$, the matrix has no inverse (it is singular).
Example 3: Finding the Inverse of a $2 \times 2$ Matrix

Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

Solution: Determinant $= (4)(3) - (5)(2) = 12 - 10 = 2$. $$ A^{-1} = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3/2 & -5/2 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} $$

Verification: Calculate $AA^{-1}$ and $A^{-1}A$ to ensure both equal $I_2$.

Inverse of an $n \times n$ Matrix

For larger matrices, use Gaussian Elimination.

Algorithm for Finding $A^{-1}$
  1. Form the augmented matrix $[A \mid I_n]$.
  2. Use elementary row operations to transform the left side ($A$) into the identity matrix $I_n$.
  3. The right side will automatically transform into $A^{-1}$. $$ [A \mid I_n] \xrightarrow{\text{row ops}} [I_n \mid A^{-1}] $$
Example 4: Finding the Inverse of a $3 \times 3$ Matrix

Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & -3 & -6 \\ -3 & 6 & 15 \end{bmatrix}$.

Solution: Start with augmented matrix $[A \mid I_3]$: $$ \left[ \begin{array}{rrr|rrr} 1 & -2 & -4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & -6 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 6 & 15 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right] $$

Perform row operations to reach reduced row-echelon form on the left: 4. $R_2 - 2R_1 \to R_2$ and $R_3 + 3R_1 \to R_3$ 5. Scale $R_3$ by $1/3$ 6. Eliminate entries above pivots ($R_1 + 2R_2$, $R_2 - 2R_3$)

Final Matrix: $$ \left[ \begin{array}{rrr|rrr} 1 & 0 & 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -4 & 1 & -2/3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1/3 \end{array} \right] $$

The right side is $A^{-1}$: $$ A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & -2/3 \\ 1 & 0 & 1/3 \end{bmatrix} $$

Verification: Check that $AA^{-1} = I_3$ and $A^{-1}A = I_3$.

Matrix Equations

Solving a Matrix Equation

A system of linear equations can be written as a single matrix equation $AX = B$, where:

  • $A$ is the coefficient matrix.
  • $X$ is the variable matrix.
  • $B$ is the constant matrix.

If $A$ is a square $n \times n$ matrix with an inverse $A^{-1}$, the solution is found by multiplying both sides by $A^{-1}$ on the left: $$ X = A^{-1}B $$

Proof: $$ \begin{aligned} AX &= B \\ A^{-1}(AX) &= A^{-1}B \quad \leftarrow \text{Multiply on left by } A^{-1} \\ (A^{-1}A)X &= A^{-1}B \quad \leftarrow \text{Associative Property} \\ I_n X &= A^{-1}B \quad \leftarrow \text{Property of Inverses} \\ X &= A^{-1}B \quad \leftarrow \text{Property of Identity Matrix} \end{aligned} $$

Example 6: Solving a System Using a Matrix Inverse

Solve the system: $$ > \begin{cases} > 2x - 5y = 15 \\ > 3x - 6y = 36 > \end{cases} > $$

(a) Write as Matrix Equation $AX=B$: $$ > \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 3 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 15 \\ 36 \end{bmatrix} > $$

(b) Solve using $X = A^{-1}B$: First, find $A^{-1}$ using the $2 \times 2$ formula. Determinant $= (2)(-6) - (-5)(3) = -12 + 15 = 3$. $$ > A^{-1} = \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} -6 & 5 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} > $$ Multiply $A^{-1}$ by $B$: $$ > \begin{aligned} > X &= A^{-1}B \\ > \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} -6 & 5 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 15 \\ 36 \end{bmatrix} \\ > &= \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} (-6)(15) + (5)(36) \\ (-3)(15) + (2)(36) \end{bmatrix} \\ > &= \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} -90 + 180 \\ -45 + 72 \end{bmatrix} \\ > &= \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 90 \\ 27 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 30 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} > \end{aligned} > $$ Solution: $x = 30, y = 9$.

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 708)
