1 Calculate and Interpret the Slope of a Line

Note

A linear equation is an equation in two variables whose graph is a straight line. The defining characteristic of a line is its slope, a numerical measure of its steepness.

Linear 100 FORMAL SCIENCES/110 Pure Mathematics/111 Foundations/Functions/Functions

A linear function is a function of the form: $$f(x) = ax + b$$

  • Graph: A line
  • Slope: $a$
  • y-intercept: $b$

The Concept: Rise over Run

Imagine a staircase. The steepness is determined by the ratio of the vertical step (Rise) to the horizontal step (Run).

Diagram of a line with a "staircase" showing Rise and Run:

Definition: Slope

Let $P = (x_1, y_1)$ and $Q = (x_2, y_2)$ be two distinct points on a nonvertical line $L$. The slope $m$ of $L$ is: $$ m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \qquad (x_1 \neq x_2) $$

This can be interpreted as: $$ m = \frac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \frac{\text{Change in } y}{\text{Change in } x} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} $$

Visual derivation of the slope formula showing a right triangle formed by points P and Q:

Vertical Lines

If $x_1 = x_2$, the line is vertical. The slope is undefined because division by zero is not allowed.

Key Properties of Slope

  1. Consistency: The slope is constant. You can use any two distinct points on the line to calculate it. (Based on similar triangles).
  2. Direction Independence: It doesn't matter which point is $P$ and which is $Q$. $$ \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \frac{y_1 - y_2}{x_1 - x_2} $$

Examples and Interpretation

EXAMPLE 1 Finding and Interpreting Slope:

Find the slope of the line containing $(1, 2)$ and $(5, -3)$.

$$ m = \frac{-3 - 2}{5 - 1} = \frac{-5}{4} = -\frac{5}{4} $$

Interpretation: The slope is $-\frac{5}{4}$. This means for every 4-unit increase in $x$ (run), $y$ decreases by 5 units (rise). The average rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ is $-\frac{5}{4}$.

EXAMPLE 2 Visualizing Slope Variations:

Consider four different lines ($L_1, L_2, L_3, L_4$) all passing through the point $P(2, 3)$.

1. Positive Slope ($L_1$) Passes through $Q_1(-1, -2)$. $$ \color{RubineRed}{m_1} = \frac{-2 - 3}{-1 - 2} = \frac{-5}{-3} = \frac{5}{3} $$

  • Visual: Slants upward from left to right.

2. Negative Slope ($L_2$) Passes through $Q_2(3, -1)$. $$ \color{orange}m_2 = \frac{-1 - 3}{3 - 2} = \frac{-4}{1} = -4 $$

  • Visual: Slants downward from left to right.

3. Zero Slope ($L_3$) Passes through $Q_3(5, 3)$. $$ \color{cyan}m_3 = \frac{3 - 3}{5 - 2} = \frac{0}{3} = 0 $$

  • Visual: Horizontal line.

4. Undefined Slope ($L_4$) Passes through $Q_4(2, 5)$. $$ \color{green}m_4 \text{ is undefined because } x_1 = x_2 = 2 $$

  • Visual: Vertical line.

Summary: Geometry of Slope

Slope Value ($m$) Geometric Behavior Example
$m > 0$ Line rises (slants up) from left to right. $y = 2x$
$m < 0$ Line falls (slants down) from left to right. $y = -x$
$m = 0$ Line is Horizontal. $y = 3$
Undefined Line is Vertical. $x = 2$

Steepness

The absolute value of the slope determines steepness.

  • $|m|$ is large $\rightarrow$ Steep line (closer to vertical).
  • $|m|$ is small $\rightarrow$ Flat line (closer to horizontal).

Family of lines with positive slopes $0, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 6$ getting steeper:

Family of lines with negative slopes $0, -1/4, -1/2, -1, -2, -6$ getting steeper:

2 Graph Lines Given a Point and the Slope

If you know a point on a line and its slope, you can graph the line perfectly without finding the equation first. The secret lies in interpreting the slope as a set of instructions for movement: Rise over Run.

$$ m = \frac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \frac{\text{Vertical Change}}{\text{Horizontal Change}} $$

EXAMPLE 3: Graphing from a Point and Slope

Task: Draw the line containing the point $(3, 2)$ with the given slopes.

(a) Slope $m = \frac{3}{4}$

  • Interpretation: Rise = $+3$, Run = $+4$.
  • Movement: From $(3, 2)$, move 4 units Right and 3 units Up.
  • New Point: $(3+4, 2+3) = (7, 5)$.
  • Graph: Draw a line through $(3, 2)$ and $(7, 5)$.

(b) Slope $m = -\frac{4}{5}$

A negative slope can be interpreted in two valid ways. Both lead to the same line.

Method 1: Down and Right Write slope as $\frac{-4}{5}$.

  • Interpretation: Rise = $-4$, Run = $+5$.
  • Movement: From $(3, 2)$, move 5 units Right and 4 units Down.
  • New Point: $(3+5, 2-4) = (8, -2)$.

Method 2: Up and Left Write slope as $\frac{4}{-5}$.

  • Interpretation: Rise = $+4$, Run = $-5$.
  • Movement: From $(3, 2)$, move 5 units Left and 4 units Up.
  • New Point: $(3-5, 2+4) = (-2, 6)$.

Graph: Draw a line through $(3, 2)$ and either $(8, -2)$ or $(-2, 6)$.

Quick Reference for Slope Movement
Slope Sign Direction
Positive (+) Uphill (Right & Up) OR (Left & Down)
Negative (-) Downhill (Right & Down) OR (Left & Up)

3 Find the Equation of a Vertical Line

Vertical lines are unique because their x-coordinate never changes, regardless of the y-value. This results in an undefined slope.

EXAMPLE 4 Graphing a Vertical Line

Graph the equation: $x = 3$

Solution: To graph $x = 3$, we look for all points $(x, y)$ where the x-coordinate is always 3.

  • Points: $(3, -1), (3, 0), (3, 1), (3, 2), (3, 3), \dots$

The graph is a vertical line with an x-intercept of 3.

Theorem: Equation of a Vertical Line

A vertical line is given by an equation of the form: $$ x = a $$ where $a$ is the x-intercept.

Key Properties:

  • The slope is undefined.
  • The line is perpendicular to the x-axis.
  • It is not a function (fails the vertical line test).

4 Use the Point-Slope Form of a Line; Identify Horizontal Lines

When you know a specific point on a line and its slope, you can derive the equation using the Point-Slope Form.

Derivation

Let $L$ be a nonvertical line with slope $m$ containing the point $(x_1, y_1)$. For any other point $(x, y)$ on the line, the slope formula tells us: $$ m = \frac{y - y_1}{x - x_1} $$ Multiplying both sides by $(x - x_1)$ gives us the standard Point-Slope equation.

Theorem: Point-Slope Form of an Equation of a Line

An equation of a nonvertical line with slope $m$ that contains the point $(x_1, y_1)$ is: $$ y - y_1 = m(x - x_1) \tag{2} $$

EXAMPLE 5 Using the Point-Slope Form of a Line

Problem: Find the equation of the line with slope $4$ containing the point $(1, 2)$.

Solution: Substitute $m = 4, x_1 = 1, y_1 = 2$ into the formula: $$ > \begin{aligned} > y - y_1 &= m(x - x_1) \\ > y - 2 &= 4(x - 1) \\ > y - 2 &= 4x - 4 \\ > y &= 4x - 2 > \end{aligned} > $$

EXAMPLE 6 Finding the Equation of a Horizontal Line

Problem: Find an equation of the horizontal line containing the point $(3, 2)$.

Solution: A horizontal line has a slope of 0 ($m=0$). Using the point-slope form with $m=0, x_1=3, y_1=2$: $$ > \begin{aligned} > y - y_1 &= m(x - x_1) \\ > y - 2 &= 0 \cdot (x - 3) \\ > y - 2 &= 0 \\ > y &= 2 > \end{aligned} > $$

Key Insight: On a horizontal line, the y-value is constant. Since the line passes through $y=2$, the equation is simply $y=2$.

Theorem: Equation of a Horizontal Line

A horizontal line is given by an equation of the form: $$ y=b $$ where $b$ is the $y$-intercept.

5 Find the Equation of a Line Given Two Points

If you have two points, you have enough information to write the line's equation. The strategy is a two-step process: Find the Slope $\rightarrow$ Use Point-Slope Form.

EXAMPLE 7: Finding an Equation from Two Points

Problem: Find the equation of the line containing $(2, 3)$ and $(-4, 5)$.

Step 1: Calculate Slope $$ m = \frac{5 - 3}{-4 - 2} = \frac{2}{-6} = -\frac{1}{3} $$

Step 2: Use Point-Slope Form Use the slope $m = -\frac{1}{3}$ and either point. Let's use $(2, 3)$: $$ y - 3 = -\frac{1}{3}(x - 2) $$

[Figure 38: Graph of the line passing through $(2, 3)$ and $(-4, 5)$.]

[!tip] Tip You could have used the other point $(-4, 5)$. The equation $y - 5 = -\frac{1}{3}(x + 4)$ looks different, but simplifies to the same line!

6 Write the Equation of a Line in Slope-Intercept Form

The Slope-Intercept Form is the most useful form for graphing and understanding a line because it reveals the two most important features directly: the slope and the y-intercept.

Derivation

We know the point-slope form: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$. If the line crosses the y-axis at $(0, b)$, we can use this point as $(x_1, y_1)$.

$$ \begin{aligned} y - b &= m(x - 0) \\ y - b &= mx \\ y &= mx + b \end{aligned} $$

Theorem: Slope-Intercept Form

An equation of a line with slope $m$ and y-intercept $b$ is: $$ y = mx + b \tag{3} $$

  • $m$ = Slope (steepness/direction)
  • $b$ = y-intercept (where it crosses the vertical axis)

Understanding the Roles of $m$ and $b$

We can visualize how $m$ and $b$ affect the graph by looking at families of lines.

1. Changing the Slope ($m$)

Consider the family of lines $y = mx + 2$. The y-intercept is fixed at $2$.

  • Observation: As you change $m$, the lines rotate around the fixed point $(0, 2)$.
  • Conclusion: The slope determines the angle of the line.
  • $Y_1 = 2$ (Slope 0, horizontal)
  • $Y_4 = 3x + 2$ (Positive slope)
  • $Y_5 = -3x + 2$ (Negative slope)

2. Changing the Intercept ($b$)

Consider the family of lines $y = 2x + b$. The slope is fixed at $2$.

  • Observation: The lines never cross each other; they look like a "ladder" shifted up and down.
  • Conclusion: Lines with the same slope are parallel. Changing $b$ shifts the line vertically.
  • $Y_2 = 2x + 1$
  • $Y_4 = 2x + 4$
  • $Y_5 = 2x - 4$

7 Identify the Slope and y-Intercept of a Line from Its Equation

When an equation is in slope-intercept form ($y = mx + b$), finding the slope and intercept is immediate.

Quick Identification: For the equation $y = -2x + 7$:

  • Compare to $y = \textcolor{red}{m}x + \textcolor{blue}{b}$
  • Slope ($m$): $-2$
  • y-intercept ($b$): $7$
EXAMPLE 8: Finding Slope and y-Intercept

Problem: Find the slope $m$ and y-intercept $b$ of $2x + 4y = 8$. Graph the equation.

Step 1: Convert to Slope-Intercept Form Solve for $y$: $$ > \begin{aligned} > 2x + 4y &= 8 \\ > 4y &= -2x + 8 \\ > y &= \frac{-2x}{4} + \frac{8}{4} \\ > y &= -\frac{1}{2}x + 2 > \end{aligned} > $$

Step 2: Identify Features

  • Slope ($m$): $-\frac{1}{2}$
  • y-intercept ($b$): $2$

Step 3: Graph the Line

  1. Plot the y-intercept at $(0, 2)$.
  2. Use the slope $m = -\frac{1}{2}$ (Rise $-1$, Run $2$).
  3. From $(0, 2)$, move right 2 and down 1 to reach $(2, 1)$.
  4. Draw the line through these points.

8 Graph Lines Written in General Form Using Intercepts

While Slope-Intercept Form ($y=mx+b$) is great for seeing slope, equations are often given in General Form. You don't always need to rearrange the equation to graph it; you can simply find the "bookends" where the line hits the axes.

Definition: General Form

The equation of a line is in general form when written as: $$ Ax + By = C \tag{4} $$ where $A, B,$ and $C$ are real numbers, and $A$ and $B$ are not both $0$.

The "Two-Intercept" Graphing Strategy

To graph a line in general form quickly, find the two points where it crosses the axes.

  1. Find x-intercept: Let $y = 0$ and solve for $x$.
  2. Find y-intercept: Let $x = 0$ and solve for $y$.
  3. Connect: Draw a line through these two points.
EXAMPLE 9: Graphing Using Intercepts

Equation: $2x + 4y = 8$

Step 1: Find the x-intercept Set $y = 0$: $$ 2x + 4(0) = 8 \implies 2x = 8 \implies x = 4 $$ Point: $(4, 0)$

Step 2: Find the y-intercept Set $x = 0$: $$ 2(0) + 4y = 8 \implies 4y = 8 \implies y = 2 $$ Point: $(0, 2)$

Step 3: Graph Plot $(4, 0)$ and $(0, 2)$ and draw the line connecting them.

Special Cases in General Form

Vertical and horizontal lines are just specific versions of $Ax + By = C$ where one coefficient is zero.

Line Type Equation General Form Version Graph Description
Vertical $x = a$ $1\cdot x + 0\cdot y = a$ Crosses x-axis at $a$; slope undefined.
Horizontal $y = b$ $0\cdot x + 1\cdot y = b$ Crosses y-axis at $b$; slope is 0.
Definition: Linear Equation

Because every line can be written in general form, any equation equivalent to $Ax + By = C$ is called a linear equation.

9 Find Equations of Parallel Lines

Two lines in the same plane are parallel if they never intersect (they have no points in common).

Theorem: Criterion for Parallel Lines

Two non-vertical lines are parallel if and only if:

  1. Their slopes are equal ($m_1 = m_2$).
  2. They have different y-intercepts ($b_1 \neq b_2$).

EXAMPLE 10: Showing Two Lines Are Parallel

Problem: Show that $L_1: 2x + 3y = 6$ and $L_2: 4x + 6y = 0$ are parallel.

Strategy: Convert both to Slope-Intercept Form ($y=mx+b$) to compare their $m$ and $b$ values.

Line $L_1$: $$ \begin{aligned} 2x + 3y &= 6 \\ 3y &= -2x + 6 \\ y &= -\frac{2}{3}x + 2 \end{aligned} $$

  • Slope $m_1 = -\frac{2}{3}$
  • Intercept $b_1 = 2$

Line $L_2$: $$ \begin{aligned} 4x + 6y &= 0 \\ 6y &= -4x \\ y &= -\frac{4}{6}x \\ y &= -\frac{2}{3}x \end{aligned} $$

  • Slope $m_2 = -\frac{2}{3}$
  • Intercept $b_2 = 0$

Conclusion: Since the slopes are equal ($-\frac{2}{3}$) but the intercepts are different ($2 \neq 0$), the lines are parallel.

Graph showing two parallel lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ running side-by-side.

EXAMPLE 11: Finding the Equation of a Parallel Line

Problem: Find the equation of the line containing $(2, -3)$ and parallel to $2x + y = 6$.

Step 1: Find the slope of the reference line. Convert $2x + y = 6$ to slope-intercept form: $$ y = -2x + 6 $$ The slope is $m = -2$. Note: Parallel lines have the same slope, so our new line must also have $m = -2$.

Step 2: Use Point-Slope Form. Use slope $m = -2$ and point $(x_1, y_1) = (2, -3)$.

$$ \begin{aligned} y - y_1 &= m(x - x_1) \\ y - (-3) &= -2(x - 2) \\ y + 3 &= -2x + 4 \\ y &= -2x + 1 \quad & \leftarrow \text{Slope-Intercept Form} \\ 2x + y &= 1 \quad & \leftarrow \text{General Form} \end{aligned} $$

10 Find Equations of Perpendicular Lines

Two lines are perpendicular if they intersect at a right angle ($90^\circ$).

Theorem: Criterion for Perpendicular Lines

Two nonvertical lines are perpendicular if and only if the product of their slopes is $-1$ $$ m_1 m_2 = -1 $$

In other words: The slopes must be negative reciprocals of each other. If $m_1 = \frac{a}{b}$, then $m_2 = -\frac{b}{a}$.

Proof Sketch (Using Distance Formula)

By placing two perpendicular lines at the origin, we form a right triangle with vertices $O(0,0)$, $A(1, m_2)$, and $B(1, m_1)$. Applying the Pythagorean Theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$) to the distances between these points: $$ [d(O, A)]^2 + [d(O, B)]^2 = [d(A, B)]^2 $$ Simplifying the distance formulas leads directly to the result: $$ m_1 m_2 = -1 $$

EXAMPLE 12 Finding the Slope of a Perpendicular Line

If a line has slope $\frac{3}{2}$, any line perpendicular to it must have the negative reciprocal slope. $$ m_{\perp} = -\frac{2}{3} $$ Check: $\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) \cdot \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -1$.

EXAMPLE 13 Finding the Equation of a Perpendicular Line

Problem: Find the equation of the line containing $(1, -2)$ and perpendicular to $x + 3y = 6$.

Step 1: Find the slope of the given line. Rewrite $x + 3y = 6$ in slope-intercept form: $$ \begin{aligned} 3y &= -x + 6 \\ y &= -\frac{1}{3}x + 2 \end{aligned} $$ The slope is $m = -\frac{1}{3}$.

Step 2: Find the perpendicular slope. The negative reciprocal of $-\frac{1}{3}$ is $3$.

Step 3: Use Point-Slope Form. Use point $(1, -2)$ and slope $m = 3$: $$ \begin{aligned} y - y_1 &= m(x - x_1) \\ y - (-2) &= 3(x - 1) \\ y + 2 &= 3x - 3 \\ y &= 3x - 5 \quad & \leftarrow \text{Slope-Intercept Form} \\ 3x - y &= 5 \quad & \leftarrow \text{General Form} \end{aligned} $$

Graph showing the two lines intersecting at a right angle at point (1, -2)

References

  • Precalculus, 9th Edition (Michael Sullivan) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf, (p. 19 - 28)

notes.html:
Graphs of Functions and the Vertical Line Test

Visualizing Relationships

In applications, a graph often demonstrates the relationship between two variables more clearly than a table or equation.

Example: Gas Prices (1980–2009) Table 1 lists average gas prices over time. When plotted, these points form a line graph.

Key Observation: For each date on the horizontal axis, there is only one price on the vertical axis. This confirms that the graph represents a function, even though we don't have a specific algebraic equation for it.

1. Identify the Graph of a Function

The Graph of a Function

If $f$ is a function with domain $A$, the graph of $f$ is the set of ordered pairs: $$ \{(x, f(x)) \mid x \in A\} $$ plotted in a coordinate plane.

  • The graph is the set of all points $(x, y)$ such that $y = f(x)$.
  • The graph of $f$ is identical to the graph of the equation $y = f(x)$
  • Each number $x$ in the domain must have exactly one image $y$ in the range.
Theorem: Vertical-Line Test

A set of points in the $xy$-plane is the graph of a function if and only if every vertical line intersects the graph in at most one point.

EXAMPLE 1: Identifying the Graph of a Function

Which of the graphs in the Figure are graphs of functions?

Analysis:

Graph Equation Vertical Line Test Conclusion
(a) $y = x^2$ ✅ Passes. Every vertical line hits the curve at most once. Function
(b) $y = x^3$ ✅ Passes. Every vertical line hits the curve at most once. Function
(c) $x = y^2$ ❌ Fails. A vertical line (e.g., at $x=1$) hits the graph at two points ($y=1$ and $y=-1$). Not a Function
(d) $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ ❌ Fails. A vertical line intersects the circle at two points. Not a Function

2.2 The Graph of a Function: Analysis and Information

Core Concept: Points on a Graph

If $(x, y)$ is a point on the graph of a function $f$, then: $$ y = f(x) $$

  • Input: $x$ is the value of the function at $x$.
  • Output: $y$ is the image of $x$.
EXAMPLE 2: Obtaining Information from a Graph

Context: Let $f$ represent the distance $y$ of a pendulum bob from its at-rest position at time $x$.

(a) Find specific values: Look for the y-coordinate at the given x.

  • $f(0) = 4$ (Point $(0, 4)$ is on the graph)
  • $f(\frac{3\pi}{2}) = 0$ (Point $(\frac{3\pi}{2}, 0)$ is on the graph)
  • $f(3\pi) = -4$ (Point $(3\pi, -4)$ is on the graph)

(b) Find the Domain: Look at the "shadow" of the graph on the x-axis.

  • The graph exists for $x$ between $0$ and $4\pi$.
  • Domain: $[0, 4\pi]$

(c) Find the Range: Look at the "shadow" of the graph on the y-axis.

  • The graph oscillates between $-4$ and $4$.
  • Range: $[-4, 4]$

(d) List the Intercepts: Points where the graph touches the axes.

  • y-intercept: $(0, 4)$
  • x-intercepts: $(\frac{\pi}{2}, 0), (\frac{3\pi}{2}, 0), (\frac{5\pi}{2}, 0), (\frac{7\pi}{2}, 0)$

(e) Intersections with a Horizontal Line: How many times does the line $y = 2$ intersect the graph?

  • Draw a horizontal line at height 2. It hits the wave 4 times.

(f) Solve $f(x) = -4$: Find the x-values where the graph is at its lowest point ($y=-4$).

  • $x = \pi$ and $x = 3\pi$.

(g) Solve $f(x) > 0$: Where is the graph above the x-axis?

  • Intervals: $[0, \frac{\pi}{2}) \cup (\frac{3\pi}{2}, \frac{5\pi}{2}) \cup (\frac{7\pi}{2}, 4\pi]$

Graphing Piecewise-Defined Functions

A piecewise-defined function is defined by different formulas on different parts of its domain. The graph consists of separate pieces.

Example 4: Graph of a Piecewise-Defined Function

Sketch the graph of: $$f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & \text{if } x \le 1 \\ 2x + 1 & \text{if } x > 1 \end{cases}$$

Solution

Interval Function Graph Piece
$x \le 1$ $f(x) = x^2$ Parabola to the left of $x = 1$
$x > 1$ $f(x) = 2x + 1$ Line to the right of $x = 1$

Key Points

  • At $x = 1$: $(1, 1)$ is included (solid dot) $\leftarrow$ from $x^2$
  • At $x = 1$: $(1, 3)$ is excluded (open dot) $\leftarrow$ from $2x + 1$

Visualizing Domain and Range (The Shadow Test)

When looking at a graph, you can determine the domain and range using "light beams":

  • Domain: Imagine vertical beams of light shining down from the top. The shadow cast on the x-axis is the domain.
  • Range: Imagine horizontal beams of light shining from the side. The shadow cast on the y-axis is the range.
EXAMPLE 3: Obtaining Information from an Equation

Function: $f(x) = \frac{x + 1}{x + 2}$

(a) Find the Domain: The denominator cannot be zero. $x + 2 \neq 0 \implies x \neq -2$. Domain: $\{x \mid x \neq -2\}$

(b) Is the point $(1, \frac{1}{2})$ on the graph? Evaluate $f(1)$: $$ f(1) = \frac{1 + 1}{1 + 2} = \frac{2}{3} $$ Since $f(1) = \frac{2}{3} \neq \frac{1}{2}$, the point $(1, \frac{1}{2})$ is NOT on the graph. The point $(1, \frac{2}{3})$ IS on the graph.

(c) If $x = 2$, what is $f(x)$? $$ f(2) = \frac{2 + 1}{2 + 2} = \frac{3}{4} $$ The point $(2, \frac{3}{4})$ is on the graph.

(d) If $f(x) = 2$, what is $x$? Set the equation equal to 2 and solve: $$ \frac{x + 1}{x + 2} = 2 $$ $$ x + 1 = 2(x + 2) $$ $$ x + 1 = 2x + 4 $$ $$ -3 = x $$ The point $(-3, 2)$ is on the graph.

(e) Find the x-intercepts: Set $f(x) = 0$. A fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero (and denominator is not). $$ x + 1 = 0 \implies x = -1 $$ The x-intercept is $-1$. The point $(-1, 0)$ is on the graph.

References

  • Precalculus, 9th Edition (Michael Sullivan) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf, (p. 60 - 63)

notes.html:
8.2 Graphs of Polar Equations

Graphing Polar Equations

The graph of $r = f(\theta)$ consists of all points $P(r, \theta)$ satisfying the equation.

  • Use a polar grid (concentric circles and rays from the pole) for plotting.
  • Basic shapes have simple polar equations:
    • $r = a$: Circle of radius $|a|$ centered at origin ($x^2 + y^2 = a^2$).
    • $\theta = c$: Line through origin with slope $\tan c$ ($y = (\tan c)x$).
Example 1: Sketching $r = 3$

Graph is a circle of radius 3 centered at origin. Rectangular form: $x^2 + y^2 = 9$.

Example 2: Sketching $\theta = \pi/3$

Graph is a line through origin making angle $\pi/3$ with polar axis. Rectangular form: $y = \sqrt{3}x$.

Example 3: Sketching $r = 2 \sin \theta$

Plot points for $\theta \in [0, \pi]$. The graph is a circle. Rectangular form: $x^2 + (y-1)^2 = 1$ (Circle of radius 1 centered at $(0,1)$).

General Circle Forms

Equations of the form: $$ r = 2a \sin \theta \quad \text{or} \quad r = 2a \cos \theta $$ represent circles with radius $|a|$ centered at $(a, \pi/2)$ and $(a, 0)$ respectively.

Sketching Complex Curves

To sketch curves like cardioids or roses, first graph $r = f(\theta)$ in rectangular coordinates (r on y-axis, $\theta$ on x-axis). This acts as a "table of values" to guide the polar sketch.

Example 4: Sketching a Cardioid ($r = 2 + 2 \cos \theta$)
  1. Graph $r = 2 + 2 \cos \theta$ in rectangular coordinates (Figure 5).
  2. Trace polar graph as $\theta$ increases:
    • $\theta: 0 \to \pi/2$: $r$ decreases $4 \to 2$.
    • $\theta: \pi/2 \to \pi$: $r$ decreases $2 \to 0$.
    • $\theta: \pi \to 3\pi/2$: $r$ increases $0 \to 2$ (negative r values plot in opposite quadrant).
    • $\theta: 3\pi/2 \to 2\pi$: $r$ increases $2 \to 4$.
Cardioids

Equations of the form: $$ r = a(1 \pm \cos \theta) \quad \text{or} \quad r = a(1 \pm \sin \theta) $$ produce heart-shaped curves called cardioids.

Example 5: Sketching a Four-Leaved Rose ($r = \cos 2\theta$)

Graph $r = \cos 2\theta$ in rectangular coordinates to see sign changes.

  • As $\theta$ goes $0 \to \pi/4$, $r$ goes $1 \to 0$ (Leaf 1 in QI).
  • As $\theta$ goes $\pi/4 \to \pi/2$, $r$ goes $0 \to -1$ (Leaf 2 in QIV, because r is negative).
Rose Curves

Equations of the form: $$ r = a \cos n\theta \quad \text{or} \quad r = a \sin n\theta $$

  • If $n$ is odd: n-leaved rose.
  • If $n$ is even: 2n-leaved rose.

Symmetry Tests

Symmetry simplifies graphing. If a test holds, the graph has that symmetry.

Types of Symmetry
Symmetry Test Property
Polar Axis (x-axis) Replace $\theta$ by $-\theta$. Equation unchanged. Graph unchanged when reflected about polar axis.
Pole (origin) Replace $r$ by $-r$ OR $\theta$ by $\theta + \pi$. Equation unchanged. Graph unchanged when rotated $\pi$ about pole.
Line $\theta = \pi/2$ (y-axis) Replace $\theta$ by $\pi - \theta$. Equation unchanged. Graph unchanged when reflected about vertical line $\theta = \pi/2$.
Example 6: Using Symmetry to Sketch a Limaçon ($r = 1 + 2 \cos \theta$)
  1. Symmetry: Replacing $\theta$ with $-\theta$ gives $1 + 2\cos(-\theta) = 1 + 2\cos\theta$. Symmetric about polar axis.
  2. Zeros: Solve $1 + 2\cos\theta = 0 \implies \cos\theta = -1/2 \implies \theta = 2\pi/3, 4\pi/3$. These are where graph crosses the pole.
  3. Table: Sketch rectangular graph of $r$ vs $\theta$ to guide polar plotting for $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, then reflect.

.

Limaçons

Equations of the form: $$ r = a \pm b \cos \theta \quad \text{or} \quad r = a \pm b \sin \theta $$ Shape depends on ratio $a/b$ (dimpled, convex, or with inner loop).

Graphing with Devices (Periodicity)

To graph $r = f(\theta)$ on a calculator, determine the domain $[0, P]$ required for one complete trace.

Example 7: Domain for $r = \cos(2\theta/3)$

Find smallest integer $n$ such that the period repeats: $$ \cos\left(\frac{2(\theta + 2n\pi)}{3}\right) = \cos\left(\frac{2\theta}{3}\right) $$ This requires $\frac{4n\pi}{3}$ to be a multiple of $2\pi$. Smallest integer $n=3$. Domain: $\theta \in [0, 6\pi]$.

Families of Polar Equations and Common Curves

Example 8: A Family of Polar Equations

Graph $r = 1 + c \sin \theta$ for $c = 3, 2.5, 2, 1.5, 1$.

Observation:

  • $c > 1$: Graph is a limaçon with an inner loop. As $c$ decreases toward 1, the loop shrinks.
  • $c = 1$: The loop disappears, and the graph becomes a cardioid.
Some Common Polar Curves

A summary of standard polar graphs used in calculus.

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 610)

notes.html:
8.1 Polar Coordinates

Definition of Polar Coordinates

The polar coordinate system specifies a point $P$ in the plane by:

  • Pole: Fixed point $O$ (origin).
  • Polar axis: Ray from $O$ (usually positive x-axis).
  • Coordinates: $P(r, \theta)$ where:
    • $r$ is the directed distance from $O$ to $P$.
    • $\theta$ is the directed angle from the polar axis to segment $\overline{OP}$.

Sign Conventions:

  • $\theta > 0$: Counterclockwise rotation.
  • $\theta < 0$: Clockwise rotation.
  • $r < 0$: Point lies $|r|$ units from the pole in the direction opposite to the terminal side of $\theta$.
Multiple Representations

A single point has infinitely many polar representations. For any integer $n$: $$ (r, \theta) \equiv (r, \theta + 2n\pi) $$ $$ (r, \theta) \equiv (-r, \theta + (2n+1)\pi) $$

Note: $(r, \theta)$ and $(-r, \theta + \pi)$ represent the same point.

Example 1: Plotting Points

Plot points: (a) $(1, 3\pi/4)$, (b) $(3, -\pi/6)$, (c) $(3, 3\pi)$, (d) $(-4, \pi/4)$.

Solution:

  • (d) For $r=-4$, move 4 units in the direction opposite to $\pi/4$ (which is $5\pi/4$).
Example 2: Different Polar Coordinates for the Same Point

Given $P(2, \pi/3)$. Find other representations with $r > 0$ and $r < 0$.

Solution:

  • $r > 0$: Add multiples of $2\pi$ to $\theta$. $$ \left(2, \frac{\pi}{3} + 2\pi\right) = \left(2, \frac{7\pi}{3}\right) $$ $$ \left(2, \frac{\pi}{3} - 2\pi\right) = \left(2, -\frac{5\pi}{3}\right) $$
  • $r < 0$: Replace $r$ with $-r$ and add/subtract $\pi$ to $\theta$. $$ \left(-2, \frac{\pi}{3} + \pi\right) = \left(-2, \frac{4\pi}{3}\right) $$ $$ \left(-2, \frac{\pi}{3} - \pi\right) = \left(-2, -\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) $$
Relationship Between Polar and Rectangular Coordinates

Assume the polar axis coincides with the positive x-axis.

Polar to Rectangular: $$ x = r \cos \theta \quad \text{and} \quad y = r \sin \theta $$

Rectangular to Polar: $$ r^2 = x^2 + y^2 \quad \text{and} \quad \tan \theta = \frac{y}{x} \quad (x \neq 0) $$

Example 3: Converting Polar to Rectangular

Convert $(4, 2\pi/3)$ to rectangular coordinates.

Solution: Given $r=4, \theta=2\pi/3$: $$ x = 4 \cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = 4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -2 $$ $$ y = 4 \sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = 4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 2\sqrt{3} $$ Rectangular coordinates: $(-2, 2\sqrt{3})$.

Example 4: Converting Rectangular to Polar

Convert $(2, -2)$ to polar coordinates.

Solution: Given $x=2, y=-2$: $$ r^2 = 2^2 + (-2)^2 = 8 \implies r = \pm 2\sqrt{2} $$ $$ \tan \theta = \frac{-2}{2} = -1 $$ Since the point $(2, -2)$ is in Quadrant IV:

  • If $r > 0$, $\theta = -\pi/4$ (or $7\pi/4$).
  • If $r < 0$, $\theta = 3\pi/4$.

Polar coordinates: $(2\sqrt{2}, -\pi/4)$ or $(-2\sqrt{2}, 3\pi/4)$.

Polar Equations

Polar Equation: Equation in $r$ and $\theta$. Rectangular Equation: Equation in $x$ and $y$.

Example 5: Rectangular to Polar Equation

Express $x^2 = 4y$ in polar coordinates.

Solution: Substitute $x = r \cos \theta, y = r \sin \theta$: $$ > \begin{aligned} > (r \cos \theta)^2 &= 4(r \sin \theta) \\ > r^2 \cos^2 \theta &= 4r \sin \theta \\ > r &= \frac{4 \sin \theta}{\cos^2 \theta} \\ > r &= 4 \sec \theta \tan \theta > \end{aligned} > $$

Example 6: Polar to Rectangular Equations

Express in rectangular coordinates.

(a) $r = 5 \sec \theta$ Multiply by $\cos \theta$: $$ r \cos \theta = 5 \implies x = 5 $$ (Vertical line) (b) $r = 2 \sin \theta$ Multiply by $r$: $$ > \begin{aligned} > r^2 &= 2r \sin \theta \\ > x^2 + y^2 &= 2y \\ > x^2 + (y-1)^2 &= 1 > \end{aligned} > $$ (Circle of radius 1 centered at $(0,1)$) (c) $r = 2 + 2 \cos \theta$ Multiply by $r$: $$ > \begin{aligned} > r^2 &= 2r + 2r \cos \theta \\ > x^2 + y^2 &= 2r + 2x \\ > x^2 + y^2 - 2x &= 2r \\ > (x^2 + y^2 - 2x)^2 &= 4r^2 \\ > (x^2 + y^2 - 2x)^2 &= 4(x^2 + y^2) > \end{aligned} > $$ (Rectangular form is more complex; graphing in polar is preferred.)

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 592)

notes.excerpt: --- Addition and Subtraction Formulas [!info] Addition and Subtraction Formulas Formulas for Sine: $$ \sin(s + t) \sin s \cos t + \cos s \sin t $$ $$ \sin(s - t) \sin s \cos t - \cos s \sin t $$ Formu
notes.html:
Addition and Subtraction Formulas

Addition and Subtraction Formulas

Formulas for Sine: $$ > \sin(s + t) = \sin s \cos t + \cos s \sin t > $$ $$ > \sin(s - t) = \sin s \cos t - \cos s \sin t > $$

Formulas for Cosine: $$ > \cos(s + t) = \cos s \cos t - \sin s \sin t > $$ $$ > \cos(s - t) = \cos s \cos t + \sin s \sin t > $$

Formulas for Tangent: $$ > \tan(s + t) = \frac{\tan s + \tan t}{1 - \tan s \tan t} > $$ $$ > \tan(s - t) = \frac{\tan s - \tan t}{1 + \tan s \tan t} > $$

$\tan(2\pi​−u)=\frac{\sin(2\pi−u)}{\cos(2\pi​−u)​}$

Proof of Addition Formula for Cosine

To prove $\cos(s + t) = \cos s \cos t - \sin s \sin t$, we use the unit circle and distance formula.

Consider points on the unit circle:

  • $P_0(1, 0)$ and $P_1(\cos(s+t), \sin(s+t))$ determine arc $s+t$.
  • $Q_0(\cos(-s), \sin(-s)) = (\cos s, -\sin s)$ and $Q_1(\cos t, \sin t)$ determine arc $t - (-s) = s+t$.

Since the arcs are equal in length, the chords subtending them are equal in length: $d(P_0, P_1) = d(Q_0, Q_1)$.

Using the Distance Formula: $$ \sqrt{[\cos(s+t) - 1]^2 + [\sin(s+t) - 0]^2} = \sqrt{(\cos t - \cos s)^2 + (\sin t + \sin s)^2} $$

Squaring both sides and expanding: $$ \begin{aligned} &\cos^2(s+t) - 2\cos(s+t) + 1 + \sin^2(s+t) \\ &\quad = \cos^2 t - 2\cos s \cos t + \cos^2 s + \sin^2 t + 2\sin s \sin t + \sin^2 s \end{aligned} $$

Apply Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta = 1$ three times (for angle $s+t$, angle $t$, and angle $s$): $$ \begin{aligned} \underbrace{\cos^2(s+t) + \sin^2(s+t)}_{1} + 1 - 2\cos(s+t) &= \underbrace{(\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t)}_{1} + \underbrace{(\cos^2 s + \sin^2 s)}_{1} - 2\cos s \cos t + 2\sin s \sin t \\ 2 - 2\cos(s+t) &= 2 - 2\cos s \cos t + 2\sin s \sin t \end{aligned} $$

Subtract 2 from both sides and divide by $-2$: $$ \boxed{\cos(s+t) = \cos s \cos t - \sin s \sin t} \quad \blacksquare $$

Proof of Subtraction Formula for Cosine

Replace $t$ with $-t$ in the Addition Formula for Cosine:

$$ \begin{aligned} \cos(s - t) &= \cos(s + (-t)) \\ &= \cos s \cos(-t) - \sin s \sin(-t) \quad \leftarrow \text{Addition Formula for Cosine} \\ &= \boxed{\cos s \cos t + \sin s \sin t} \quad \leftarrow \text{Even-odd identities } (\cos(-t)=\cos t, \sin(-t)=-\sin t) \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

Applications of Addition and Subtraction Formulas

Example 3: Proving a Cofunction Identity

Prove the cofunction identity $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - u\right) = \sin u$.

Solution

By the Subtraction Formula for Cosine: $$ \begin{aligned} \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - u\right) &= \cos\frac{\pi}{2} \cos u + \sin\frac{\pi}{2} \sin u \\ &= 0 \cdot \cos u + 1 \cdot \sin u \\ &= \sin u \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

Example 4: Proving an Identity

Verify the identity $\dfrac{1 + \tan x}{1 - \tan x} = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + x\right)$.

Solution

Start with the right-hand side (RHS) and apply the Addition Formula for Tangent:

$$ \begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + x\right) \\ &= \frac{\tan\frac{\pi}{4} + \tan x}{1 - \tan\frac{\pi}{4} \tan x} \quad \leftarrow \text{Addition Formula for Tangent} \\ &= \frac{1 + \tan x}{1 - 1 \cdot \tan x} \quad \leftarrow \tan\frac{\pi}{4} = 1 \\ &= \frac{1 + \tan x}{1 - \tan x} = \text{LHS} \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

Expressions Involving Trigonometric Functions of a Sum

Expressions involving trigonometric functions and their inverses often arise in calculus. To evaluate them, define angles for the inverse functions, draw reference triangles to find missing sides, and apply addition/subtraction formulas.

Example 6: Simplifying an Expression Involving Inverse Trigonometric Functions

Write $\sin(\cos^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y)$ as an algebraic expression in $x$ and $y$, where $-1 \le x \le 1$.

Solution

Let $\theta = \cos^{-1}x$ and $\phi = \tan^{-1}y$. This implies $\cos \theta = x$ and $\tan \phi = y$.

Construct reference triangles to determine the remaining trigonometric ratios:

  • Triangle for $\theta$: Adjacent $= x$, Hypotenuse $= 1 \implies$ Opposite $= \sqrt{1-x^2}$. $$ \sin \theta = \sqrt{1-x^2} $$
  • Triangle for $\phi$: Opposite $= y$, Adjacent $= 1 \implies$ Hypotenuse $= \sqrt{1+y^2}$. $$ \cos \phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+y^2}}, \quad \sin \phi = \frac{y}{\sqrt{1+y^2}} $$

Apply the Addition Formula for Sine:

$$ \begin{aligned} \sin(\cos^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y) &= \sin(\theta + \phi) \\ &= \sin \theta \cos \phi + \cos \theta \sin \phi \qquad \leftarrow \text{Addition Formula for Sine} \\ &= \sqrt{1-x^2} \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+y^2}} \right) + x \left( \frac{y}{\sqrt{1+y^2}} \right) \qquad \leftarrow \text{Substitute from triangles} \\ &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+y^2}} \left( \sqrt{1-x^2} + xy \right) \qquad \leftarrow \text{Factor out } \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+y^2}} \end{aligned} $$

Evaluating Expressions Involving Trigonometric Functions

Example 7: Evaluating an Expression Involving Trigonometric Functions

Evaluate $\sin(\theta + \phi)$, where $\sin \theta = \frac{12}{13}$ with $\theta$ in Quadrant II and $\tan \phi = \frac{3}{4}$ with $\phi$ in Quadrant III.

Solution

Step 1: Find missing values for $\theta$ (Quadrant II) Given $\sin \theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{12}{13}$, we have $y=12, r=13$. Use Pythagorean Theorem ($x^2 + y^2 = r^2$): $$ \begin{aligned} x^2 + 12^2 &= 13^2 \\ x^2 &= 25 \\ x &= -5 \quad \leftarrow x < 0 \text{ in Quadrant II} \end{aligned} $$ Thus, $\cos \theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{5}{13}$.

Step 2: Find missing values for $\phi$ (Quadrant III) Given $\tan \phi = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{3}{4}$. In Quadrant III, both $x$ and $y$ are negative, so $y=-3, x=-4$. Hypotenuse $r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-4)^2} = 5$. Thus, $\sin \phi = -\frac{3}{5}$ and $\cos \phi = -\frac{4}{5}$.

Step 3: Apply Addition Formula for Sine $$ \begin{aligned} \sin(\theta + \phi) &= \sin \theta \cos \phi + \cos \theta \sin \phi \quad \leftarrow \text{Addition Formula} \\ &= \left(\frac{12}{13}\right)\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right) + \left(-\frac{5}{13}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right) \quad \leftarrow \text{Substitute values} \\ &= -\frac{48}{65} + \frac{15}{65} \\ &= -\frac{33}{65} \end{aligned} $$

Expressions of the Form $A \sin x + B \cos x$

Linear combinations of sine and cosine can be rewritten as a single sine function using the Addition Formula.

Sums of Sines and Cosines

If $A$ and $B$ are real numbers, then: $$ > A \sin x + B \cos x = k \sin(x + \phi) > $$ where $k = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$ and $\phi$ satisfies: $$ > \cos \phi = \frac{A}{k} \quad \text{and} \quad \sin \phi = \frac{B}{k} > $$

Geometric Interpretation: The angle $\phi$ corresponds to the point $(A, B)$ in the plane, where $k$ is the distance from the origin.

Example 8: A Sum of Sine and Cosine Terms

Express $3 \sin x + 4 \cos x$ in the form $k \sin(x + \phi)$.

Solution Identify $A=3, B=4$. Calculate amplitude $k$: $$ k = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5 $$

Determine $\phi$: $$ \cos \phi = \frac{3}{5}, \quad \sin \phi = \frac{4}{5} $$ Since both are positive, $\phi$ is in Quadrant I. $$ \phi = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) \approx 53.1^\circ $$

Result: $$ 3 \sin x + 4 \cos x \approx 5 \sin(x + 53.1^\circ) $$

Example 9: Graphing a Trigonometric Function

Write $f(x) = -\sin 2x + \sqrt{3} \cos 2x$ in the form $k \sin(2x + \phi)$ and graph it.

Solution Identify $A=-1, B=\sqrt{3}$. $$ k = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{4} = 2 $$

Determine $\phi$: $$ \cos \phi = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad \sin \phi = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $$ Cosine is negative, sine is positive $\implies$ $\phi$ is in Quadrant II. $$ \phi = \frac{2\pi}{3} $$

Rewrite function: $$ f(x) = 2 \sin\left(2x + \frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = 2 \sin 2\left(x + \frac{\pi}{3}\right) $$

Graphing Properties:

  • Amplitude: $2$
  • Period: $\frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi$
  • Horizontal Shift: $-\frac{\pi}{3}$ (left by $\pi/3$)

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 561)

notes.html:
Chapter 7 Review: Analytic Trigonometry

Fundamental Trigonometric Identities

Reciprocal Identities $$ \csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x}, \quad \sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}, \quad \cot x = \frac{1}{\tan x} $$ $$ \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}, \quad \cot x = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x} $$

Pythagorean Identities $$ \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1, \quad \tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x, \quad 1 + \cot^2 x = \csc^2 x $$

Even-Odd Identities $$ \sin(-x) = -\sin x, \quad \cos(-x) = \cos x, \quad \tan(-x) = -\tan x $$

Cofunction Identities $$ \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \cos x, \quad \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \sin x, \quad \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \cot x $$ $$ \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \csc x, \quad \csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \sec x, \quad \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \tan x $$

Proving Trigonometric Identities

Guidelines:

  1. Start with one side: Choose the more complicated side.
  2. Use known identities: Algebra, factoring, common denominators.
  3. Convert to sines and cosines: If stuck, rewrite everything in terms of $\sin$ and $\cos$.

Warning: Do not operate on both sides simultaneously (unless steps are reversible).

Addition and Subtraction Formulas

Formulas for Sine $$ \sin(s+t) = \sin s \cos t + \cos s \sin t $$ $$ \sin(s-t) = \sin s \cos t - \cos s \sin t $$

Formulas for Cosine $$ \cos(s+t) = \cos s \cos t - \sin s \sin t $$ $$ \cos(s-t) = \cos s \cos t + \sin s \sin t $$

Formulas for Tangent $$ \tan(s+t) = \frac{\tan s + \tan t}{1 - \tan s \tan t}, \quad \tan(s-t) = \frac{\tan s - \tan t}{1 + \tan s \tan t} $$

Sums of Sines and Cosines

Expression $A \sin x + B \cos x$ can be written as $k \sin(x + \phi)$ where: $$ k = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}, \quad \cos \phi = \frac{A}{k}, \quad \sin \phi = \frac{B}{k} $$

Double-Angle Formulas

Sine $$ \sin 2x = 2 \sin x \cos x $$

Cosine $$ \cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 $$

Tangent $$ \tan 2x = \frac{2 \tan x}{1 - \tan^2 x} $$

Formulas for Lowering Powers

$$ \sin^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}, \quad \cos^2 x = \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}, \quad \tan^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{1 + \cos 2x} $$

Half-Angle Formulas

$$ \sin \frac{u}{2} = \pm \sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos u}{2}}, \quad \cos \frac{u}{2} = \pm \sqrt{\frac{1 + \cos u}{2}} $$ $$ \tan \frac{u}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos u}{\sin u} = \frac{\sin u}{1 + \cos u} $$ Note: The sign ($\pm$) depends on the quadrant of $u/2$.

Product-Sum and Sum-to-Product Formulas

Product-to-Sum $$ \sin u \cos v = \frac{1}{2}[\sin(u+v) + \sin(u-v)] $$ $$ \cos u \sin v = \frac{1}{2}[\sin(u+v) - \sin(u-v)] $$ $$ \cos u \cos v = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(u+v) + \cos(u-v)] $$ $$ \sin u \sin v = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(u-v) - \cos(u+v)] $$

Sum-to-Product $$ \sin x + \sin y = 2 \sin\frac{x+y}{2} \cos\frac{x-y}{2} $$ $$ \sin x - \sin y = 2 \cos\frac{x+y}{2} \sin\frac{x-y}{2} $$ $$ \cos x + \cos y = 2 \cos\frac{x+y}{2} \cos\frac{x-y}{2} $$ $$ \cos x - \cos y = -2 \sin\frac{x+y}{2} \sin\frac{x-y}{2} $$

Trigonometric Equations

Basic Equation: $T(\theta) = c$ (where $T$ is a trig function).

Solving Strategy:

  1. Find solutions in one period: Solve for $\theta$ in an interval of length $2\pi$ (for sin/cos) or $\pi$ (for tan).
  2. Find all solutions: Add integer multiples of the period ($2k\pi$ or $k\pi$) to the solutions found in Step 1.

Advanced Techniques:

  • Factoring: Use Zero-Product Property.
  • Identities: Rewrite to isolate a single function.
  • Multiples of Angles: Solve for the multiple (e.g., $3\theta$) first, then divide by the coefficient.
  • Squaring: Check for extraneous solutions.

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 592)

notes.html:
Basic Trigonometric Equations

Definition

A trigonometric equation contains trigonometric functions.

  • Identity: True for all values (e.g., $\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta = 1$).
  • Equation: True only for specific values of the variable.

Basic Form: $T(\theta) = c$, where $T$ is a trig function and $c$ is a constant.

Guidelines for Solving Basic Trigonometric Equations
  1. Find solutions in one period: Find all solutions within an interval of length equal to the function's period ($2\pi$ for sin/cos, $\pi$ for tan).
  2. Find all solutions: Add integer multiples of the period to the solutions found in Step 1.
    • For $\sin$ and $\cos$: Add $2k\pi$.
    • For $\tan$: Add $k\pi$.
Example 1: Solving $\sin \theta = \frac{1}{2}$

1. Solutions in one period $[0, 2\pi)$: Sine is positive in QI and QII. Reference angle is $\pi/6$. $$ \theta = \frac{\pi}{6}, \quad \theta = \frac{5\pi}{6} $$

2. All solutions: $$ \theta = \frac{\pi}{6} + 2k\pi, \quad \theta = \frac{5\pi}{6} + 2k\pi $$ where $k$ is any integer.

Example 2: Solving $\cos \theta = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

1. Solutions in one period $[0, 2\pi)$: Cosine is negative in QII and QIII. Reference angle is $\pi/4$. $$ \theta = \frac{3\pi}{4}, \quad \theta = \frac{5\pi}{4} $$

2. All solutions: $$ \theta = \frac{3\pi}{4} + 2k\pi, \quad \theta = \frac{5\pi}{4} + 2k\pi $$

Specific solutions (for $k = -1, 0, 1$): $$ -\frac{5\pi}{4}, -\frac{3\pi}{4}, \frac{3\pi}{4}, \frac{5\pi}{4}, \frac{11\pi}{4}, \frac{13\pi}{4} $$

Example 3: Solving $\cos \theta = 0.65$ (Calculator)

1. Solutions in one period: Find reference angle using inverse cosine: $\theta = \cos^{-1}(0.65) \approx 0.86$ rad. Cosine is positive in QI and QIV.

  • QI: $\theta \approx 0.86$
  • QIV: $\theta \approx 2\pi - 0.86 \approx 5.42$

2. All solutions: $$ \theta \approx 0.86 + 2k\pi, \quad \theta \approx 5.42 + 2k\pi $$

Example 4: Solving $\tan \theta = 2$

1. Solutions in one period: $\theta = \tan^{-1}(2) \approx 1.12$. Tangent has period $\pi$, so we only need one solution in $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$.

2. All solutions: Add multiples of $\pi$: $$ \theta \approx 1.12 + k\pi $$

Solving by Isolating the Function

Example 5: Algebraic Equivalents

(a) $2 \sin \theta - 1 = 0$ Isolate $\sin \theta$: $$ \sin \theta = \frac{1}{2} $$ This is Example 1. Solutions: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{6} + 2k\pi, \frac{5\pi}{6} + 2k\pi$.

(b) $\tan^2 \theta - 3 = 0$ Isolate $\tan \theta$: $$ \tan^2 \theta = 3 \implies \tan \theta = \pm \sqrt{3} $$ In interval $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$, solutions are $\pi/3$ and $-\pi/3$. Add multiples of period $\pi$: $$ \theta = \frac{\pi}{3} + k\pi, \quad \theta = -\frac{\pi}{3} + k\pi $$

Solving Trigonometric Equations by Factoring

Use the Zero-Product Property: If $AB = 0$, then $A=0$ or $B=0$.

Example 6: Quadratic Type

Solve $2 \cos^2 \theta - 7 \cos \theta + 3 = 0$.

Factor the quadratic form $(2C-1)(C-3)=0$: $$ (2 \cos \theta - 1)(\cos \theta - 3) = 0 $$

Set factors to zero:

  1. $2 \cos \theta - 1 = 0 \implies \cos \theta = \frac{1}{2}$ Solutions in $[0, 2\pi)$: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{5\pi}{3}$. General: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3} + 2k\pi, \frac{5\pi}{3} + 2k\pi$.

  2. $\cos \theta - 3 = 0 \implies \cos \theta = 3$ No solution (range of cosine is $[-1, 1]$).

Example 7: Common Factor

Solve $5 \sin \theta \cos \theta + 4 \cos \theta = 0$.

Factor out $\cos \theta$: $$ \cos \theta (5 \sin \theta + 4) = 0 $$

Set factors to zero:

  1. $\cos \theta = 0$ Solutions in $[0, 2\pi)$: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}$.

  2. $5 \sin \theta + 4 = 0 \implies \sin \theta = -0.8$ Reference angle: $\sin^{-1}(0.8) \approx 0.93$. Sine is negative in QIII and QIV.

    • QIII: $\theta \approx \pi + 0.93 \approx 4.07$
    • QIV: $\theta \approx 2\pi - 0.93 \approx 5.35$ (or simply use negative angle $-0.93$)

All solutions: $$ \theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pi, \quad \theta = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 2k\pi $$ $$ \theta \approx -0.93 + 2k\pi, \quad \theta \approx 4.07 + 2k\pi $$

More Trigonometric Equations

Solving by Using Identities

Use identities to rewrite equations in terms of a single trig function, then factor.

Example 1: Using a Trigonometric Identity

Solve $1 + \sin\theta = 2\cos^2\theta$.

Solution

Convert to single function using Pythagorean identity:

$$ \begin{aligned} 1 + \sin\theta &= 2\cos^2\theta \quad \leftarrow \text{Given} \\ 1 + \sin\theta &= 2(1 - \sin^2\theta) \quad \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ 2\sin^2\theta + \sin\theta - 1 &= 0 \quad \leftarrow \text{Rearrange} \\ (2\sin\theta - 1)(\sin\theta + 1) &= 0 \quad \leftarrow \text{Factor} \end{aligned} $$

Set each factor to zero:

  • $\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2} \implies \theta = \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{5\pi}{6}$ in $[0, 2\pi)$
  • $\sin\theta = -1 \implies \theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}$ in $[0, 2\pi)$

All solutions: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{6} + 2k\pi, \quad \theta = \frac{5\pi}{6} + 2k\pi, \quad \theta = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 2k\pi$

Example 2: Using Double-Angle Formula

Solve $\sin 2\theta - \cos\theta = 0$.

Solution

$$ \begin{aligned} \sin 2\theta - \cos\theta &= 0 \\ 2\sin\theta\cos\theta - \cos\theta &= 0 \quad \leftarrow \text{Double-Angle Formula} \\ \cos\theta(2\sin\theta - 1) &= 0 \quad \leftarrow \text{Factor} \end{aligned} $$

  • $\cos\theta = 0 \implies \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}$
  • $\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2} \implies \theta = \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{5\pi}{6}$

All solutions: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pi, \quad \theta = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 2k\pi, \quad \theta = \frac{\pi}{6} + 2k\pi, \quad \theta = \frac{5\pi}{6} + 2k\pi$

Extraneous Solutions from Squaring

When squaring both sides, always check solutions in the original equation. Squaring can introduce extraneous solutions.

Example 3: Squaring and Using an Identity

Solve $\cos\theta + 1 = \sin\theta$ in $[0, 2\pi)$.

Solution

$$ \begin{aligned} \cos\theta + 1 &= \sin\theta \\ \cos^2\theta + 2\cos\theta + 1 &= \sin^2\theta \quad \leftarrow \text{Square both sides} \\ \cos^2\theta + 2\cos\theta + 1 &= 1 - \cos^2\theta \quad \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ 2\cos^2\theta + 2\cos\theta &= 0 \\ 2\cos\theta(\cos\theta + 1) &= 0 \end{aligned} $$

  • $\cos\theta = 0 \implies \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}$
  • $\cos\theta = -1 \implies \theta = \pi$

Check in original equation:

  • $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$: $0 + 1 = 1$ ✓
  • $\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}$: $0 + 1 \neq -1$ (extraneous)
  • $\theta = \pi$: $-1 + 1 = 0$ ✓

Solutions: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi$

Finding Intersection Points

Example 4: Intersection of $f(x) = \sin x$ and $g(x) = \cos x$

Graphical: $x \approx 0.785, 3.927$ (from graphing device)

Algebraic: $$ \begin{aligned} \sin x &= \cos x \\ \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} &= 1 \quad \leftarrow \text{Divide by } \cos x \text{ (valid since } \cos x \neq 0\text{)} \\ \tan x &= 1 \\ x &= \frac{\pi}{4} + k\pi \end{aligned} $$

Equations with Multiples of Angles

Strategy: Solve for the multiple of the angle first, then divide.

Example 5: Multiple of an Angle

Solve $2\sin 3\theta - 1 = 0$.

(a) All solutions:

$$ \begin{aligned} 2\sin 3\theta &= 1 \\ \sin 3\theta &= \frac{1}{2} \end{aligned} $$

Solve for $3\theta$ in $[0, 2\pi)$: $3\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{5\pi}{6}$

General solutions for $3\theta$: $$ 3\theta = \frac{\pi}{6} + 2k\pi, \quad 3\theta = \frac{5\pi}{6} + 2k\pi $$

Divide by 3: $$ \theta = \frac{\pi}{18} + \frac{2k\pi}{3}, \quad \theta = \frac{5\pi}{18} + \frac{2k\pi}{3} $$

(b) Solutions in $[0, 2\pi)$ (use $k = 0, 1, 2$):

$$ \theta = \frac{\pi}{18}, \frac{5\pi}{18}, \frac{13\pi}{18}, \frac{17\pi}{18}, \frac{25\pi}{18}, \frac{29\pi}{18} $$

Example 6: Half-Angle Equation

Solve $\sqrt{3}\tan\frac{\theta}{2} - 1 = 0$.

(a) All solutions:

$$ \begin{aligned} \sqrt{3}\tan\frac{\theta}{2} &= 1 \\ \tan\frac{\theta}{2} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned} $$

Solve for $\frac{\theta}{2}$ in $(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2})$: $\frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{\pi}{6}$

General solutions for $\frac{\theta}{2}$ (period $\pi$): $$ \frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{\pi}{6} + k\pi $$

Multiply by 2: $$ \theta = \frac{\pi}{3} + 2k\pi $$

(b) Solutions in $[0, 4\pi)$ (use $k = 0, 1$):

$$ \theta = \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{7\pi}{3} $$

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 580)

notes.html:
Double-Angle Formulas

Double-Angle Formulas

Formula for sine: $$ \sin 2x = 2 \sin x \cos x $$

Formulas for cosine: $$ \cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 1 - 2 \sin^2 x = 2 \cos^2 x - 1 $$

Formula for tangent: $$ \tan 2x = \frac{2 \tan x}{1 - \tan^2 x} $$

Proofs

Proof of Double-Angle Formulas for Cosine Using the Addition Formula for Cosine with $x+x$: $$ \begin{aligned} \cos 2x &= \cos(x + x) \\ &= \cos x \cos x - \sin x \sin x \quad \leftarrow \text{Addition Formula} \\ &= \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x \end{aligned} $$ Deriving the other forms using $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$:

  1. Substitute $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$: $$ \cos 2x = (1 - \sin^2 x) - \sin^2 x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x $$
  2. Substitute $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$: $$ \cos 2x = \cos^2 x - (1 - \cos^2 x) = 2\cos^2 x - 1 \quad \blacksquare $$
Example 1: Using the Double-Angle Formulas

If $\cos x = -\frac{2}{3}$ and $x$ is in Quadrant II, find $\cos 2x$ and $\sin 2x$.

Solution

Find $\cos 2x$: $$ \begin{aligned} \cos 2x &= 2 \cos^2 x - 1 \quad \leftarrow \text{Double-Angle Formula} \\ &= 2\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^2 - 1 \\ &= \frac{8}{9} - 1 = -\frac{1}{9} \end{aligned} $$

Find $\sin 2x$: First find $\sin x$. Since $x$ is in QII, $\sin x > 0$: $$ \sin x = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2 x} = \sqrt{1 - \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^2} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3} $$ Now apply the sine double-angle formula: $$ \begin{aligned} \sin 2x &= 2 \sin x \cos x \quad \leftarrow \text{Double-Angle Formula} \\ &= 2\left(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\right)\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) \\ &= -\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{9} \end{aligned} $$

Example 2: A Triple-Angle Formula

Write $\cos 3x$ in terms of $\cos x$.

Solution $$ \begin{aligned} \cos 3x &= \cos(2x + x) \\ &= \cos 2x \cos x - \sin 2x \sin x \quad \leftarrow \text{Addition formula} \\ &= (2 \cos^2 x - 1) \cos x - (2 \sin x \cos x) \sin x \quad \leftarrow \text{Double-Angle Formulas} \\ &= 2 \cos^3 x - \cos x - 2 \sin^2 x \cos x \quad \leftarrow \text{Expand} \\ &= 2 \cos^3 x - \cos x - 2 \cos x (1 - \cos^2 x) \quad \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ &= 2 \cos^3 x - \cos x - 2 \cos x + 2 \cos^3 x \quad \leftarrow \text{Expand} \\ &= 4 \cos^3 x - 3 \cos x \quad \leftarrow \text{Simplify} \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

Polynomial Property

$\cos nx$ can always be written as a polynomial of degree $n$ in $\cos x$. The analogous result for $\sin nx$ is not true in general.

Example 3: Proving an Identity

Prove the identity $\frac{\sin 3x}{\sin x \cos x} = 4 \cos x - \sec x$.

Solution Start with the left-hand side: $$ \begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \frac{\sin 3x}{\sin x \cos x} = \frac{\sin(x + 2x)}{\sin x \cos x} \\ &= \frac{\sin x \cos 2x + \cos x \sin 2x}{\sin x \cos x} \quad \leftarrow \text{Addition Formula} \\ &= \frac{\sin x (2 \cos^2 x - 1) + \cos x (2 \sin x \cos x)}{\sin x \cos x} \quad \leftarrow \text{Double-Angle Formulas} \end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} &= \frac{2 \sin x \cos^2 x - \sin x + 2 \sin x \cos^2 x}{\sin x \cos x} \quad \leftarrow \text{Expand numerator} \\ &= \frac{4 \sin x \cos^2 x - \sin x}{\sin x \cos x} \quad \leftarrow \text{Combine like terms} \\ &= \frac{\sin x (4 \cos^2 x - 1)}{\sin x \cos x} \quad \leftarrow \text{Factor out } \sin x \\ &= \frac{4 \cos^2 x - 1}{\cos x} \quad \leftarrow \text{Cancel } \sin x \\ &= \frac{4 \cos^2 x}{\cos x} - \frac{1}{\cos x} \quad \leftarrow \text{Separate fraction} \\ &= 4 \cos x - \sec x = \text{RHS} \quad \leftarrow \text{Reciprocal identity} \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

Half-Angle Formulas

These formulas allow us to rewrite trigonometric expressions involving even powers of sine and cosine in terms of the first power of cosine only. This technique is crucial for integration in calculus.

Formulas for Lowering Powers

$$ > \sin^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2} \qquad \cos^2 x = \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2} > $$ $$ > \tan^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{1 + \cos 2x} > $$

Proof

Derived directly from the Double-Angle Formulas for Cosine:

  1. From $\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$, solve for $\sin^2 x$.
  2. From $\cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x - 1$, solve for $\cos^2 x$.
  3. The tangent formula follows from the quotient identity $\tan^2 x = \frac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}$: $$ \tan^2 x = \frac{\frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}}{\frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}} = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{1 + \cos 2x} \quad \blacksquare $$
Example 4: Lowering Powers in a Trigonometric Expression

Express $\sin^2 x \cos^2 x$ in terms of the first power of cosine.

Solution

Method 1: Using Power-Lowering Formulas Repeatedly

$$ \begin{aligned} \sin^2 x \cos^2 x &= \left( \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2} \right) \left( \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2} \right) \\ &= \frac{1 - \cos^2 2x}{4} \\ &= \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} \cos^2 2x \\ &= \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{1 + \cos(2 \cdot 2x)}{2} \right) \quad \leftarrow \text{Apply formula to } \cos^2 2x \\ &= \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{8} \cos 4x \\ &= \frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{8} \cos 4x \\ &= \frac{1}{8}(1 - \cos 4x) \end{aligned} $$

Method 2: Using the Double-Angle Formula for Sine

Recall that $\sin x \cos x = \frac{1}{2} \sin 2x$. Thus:

$$ \begin{aligned} \sin^2 x \cos^2 x &= (\sin x \cos x)^2 \\ &= \left( \frac{1}{2} \sin 2x \right)^2 \\ &= \frac{1}{4} \sin^2 2x \\ &= \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{1 - \cos 4x}{2} \right) \quad \leftarrow \text{Apply power-lowering to } \sin^2 2x \\ &= \frac{1}{8}(1 - \cos 4x) \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

Half-Angle Formulas

Half-Angle Formulas

$$ > \sin \frac{u}{2} = \pm \sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos u}{2}} \qquad \cos \frac{u}{2} = \pm \sqrt{\frac{1 + \cos u}{2}} > $$ $$ > \tan \frac{u}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos u}{\sin u} = \frac{\sin u}{1 + \cos u} > $$ The choice of the $+$ or $-$ sign depends on the quadrant in which $u/2$ lies.

Proof of Tangent Half-Angle Formula

Substitute $x = u/2$ into the formulas for lowering powers and take the square root. For tangent:

$$ \begin{aligned} \tan \frac{u}{2} &= \pm \sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos u}{1 + \cos u}} \\ &= \pm \sqrt{\left( \frac{1 - \cos u}{1 + \cos u} \right) \left( \frac{1 - \cos u}{1 - \cos u} \right)} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Multiply num and den by } 1 - \cos u \\ &= \pm \sqrt{\frac{(1 - \cos u)^2}{1 - \cos^2 u}} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Simplify} \\ &= \pm \frac{|1 - \cos u|}{|\sin u|} \qquad \leftarrow \sqrt{A^2} = |A| \text{ and } 1-\cos^2 u = \sin^2 u \end{aligned} $$

Since $1 - \cos u \ge 0$ for all $u$, and $\sin u$ and $\tan(u/2)$ always have the same sign, the $\pm$ and absolute values resolve to:

$$ \tan \frac{u}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos u}{\sin u} $$

The other form, $\frac{\sin u}{1 + \cos u}$, is derived by multiplying numerator and denominator by $1 + \cos u$. $\blacksquare$

Example 5: Using a Half-Angle Formula

Find the exact value of $\sin 22.5^\circ$.

Solution

Since $22.5^\circ$ is half of $45^\circ$, use the Half-Angle Formula for Sine with $u = 45^\circ$. Choose the $+$ sign because $22.5^\circ$ is in Quadrant I.

$$ \begin{aligned} \sin \frac{45^\circ}{2} &= \sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos 45^\circ}{2}} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Half-Angle Formula} \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{1 - \sqrt{2}/2}{2}} \qquad \leftarrow \cos 45^\circ = \sqrt{2}/2 \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{2 - \sqrt{2}}{4}} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Common denominator} \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2 - \sqrt{2}} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Simplify} \end{aligned} $$

Example 6: Using a Half-Angle Formula

Find $\tan(u/2)$ if $\sin u = \frac{2}{5}$ and $u$ is in Quadrant II.

Solution

First find $\cos u$. Since cosine is negative in Quadrant II:

$$ \begin{aligned} \cos u &= -\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 u} \\ &= -\sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2} \\ &= -\sqrt{\frac{21}{25}} = -\frac{\sqrt{21}}{5} \end{aligned} $$

Now apply the Half-Angle Formula for Tangent (using the form without square roots to avoid sign ambiguity):

$$ \begin{aligned} \tan \frac{u}{2} &= \frac{1 - \cos u}{\sin u} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Half-Angle Formula} \\ &= \frac{1 - (-\sqrt{21}/5)}{2/5} \\ &= \frac{1 + \sqrt{21}/5}{2/5} \\ &= \frac{5 + \sqrt{21}}{2} \end{aligned} $$

Expressions Involving Inverse Trigonometric Functions

Expressions involving trigonometric functions and their inverses are evaluated by defining an angle $\theta$ for the inverse part, drawing a reference triangle to find missing sides, and applying fundamental identities (like Double-Angle Formulas).

Example 7: Evaluating an Expression Involving an Inverse Trigonometric Function

Evaluate $\sin(2 \cos^{-1}(-\frac{2}{5}))$.

Solution

Let $\theta = \cos^{-1}(-\frac{2}{5})$. By definition, $\cos \theta = -\frac{2}{5}$ with $\theta$ in Quadrant II ($0 \le \theta \le \pi$).

1. Find missing side using Pythagorean Theorem: Since $\cos \theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{2}{5}$, let $x = -2$ and $r = 5$. $$ \begin{aligned} x^2 + y^2 &= r^2 \qquad \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean Theorem} \\ (-2)^2 + y^2 &= 5^2 \qquad \leftarrow x = -2, r = 5 \\ y^2 &= 21 \\ y &= \sqrt{21} \qquad \leftarrow y > 0 \text{ in QII} \end{aligned} $$

2. Apply Double-Angle Formula for Sine: $$ \begin{aligned} \sin(2 \cos^{-1}(-\tfrac{2}{5})) &= \sin 2\theta \\ &= 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta \qquad \leftarrow \text{Double-Angle Formula} \\ &= 2 \left( \frac{\sqrt{21}}{5} \right) \left( -\frac{2}{5} \right) \qquad \leftarrow \text{From triangle: } \sin \theta = \frac{y}{r}, \cos \theta = \frac{x}{r} \\ &= -\frac{4\sqrt{21}}{25} \end{aligned} $$

Example 8: Simplifying an Expression Involving an Inverse Trigonometric Function

Write $\sin(2 \cos^{-1} x)$ as an algebraic expression in $x$ only, where $-1 \le x \le 1$.

Solution

Let $\theta = \cos^{-1} x$. Then $\cos \theta = x$. Construct a right triangle where adjacent side $= x$ and hypotenuse $= 1$. Opposite side $= \sqrt{1^2 - x^2} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}$.

We need to find $\sin 2\theta$. Use the Double-Angle Formula for Sine:

$$ \begin{aligned} \sin(2 \cos^{-1} x) &= \sin 2\theta \qquad \leftarrow \cos^{-1} x = \theta \\ &= 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta \qquad \leftarrow \text{Double-Angle Formula} \\ &= 2 (\sqrt{1 - x^2}) (x) \qquad \leftarrow \text{From triangle: } \sin \theta = \frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{1}, \cos \theta = x \\ &= 2x\sqrt{1 - x^2} \end{aligned} $$

Product-Sum and Sum-to-Product Formulas

Product-to-Sum Formulas

Derived by adding or subtracting the Addition and Subtraction Formulas. For example, adding the formulas for $\sin(u+v)$ and $\sin(u-v)$:

$$ \begin{aligned} \sin(u+v) &= \sin u \cos v + \cos u \sin v \\ \sin(u-v) &= \sin u \cos v - \cos u \sin v \\ \hline \sin(u+v) + \sin(u-v) &= 2 \sin u \cos v \end{aligned} $$

Dividing by 2 gives the first formula.

Product-to-Sum Formulas

$$ > \begin{aligned} > \sin u \cos v &= \tfrac{1}{2}[\sin(u+v) + \sin(u-v)] \\ > \cos u \sin v &= \tfrac{1}{2}[\sin(u+v) - \sin(u-v)] \\ > \cos u \cos v &= \tfrac{1}{2}[\cos(u+v) + \cos(u-v)] \\ > \sin u \sin v &= \tfrac{1}{2}[\cos(u-v) - \cos(u+v)] > \end{aligned} > $$

Example 9: Expressing a Trigonometric Product as a Sum

Express $\sin 3x \sin 5x$ as a sum of trigonometric functions.

Solution Use the fourth Product-to-Sum Formula with $u = 3x$ and $v = 5x$. Note that cosine is an even function ($\cos(-\theta) = \cos \theta$).

$$ \begin{aligned} \sin 3x \sin 5x &= \tfrac{1}{2}[\cos(3x - 5x) - \cos(3x + 5x)] \\ &= \tfrac{1}{2}[\cos(-2x) - \cos 8x] \\ &= \tfrac{1}{2} \cos 2x - \tfrac{1}{2} \cos 8x \end{aligned} $$

Sum-to-Product Formulas

These are the reverse of the Product-to-Sum formulas. By substituting $u = \frac{x+y}{2}$ and $v = \frac{x-y}{2}$ into the Product-to-Sum formulas, we obtain:

Sum-to-Product Formulas

$$ > \begin{aligned} > \sin x + \sin y &= 2 \sin\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{x-y}{2}\right) \\ > \sin x - \sin y &= 2 \cos\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{x-y}{2}\right) \\ > \cos x + \cos y &= 2 \cos\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{x-y}{2}\right) \\ > \cos x - \cos y &= -2 \sin\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{x-y}{2}\right) > \end{aligned} > $$

Example 10: Proving an Identity

Prove the identity $\frac{\sin 3t + \sin 5t}{\cos 3t - \cos 5t} = \cot t$.

Solution Apply Sum-to-Product formulas to the numerator and denominator.

$$ \begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \frac{\sin 3t + \sin 5t}{\cos 3t - \cos 5t} \\ &= \frac{2 \sin\left(\frac{3t+5t}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{3t-5t}{2}\right)}{-2 \sin\left(\frac{3t+5t}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{3t-5t}{2}\right)} \quad \leftarrow \text{Sum-to-Product} \\ &= \frac{2 \sin 4t \cos(-t)}{-2 \sin 4t \sin(-t)} \\ &= \frac{\cos(-t)}{-\sin(-t)} \quad \leftarrow \text{Cancel } 2 \sin 4t \\ &= \frac{\cos t}{-(-\sin t)} \quad \leftarrow \text{Even-Odd identities} \\ &= \frac{\cos t}{\sin t} = \cot t = \text{RHS} \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

Example 11: Solving a Trigonometric Equation

Solve the equation $\sin 5x = \sin 3x$.

Solution Move all terms to one side to use Sum-to-Product formulas.

$$ \begin{aligned} \sin 5x - \sin 3x &= 0 \\ 2 \cos\left(\frac{5x+3x}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{5x-3x}{2}\right) &= 0 \quad \leftarrow \text{Sum-to-Product} \\ 2 \cos 4x \sin x &= 0 \end{aligned} $$

Set each factor to zero:

  1. $\cos 4x = 0 \implies 4x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \implies x = \frac{\pi}{8} + \frac{n\pi}{4}$
  2. $\sin x = 0 \implies x = n\pi$

where $n$ is an integer.

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 570)

notes.html:
Trigonometric Identities

Fundamental Trigonometric Identities

Reciprocal Identities $$ > \csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x} \quad \sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x} \quad \cot x = \frac{1}{\tan x} > $$ $$ > \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \quad \cot x = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x} > $$

Pythagorean Identities $$ > \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1 \quad \tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x \quad 1 + \cot^2 x = \csc^2 x > $$

Even-Odd Identities $$ > \sin(-x) = -\sin x \quad \cos(-x) = \cos x \quad \tan(-x) = -\tan x > $$

Cofunction Identities $$ > \begin{aligned} > \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) &= \cos x & \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) &= \cot x & \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) &= \csc x \\ > \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) &= \sin x & \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) &= \tan x & \csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) &= \sec x > \end{aligned} > $$

Identity vs. Equation: An identity is true for all values of the variable(s) for which both sides are defined. An equation is true only for specific values.

Simplifying Trigonometric Expressions

Use fundamental identities, factoring, common denominators, and algebraic techniques to rewrite complex expressions into simpler forms.

Example 1: Simplifying a Trigonometric Expression

Simplify $\cos t + \tan t \sin t$.

Solution Rewrite in terms of sine and cosine: $$ \begin{aligned} \cos t + \tan t \sin t &= \cos t + \left(\frac{\sin t}{\cos t}\right) \sin t && \leftarrow \text{Reciprocal identity} \\ &= \frac{\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t}{\cos t} && \leftarrow \text{Common denominator} \\ &= \frac{1}{\cos t} && \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ &= \sec t && \leftarrow \text{Reciprocal identity} \end{aligned} $$

Example 2: Simplifying by Combining Fractions

Simplify $\frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta} + \frac{\cos \theta}{1 + \sin \theta}$.

Solution Combine fractions using a common denominator: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta} + \frac{\cos \theta}{1 + \sin \theta} &= \frac{\sin \theta(1 + \sin \theta) + \cos^2 \theta}{\cos \theta(1 + \sin \theta)} && \leftarrow \text{Common denominator} \\ &= \frac{\sin \theta + \sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta}{\cos \theta(1 + \sin \theta)} && \leftarrow \text{Distribute } \sin \theta \\ &= \frac{\sin \theta + 1}{\cos \theta(1 + \sin \theta)} && \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ &= \frac{1}{\cos \theta} = \sec \theta && \leftarrow \text{Cancel, use reciprocal identity} \end{aligned} $$

Proving Trigonometric Identities

Guidelines for Proving Trigonometric Identities
  1. Start with One Side: Choose one side (usually the more complicated) and transform it into the other side.
  2. Use Known Identities: Apply algebra and fundamental identities. Bring fractions to common denominator, factor, simplify.
  3. Convert to Sines and Cosines: If stuck, rewrite all functions in terms of $\sin$ and $\cos$.
Critical Rule: Do NOT Operate on Both Sides

To prove an identity, we do not perform the same operations on both sides. Operations like squaring are not reversible — they can transform a non-identity into an identity.

Example: $\sin x = -\sin x$ is not an identity, but squaring both sides gives $\sin^2 x = \sin^2 x$, which is an identity. This doesn't prove the original.

Only reversible operations preserve identity status.

Disproving an Identity

To show an equation is not an identity, find one counterexample value where it fails.

Example: $\sin x + \cos x = 1$ is not an identity because at $x = \frac{\pi}{4}$: $$ \sin\frac{\pi}{4} + \cos\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \sqrt{2} \neq 1 $$

Example 3: Proving an Identity by Rewriting in Terms of Sine and Cosine

Verify that $\cos\theta(\sec\theta - \cos\theta) = \sin^2\theta$ is an identity.

(a) Algebraic Proof

Start with the more complicated side (LHS):

$$ \begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \cos\theta(\sec\theta - \cos\theta) \\ &= \cos\theta\left(\frac{1}{\cos\theta} - \cos\theta\right) && \leftarrow \text{Reciprocal identity} \\ &= 1 - \cos^2\theta && \leftarrow \text{Expand} \\ &= \sin^2\theta && \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ &= \text{RHS} \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

(b) Graphical Confirmation

Graphs coincide → confirms identity.

Reversibility Insight

Each step in Example 3 is reversible, so the proof could work backward from RHS to LHS. However, it's typically easier to transform the more complicated side into the simpler side.

Example 4: Proving an Identity by Combining Fractions

Verify the identity $2 \tan x \sec x = \dfrac{1}{1 - \sin x} - \dfrac{1}{1 + \sin x}$.

Solution

Start with the right-hand side (RHS), finding a common denominator:

$$ \begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= \frac{1}{1 - \sin x} - \frac{1}{1 + \sin x} \\ &= \frac{(1 + \sin x) - (1 - \sin x)}{(1 - \sin x)(1 + \sin x)} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Common denominator} \\ &= \frac{2 \sin x}{1 - \sin^2 x} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Simplify numerator} \\ &= \frac{2 \sin x}{\cos^2 x} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ &= 2 \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \left(\frac{1}{\cos x}\right) \qquad \leftarrow \text{Factor} \\ &= 2 \tan x \sec x = \text{LHS} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Reciprocal identities} \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

Strategy: Introducing an Extra Factor

If stuck, multiply the numerator and denominator by a chosen trigonometric expression (often a conjugate) to simplify the result.

Example: Multiplying by $(1 + \sin u)$ exploits the difference of squares: $(1 - \sin u)(1 + \sin u) = 1 - \sin^2 u = \cos^2 u$

Example 5: Proving an Identity by Introducing Something Extra

Verify the identity $\dfrac{\cos u}{1 - \sin u} = \sec u + \tan u$.

Solution

Start with the left-hand side (LHS) and multiply numerator and denominator by $1 + \sin u$:

$$ \begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \frac{\cos u}{1 - \sin u} \\ &= \frac{\cos u}{1 - \sin u} \cdot \frac{1 + \sin u}{1 + \sin u} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Multiply num and den by } 1 + \sin u \\ &= \frac{\cos u(1 + \sin u)}{1 - \sin^2 u} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Expand denominator} \\ &= \frac{\cos u(1 + \sin u)}{\cos^2 u} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ &= \frac{1 + \sin u}{\cos u} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Cancel common factor} \\ &= \frac{1}{\cos u} + \frac{\sin u}{\cos u} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Separate into two fractions} \\ &= \sec u + \tan u = \text{RHS} \qquad \leftarrow \text{Reciprocal identities} \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} $$

Proving Identities and Trigonometric Substitution

Strategy: Working with Both Sides Separately

If transforming one side into the other is difficult, transform each side separately into the same third expression. If $\text{LHS} = \text{Expression}_3$ and $\text{RHS} = \text{Expression}_3$, then $\text{LHS} = \text{RHS}$.

Example 6: Proving an Identity by Working with Both Sides Separately

Verify the identity $\dfrac{1 + \cos \theta}{\cos \theta} = \dfrac{\tan^2 \theta}{\sec \theta - 1}$.

Solution

Transform LHS and RHS independently to reach a common result:

$$ \begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \frac{1 + \cos \theta}{\cos \theta} \\ &= \frac{1}{\cos \theta} + \frac{\cos \theta}{\cos \theta} \\ &= \sec \theta + 1 \end{aligned} \qquad \begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= \frac{\tan^2 \theta}{\sec \theta - 1} \\ &= \frac{\sec^2 \theta - 1}{\sec \theta - 1} \quad \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ &= \frac{(\sec \theta - 1)(\sec \theta + 1)}{\sec \theta - 1} \quad \leftarrow \text{Factor} \\ &= \sec \theta + 1 \end{aligned} $$

Since $\text{LHS} = \sec \theta + 1$ and $\text{RHS} = \sec \theta + 1$, the equation is an identity. $\blacksquare$

Trigonometric Substitution

Concept: Replace an algebraic variable $x$ with a trigonometric function (e.g., $x = \sin \theta$) to simplify expressions, particularly those involving square roots like $\sqrt{1-x^2}$. This is foundational for integration in calculus.

Example 7: Trigonometric Substitution

Substitute $x = \sin \theta$ in the expression $\sqrt{1 - x^2}$ and simplify. Assume $0 \le \theta \le \pi/2$.

Solution

$$ \begin{aligned} \sqrt{1 - x^2} &= \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \theta} \quad \leftarrow \text{Substitute } x = \sin \theta \\ &= \sqrt{\cos^2 \theta} \quad \leftarrow \text{Pythagorean identity} \\ &= \cos \theta \quad \leftarrow \text{Take square root} \end{aligned} $$

Domain Constraints & Absolute Values

Normally, $\sqrt{u^2} = |u|$. Here, $\sqrt{\cos^2 \theta} = |\cos \theta|$. However, because the problem restricts $\theta$ to $[0, \pi/2]$, we know $\cos \theta \ge 0$. Thus, $|\cos \theta| = \cos \theta$.

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 554)

notes.excerpt: --- Angle Measure & Radian Definition [!info] Angle Basics - Angle: Rotation of ray $R_1$ (initial side) onto $R_2$ (terminal side) about vertex $O$. - Sign: Counterclockwise → positive; Clockwise → n
notes.html:
Angle Measure & Radian Definition

Angle Basics
  • Angle: Rotation of ray $R_1$ (initial side) onto $R_2$ (terminal side) about vertex $O$.
  • Sign: Counterclockwise → positive; Clockwise → negative.
  • Notation: Greek letters ($\alpha, \beta, \theta$) or uppercase ($A, B, C$).
Radian Measure (Definition)

For a circle of radius 1 centered at the angle’s vertex:
The radian measure of $\theta$ is the length of the arc it subtends.

Key benchmarks (unit circle circumference = $2\pi$):

  • Full revolution: $2\pi$ rad
  • Straight angle: $\pi$ rad
  • Right angle: $\frac{\pi}{2}$ rad
  • Arc length 2 on unit circle → angle = 2 rad

Degrees ↔ Radians Conversion

Core Relationship

$$ > 180^\circ = \pi \text{ rad} > \quad \Rightarrow \quad > 1^\circ = \frac{\pi}{180} \text{ rad}, \quad > 1 \text{ rad} = \left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^\circ \approx 57.296^\circ > $$

Conversion Rules:

  • Degrees → Radians: Multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$
  • Radians → Degrees: Multiply by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$
Example 1: Converting Between Radians and Degrees

(a) $60^\circ = 60 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ rad}$
(b) $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ rad} = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \cdot \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 30^\circ$

Angles in Standard Position & Coterminal Angles

Standard Position

An angle is in standard position if:

  • Vertex at origin $(0,0)$
  • Initial side along positive $x$-axis
  • Terminal side determined by rotation (CCW = positive, CW = negative)
Coterminal Angles

Two angles are coterminal if their terminal sides coincide.

To find coterminal angles:

  • Degrees: Add/subtract multiples of $360^\circ$
  • Radians: Add/subtract multiples of $2\pi$
Example 2: Coterminal Angles

(a) $\theta = 30^\circ$
Positive: $30^\circ + 360^\circ = 390^\circ$, $30^\circ + 720^\circ = 750^\circ$
Negative: $30^\circ - 360^\circ = -330^\circ$, $30^\circ - 720^\circ = -690^\circ$

(b) $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$
Positive: $\frac{\pi}{3} + 2\pi = \frac{7\pi}{3}$, $\frac{\pi}{3} + 4\pi = \frac{13\pi}{3}$
Negative: $\frac{\pi}{3} - 2\pi = -\frac{5\pi}{3}$, $\frac{\pi}{3} - 4\pi = -\frac{11\pi}{3}$

General Form

All angles coterminal with $\theta$:

  • Degrees: $\theta + 360^\circ \cdot n$,$n \in \mathbb{Z}$
  • Radians: $\theta + 2\pi \cdot n$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$

Coterminal angles have identical trig function values.

Length of a Circular Arc

Arc Length Formula

For a circle of radius $r$, central angle $\theta$ (in radians), arc length $s$: $$ > s = r\theta > $$

Solve for angle:
$$ > \theta = \frac{s}{r} > $$

Radians Required

The formula $s = r\theta$ only holds when $\theta$ is in radians. Convert degrees first if needed.

Example 4: Arc Length and Angle Measure

(a) Radius $10$ m, angle $30^\circ = \frac{\pi}{6}$ rad →
$s = 10 \cdot \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{3}$ m

(b) Radius $4$ m, arc $6$ m →
$\theta = \frac{6}{4} = \frac{3}{2}$ rad

Intuition

Radian measure = how many radii fit along the arc.
So $\theta = \frac{s}{r}$ is literally “arc length divided by radius”.

Always check units: $s$ and $r$ must be same unit; $\theta$ dimensionless (radians).

Area of a Circular Sector

Sector Area Formula

For a circle of radius $r$, central angle $\theta$ (in radians), sector area $A$: $$ > A = \frac{1}{2} r^2 \theta > $$

Radians Required

The formula $A = \frac{1}{2} r^2 \theta$ only holds when $\theta$ is in radians. Convert degrees first if needed.

Example 5: Area of a Sector

Radius $3$ m, angle $60^\circ = \frac{\pi}{3}$ rad →
$$ > A = \frac{1}{2}(3)^2\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{9}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{3\pi}{2} \text{ m}^2 > $$

Derivation Insight

Sector area = fraction of full circle:
$\frac{\theta}{2\pi} \cdot \pi r^2 = \frac{1}{2} r^2 \theta$

Always verify units: $r$ in length → $A$ in square length; $\theta$ dimensionless (radians).

Circular Motion: Linear & Angular Speed

Definitions

For a point moving on circle of radius $r$, traversing angle $\theta$ (rad) in time $t$:

  • Angular speed: $\omega = \dfrac{\theta}{t}$ (rad per unit time)
  • Linear speed: $v = \dfrac{s}{t} = \dfrac{r\theta}{t} = r\omega$ (distance per unit time)
Example 6: Finding Linear and Angular Speed

Stone on 3-ft sling, 15 rev / 10 s.

Angular speed:
$\theta = 15 \cdot 2\pi = 30\pi$ rad →
$\omega = \dfrac{30\pi}{10} = 3\pi$ rad/s

Linear speed:
$s = 15 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 3 = 90\pi$ ft →
$v = \dfrac{90\pi}{10} = 9\pi$ ft/s
(or use $v = r\omega = 3 \cdot 3\pi = 9\pi$)

Key Relation

$$ > v = r\omega > $$ Always ensure $\theta$ is in radians for these formulas.

Units:

  • $\omega$: rad/s, rad/min, etc.
  • $v$: ft/s, m/s, etc. (same as distance/time)

References

  • Precalculus - Mathematics for Calculus 8th Edition (James Stewart, Lothar Redlin, Saleem Watson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf (p. 486)
