notes.html:
CH1: Tribu

Note

une famille $\tau$ de partie d'un ensemble $X$ ne tribu ou $\sigma$-algebre s'il verifier les proprietes suivant:

  1. $X \in \tau$

  2. si $A \in \tau$ alors $A^c \in \tau$

  3. $\cup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n \in \tau$ pour toute suite $(A_n) \subset \tau$

Proposition

  1. $\emptyset$ est un ensemble mesurable
  2. $\cup^N_{n \geq 0} A_n$ et $\cap^N_{n \geq 0} A_n$ sont des ensembles mesurable
  3. si $A$ et $B$ sont mesurable, $A\setminus B$ et aussi mesurable

Mesure positive

une mesure positive sur $(X,\tau)$ toute application $\mu$

$$\mu : \tau \longrightarrow [0, +\infty[$$

qui vérifie les propriétés suivantes

  1. $\mu(\emptyset)=0$

  2. $\mu$ est $\sigma$-additive:

    $A_i \cap A_j=\emptyset$ (disjoint 2 a 2), On a $\mu(\cup_{n\in \mathbb{N}} A_n)= \sum^{+\infty}_{i=0}\mu(A_i)$

Proposition

Soit $(X,\tau, \mu)$ un espace mesure

1. Si $A_1,A_2,...,A_n$ sont des ensembles mesurable disjoint 2 a 2 alors $\mu(\cup^{n}_{k=1} A_n)= \sum^{n}_{k=1}\mu(A_i)$

Preuve : on pose $A_p=\emptyset, p > n$

2. $\forall A,B \in \tau$ avec $A \subset B$, on a $\mu(A \setminus B)=\mu(B)-\mu(A)$ (Preuve : $B= A\cup (B\setminus A)$)

et $\mu(A) \leq \mu(B)$ (Preuve : $\mu(A \setminus B)=\mu(B)-\mu(A)$ et $\mu(A \setminus B) \geq 0$)

3. $\forall A,B \in \tau, \mu(A \cap B) < +\infty$, On a : $\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) +\mu(B) -\mu(A\cap B)$

Preuve : ![[Excalidraw/Drawing 2026-02-21 13.23.21.excalidraw.md#^frame=trbiuebbprop 3]]

4. $\forall A,B \in \tau$

$\mu(A\cup B) \leq \mu(A)+\mu(B)$ (Preuve : $\mu(A\cap B)\geq 0$, donc $\mu(A)+\mu(B)-\mu(A\cup B) \geq 0$)

$\mu(A\cap B) \leq \min(\mu(A),\mu(B))$ (Preuve : $A\cap B \subset A$ et $A\cap B \subset B$)

$\mu(A \cup B) \geq \max(\mu(A),\mu(B))$ (Preuve : $A \subset A\cup B$ et $B \subset A\cup B$)

5. Pour toute suite $(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ d'element de $\tau$, $(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \tau$

$$\cup^{+\infty}_{i=1} A_i \in \tau, \text{ On a, } \quad \mu(\cup^{+\infty}_{i=1} A_i) \leq \sum^{+ \infty}_{i=1} \mu(A_i)$$

Demonstration: On pose $B_1 = A_1$, $\forall n \geq 2$ $B_n = A_n \setminus \cup^{n-1}_{k=1} B_k$ On vérifie une $B_j \cap B_i =\emptyset$ montrons par récurrence $B_1=A_1$ , $B_2 =A_2 \setminus A_1$ donc $B_1 \cap B_2 =\emptyset$ donc c'est claire que $B_n \subset A_n$ Montrer par récurrence $\cup^n_{k=1} B_k = \cup^n_{k=1} A_k$ alors $\cup^{+ \infty}_{k=1} B_k = \cup^{+ \infty}_{k=1} A_k$ Finalement: $$\mu(\cup^{+\infty}_{k=1} A_k)=\mu(\cup^{+\infty}_{k=1} B_k)= \sum^{+ \infty}_{k=1} \mu(B_k)\leq \sum^{+ \infty}_{k=1} \mu(A_k)$$

6. Si $(A_n)$ est une suite croissante la suite $\mu(A_i)$ est croissante et converge vers $\mu(A)=\mu(\cup^{+\infty}_{n=0})$

$$\lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \mu(A_n)=\mu(\cup^{+\infty}_{n=0} A_n)=\mu(A)$$

Demonstration: On pose: $B_0=A_0$ et $B_n=A_n \setminus A_{n-1}$

On m.q: $\forall i \not = j, B_i \cap B_j = \emptyset$

$$\begin{align} i < j &\Rightarrow i \leq j-1\\ B_i&=A_i \setminus A_{i-1}\\ B_j&=A_j \setminus A_{j-1}\\ A_i \subset A_{j-1} &\text{ donc sont disjoint 2 a 2} \end{align}$$

On m.q: $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, A_n=\cup^{n}_{k=0} B_k$

$$\begin{align} \cup^{n}_{k=0} B_k &= A_0 \cup (A_1 \setminus A_0) \cup ... \cup (A_n \setminus A_{n-1})\\ & = A_0 \cup A_1 ... \cup A_n \\ &=A_n \end{align}$$ Alors $\cup^{+ \infty}_{k=1} B_k = \cup^{+ \infty}_{k=1} A_k$ Finalement: $$\mu(\cup^{+ \infty}_{k=0} A_k) = \mu(\cup^{+ \infty}_{k=0} B_k)=\sum^{+ \infty}_{k=0} \mu(B_k)= \lim_{n \rightarrow + \infty} \sum^{n}_{k=0} \mu(B_k)=\lim_{n\rightarrow +\infty} \mu(\cup^n_{k=0}B_k)=\lim_{n \rightarrow + \infty} \mu(A_n)$$

7. Si $(A_n)$ est une suite décroissante la suite $\mu(A_i)$ est décroissante et converge vers $\mu(A)=\mu(\cap^{+\infty}_{n=0} A_n)$

$$\lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \mu(A_n)=\mu(\cap^{+\infty}_{n=0} A_n)=\mu(A)$$

Demonstration: On pose $B_0=\emptyset$, $B_n= A_0 \setminus A_n$

On m.q: Si $A_n$ décroissante donc $B_n$ croissante

On m.q : Si $A_n$ est décroissante donc $\mu(A_n)$ est décroissante

$A_{n+1} \subset A_n$ donc $\mu(A_{n+1}) \leq \mu(A_n)$ donc $\mu(A_n)$ est décroissante

On m.q: $\cup^{+ \infty}_{n=0}(A_0 \setminus A_n)=A_0 \setminus (\cap^{+ \infty}_{n=0} A_n)$

Finalement $B_n$ croissante donc $\lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \mu(B_n)=\mu(\cup^{+\infty}_{n=0} B_n)$

a. $\lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \mu(B_n)=\lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \mu(A_0 \setminus A_n)$

b. $\mu(\cup^{+\infty}_{n=0} B_n)=\mu(A_0 \setminus (\cap^{+ \infty}_{n=0} A_n))$

Alors:

$$\lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \mu(A_n)=\mu(\cap^{+\infty}_{n=0} A_n)$$

CH 2: Calcul de Probabilité

  • $\overline{\lim} A_n=\cap_{k \in \mathbb{N}}(\cup_{n \geq k} A_n)$

  • $\underline{\lim} A_n=\cup_{k \in \mathbb{N}}(\cap_{n \geq k} A_n)$

$$P(A)=\frac{Card(A)}{Card(\Omega)}$$

Probabilité conditionné par un évènement

$$P(A / B)=\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$$

Formule de Bayes

$$P(A_n / B)=\frac{P(B / A_n)P(A_n)}{\sum^{+\infty}_{k=1}P(B / A_k)\times P(A_k)}$$

Evènement indépendant

$$P(A/B)=P(A) \quad \text{ et } \quad P(B/A)=P(B)$$

$$P(A \cap B)= P(A) \times P(B)$$

Lemme de Borel-Cantelli

  1. Si $\sum_{n \geq 1} P(A_n) < +\infty$ donc $P(\overline{\lim}A_n)=0$

  2. Si les $(A_n)_{n \geq 1}$ sont indépendants et $\sum_{n \geq 1} P(A_n) = +\infty$ donc $P(\overline{\lim}A_n)=1$

CH 3: Variables Aléatoires Réelles

On appelle variable aléatoire réelle (v.a.r) toute application mesurable de $(\Omega,F)$ dans $(\mathbb{R},B(\mathbb{R}))$.

$$\forall A \in B(\mathbb{R}), \quad X^{-1}(A) \in F$$

Variable Aléatoire Discrète (v.a.d)

$$X:(\Omega , F)\rightarrow (\mathbb{R},B(\mathbb{R})) \quad \text{ est v.a.d si:}$$

  • $X(\Omega)=S$ est au plus dénombrable, $S=\{x_1,.....x_k,....\}$

  • $\forall x_k \in S, X^{-1}(\{x_k\}) \in F$

Notation

$$X^{-1} (\{x_k\})=\{\omega \in \Omega / X(\omega)=x_k\}=(X=x_k)$$

Loi de Proba d'une v.a.d

On appelle fonction de répartition de $X$ la fonction réelle définie par:

$$\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\quad F_X(x)=\sum_{x_k \leq x} P(X=x_k)$$

$F_X$ est une fonction croissante, continue à droite en tout point.

  • $\lim_{x \rightarrow + \infty} F(x)=1$

  • $\lim_{x \rightarrow - \infty} F(x)=0$

Loi de probabilité usuelle

Soit $(\Omega , F, P)$ un espace probabilise

Loi de Bernouille

Une experience aléatoire a deux issues possible (succès ou échec) $$ \begin{align} X \sim &\mathcal{B(p)} \\ P(X=1)=p \quad\text{ et }& \quad P(X=0)=1-p \\ \text{Esperence: }\quad & E(X)=p\\ \text{Variance: }\quad & V(X)=p \cdot (1-p) \end{align} $$

Loi Binomiale

Une répétition n fois d'une experience de Bernouille d'une façons indépendant Compter le nombre de success parmi n essais $$ \begin{align} X &\sim \mathcal{B}(n,p) \\ P(X=k)=&\binom{n}{k}\cdot p^k \cdot (1-p)^{n-k}\\ \text{Esperence: }\quad & E(X)=np\\ \text{Variance: }\quad & V(X)=np \cdot (1-p) \end{align} $$

Loi Uniforme Discrete

Chaque issue possible a la meme probabilité de se produire Equiprobabilité parfaite $$ \begin{align} X \sim &U({x_1,....,x_n})\\ \forall x_k \in S \Rightarrow &P(X=x_k)=\frac{1}{n} \\ n=&Card(S)\\ \text{Esperence: }\quad & E(X)=\frac{n +1}{2}\\ \text{Variance: }\quad & V(X)=\frac{n^2 -1}{12} \end{align} $$

Loi Géométrique

Modélise le temps d'attente de premier success Nombre d'essais necessaire pour obtenir le premiere succès $$ \begin{align} X \sim &\mathcal{G}(p)\\ P(X=k)=&(1-p)^{k-1}\cdot p \\ \text{Esperence: }\quad & E(X)=\frac{1}{p}\\ \text{Variance: }\quad & V(X)=\frac{1-p}{p} \end{align} $$

Loi de Poisson

Montre un évènement qui se produisent dans un lapse de temps $$ \begin{align} X \sim &\mathcal{P}(\lambda)\\ P(X=k)=&\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}\\ \text{Esperence: }\quad & E(X)=\lambda\\ \text{Variance: }\quad & V(X)=\lambda \end{align} $$

Loi Hypergéométrique

On dispose de N objet dont n sont défectueuse, On prélevé un échantillon de taille k (sans remise), k objet pour N $X$ : nombre de piece défectueuse parmi k pieces $$ \begin{align} X \sim &\mathcal{H}(N,n,k)\\ P(X=x)=&\frac{C^x_n \cdot C^{k-x}_{N-n}}{C^k_N} \\ \text{Esperence: }\quad & E(X)=n\frac{k}{N}\\ \text{Variance: }\quad & V(X)=n\frac{k}{N}(1-\frac{k}{N})\frac{N-n}{N-1} \end{align} $$

Espérance d'une v.a.d

Si $\sum_{x \in S} |x| \cdot P(X=x) < + \infty$, alors l'espérance mathématique de $X$ est :

$$E(X)=\sum_{x \in S} \; x \cdot P(X=x)$$

Proposition (Espérance)

  1. Si $X=a$ (constante), donc $E(X)=a$

  2. Soit $Y=aX+b$ alors $E(Y)=aE(X)+b$

  3. $E(aX+bY)=aE(X)+bE(Y)$

  4. Si $X \leq Y$ P.p.s, alors $E(X) \leq E(Y)$

Variance et Ecart-type d'une v.a.d

Soit $E(X)=m < +\infty$.

Si $\sum_{x \in S} (x-m)^2 \cdot P(X=x) < + \infty$, on appelle variance de $X$ (notée $V(X)$ ou $\sigma^2_X$) la quantité :

$$V(X)=\sum_{x \in S} (x-m)^2 \cdot P(X=x)$$

Remarques :

  • L'écart-type est défini par : $\sigma_X = \sqrt{V(X)}$

  • Moment centré d'ordre 2 : $V(X)=E(X^2)-(E(X))^2$

Propriétés de la Variance

  1. $V(X) \geq 0$

  2. Pour $Y=aX+b$, on a : $V(Y)= a^2 V(X)$

  3. Centrage et Réduction : Soit $X$ avec $E(X)=m$.

    $E\left(\frac{X-m}{\sigma}\right)=0$ $V\left(\frac{X-m}{\sigma}\right)=1$ On dit qu'on a centré et réduit $X$.

Variable Aléatoire Continue (v.a.c)

Soit $X$ une variable aléatoire définie sur $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$. $X$ est une variable aléatoire continue si sa loi $P_X$ admet une densité $f$ par rapport à la mesure de Lebesgue $\lambda$ sur $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))$.

Fonction de Répartition (f.d.r) d'une v.a.c

La fonction de répartition $F_X(x)$ de $X$ est donnée par :

$$F_X(x) = P_X(]-\infty, x]) = P(X \le x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t) d\lambda(t)$$

Propriétés de la fonction de repartition:

  • $F_X$ est croissante ($x \le y \Rightarrow F_X(x) \le F_X(y)$).

  • $F_X$ est continue à droite en tout point de $\mathbb{R}$.

  • $\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = 0$ et $\lim_{x \to +\infty} F_X(x) = l$.

  • $F_X$ est absolument continue par rapport à $\lambda$ ($P_X \ll \lambda$).

  • $F'_X(x) = f(x)$ presque partout.

Espérance et Intégration (v.a.c)

Si $P_X$ admet une densité $f$ par rapport à la mesure de Lebesgue :

$$E(X) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} x \cdot f(x) d\lambda(x)$$

Théorème de transfert : Pour une fonction mesurable $g$ :

$$E(g(X)) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} g(x) \cdot f(x) d\lambda(x)$$

Lois de Probabilités Continues Usuelles

1. Loi Uniforme

$X$ suit la loi uniforme sur l'intervalle $[a, b]$ si sa densité $f_X$ est :

$$\begin{align} X \sim &\mathcal{U}_{[a,b]}\\ f_X(x) =& \frac{1}{b-a} \cdot \mathcal{I}_{[a,b]}(x) \end{align}$$

  • Espérance : $E(X) = \frac{a+b}{2}$

  • Variance : $V(X) = \frac{(b-a)^2}{12}$

2. Loi Normale (Gaussienne)

$X$ suit une loi normale d'espérance $m$ et de variance $\sigma^2$ si sa densité est :

$$\begin{align} X \sim &\mathcal{N}(m, \sigma^2)\\ f_X(x) =& \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-m}{\sigma}\right)^2} \end{align}$$

Note

Si $m=0$ et $\sigma^2=1$, on dit que $X$ est centrée réduite, notée $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$.

3. Loi Exponentielle

$X$ suit une loi exponentielle de paramètre $\lambda > 0$ si sa densité est :

$$\begin{align} X \sim &\mathcal{E}(\lambda)\\ f_X(x) =& \lambda e^{-\lambda x} \quad \text{pour } x \ge 0 \end{align}$$

  • Fonction de répartition : $F_X(x) = (1 - e^{-\lambda x})\mathcal{I}_{x \ge 0}$

4. Loi de Cauchy

$X$ suit une loi de Cauchy de paramètres $a$ et $b$ si sa densité est :

$$\begin{align} X \sim &\mathcal{C}(a,b)\\ f_X(x) =& \frac{1}{\pi} \frac{a}{a^2 + (x-b)^2} \end{align}$$

  • L'espérance $E(X)$ n'existe pas (elle vaut $+\infty$).

Moments et Paramètres de Position

  • Moment d'ordre $n$ : $E(X^n) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x^n f(x) dx$

  • Moment centré d'ordre $n$ : $\mu_n = E((X - E(X))^n)$

  • Médiane : Un réel $\alpha$ tel que $P(X \ge \alpha) \ge \frac{1}{2}$ et $P(X \le \alpha) \ge \frac{1}{2}$. Si $F$ est continue, on résout $F(\alpha) = \frac{1}{2}$.

  • Quantile d'ordre $\alpha$ : Un réel $q_\alpha$ tel que $P(X \ge q_\alpha) \ge 1 - \alpha$ et $P(X \le q_\alpha) \ge \alpha$.

  • Mode : C'est la valeur pour laquelle la fonction de densité $f(x)$ est maximale (quand elle existe).

Inégalités Fondamentales

Inégalité de Markov : Pour une v.a. $X$ positive et $\epsilon > 0$ :

$$P(X \ge \epsilon) \le \frac{E(X)}{\epsilon}$$

Inégalité de Bienaymé-Tchebychev : Si $X$ possède une variance finie $\sigma_X^2$, pour tout $\epsilon > 0$ :

$$P(|X - E(X)| > \epsilon) \le \frac{V(X)}{\epsilon^2}$$

CH 4: Couples Aléatoires (Rappels)

Soit un couple aléatoire $(X, Y)$.

I. Variable Aléatoire Bivariée Discrète

Distribution conjointe : $P(X=x, Y=y)$.

  1. Distribution marginale de X :

    $$P(X=x) = \sum_y P(X=x, Y=y)$$

  2. Espérance marginale de g(X) :

    $$E(g(X)) = \sum_x g(x) P(X=x)$$

    $$E(X) = \sum_x x P(X=x)$$

  3. Distribution conditionnelle de Y sachant X=x :

    $$P(Y=y / X=x) = \frac{P(X=x, Y=y)}{P(X=x)} \quad \text{avec } P(X=x) \neq 0$$

  4. Espérance conditionnelle de g(Y) sachant X=x :

    $$E(g(Y)/X=x) = \sum_y g(y) P(Y=y/X=x)$$

  5. Espérance de g(X,Y) :

    $$E(g(X,Y)) = \sum_x \sum_y g(x,y) P(X=x, Y=y)$$

II. Variable Aléatoire Bivariée Continue

Densité conjointe : $f(x,y)$.

  1. Densité marginale de X :

    $$f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x,y) dy$$

  2. Espérance marginale de g(X) :

    $$E(g(X)) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} g(x) f_X(x) dx$$

  3. Densité conditionnelle de Y sachant X=x :

    $$f_{Y/X=x}(y) = \frac{f(x,y)}{f_X(x)} \quad \text{avec } f_X(x) \neq 0$$

  4. Espérance conditionnelle de g(Y) sachant X=x :

    $$E(g(Y)/Y=x) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} g(y) f_{Y/X=x}(y) dy$$

  5. Espérance de g(X,Y) :

    $$E(g(X,Y)) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} g(x,y) f(x,y) dx dy$$

CH 5: Indépendance et Moments

1. Matrice de Covariance

Soit $X=(X_1, X_2)$ défini sur $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ à valeurs dans $\mathbb{R}^2$ tel que $E(X_1) < +\infty$ et $E(X_2) < +\infty$.

La matrice de covariance $C_X$ est définie par :

$$C_X = \begin{pmatrix} V(X_1) & Cov(X_1, X_2) \\ Cov(X_2, X_1) & V(X_2) \end{pmatrix}$$

Définition de la covariance :

$$Cov(X_1, X_2) = E[(X-E(X))(Y-E(Y))] = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y)$$

Propriété de la Matrice

$C_X$ est une matrice symétrique définie positive (ou semi-définie positive), c'est-à-dire :

$\forall \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^2, \quad \alpha^T C_X \alpha \geq 0$.

2. Corrélation entre X et Y

Le coefficient de corrélation linéaire est :

$$\rho_{XY} = \frac{Cov(X,Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y} \quad \text{et on a } |\rho_{XY}| \leq 1$$

Remarque : $Cov(X,Y) = 0 \iff X$ et $Y$ sont non corrélés.

3. Indépendance Stochastique

$X$ et $Y$ sont indépendants si et seulement si l'une des conditions suivantes est vérifiée :

  1. $P(X \leq x \cap Y \leq y) = P(X \leq x) \cdot P(Y \leq y)$

  2. $F_{(X,Y)}(x,y) = F_X(x) \cdot F_Y(y)$

  3. $f_{(X,Y)}(x,y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y)$ (Cas continu)

  4. $E(XY) = E(X)E(Y)$

  5. $\forall g$ réelle mesurable bornée ou positive, $E(g(X)g(Y)) = E(g(X)) \cdot E(g(Y))$

Implications :

  • $X$ et $Y$ indépendants $\implies Cov(X,Y) = 0$.

  • Si $X$ et $Y$ suivent la loi Normale, alors :

    $X$ et $Y$ indépendants $\iff Cov(X,Y) = 0$.

CH 6: Opérations et Théorèmes Limites

Propriétés des opérateurs Espérances et Variances

Soient $X$ et $Y$ deux v.a. et $a, b$ deux réels.

  1. Linéarité : $E(aX + bY) = aE(X) + bE(Y)$

  2. Variance : $Var(aX + bY) = a^2 Var(X) + b^2 Var(Y) + 2ab Cov(X,Y)$

  3. Si X et Y sont indépendants :

    • $V(X+Y) = V(X) + V(Y)$

    • $V(X-Y) = V(X) + V(Y)$

Théorème d'Addition (Stabilité)

Soient $X$ et $Y$ deux v.a. indépendantes.

  1. Loi Binomiale :

    Si $X \sim \mathcal{B}(n_1, p)$ et $Y \sim \mathcal{B}(n_2, p) \implies X+Y \sim \mathcal{B}(n_1+n_2, p)$

  2. Loi de Poisson :

    Si $X \sim \mathcal{P}(\lambda_1)$ et $Y \sim \mathcal{P}(\lambda_2) \implies X+Y \sim \mathcal{P}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$

  3. Loi Normale :

    Si $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)$ et $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)$, alors :

    $$aX + bY \sim \mathcal{N}(a\mu_1 + b\mu_2, a^2\sigma_1^2 + b^2\sigma_2^2)$$

Vecteurs Gaussiens

On dit que $X = (X_1, ..., X_n)$ (dans $\mathbb{R}^n$) est un vecteur aléatoire gaussien ssi :

$\forall (\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, la combinaison linéaire $\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i X_i$ est une variable aléatoire gaussienne dans $\mathbb{R}$.

Fonction Caractéristique

Soit $X$ une v.a. sur $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$. La fonction caractéristique de $X$ est :

$$\phi_X(t) = E(e^{itX})$$

  • Cas continu : $\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{itx} f_X(x) dx$

  • Cas discret : $\sum_{k} e^{itk} P(X=k)$

Remarque : La fonction caractéristique détermine d'une façon unique la loi de probabilité.

Annexe : Quelques Approximations Usuelles

Conditions et schémas d'approximation des lois :

  1. Binomiale vers Poisson : $\mathcal{B}(n, p) \to \mathcal{P}(\lambda)$

    • Conditions : $n \ge 30$, $p \le 0.1$, $np < 15$.

    • Paramètre : $\lambda = np$

  2. Binomiale vers Normale : $\mathcal{B}(n, p) \to \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$

    • Conditions : $np \ge 5$ et $n(1-p) \ge 5$ (ou $n$ grand et $p$ pas trop proche de 0 ou 1).

    • Paramètres : Approximée par $\mathcal{N}(np, np(1-p))$

  3. Poisson vers Normale : $\mathcal{P}(\lambda) \to \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$

    • Condition : $\lambda \ge 15$ (grandes valeurs de $\lambda$).

    • Paramètres : Approximée par $\mathcal{N}(\lambda, \lambda)$

CH 7: Convergence Stochastique

Soit $(X_n)_{n \ge 1}$ une suite de variables aléatoires et $X$ une variable aléatoire définies sur $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$.

1. Convergence en Probabilité

$X_n$ converge en probabilité vers $X$ lorsque $n \to +\infty$ si, pour tout $\epsilon > 0$ :

$$\lim_{n \to +\infty} P(|X_n - X| > \epsilon) = 0$$

2. Convergence Presque Sûre (p.s.)

$X_n$ converge presque sûrement vers $X$ si la probabilité de l'ensemble des éventualités $\omega$ pour lesquelles $X_n(\omega)$ converge vers $X(\omega)$ est égale à 1.

$$P(\{\omega / X_n(\omega) \to X(\omega)\}) = 1$$

  • Condition suffisante de cv p.s : Si $\sum_{n \ge 1} P(|X_n - X| > \epsilon) < +\infty$, alors $X_n \xrightarrow{p.s} X$.

3. Loi des Grands Nombres (LGN)

Soit $(X_n)_{n \ge 1}$ une suite de variables aléatoires indépendantes et de même loi (i.i.d 'Independent and identically distributed') avec une espérance $E(X_i) = m$. On définit la moyenne arithmétique (empirique) $\overline{X}_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$.

  • Loi Faible des Grands Nombres : $\overline{X}_n$ converge en probabilité vers la vraie moyenne $m$.

  • Loi Forte des Grands Nombres : $\overline{X}_n$ converge presque sûrement (p.s.) vers $m$.

Intérêt Pratique des LGN

Dans la pratique, la moyenne théorique (l'espérance) d'une v.a. est inconnue. Prendre plusieurs observations indépendantes $X_i$ permet d'estimer cette moyenne avec certitude via la moyenne arithmétique, car celle-ci converge vers la vraie espérance.

4. Théorème Central Limite (TCL)

Soit $(X_n)$ une suite de v.a. i.i.d avec $E(X_n) = m$ et de variance $V(X_n) = \sigma^2$. La variable centrée et réduite approchée $Z_n$ converge vers la loi normale standard $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ quand $n \to +\infty$.

$$Z_n = \frac{\overline{X}_n - m}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}} \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}} \mathcal{N}(0,1)$$

notes.html:
Deductive Reasoning and Logical Connectives

Proofs play a central role in mathematics, and deductive reasoning is the foundation on which proofs are based. In deductive reasoning, we arrive at a conclusion based on the assumption that other statements, called premises, are true.

Examples of Deductive Reasoning

  1. It will either rain or snow tomorrow. It's too warm for snow. Therefore, it will rain.

  2. If today is Sunday, then I don't have to go to work today. Today is Sunday. Therefore, I don't have to go to work today.

  3. I will go to work either tomorrow or today. I'm going to stay home today. Therefore, I will go to work tomorrow.

Validity of Arguments

In a deductive argument, the conclusion seems to be forced on us by the premises.

Valid Argument

An argument is considered valid if the premises cannot all be true without the conclusion being true as well. If both premises are true, we can be sure that the conclusion is also true.

An argument can be invalid if the conclusion could be false even when both premises are true.

Invalid Deductive Argument

Either the butler is guilty or the maid is guilty.

Either the maid is guilty or the cook is guilty.

Therefore, either the butler is guilty or the cook is guilty.

Why it's invalid: If the maid were guilty, but the butler and the cook were both innocent, then both premises would be true and the conclusion would be false.

Logical Form and Connectives

What makes an argument valid is its form, not its subject matter. For instance, the first and third arguments in the initial example share the same underlying logic:

$$P \text{ or } Q.$$

$$\text{not } Q.$$

$$\text{Therefore, } P.$$

Replacing specific statements with letters (such as $P$ and $Q$) keeps us from being distracted by aspects of the argument that don't affect its validity. Ultimately, the meanings of a few connecting words—like or and not—give the key to understanding what makes reasoning valid or invalid.

Connective Symbols
Symbol Meaning
$\lor$ or
$\land$ and
$\lnot$ not
Logical Connective Terminology

  • The statement $P \lor Q$ is called the disjunction of $P$ and $Q$.

  • The statement $P \land Q$ is called the conjunction of $P$ and $Q$.

  • The statement $\lnot P$ is called the negation of $P$.

When analyzing complex statements, it is often helpful to progressively break down the logical components and extract implicit negations.

Analyzing Logical Forms

Statement: Joe is going to leave home and not come back.

Initial Analysis: If we let $P$ stand for "Joe is going to leave home" and $Q$ stand for "Joe is not going to come back," we could represent this as $P \land Q$.

Improved Analysis: The first analysis misses an important feature: it doesn't indicate that $Q$ is a negative statement. By letting $R$ stand for "Joe is going to come back," we can write $Q$ as $\lnot R$. Plugging this in gives the improved symbolic representation $P \land \lnot R$.

Statement: Either Bill is at work and Jane isn't, or Jane is at work and Bill isn't.

Analysis: Let $B$ be "Bill is at work" and $J$ be "Jane is at work." The first half is $B \land \lnot J$, and the second half is $J \land \lnot B$. To represent the entire statement, we combine them with a disjunction: $(B \land \lnot J) \lor (J \land \lnot B)$.

Order of Operations for Negation

The negation symbol $\lnot$ always applies only to the statement that comes immediately after it. For example, $\lnot P \land Q$ means $(\lnot P) \land Q$, rather than $\lnot(P \land Q)$. Similar to algebra, parentheses should be used to unambiguously indicate which statements are being combined.

Key Takeaways

  • Deductive reasoning relies on arguments where the truth of the premises guarantees the truth of the conclusion; an argument is valid if the premises cannot all be true without the conclusion also being true.

  • The validity of an argument is determined by its logical form rather than its subject matter, which allows us to replace statements with abstract variables.

  • Complex logical statements are constructed using standard connective symbols: $\lor$ (disjunction/or), $\land$ (conjunction/and), and $\lnot$ (negation/not).

  • The negation symbol ($\lnot$) binds strictly to the proposition immediately following it; parentheses are essential for establishing unambiguous order of operations in compound expressions.

Translating Between English and Logic

When translating complex expressions between logical symbols and natural language, the placement of specific English words can help clarify where parentheses belong.

Example 1.1.3: Translating Logical Expressions

Suppose $S$ stands for "John is stupid" and $L$ stands for "John is lazy." We can translate the following symbolic expressions into English:

  1. $(\lnot S \land L) \lor S$: "Either John isn't stupid and he is lazy, or he's stupid."

  2. $\lnot S \land (L \lor S)$: "John isn't stupid, and either he's lazy or he's stupid." Notice how the placement of the word either changes based on the parentheses.

  3. $\lnot(S \land L) \lor S$: "Either John isn't both stupid and lazy, or John is stupid." Here, the word both helps distinguish the parenthesis position.

Translation Traps

  • Non-logical uses of "and": The symbol $\land$ cannot represent the word and in the sentence "John and Bill are friends," because it is not combining two statements.

  • "But" often means "And": The word but is frequently used in English to mean and (conjunction), particularly when conveying a contrast (e.g., "John isn't stupid but he is lazy").

  • Meaning over word-for-word translation: A statement like "Rain and snow are the only two possibilities" uses the word and, but logically expresses a disjunction (either rain or snow). Always determine the logical form by analyzing what the statement means, rather than translating it strictly word by word.

Well-Formed Formulas

The connective symbols have strict grammatical rules, much like arithmetic operators in algebra. The symbols $\land$ and $\lor$ act as operators between two statements, whereas the symbol $\lnot$ is applied before a statement to negate it.

Well-Formed Formulas

Meaningless, "ungrammatical" strings of logical symbols (such as $P \lnot \land Q$ or $P - Q$) are invalid. "Grammatical" expressions that correctly follow the syntactic rules of logical connectives are called well-formed formulas, or simply formulas.

Hidden Logical Connectives in Mathematics

Sometimes logical words are embedded implicitly within standard mathematical notation.

Unpacking Mathematical Notation

  • Simple inequalities: The statement $3 \le \pi$ appears to contain no logical words, but read aloud, it means $3 < \pi$ or $3 = \pi$. Instead of abbreviating these short statements with variables, we can write the logical form directly as $(3 < \pi) \lor (3 = \pi)$.

  • Compound inequalities: The statement $3 \le \pi < 4$ combines multiple relations. It means $3 \le \pi$ and $\pi < 4$. Expanding the hidden logic of both parts yields the full formula: $[(3 < \pi) \lor (3 = \pi)] \land (\pi < 4)$. Uncovering this logical form is often crucial for understanding mathematical reasoning.

Key Takeaways

  • Natural language requires careful analysis to translate into logic; words like "but" often represent logical conjunction ($\land$), and words like "either" or "both" dictate the placement of parentheses.

  • Logical symbols must follow strict grammatical rules to create meaningful expressions, known as well-formed formulas.

  • Standard mathematical notations (like $\le$ or chained inequalities) frequently hide implicit logical connectives ($\lor$ and $\land$) that must be explicitly unpacked to reveal the statement's true logical form.

References

How_to_Prove_It_A_Structured_Approach_Daniel_J_Velleman_z_library.pdf (p, 8)

notes.html:
1.5 The Conditional and Biconditional Connectives

Conditional Statements
  • The connective $\to$ represents the conditional statement "If $P$ then $Q$".
  • In the formula $P \to Q$, $P$ is called the antecedent and $Q$ is called the consequent.
Conditional Truth Table
$P$ $Q$ $P \to Q$
F F T
F T T
T F F
T T T
Understanding the "False Antecedent" Cases
  • To understand why F $\to$ F and F $\to$ T evaluate to True, consider the universally true statement "If $x > 2$ then $x^2 > 4$".
  • Plugging in $x = 1$ yields false $\to$ false, which must evaluate to true to preserve the statement's overall truth.
  • Plugging in $x = -5$ yields false $\to$ true, which also must evaluate to true.
  • Therefore, the only scenario where $P \to Q$ is false is when a true antecedent leads to a false consequent.

Equivalences and Terminology

Conditional Equivalences

  • Conditional laws:

  • $P \to Q$ is equivalent to $\lnot P \lor Q$.

  • $P \to Q$ is equivalent to $\lnot(P \land \lnot Q)$.

  • Contrapositive law:

  • The contrapositive of $P \to Q$ is the formula $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$.

  • $P \to Q$ is logically equivalent to $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$.

Mathematical phrasing often expresses $P \to Q$ in formats other than "If $P$ then $Q$".

Alternative Phrasings for $P \to Q$
  • $P$ implies $Q$.
  • $Q$, if $P$.
  • $P$ only if $Q$.
  • $P$ is a sufficient condition for $Q$ (the truth of $P$ guarantees the truth of $Q$).
  • $Q$ is a necessary condition for $P$ (in order for $P$ to be true, $Q$ must be true; if $\lnot Q$, then $\lnot P$).
The Converse Trap
  • The converse of $P \to Q$ is the formula $Q \to P$.
  • A conditional statement ($P \to Q$) and its converse ($Q \to P$) do not mean the same thing and are not logically equivalent.
  • Inferring $P$ from the premises $P \to Q$ and $Q$ is an invalid argument form.

The Biconditional Connective

When both a conditional statement and its converse are true, we use the biconditional connective.

Biconditional Statements
  • The connective $\leftrightarrow$ expresses that both $P \to Q$ and $Q \to P$ are true.
  • $P \leftrightarrow Q$ is an abbreviation for $(P \to Q) \land (Q \to P)$.
  • This is commonly read as "$P$ if and only if $Q$", abbreviated in mathematics as "$P$ iff $Q$".
  • It can also be phrased as "$P$ is a necessary and sufficient condition for $Q$".
Biconditional Truth Table
$P$ $Q$ $P \leftrightarrow Q$
F F T
F T F
T F F
T T T
Everyday Language vs. Mathematics
  • In everyday speech, people frequently use an "if" statement when they actually mean to convey a biconditional "iff" (e.g., "If you don't eat your dinner, you won't get dessert" implies the converse is also true).
  • This blurring of terminology is never acceptable in mathematics. You must strictly differentiate between "if" ($\to$) and "iff" ($\leftrightarrow$).

Key Takeaways

  • The conditional statement $P \to Q$ is only false in the single case where $P$ is true and $Q$ is false.
  • A conditional statement is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ($\lnot Q \to \lnot P$) but must never be confused with its converse ($Q \to P$).
  • The phrasing "$P$ is a sufficient condition for $Q$" translates to $P \to Q$, whereas "$P$ is a necessary condition for $Q$" translates to $Q \to P$.
  • The biconditional connective $\leftrightarrow$ means "$P$ if and only if $Q$" and evaluates to true only when $P$ and $Q$ share the exact same truth value.

References

How_to_Prove_It_A_Structured_Approach_Daniel_J_Velleman_z_library.pdf (p, 44)

notes.html:
1.2 Truth Tables

To understand how words such as and, or, and not affect the validity of arguments, we must examine how they contribute to the truth or falsity of the statements containing them.

Truth Value

When we evaluate the truth or falsity of a statement, we assign it one of the labels true or false; this label is called its truth value.

We can summarize all the possibilities for a logical formula using a truth table, where each row represents one of the possible combinations of truth values for the component statements.

Basic Truth Tables
P Q P∧Q P∨Q ¬P
F F F F T
F T F T T
T F F T
T T T T
Inclusive vs. Exclusive Or

The word or can be interpreted in two ways: the inclusive or (which includes the possibility of both statements being true) and the exclusive or (meaning "$P$ or $Q$ but not both"). In mathematics, or always means the inclusive or unless specified otherwise.

Constructing Complex Truth Tables

Using the fundamental rules for $\land$, $\lor$, and $\lnot$, we can work out truth tables for more complex formulas one step at a time. If a formula contains three letters, it requires eight lines to list all possible combinations of truth values.

Compact Truth Tables and the Main Connective

Instead of using separate columns to list the truth values for every component part of a formula, you can list the truth values directly below the corresponding connective symbol in the original formula.

For example, in evaluating $\lnot(P \lor \lnot Q)$, you would first list the values for $P$ and $Q$, then evaluate $\lnot Q$, then combine $P$ and $\lnot Q$ under the $\lor$ symbol, and finally negate those results under the initial $\lnot$ symbol. The symbol under which the final truth value for the entire formula is listed is called the main connective.

Verifying Arguments with Truth Tables

Verification Strategy: Truth Tables for Arguments

To verify if a deductive argument is valid using truth tables:

  1. Construct a truth table that includes columns for all the argument's premises and its conclusion.

  2. Identify every row where all the premises are true.

  3. If the conclusion is also true in every one of those rows, the argument is valid.

  4. If there is even one row where the premises are all true but the conclusion is false, the argument is invalid.

Evaluating Argument Validity

Premise 1: $(\lnot S \land L) \lor S$ (Either John isn't stupid and he is lazy, or he's stupid).

Premise 2: $S$ (John is stupid).

Conclusion: $\lnot L$ (John isn't lazy).

Constructing a truth table reveals a row where $S$ is True and $L$ is True. In this row, both premises evaluate to True, but the conclusion $\lnot L$ evaluates to False. Because it is possible for both premises to be true while the conclusion is false, this argument is invalid.

Logical Equivalences

Equivalent Formulas

Formulas that always have the same truth value, no matter what statements the letters in them stand for, are equivalent. If two formulas are equivalent, you can always substitute one for the other in any expression, and the results will remain equivalent.

Common Logical Equivalences

  • DeMorgan's laws:

    • $\lnot(P \land Q)$ is equivalent to $\lnot P \lor \lnot Q$.

    • $\lnot(P \lor Q)$ is equivalent to $\lnot P \land \lnot Q$.

  • Commutative laws:

    • $P \land Q$ is equivalent to $Q \land P$.

    • $P \lor Q$ is equivalent to $Q \lor P$.

  • Associative laws:

    • $P \land (Q \land R)$ is equivalent to $(P \land Q) \land R$.

    • $P \lor (Q \lor R)$ is equivalent to $(P \lor Q) \lor R$.

  • Idempotent laws:

    • $P \land P$ is equivalent to $P$.

    • $P \lor P$ is equivalent to $P$.

  • Distributive laws:

    • $P \land (Q \lor R)$ is equivalent to $(P \land Q) \lor (P \land R)$.

    • $P \lor (Q \land R)$ is equivalent to $(P \lor Q) \land (P \lor R)$.

  • Absorption laws:

    • $P \lor (P \land Q)$ is equivalent to $P$.

    • $P \land (P \lor Q)$ is equivalent to $P$.

  • Double Negation law:

    • $\lnot\lnot P$ is equivalent to $P$.

Notice that because of the Associative laws, we can leave out parentheses in formulas like $P \land Q \land R$ without worrying about ambiguity, as either way of filling in the parentheses leads to equivalent formulas.

Tautologies and Contradictions

Tautologies and Contradictions

  • Tautologies are formulas that are always true, regardless of the truth values of their component variables (e.g., $P \lor \lnot P$).

  • Contradictions are formulas that are always false (e.g., $P \land \lnot P$).

Tautology and Contradiction Laws

Tautology laws:

  • $P \land (\text{a tautology})$ is equivalent to $P$.

  • $P \lor (\text{a tautology})$ is a tautology.

  • $\lnot(\text{a tautology})$ is a contradiction.

Contradiction laws:

  • $P \land (\text{a contradiction})$ is a contradiction.

  • $P \lor (\text{a contradiction})$ is equivalent to $P$.

  • $\lnot(\text{a contradiction})$ is a tautology.

Using Laws to Find Simpler Formulas

Find a simpler formula equivalent to $\lnot(Q \land \lnot P) \lor P$:

$\lnot(Q \land \lnot P) \lor P$

is equivalent to $(\lnot Q \lor \lnot\lnot P) \lor P$ (DeMorgan's law)

is equivalent to $(\lnot Q \lor P) \lor P$ (Double negation law)

is equivalent to $\lnot Q \lor (P \lor P)$ (Associative law)

is equivalent to $\lnot Q \lor P$ (Idempotent law)

Key Takeaways

  • Truth tables provide a mechanical, exhaustive method for determining the validity of deductive arguments; an argument is only valid if every scenario that makes the premises true also makes the conclusion true.

  • Equivalent formulas share identical truth conditions and can be freely substituted for one another.

  • Standard algebraic laws of logic (such as DeMorgan's laws, Distributive laws, and Associative laws) allow for the simplification of complex propositions without altering their semantic meaning.

  • Recognizing tautologies (universally true statements) and contradictions (universally false statements) unlocks additional rules for simplifying logical expressions.

References

How_to_Prove_It_A_Structured_Approach_Daniel_J_Velleman_z_library.pdf (p, 14)

notes.excerpt: --- When negating statements containing quantifiers, the negation symbol can be pushed through the quantifier by flipping the quantifier to its opposite type. [!important] Quantifier Negation Laws $\l
notes.html:
When negating statements containing quantifiers, the negation symbol can be pushed through the quantifier by flipping the quantifier to its opposite type.

Quantifier Negation Laws

  • $\lnot \exists x P(x)$ is equivalent to $\forall x \lnot P(x)$.

  • $\lnot \forall x P(x)$ is equivalent to $\exists x \lnot P(x)$.

Combining quantifier negation laws with established propositional equivalences (like De Morgan's laws or conditional laws) allows us to re-express complex negative statements as simpler, equivalent positive statements.

Negating a Universal Statement

To find a positive equivalent for $\lnot(A \subseteq B)$:

  1. Expand the subset definition: $\lnot \forall x(x \in A \to x \in B)$.

  2. Apply Quantifier Negation Law: $\exists x \lnot(x \in A \to x \in B)$.

  3. Apply Conditional Law: $\exists x \lnot(x \notin A \lor x \in B)$.

  4. Apply De Morgan's Law: $\exists x(x \in A \land x \notin B)$.

Conclusion: Saying $A$ is not a subset of $B$ means there is something in $A$ that is not in $B$.

Swapping Quantifiers

Rules for Reversing Quantifier Order

  • Same Type: Two consecutive universal quantifiers ($\forall x \forall y$) or two existential quantifiers ($\exists x \exists y$) can always be switched without changing the meaning of the formula.

  • Mixed Types: As established in Section 2.1, reversing the order of different quantifiers (e.g., $\exists x \forall y$ to $\forall y \exists x$) generally changes the meaning of the formula and is not an equivalence.

The Unique Existential Quantifier

Mathematical statements frequently declare that exactly one object satisfies a condition.

Unique Existential Notation

  • Symbol: $\exists ! x P(x)$.

  • Meaning: "There is exactly one value of $x$ such that $P(x)$ is true," or "There is a unique $x$ such that $P(x)$".

  • Formal Abbreviation: $\exists ! x P(x)$ is an abbreviation for the formal logic expression: $\exists x(P(x) \land \lnot \exists y(P(y) \land y \neq x))$.

Bounded Quantifiers

To specify the universe $(A)$ of discourse directly within a formula, or to restrict attention to a specific subset of the universe, bounded quantifiers are used.

Bounded Quantifier Abbreviations

  • Universal: $\forall x \in A P(x)$ is an abbreviation for $\forall x(x \in A \to P(x))$.

  • Existential: $\exists x \in A P(x)$ is an abbreviation for $\exists x(x \in A \land P(x))$.

Bounded quantifiers follow the same negation rules as standard quantifiers:

  • $\lnot \forall x \in A P(x)$ is equivalent to $\exists x \in A \lnot P(x)$.

  • $\lnot \exists x \in A P(x)$ is equivalent to $\forall x \in A \lnot P(x)$.

Vacuously True Statements

When dealing with bounded quantifiers over an empty set ($A = \emptyset$), the resulting truth values are strictly governed by the underlying logical connectives.

Vacuously True

  • Existential on Empty Sets: $\exists x \in \emptyset P(x)$ is always false, because there is nothing in the empty set to satisfy $P(x)$.

  • Universal on Empty Sets: $\forall x \in \emptyset P(x)$ is always true. Expanding its definition gives $\forall x(x \in \emptyset \to P(x))$. Since $x \in \emptyset$ is always false, the conditional $F \to P(x)$ evaluates to true for every possible $x$. Statements that are true simply because the antecedent is impossible are called vacuously true.

  • Application: This principle proves that the empty set is a subset of every set ($\emptyset \subseteq B$). The definition $\forall x(x \in \emptyset \to x \in B)$ is vacuously true.

Distributive Laws for Quantifiers

Distributing Quantifiers

  • Valid: The universal quantifier distributes over conjunction: $\forall x(P(x) \land Q(x))$ is logically equivalent to $\forall x P(x) \land \forall x Q(x)$.

  • Invalid: The existential quantifier does not distribute over conjunction: $\exists x(P(x) \land Q(x))$ is not equivalent to $\exists x P(x) \land \exists x Q(x)$.

Key Takeaways

  • Negating a quantified statement flips universal quantifiers ($\forall$) to existential ($\exists$) and vice versa, while negating the inner proposition.

  • Adjacent quantifiers of the same type can be freely swapped; adjacent quantifiers of different types cannot.

  • Bounded quantifiers ($\forall x \in A$, $\exists x \in A$) are shorthand for conditional and conjunctive expressions, respectively.

  • A universal claim restricted to an empty set is automatically "vacuously true" because its underlying conditional premise is always false.

References

How_to_Prove_It_A_Structured_Approach_Daniel_J_Velleman_z_library.pdf (p, 64)

notes.excerpt: --- [!abstract] Universal and Existential Quantifiers Universal Quantifier ($\forall$): $\forall x P(x)$ reads "For all $x$, $P(x)$". It asserts that the truth set of $P(x)$ equals the entire universe
notes.html:
Universal and Existential Quantifiers

  • Universal Quantifier ($\forall$): $\forall x P(x)$ reads "For all $x$, $P(x)$". It asserts that the truth set of $P(x)$ equals the entire universe of discourse $U$.

  • Existential Quantifier ($\exists$): $\exists x P(x)$ reads "There exists an $x$ such that $P(x)$". It asserts that the truth set of $P(x)$ contains at least one element, meaning it is not equal to $\emptyset$.

Variable Binding and Scope

  • Quantifiers bind variables. In $\forall x L(x, y)$, $x$ is a bound variable, while $y$ is a free variable.

  • Bound variables are placeholders and can be freely renamed without changing the statement's meaning (e.g., $\forall x L(x, y)$ is equivalent to $\forall w L(w, y)$).

  • Scope constraint: The expressions $\forall x$ and $\exists x$ apply only to the statement that comes immediately after them. Thus, the formula $\forall x P(x) \to Q(x)$ strictly means $(\forall x P(x)) \to Q(x)$, not $\forall x(P(x) \to Q(x))$.

Translating Natural Language to Quantificational Logic

  • "Everyone/Everything": Generally indicates a universal quantifier.

  • Example: "Everything in that store is either overpriced or poorly made" translates to $\forall x(S(x) \to (O(x) \lor P(x)))$. Notice the common pattern of a universal quantifier applied to a conditional statement to restrict the logical claim to a specific category.

  • "Someone/Something": Indicates an existential quantifier.

  • Example: "Someone didn't do the homework" translates to $\exists x \lnot H(x)$.

  • "Nobody/Nothing": Indicates the negation of an existential statement.

  • Example: "Nobody's perfect" translates to $\lnot \exists x P(x)$.

  • Set Definitions: The subset relation $A \subseteq B$ translates symbolically to $\forall x(x \in A \to x \in B)$.

The Order of Multiple Quantifiers

When a statement contains multiple quantifiers, the order in which they appear fundamentally changes the meaning and truth value of the statement.

  • $\forall x \exists y (x + y = 5)$: "For every $x$, there is a corresponding $y$ that makes the equation true." This evaluates to True for real numbers, as $y$ can always be $5 - x$.

  • $\exists y \forall x (x + y = 5)$: "There is a single specific value of $y$ that works for all values of $x$." This evaluates to False for real numbers.

  • In plain English, if $L(x, y)$ means "$x$ likes $y$", then $\forall x \exists y L(x, y)$ means "Everyone likes someone," whereas $\exists y \forall x L(x, y)$ means "There is someone who is universally liked".

Key Takeaways

  • The universal quantifier ($\forall$) asserts a condition holds for every element in a universe, while the existential quantifier ($\exists$) asserts it holds for at least one element.

  • Quantifiers bind the variable immediately following them; their scope extends only to the adjacent statement unless parentheses explicitly group a larger compound statement.

  • Natural language statements about classes of objects (e.g., "All men have brown hair") are typically modeled using a universal quantifier applied to a conditional statement (e.g., $\forall x(M(x) \to B(x))$).

  • The sequence of mixed quantifiers (e.g., $\forall x \exists y$ vs. $\exists y \forall x$) is strictly non-commutative and completely alters the logical assertion being made.

References

How_to_Prove_It_A_Structured_Approach_Daniel_J_Velleman_z_library.pdf (p, 55)

notes.html:
Sets

Some of these topic are discussed in a different way in Algebra Essentials

Definition

A set is a collection of objects called elements or members of that set. The empty set (denoted $\emptyset$) is the set with no elements.

There are a few symbols that are super helpful to know as a shorthand, and will be used throughout the course. Let $S$ be a set. Then:

Symbol Meaning Symbol Meaning
$a \in S$ "$a$ is an element in $S$" $\exists$ "there exists"
$a \notin S$ "$a$ is not an element in $S$" $\exists!$ "there exists a unique"
$\forall$ "for all" $\Rightarrow$ "implies"
$:=$ "define" $\Leftrightarrow$ "if and only if"

Definition: Set Relations

We want to relate different sets, and thus we get the following notation/definitions:

  1. A set $A$ is a subset of $B$, $A \subset B$, if every element of $A$ is in $B$: Given $A \subset B$, if $a \in A \Rightarrow a\in B$.
  2. Two sets $A$ and $B$ are equal, $A = B$, if $A \subset B$ and $B \subset A$.
  3. A set $A$ is a proper subset of $B$, $A \subsetneq B$ if $A \subset B$ and $A \not= B$.

Set Building Notation

$$ \{x \in A \;|\; P(x)\} \quad \text{or} \quad \{x\;|\;P(x)\} $$ Which means "all $x\in A$ that satisfies property $P(x)$".

Examples

  1. The set of natural numbers: $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,4,...\}$
  2. The set of integers: $\mathbb{Z}=\{0,1,-1,2,-2,3,-3,...\}$
  3. The set of rational numbers: $\mathbb{Q}=\{\frac{m}{n}\;|\;m,n\in \mathbb{Z}\;\text{ and }\; n\not=0\}$
  4. The set of real numbers: $\mathbb{R}$.
  5. Odd numbers: $\{2n+1\;|\;n \in \mathbb{N}\}=\{1,3,5,...\}$

It follows: $$ \mathbb{N} \;\subset \;\mathbb{Z}\; \subset\; \mathbb{Q}\; \subset\; \mathbb{R}\; (\subset \mathbb{C}) $$

Problem

How do we Describe $\mathbb{R}$?

Check: Cantor’s Remarkable Theorem and the Rationals’ Lack of the Least Upper Bound Property and The Characterization of the Real Numbers to find out

Definitions

  1. The union of $A$ and $B$ is the set $A\cup B=\{x\;|\;x\in A \; \text{ or } \; x\in B\}$.
  2. The intersection of $A$ and $B$ is the set $A\cap B=\{x\;|\;x\in A \; \text{ and } \; x\in B\}$.
  3. The set difference of $A$ and $B$ is the set $A\setminus B=\{x\in A \; | \; x\not \in B\}$.
  4. The complement of $A$ is the set $A^c=\{x \;|\; x \not \in A\}$.
  5. $A$ and $B$ are disjoint if $A\cap B=\emptyset$

Theorem: De Morgan's Laws

If $A,B,C$ are sets then:

  1. $(B \cup C)^c=B^c\cap C^c$ ,
  2. $(B \cap C)^c=B^c\cup C^c$ ,
  3. $A\setminus (B \cup C) = (A\setminus B) \cap (A\setminus C)$ ,
  4. $A\setminus (B \cap C) = (A\setminus B) \cup (A\setminus C)$ .

Proof:

$\blacksquare$ this black square means the end of a proof.

Proof of (1): $(B \cup C)^c = B^c \cap C^c$

We must prove $(B\cup C)^c \subseteq B^c \cap C^c$ and $B^c \cap C^c \subseteq (B \cup C)^c$

$$\begin{aligned} > x \in (B \cup C)^c &\Rightarrow x \notin B \cup C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \notin B \;\text{ and }\; x \notin C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in B^c \;\text{ and }\; x \in C^c \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in B^c \cap C^c \\ > \text{Thus, }(B \cup C)^c &\subseteq B^c \cap C^c > \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} > x \in B^c \cap C^c &\Rightarrow x \in B^c \;\text{ and }\; x \in C^c \\ > &\Rightarrow x \notin B \;\text{ and }\; x \notin C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \notin B \cup C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in (B \cup C)^c \\ > \text{Thus, }B^c \cap C^c &\subseteq (B \cup C)^c \qquad \blacksquare > \end{aligned}$$

Proof of (2): $(B \cap C)^c = B^c \cup C^c$

We must prove $(B\cap C)^c \subseteq B^c \cup C^c$ and $B^c \cup C^c \subseteq (B \cap C)^c$

$$\begin{aligned} > x \in (B \cap C)^c &\Rightarrow x \notin B \cap C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \notin B \;\text{ or }\; x \notin C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in B^c \;\text{ or }\; x \in C^c \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in B^c \cup C^c \\ > \text{Thus, }(B \cap C)^c &\subseteq B^c \cup C^c > \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} > x \in B^c \cup C^c &\Rightarrow x \in B^c \;\text{ or }\; x \in C^c \\ > &\Rightarrow x \notin B \;\text{ or }\; x \notin C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \notin B \cap C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in (B \cap C)^c \\ > \text{Thus, }B^c \cup C^c &\subseteq (B \cap C)^c \qquad \blacksquare > \end{aligned}$$

Proof of (3): $A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)$

We must prove $A\setminus(B\cup C) \subseteq (A\setminus B)\cap(A\setminus C)$ and $(A\setminus B)\cap(A\setminus C) \subseteq A\setminus(B\cup C)$

$$\begin{aligned} > x \in A \setminus (B \cup C) &\Rightarrow x \in A \;\text{ and }\; x \notin B \cup C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in A \;\text{ and }\; x \notin B \;\text{ and }\; x \notin C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in A\setminus B \;\text{ and }\; x \in A\setminus C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in (A\setminus B) \cap (A\setminus C) \\ > \text{Thus, } A\setminus(B\cup C) &\subseteq (A\setminus B)\cap(A\setminus C) > \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} > x \in (A\setminus B)\cap(A\setminus C) &\Rightarrow x \in A\setminus B \;\text{ and }\; x \in A\setminus C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in A,\; x\notin B \;\text{ and }\; x\notin C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in A \;\text{ and }\; x \notin B\cup C \\ > &\Rightarrow x \in A\setminus(B\cup C) \\ > \text{Thus, }(A\setminus B)\cap(A\setminus C) &\subseteq A\setminus(B\cup C) \qquad \blacksquare > \end{aligned}$$

Proof of (4): $A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)$

We must prove $A\setminus(B\cap C) \subseteq (A\setminus B)\cup(A\setminus C)$ and $(A\setminus B)\cup(A\setminus C) \subseteq A\setminus(B\cap C)$

$$\begin{aligned} > x \in A\setminus(B\cap C) &\Rightarrow x\in A \;\text{ and }\; x \notin B\cap C \\ > &\Rightarrow x\in A \;\text{ and }\; (x\notin B \;\text{ or }\; x\notin C) \\ > &\Rightarrow (x\in A \;\text{ and }\; x\notin B) \;\text{ or }\;(x\in A \;\text{ and }\; x\notin C) \\ > &\Rightarrow x\in A\setminus B \;\text{ or }\; x\in A\setminus C \\ > &\Rightarrow x\in (A\setminus B)\cup(A\setminus C) \\ > \text{Thus, }A\setminus(B\cap C) &\subseteq (A\setminus B)\cup(A\setminus C) > \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} > x\in(A\setminus B)\cup(A\setminus C) &\Rightarrow x\in A\setminus B \;\text{ or }\; x\in A\setminus C \\ > &\Rightarrow (x\in A,\;x\notin B) \;\text{ or }\;(x\in A,\;x\notin C) \\ > &\Rightarrow x\in A \;\text{ and }\;(x\notin B \;\text{ or }\; x\notin C) \\ > &\Rightarrow x\in A \;\text{ and }\; x\notin B\cap C \\ > &\Rightarrow x\in A\setminus(B\cap C) \\ > \text{Thus, }(A\setminus B)\cup(A\setminus C) &\subseteq A\setminus(B\cap C) \qquad \blacksquare > \end{aligned}$$

see also: Mathematical Induction

References

  • mit-18-100-lecture 1.pdf (BASIC SET THEORY)
  • https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/resources/18100a-lecture-1-multicammp4/

notes.excerpt: --- Complex Expressions in Set-Builder Notation Set-builder notation can be modified by placing a complex expression before the vertical line instead of a single variable. For example, $\{n^2 \mid n \
notes.html:
Complex Expressions in Set-Builder Notation

  • Set-builder notation can be modified by placing a complex expression before the vertical line instead of a single variable.

  • For example, $\{n^2 \mid n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ defines the set of all perfect squares.

  • This notation logically translates to an elementhood test containing an existential quantifier: $\{n^2 \mid n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ means the same thing as $\{x \mid \exists n \in \mathbb{N},\quad(x = n^2)\}$.

Families of Sets & Indexing

  • Sets that contain other sets as their elements are called families of sets.

  • When the elements of a set are identified by a numbered system or an index set $I$, the set is called an indexed family.

  • The general form for an indexed family $A$ is $\{x_i \mid i \in I\}$.

  • Logically, $x \in \{x_i \mid i \in I\}$ is equivalent to $\exists i \in I, \,(x = x_i)$.

Power Sets

Power Set

  • The power set of a set $A$, denoted $\mathcal{P}(A)$, is the set whose elements are all the subsets of $A$.

  • The formal definition is $\mathcal{P}(A) = \{x \mid x \subseteq A\}$.

Evaluating a Power Set

  • If $A = \{7, 12\}$, its subsets are $\emptyset, \{7\}, \{12\}$, and $\{7, 12\}$.

  • Therefore, the power set is $\mathcal{P}(A) = \{\emptyset, \{7\}, \{12\}, \{7, 12\}\}$.

  • The power set of the empty set, $\mathcal{P}(\emptyset)$, contains exactly one element: $\{\emptyset\}$. Note that $\{\emptyset\}$ is a set with one element, meaning it is not the same as $\emptyset$.

Unions and Intersections of Families

We can generalize intersection and union operations to apply to entire families of sets.

Intersection and Union of a Family of Sets

Suppose $\mathcal{F}$ is a family of sets:

  • Intersection ($\cap \mathcal{F}$): The set containing elements that all sets in $\mathcal{F}$ have in common.

  • $\cap \mathcal{F} = \{x \mid \forall A \in \mathcal{F},\,(x \in A)\} = \{x \mid \forall A,\,(A \in \mathcal{F} \to x \in A)\}$.

  • Union ($\cup \mathcal{F}$): The set containing elements that belong to at least one set in $\mathcal{F}$.

  • $\cup \mathcal{F} = \{x \mid \exists A \in \mathcal{F},\,(x \in A)\} = \{x \mid \exists A,\,(A \in \mathcal{F} \land x \in A)\}$.

If the family of sets is an indexed family denoted as $\mathcal{F} = \{A_i \mid i \in I\}$, an alternative mathematical notation is used:

  • Intersection: $\cap_{i \in I} A_i = \{x \mid \forall i \in I(x \in A_i)\}$.

  • Union: $\cup_{i \in I} A_i = \{x \mid \exists i \in I(x \in A_i)\}$.

Analyzing Complex Statements

When writing out the meaning of complex mathematical statements in logical symbols, a good rule of thumb is to always start by applying the definition of the "outermost" symbol first.

Key Takeaways

  • Set-builder notation can accommodate expressions before the vertical bar, which implicitly introduces an existential quantifier to define elementhood.

  • The power set $\mathcal{P}(A)$ collects all subsets of $A$ into a new set, meaning the elementhood test for $x \in \mathcal{P}(A)$ is $x \subseteq A$.

  • Unions and intersections can be applied to entire families of sets, utilizing universal ($\forall$) and existential ($\exists$) quantifiers respectively to define elementhood.

  • Indexed notation (using an index set $I$) streamlines the representation of large or infinite families of sets and their corresponding unions ($\cup_{i \in I} A_i$) and intersections ($\cap_{i \in I} A_i$).

References

notes.html:
1.4 Operations on Sets

Set operations define the truth sets of compound statements such as $P(x) \land Q(x)$, $P(x) \lor Q(x)$, and $\lnot P(x)$.

Basic Set Operations
  • Intersection ($A \cap B$): $\{x \mid x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}$. Elements common to both sets.
  • Union ($A \cup B$): $\{x \mid x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$. Elements in either $A$ or $B$, inclusive.
  • Difference ($A \setminus B$): $\{x \mid x \in A \text{ and } x \notin B\}$. The set resulting from starting with $A$ and removing any elements also in $B$.
  • Symmetric Difference ($A \triangle B$): $(A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A) = (A \cup B) \setminus (A \cap B)$. Elements in either $A$ or $B$, but not both.

Venn Diagram References:

Universe of discourse $U$ containing sets $A$ and $B$.
$A \cap B$ shaded.
$A \cup B$ shaded.
$A \setminus B$ shaded.
$A \triangle B$ shaded.
Computing Operations

Let $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ and $B = \{2, 4, 6, 8, 10\}$.

  • $A \cap B = \{2, 4\}$.
  • $A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10\}$.
  • $A \setminus B = \{1, 3, 5\}$.
  • $(A \cup B) \setminus (A \cap B) = \{1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10\}$.

Translating Between Sets and Logic

Set operations ($\cap, \cup, \setminus$) parallel the logical connectives ($\land, \lor, \lnot$) via elementhood tests.

  • Truth set of $P(x) \land Q(x)$ evaluates to $A \cap B$.
  • Truth set of $P(x) \lor Q(x)$ evaluates to $A \cup B$.
  • Truth set of $\lnot P(x)$ evaluates to $U \setminus A$ (where $U$ is the universe of discourse).
Syntax Constraint

Logical connectives combine statements; set operations combine sets. Expressions like $A \land B$ or $P(x) \cap Q(x)$ are meaningless and invalid.

Deriving Set Identities via Logic

Convert the set operation into its logical elementhood test, apply established logical equivalences (like De Morgan's Laws or Distributive Laws), and translate back to set notation.

Example 1.4.4: Deriving an Identity

Show the logical equivalence for $x \in A \setminus (B \cap C)$: $x \in A \setminus (B \cap C)$ $\iff x \in A \land \lnot(x \in B \cap C)$ (definition of $\setminus$) $\iff x \in A \land \lnot(x \in B \land x \in C)$ (definition of $\cap$) $\iff x \in A \land (x \notin B \lor x \notin C)$ (De Morgan's law) $\iff (x \in A \land x \notin B) \lor (x \in A \land x \notin C)$ (Distributive law) $\iff (x \in A \setminus B) \lor (x \in A \setminus C)$ (definition of $\setminus$) $\iff x \in (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)$ (definition of $\cup$). This proves $A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)$.

Venn diagram of three sets $A, B, C$ demonstrating this distributive behavior.

Subsets and Disjoint Sets

Subsets and Disjoint Sets
  • Subset ($A \subseteq B$): Every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$.
  • Disjoint: $A$ and $B$ have no elements in common, meaning $A \cap B = \emptyset$.

Venn Diagram References:

To prove sets are disjoint, translate to logic to expose a contradiction.

  • Evaluate $x \in (A \cap B) \cap (A \setminus B)$.
  • $\iff (x \in A \land x \in B) \land (x \in A \land x \notin B)$.
  • $\iff x \in A \land (x \in B \land x \notin B)$.
  • Because $x \in B \land x \notin B$ is a contradiction, the statement is always false, proving $(A \cap B) \cap (A \setminus B) = \emptyset$.
Theorem 1.4.7

For any sets $A$ and $B$, $(A \cup B) \setminus B \subseteq A$. Proof. We must show that if something is an element of $(A \cup B) \setminus B$, then it must also be an element of $A$. Suppose $x \in (A \cup B) \setminus B$. This means $x \in A \cup B$ and $x \notin B$, or in other words $(x \in A \lor x \in B) \land x \notin B$. Notice that these statements have the logical form $P \lor Q$ and $\lnot Q$. From these premises, we can logically conclude that $P$ (or $x \in A$) must be true. Thus, anything that is an element of $(A \cup B) \setminus B$ must also be an element of $A$, so $(A \cup B) \setminus B \subseteq A$. $\blacksquare$

Key Takeaways

  • Set operations ($\cap, \cup, \setminus$) manipulate truth sets using the exact same underlying logic as compound statements ($\land, \lor, \lnot$).
  • Set identities can be rigorously proven by expanding elementhood tests into logic, applying known laws (e.g., De Morgan's), and restructuring back into set notation.
  • Mathematical proofs concerning relations like disjointness or subsets rely entirely on reducing the definitions to logical arguments (often seeking a contradiction or a forced logical conclusion).

References

How_to_Prove_It_A_Structured_Approach_Daniel_J_Velleman_z_library.pdf (p, 34)

notes.html:
Variables and Sets

In mathematical reasoning, it is often necessary to make statements about objects represented by letters called variables. If a statement involves a variable $x$, we often write it as $P(x)$ to stress that it is a statement about $x$, which makes it easy to talk about substituting specific values (e.g., $P(7)$ means plugging $7$ in for $x$). Statements can include multiple variables representing different kinds of objects, such as $D(p, q)$, and these statements can be combined using the standard logical connectives.

When evaluating these statements, their truth values often depend on the specific values of the variables involved. To formally manage this, we use concepts from set theory.

Basic Set Notation

A set is a collection of objects, which are called the elements of the set.

  • The simplest way to specify a set is by listing its elements between braces, such as $\{3, 7, 14\}$.
  • The symbol $\in$ means "is an element of" (e.g., $7 \in \{3, 7, 14\}$).
  • The symbol $\notin$ means "is not an element of" (e.g., $11 \notin \{3, 7, 14\}$).
  • A set is completely determined by its elements; the order in which elements are listed does not matter, and listing an element multiple times does not change the set.

For sets with infinitely many elements, or elements that follow a specific pattern, we can use an elementhood test rather than an explicit list.

$$B = \{x \mid x \text{ is a prime number}\}$$

This notation is read as "the set of all $x$ such that $x$ is a prime number". The statement "$x$ is a prime number" acts as the elementhood test; any value of $x$ that makes this statement come out true passes the test and is an element of the set.

Free and Bound Variables

When defining sets using elementhood tests, it is important to distinguish how variables function within the expression.

  • In the statement $y \in \{x \mid x^2 < 9\}$, $y$ is a free variable, while $x$ is a bound variable (or dummy variable).
  • Free variables stand for objects that the statement says something about; plugging in different values for a free variable affects the meaning and truth value of the statement.
  • Bound variables are simply letters used as a convenience to help express an idea, and do not stand for any particular object. The notation $\{x \mid \dots\}$ binds the variable $x$.
  • Bound variables can always be replaced by new variables, or eliminated altogether, without changing the meaning of the statement (e.g., $y \in \{x \mid x^2 < 9\}$ means the exact same thing as $y^2 < 9$). In general, $y \in \{x \mid P(x)\}$ means the same thing as $P(y)$.

Truth Sets and Universes of Discourse

To distinguish the values of a free variable $x$ that make a statement $P(x)$ true from those that make it false, we collect them into a set.

Truth Set

The truth set of a statement $P(x)$ is the set of all values of $x$ that make the statement $P(x)$ true. It is defined by using the statement $P(x)$ as an elementhood test: Truth set of $P(x) = \{x \mid P(x)\}$.

When statements contain free variables, it is usually clear from context what kind of objects those variables stand for. The set of all possible values for the variables is called the universe of discourse for the statement, and we say that the variables range over this universe.

Standard Universes of Discourse

Mathematical notation frequently utilizes standard names for common universes of discourse:

  • $\mathbb{R} = \{x \mid x \text{ is a real number}\}$
  • $\mathbb{Q} = \{x \mid x \text{ is a rational number}\}$
  • $\mathbb{Z} = \{x \mid x \text{ is an integer}\} = \{\dots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$
  • $\mathbb{N} = \{x \mid x \text{ is a natural number}\} = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$

These letters can be followed by a superscript $+$ or $-$ to restrict the set to only positive or negative numbers (e.g., $\mathbb{R}^+$ for positive real numbers). To explicitly restrict a truth set to a specific universe $U$, we write $\{x \in U \mid P(x)\}$. This notation means that among the elements of $U$, only those that pass the elementhood test $P(x)$ will actually be in the truth set. In general, $y \in \{x \in A \mid P(x)\}$ means the same thing as $y \in A \land P(y)$.

The Empty Set

If $P(x)$ is a tautology (always true), its truth set encompasses the entire universe $U$. Conversely, if $P(x)$ is a contradiction (always false for every possible value of $x$), nothing can pass the elementhood test, meaning the truth set has no elements.

The Empty Set

Because a set is completely determined once its elements are specified, there is only one set that has no elements. It is called the empty set, or the null set, and is often denoted $\emptyset$. Alternatively, it can be written as $\{ \}$.

Empty Set Notation Traps
  • The statement $x \in \emptyset$ is an example of a statement that is always false, no matter what $x$ is.
  • The notation $\{\emptyset\}$ is not correct notation for the empty set. Just as $2$ and $\{2\}$ are not the same thing, $\emptyset$ is not the same as $\{\emptyset\}$. The first is a set with no elements, whereas the second is a set with exactly one element (that element being the empty set itself).

Key Takeaways

  • Sets represent collections of objects and are primarily defined either explicitly using braces (e.g., $\{3, 7\}$) or conceptually using elementhood tests (e.g., $\{x \mid P(x)\}$).
  • In set-builder notation like $\{x \mid P(x)\}$, $x$ acts as a bound variable that can be substituted without altering the meaning, while variables in the statement outside the set-builder are free variables.
  • The set of all valid values that a variable can take is its universe of discourse (e.g., $\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}$); appending constraints like $x \in \mathbb{R}$ directly into the definition restricts the truth set to that universe.
  • A set containing absolutely zero elements is uniquely identified as the empty set ($\emptyset$ or $\{ \}$); a statement checking for elementhood within the empty set ($x \in \emptyset$) evaluates as a logical contradiction.

References

How_to_Prove_It_A_Structured_Approach_Daniel_J_Velleman_z_library.pdf (p, 26)
