notes.html:
The Seven Functions Used in Algorithm Analysis

Definitions & Properties

Algorithm analysis uses seven fundamental functions to characterize execution growth rates: Constant ($1$), Logarithmic ($\log n$), Linear ($n$), $n$-log-$n$ ($n \log n$), Quadratic ($n^2$), Cubic ($n^3$), and Exponential ($b^n$).

1. Summary of Fundamental Functions

The table below summarizes the seven primary functions used to measure algorithm running times.

Function Class Formula Typical Algorithm Context
Constant $f(n) = c$ Basic primitive operations (addition, variable assignment, comparison).
Logarithmic $f(n) = \log_b n$ Repeatedly dividing a problem or input in half (default base $b=2$).
Linear $f(n) = n$ Processing each of $n$ elements in an array or sequence.
$n$-log-$n$ $f(n) = n \log n$ Comparison-based sorting algorithms (e.g., optimal sorting bounds).
Quadratic $f(n) = n^2$ Nested loops over an $n$-element container.
Cubic $f(n) = n^3$ Multi-level nested loops or 3D grid processing.
Exponential $f(n) = b^n$ Brute-force search over all possible combinations (default base $b=2$).

2. Logarithm Rules and Identities

The logarithm function is defined as $x = \log_b n \iff b^x = n$ for base $b > 1$. By convention in computer science, $\log n = \log_2 n$.

Ceiling Approximation

For integer $n$, $\lceil \log_b n \rceil$ represents the number of times $n$ can be divided by $b$ before the result becomes $\le 1$.

  • $\lceil \log_3 27 \rceil = 3 \quad ((27/3)/3)/3 = 1$
  • $\lceil \log_4 64 \rceil = 3 \quad ((64/4)/4)/4 = 1$
  • $\lceil \log_2 12 \rceil = 4 \quad (((12/2)/2)/2)/2 = 0.75 \le 1$

Proposition 3.1 (Logarithm Rules)

For real numbers $a > 0$, $b > 1$, $c > 0$, and $d > 1$:

$$\begin{aligned} \log_b(ac) &= \log_b a + \log_b c \\ \log_b(a/c) &= \log_b a - \log_b c \\ \log_b(a^c) &= c \log_b a \\ \log_b a &= \frac{\log_d a}{\log_d b} \\ b^{\log_d a} &= a^{\log_d b} \end{aligned}$$

Base Conversion Formula

To calculate base-2 logarithms on standard base-10 calculators:

$$\log_2 n = \frac{\text{LOG } n}{\text{LOG } 2}$$

3. Polynomials & Arithmetic Summations

General Polynomial Definition

A polynomial function of degree $d$ with coefficients $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_d$ ($a_d \neq 0$) is defined as:

$$f(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} a_i n^i = a_0 + a_1 n + a_2 n^2 + \dots + a_d n^d$$

Proposition 3.3 (Arithmetic Progression Sum)

Nested loops where the inner loop step count increases by 1 each iteration result in an arithmetic summation:

$$1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + (n-1) + n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$$

Evaluating $\frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{n^2}{2} + \frac{n}{2}$ confirms a quadratic $O(n^2)$ growth rate.

Figure 3.3

4. Exponential Functions & Geometric Series

Exponent Rules

For positive integers $a$, $b$, and $c$:

$$\begin{aligned} (b^a)^c &= b^{ac} \\ b^a b^c &= b^{a+c} \\ \frac{b^a}{b^c} &= b^{a-c} \end{aligned}$$

  • Fractional Exponents: $b^{a/c} = \sqrt[c]{b^a}$
  • Negative Exponents: $b^{-d} = \frac{1}{b^d}$

Proposition 3.5 (Geometric Sums)

For integer $n \ge 0$ and real number $a > 0$ ($a \neq 1$):

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} a^i = 1 + a + a^2 + \dots + a^n = \frac{a^{n+1} - 1}{a - 1}$$

For base $a = 2$, the sum of the first $n$ powers of 2 equals:

$$1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + \dots + 2^{n-1} = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} 2^i = 2^n - 1$$

This value represents the largest integer representable in binary using $n$ bits.

References

Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 120)

notes.html:
Low-Level and Referential Arrays

Definitions & Properties

An array is a contiguous collection of memory cells used to store related variables in sequence. In Python, sequence types are implemented either as referential arrays (which store memory addresses referencing objects elsewhere in memory) or compact arrays (which store the raw bit representations of elements directly in contiguous bytes).

1. Low-Level Memory Architecture

Computer memory consists of binary bits grouped into 8-bit units called bytes. Each byte is identified by a unique integer called its memory address.

Figure 5.1

Random Access Memory (RAM)

Hardware architecture permits access to any memory byte in $O(1)$ time based directly on its memory address.

Array Memory Address Calculation

If an array starts at base memory address $\text{start}$ and each cell occupies $\text{cellsize}$ bytes, the memory address of index $i$ is computed in $O(1)$ arithmetic:

$$\text{Address}(A[i]) = \text{start} + (\text{cellsize} \cdot i)$$

Figure 5.2
Figure 5.3

2. Referential Arrays

Python lists and tuples do not store data values directly inside the array structure. Instead, they store a contiguous sequence of fixed-length memory addresses (object references) pointing to the actual objects.

  • On typical 64-bit systems, each address cell uses 8 bytes (64 bits) regardless of the size or type of the object referenced.

  • Enables lists to store heterogeneous elements and variable-length data (such as strings of arbitrary size).

Figure 5.4

Slicing and Shallow Copying

Slicing a sequence (e.g., temp = primes[3:6]) constructs a brand-new list instance. However, the cells of the new list point to the exact same element instances as the original list (shallow copy).

Figure 5.5
Figure 5.6
primes = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]

temp = primes[3:6]

print(temp)

temp[2]= 15

print(primes)

primes = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]
temp = primes[3:6]  # references elements 7, 11, 13

print(temp)

# reassigning an index in temp redirects the pointer to a new object
temp[2] = 15  # primes remains unchanged because integers are immutable

print(primes)

Reference Aliasing and Repetition

Initializing a list using multiplication (e.g., counters = [0] * 8) creates 8 cells that all point to the single integer object 0 in memory.

Figure 5.7
Figure 5.8

Reassigning an element creates a new integer instance and binds only that specific index to the new address:

counters = [0] * 8  # all 8 cells reference id(0)
print(counters)

# immutable update reassigns only index 2
counters[2] += 1  # creates integer 1, assigns reference to counters[2]
print(counters)

The extend Method

The extend method appends references to existing objects from another sequence to the end of a list without creating copies of those objects.

Figure 5.9
primes = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]
extras = [23, 29, 31]

primes.extend(extras)  # primes now contains references to objects in extras
print(primes)

3. Compact Arrays

Compact arrays store raw data directly as contiguous bytes rather than using separate pointer references. Text strings in Python are primary examples of compact arrays.

Figure 5.10

Performance and Memory Comparison

Feature Referential Array (list, tuple) Compact Array (str, array)
Cell Content 64-bit memory address Primary binary data
Memory Consumption High (64-bit pointer + object headers) Low (only the raw bytes for the data type)
Data Types Heterogeneous objects allowed Homogeneous primitive types only
CPU Cache Locality Poor (elements scattered across heap) Excellent (contiguous memory blocks)

4. Python array Module

The standard library array module provides compact storage for homogeneous primitive C data types.

Table 5.1: Type Codes Supported by the array Module

Code C Data Type Typical Size (Bytes)
'b' signed char 1
'B' unsigned char 1
'u' Unicode char 2 or 4
'h' signed short int 2
'H' unsigned short int 2
'i' signed int 2 or 4
'I' unsigned int 2 or 4
'l' signed long int 4
'L' unsigned long int 4
'f' float 4
'd' float (double precision) 8

Practical Memory Footprint Comparison

import sys
from array import array

# create identical sequences of 1000 integers
num_list = list(range(1000))
compact_arr = array('i', range(1000))

# memory consumption comparison
print("List reference array size (bytes):", sys.getsizeof(num_list))
print("Compact array buffer size (bytes):", sys.getsizeof(compact_arr))
Low-Level Custom Arrays

The array module does not support user-defined composite types. Creating compact arrays of arbitrary structs requires the lower-level ctypes module (see Section 5.3.1).

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 185)

notes.html:
Dynamic Arrays & Amortized Analysis

Definitions & Properties

A dynamic array resolves the limitation of fixed-capacity hardware arrays by allocating a larger array and migrating existing elements when the current capacity is exhausted. Python’s list class relies on dynamic array abstraction. Amortized analysis proves that occasional expensive reallocation operations are offset by a sequence of cheap insertions, yielding $O(1)$ average time per operation.

import sys

data = []
for k in range(n):
	a = len(data)
	b = sys.getsizeof(data)
	print(f'Length: {a}, Size in Bytes: {}')
	data.append(None)

1. Dynamic Array Mechanics

When creating a low-level array, the precise size must be declared to allocate consecutive memory. If capacity is exhausted during an append, the dynamic array executes the following reallocation protocol:

  1. Allocate a new array $B$ with larger capacity.

  2. Set $B[i] = A[i]$ for $i = 0, \dots, n-1$, where $n$ is the current number of items.

  3. Set $A = B$, replacing the old array reference.

  4. Insert the new element into the new array.

Figure 5.12

Python DynamicArray Implementation

import ctypes

class DynamicArray:
    """A dynamic array class akin to a simplified Python list."""
    
    def __init__(self):
        """Create an empty array."""
        self._n = 0                                    # count actual elements
        self._capacity = 1                             # default array capacity
        self._A = self._make_array(self._capacity)     # low-level array
        
    def __len__(self):
        """Return number of elements stored in the array."""
        return self._n
        
    def __getitem__(self, k):
        """Return element at index k."""
        if not 0 <= k < self._n:
            raise IndexError('invalid index')
        return self._A[k]                              # retrieve from array
        
    def append(self, obj):
        """Add object to end of the array."""
        if self._n == self._capacity:                  # not enough room
            self._resize(2 * self._capacity)           # so double capacity
        self._A[self._n] = obj
        self._n += 1
        
    def insert(self, k , value):
	    if self._n == self._capacity:
		    self._resize(2 * self._capacity)
		for j in range(self._n, k, -1):
			self._A[j] = self._A[j-1]
		self._A[k] = value
		self._n += 1
		
	def remove(self, value):
		''' Remove first occurence of value (or raise ValueError)'''
		for k in range(self._n):
			if self._A[k] == value:
				for j in range(k, self._n-1):
					self._A[j] = self._A[j+1]
				self._A[self._n-1] = None
				self._n -= 1
				return
		return ValueError('value not found')	 
        
    def _resize(self, c):                              # nonpublic utility
        """Resize internal array to capacity c."""
        B = self._make_array(c)                        # new (bigger) array
        for k in range(self._n):                       # for each existing value
            B[k] = self._A[k]
        self._A = B                                    # use the bigger array
        self._capacity = c
        
    def _make_array(self, c):                          # nonpublic utility
        """Return new array with capacity c."""
        return (c * ctypes.py_object)()                # see ctypes documentation

2. Amortized Analysis of Appends

The strategy of geometric capacity expansion (e.g., doubling the capacity when full) guarantees that $n$ append operations execute in $O(n)$ total time, yielding an amortized $O(1)$ time per append.

Proposition 5.1 (Geometric Expansion)

Let $S$ be a sequence implemented by means of a dynamic array with initial capacity one, using the strategy of doubling the array size when full. The total time to perform a series of $n$ append operations in $S$, starting from $S$ being empty, is $O(n)$.

Proof by Accounting Method (Cyber-Dollars)

Assume 1 cyber-dollar pays for inserting one element.

  • Charge each append operation 3 cyber-dollars.

  • 1 dollar pays for the immediate insertion.

  • 1 dollar is stored with the newly inserted element to pay for its future relocation.

  • 1 dollar is stored with an older element (from the first half of the array) to pay for its future relocation.

When the array overflows at size $2^i$, there are exactly $2^{i-1}$ elements inserted since the last resize. These $2^{i-1}$ elements carry 2 dollars each, perfectly covering the cost to relocate all $2^i$ elements into the new array. Because the maximum charge per operation is constant ($3$), the total time for $n$ operations is bounded by $3n \implies O(n)$.

Figure 5.14

3. The Pitfall of Arithmetic Progression

Resizing the array by a fixed constant increment $c$ (e.g., adding 100 cells at a time) destroys the amortized $O(1)$ bound.

Proposition 5.2 (Arithmetic Expansion)

Performing a series of $n$ append operations on an initially empty dynamic array using a fixed increment with each resize takes $\Omega(n^2)$ time.

Justification

During a series of $n$ appends, resizing occurs at capacities $c, 2c, 3c, \dots, mc$ where $m = \lceil n/c \rceil$. The time spent copying elements during resize events forms an arithmetic summation (see Proposition 3.3):

$$\sum_{i=1}^{m} ci = c \sum_{i=1}^{m} i = c \frac{m(m+1)}{2} \ge c \frac{\left(\frac{n}{c}\right)\left(\frac{n}{c} + 1\right)}{2} \ge \frac{n^2}{2c}$$

Therefore, the total time is $\Omega(n^2)$.

Figure 5.15

4. Python's List Class Behavior

Python's built-in list class relies on dynamic arrays but employs an internal expansion formula rather than pure geometric doubling to balance memory usage and run-time efficiency.

Empirical testing confirms the $O(1)$ amortized cost:

from time import time

def compute_average(n):
    """Perform n appends to an empty list and return average time elapsed."""
    data = []
    start = time()                             # record the start time (in seconds)
    for k in range(n):
        data.append(None)
    end = time()                               # record the end time (in seconds)
    return (end - start) / n                   # compute average per operation

Table 5.2: Average running time of append

n 100 1,000 10,000 100,000 1,000,000 10,000,000 100,000,000
$\mu s$ per operation $0.219$ $0.158$ $0.164$ $0.151$ $0.147$ $0.147$ $0.149$
Memory Usage and Shrinking

Repeatedly removing elements from a dynamic array can leave it mostly empty while retaining a large memory capacity. Robust implementations must occasionally shrink the underlying array while avoiding oscillation (e.g., shrinking only when capacity falls below $25\%$).

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 192)

notes.html:
Python Sequence Operations & Complexity

Definitions & Properties

Python's built-in sequence classes (list, tuple, str) provide a variety of standard behaviors. Nonmutating behaviors do not change the underlying sequence and are supported by both list and tuple. Mutating behaviors alter the sequence contents and are exclusively supported by the mutable list class.

1. Nonmutating Operations (Lists & Tuples)

Tuples are typically more memory efficient than lists because their immutability negates the need for dynamic array surplus capacity. Both classes share identical asymptotic efficiencies for nonmutating operations.

Table 5.3: Asymptotic Performance of Nonmutating Behaviors

Let $n, n_1, n_2$ be lengths of respective sequences. Let $k$ denote the index of the leftmost occurrence of a searched value (or $n$ if absent).

Operation Syntax Running Time Explanation
Length len(data) $O(1)$
 Retrieves cached instance state variable.
Index Access data[j] $O(1)$ Direct memory address calculation via offset.
Index Lookup data.index(value) $O(k + 1)$
 Iterates left-to-right until match is found.
Containment value in data $O(k + 1)$
 Short-circuits loop immediately upon finding match.
Comparison data1 == data2 $O(k + 1)$ Lexicographical evaluation stops at first mismatched index $k$.
Slicing data[j:k] $O(k - j + 1)$
 Instantiates a new sequence proportional to the slice length.
Concatenation data1 + data2 $O(n_1 + n_2)$
 Creates a new sequence copying all elements from both operands.
Repetition c * data $O(cn)$
 Creates a new sequence of total length $c \cdot n$.

2. Mutating Operations (Lists Only)

Mutating operations alter the structure or contents of a list. Operations that insert or delete elements may trigger an $O(n)$ dynamic array resize or require shifting subsequent elements in memory.

Table 5.4: Asymptotic Performance of Mutating Behaviors

Operation Syntax Running Time Explanation
Assignment data[j] = val $O(1)$ Replaces object reference at index $j$; no shifting required.
Append data.append(val) $O(1)^*$ Amortized cost; occasionally requires $O(n)$ reallocation.
Insert data.insert(k, val) $O(n - k + 1)^*$ Amortized reallocation; shifts $n - k$ elements rightward.
Pop End data.pop() $O(1)^*$ Amortized; removes last element without shifting.
Pop Index data.pop(k) $O(n - k)^*$ Amortized; shifts $n - k$ elements leftward to fill gap.
Delete Index del data[k] $O(n - k)^*$ Same shifting mechanics as pop(k).
Remove Value data.remove(val) $O(n)^*$ Iterates up to index $k$ to find match, then shifts $n - k$ elements.
Extend data1.extend(data2) $O(n_2)^*$ Highly optimized amortized bulk append; resizes array at most once.
Reverse data.reverse() $O(n)$ Swaps $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ pairs in-place.
Sort data.sort() $O(n \log n)$ Uses Timsort algorithm (hybrid merge/insertion sort).

(Asterisk $*$ denotes an amortized running time bound.)

Figure 5.16
Figure 5.17

Insertion Efficiency (Table 5.5)

Empirical testing confirms insert(k, val) execution time depends directly on the location of $k$:

  • Beginning ($k = 0$): Slowest ($\Omega(n)$); shifts all elements.

  • Middle ($k = n // 2$): Faster ($\Omega(n)$); shifts half the elements.

  • End ($k = n$): Fastest ($O(1)$ amortized); behaves identically to append.

List Extension

While data.extend(other) and a for loop calling data.append() both run in proportional time, extend is significantly faster in practice:

  1. Implemented natively in compiled C code, minimizing interpreter loop overhead.

  2. Computes final capacity needed and performs at most one underlying array reallocation.

3. Python's String Class

Strings (str) are compact arrays of characters and are immutable.

Naive String Concatenation Trap

Concatenating strings iteratively creates a new string instance per loop, leading to catastrophic quadratic $O(n^2)$ behavior:

# WARNING: O(n^2) running time
letters = ''
for c in document:
    if c.isalpha():
        letters += c  # creates a new string instance each iteration

(Note: Some Python interpreters apply a runtime optimization if letters has no other references, temporarily mutating the string, but this behavior is not guaranteed).

Optimal String Composition Methods

For guaranteed $O(n)$ execution, construct a temporary list of characters and use "".join().

Method 1: List Construction

temp = []
for c in document:
    if c.isalpha():
        temp.append(c)          # O(1) amortized
letters = ''.join(temp)         # O(n) final string composition

Method 2: List Comprehension

letters = ''.join([c for c in document if c.isalpha()])

Method 3: Generator Expression (Most Memory Efficient)

letters = ''.join(c for c in document if c.isalpha())

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 202)

notes.excerpt: --- Array Applications & Insertion Sort [!info] Definitions & Properties Array-based sequences support practical storage, sorting, and transformation tasks. Managing ordered collections with fixed cap
notes.html:
Array Applications & Insertion Sort

Definitions & Properties Array-based

sequences support practical storage, sorting, and transformation tasks. Managing ordered collections with fixed capacity requires shifting elements during insertion, a mechanic shared by both high-score boards and insertion sort. Cryptographic substitution leverages character-to-index conversions and modulo arithmetic over contiguous arrays.

1. Storing High Scores (Scoreboard Application)

Maintaining a ranked list of game scores illustrates fixed-capacity array management.

The GameEntry Class

The GameEntry class encapsulates a player's name and score.

class GameEntry:
    """Represents one entry of a list of high scores."""

    def __init__(self, name, score):
        self._name = name
        self._score = score

    def get_name(self):
        return self._name

    def get_score(self):
        return self._score

    def __str__(self):
        return '({0}, {1})'.format(self._name, self._score)  # e.g., '(Bob, 98)'

The Scoreboard Class

A Scoreboard maintains entries in non-increasing order up to a fixed maximum capacity.

Figure 5.18
class Scoreboard:
    """Fixed-length sequence of high scores in nondecreasing order."""

    def __init__(self, capacity=10):
        """Initialize scoreboard with given maximum capacity.

        All entries are initially None.
        """
        self._board = [None] * capacity        # reserve space for future scores
        self._n = 0                            # number of actual entries

    def __getitem__(self, k):
        """Return entry at index k."""
        return self._board[k]

    def __str__(self):
        """Return string representation of the high score list."""
        return '\n'.join(str(self._board[j]) for j in range(self._n))

    def add(self, entry):
        """Consider adding entry to high scores."""
        score = entry.get_score()

        # Does new entry qualify as a high score?
        # Answer is yes if board not full or score is higher than last entry
        good = self._n < len(self._board) or score > self._board[-1].get_score()

        if good:
            if self._n < len(self._board):      # no score drops from list
                self._n += 1                   # so overall number increases

            # shift lower scores rightward to make room for new entry
            j = self._n - 1
            while j > 0 and self._board[j - 1].get_score() < score:
                self._board[j] = self._board[j - 1]  # shift entry from j-1 to j
                j -= 1                               # and decrement j
            self._board[j] = entry                   # when done, add new entry
Figure 5.19

Insertion and Shifting Mechanics

  • Qualification: A score qualifies if the board is not full ($n < \text{capacity}$) or if it exceeds the lowest recorded score ($score > \text{board}[-1].\text{get\_score()}$).

  • Rightward Shifting: Lower scores shift rightward by one position starting from the tail to avoid overwriting elements.

  • Worst-Case Cost: When an entry becomes the highest score, all $n$ existing entries shift rightward, taking $O(n)$ time.

2. Sorting a Sequence: Insertion-Sort

Insertion-sort iteratively places each element into its proper position within an already sorted prefix.

High-Level Algorithm Trace

  1. Consider the first element $A[0]$ sorted.

  2. For each element $A[k]$ from $k = 1$ to $n - 1$, cache $A[k]$ in variable cur.

  3. Shift elements greater than cur in subarray $A[0 \dots k-1]$ rightward by one cell.

  4. Insert cur into the resulting vacancy.

def insertion_sort(A):
    """Sort list of comparable elements into nondecreasing order."""
    for k in range(1, len(A)):         # from 1 to n-1
        cur = A[k]                     # current element to be inserted
        j = k                          # find correct index j for current
        while j > 0 and A[j - 1] > cur: # element A[j-1] must be after current
            A[j] = A[j - 1]
            j -= 1
        A[j] = cur                     # cur is now in the right place
Figure 5.20

Complexity Analysis

The running time depends on the initial order of elements:

  • Worst-Case: If the array is in reverse order, each step $k$ shifts all $k$ preceding elements:

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k = \frac{(n-1)n}{2} \implies O(n^2)$$

  • Best-Case: If the array is already sorted, the while loop condition A[j - 1] > cur evaluates to False immediately on every pass. The algorithm performs no element shifts and completes in $O(n)$ time.

3. Simple Cryptography: The Caesar Cipher

The Caesar cipher is an ancient substitution cipher that shifts each uppercase Latin letter by a fixed rotation value $r$.

Modular Arithmetic Equations

Let index $i \in \{0, 1, \dots, 25\}$ represent letters $\text{A}$ through $\text{Z}$.

$$\text{Encryption: } C = (i + r) \pmod{26}$$ $$\text{Decryption: } P = (i - r) \pmod{26}$$

Character-to-Index Conversion

Python uses Unicode code points to compute array offsets:

  • ord(c) returns the integer code point for character c.

  • chr(j) returns the character for code point j.

  • Letter index: $j = \text{ord}(c) - \text{ord}(\text{'A'})$.

Figure 5.21
class CaesarCipher:
    """Class for doing encryption and decryption using a Caesar cipher."""

    def __init__(self, shift):
        """Construct Caesar cipher using given integer shift for rotation."""
        encoder = [None] * 26                  # temp array for encryption
        decoder = [None] * 26                  # temp array for decryption
        for k in range(26):
            encoder[k] = chr((k + shift) % 26 + ord('A'))
            decoder[k] = chr((k - shift) % 26 + ord('A'))
        self._forward = ''.join(encoder)       # will store as string
        self._backward = ''.join(decoder)      # since fixed

    def encrypt(self, message):
        """Return string representing encrypted message."""
        return self._transform(message, self._forward)

    def decrypt(self, secret):
        """Return decrypted message given encrypted secret."""
        return self._transform(secret, self._backward)

    def _transform(self, original, code):
        """Utility to perform transformation based on given code string."""
        msg = list(original)
        for k in range(len(msg)):
            if msg[k].isupper():
                j = ord(msg[k]) - ord('A')     # index from 0 to 25
                msg[k] = code[j]               # replace this character
        return ''.join(msg)

4. Algorithmic Comparison

Application Primary Data Structure Key Array Operation Best-Case Time Worst-Case Time Auxiliary Space
Scoreboard Insertion Fixed-capacity list Backward scan and rightward element shift $O(1)$ $O(n)$ $O(1)$
Insertion-Sort Dynamic array / list In-place shifting within sorted prefix $O(n)$ $O(n^2)$ $O(1)$
Caesar Cipher Lookup strings / character list Array indexing via offset arithmetic $O(n)$ $O(n)$ $O(n)$

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 210)

notes.html:
Multidimensional Data & Matrices

A two-dimensional array is often called a matrix. It is accessed using two indices, $i$ (row) and $j$ (column), which are traditionally zero-indexed in computer science. $$M = \begin{bmatrix} data[0][0] & \dots & data[0][c-1] \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ data[r-1][0] & \dots & data[r-1][c-1] \end{bmatrix}$$

In Python, the most common representation for a 2D array is a list of lists.

# Example: 8 rows, 10 columns
# Accessing row 1, column 3:
value = data[1][3]

Constructing a Multidimensional List (The Aliasing Trap)

CRITICAL ENGINEERING CONCEPT: Reference Aliasing

When creating a list of lists, you must ensure each row is an independent instance. If you use the multiplication operator * on a list of lists, you create multiple references to the same underlying list object. Modifying one row will modify all rows.

Comparison of Initialization Methods

Method Code Syntax Result Verdict
1D Flattened data = ([0] * c) * r Creates a single 1D list of length $r \cdot c$. ❌ Wrong Structure
Aliasing (Shallow) data = [[0] * c] * r Creates $r$ references to the same inner list. data[0] is data[1] is True. ❌ Dangerous Bug
List Comprehension data = [[0] * c for j in range(r)] Creates $r$ distinct, independent secondary lists. ✅ Correct
The Rule for 2D Lists

Always use list comprehension to initialize multidimensional lists to guarantee independent memory allocation for each row.

# Correct way to initialize an r x c matrix of zeros
data = [[0] * c for j in range(r)]

Two-Dimensional Arrays and Positional Games

Positional games (like Tic-Tac-Toe, Chess, Checkers) naturally map to 2D arrays.

Tic-Tac-Toe Implementation

Representation: A $3 \times 3$ list of lists of characters.

  • 'X' or 'O': Player moves.
  • ' ': Empty space.
# Internal representation of a board state
board = [
    ['O', 'X', 'O'], 
    [' ', 'X', ' '], 
    [' ', 'O', 'X']
]

Complete Python Class Implementation

Design Pattern

This class manages state and rules, but does not contain AI strategy. It separates game logic from game playing.

class TicTacToe:
    """Management of a Tic-Tac-Toe game (does not do strategy)."""

    def __init__(self):
        """Start a new game."""
        self._board = [[' '] * 3 for j in range(3)] # Independent rows!
        self._player = 'X'

    def mark(self, i, j):
        """Put an X or O mark at position (i,j) for next player's turn."""
        if not (0 <= i <= 2 and 0 <= j <= 2):
            raise ValueError('Invalid board position')
        if self._board[i][j] != ' ':
            raise ValueError('Board position occupied')
        if self.winner() is not None:
            raise ValueError('Game is already complete')
        
        self._board[i][j] = self._player
        if self._player == 'X':
            self._player = 'O'
        else:
            self._player = 'X'

    def _is_win(self, mark):
        """Check whether the board configuration is a win for the given player."""
        board = self._board # local variable for shorthand
        return (
            mark <mark> board[0][0] </mark> board[0][1] == board[0][2] or  # row 0
            mark <mark> board[1][0] </mark> board[1][1] == board[1][2] or  # row 1
            mark <mark> board[2][0] </mark> board[2][1] == board[2][2] or  # row 2
            mark <mark> board[0][0] </mark> board[1][0] == board[2][0] or  # col 0
            mark <mark> board[0][1] </mark> board[1][1] == board[2][1] or  # col 1
            mark <mark> board[0][2] </mark> board[1][2] == board[2][2] or  # col 2
            mark <mark> board[0][0] </mark> board[1][1] == board[2][2] or  # diag
            mark <mark> board[0][2] </mark> board[1][1] == board[2][0]     # rev diag
        )

    def winner(self):
        """Return mark of winning player, or None to indicate a tie."""
        for mark in 'XO':
            if self._is_win(mark):
                return mark
        return None

    def __str__(self):
        """Return string representation of current game board."""
        rows = ['|'.join(self._board[r]) for r in range(3)]
        return '\n-----\n'.join(rows)

Usage Example

game = TicTacToe()

# X moves
game.mark(1, 1);  game.mark(0, 2)  # O moves
game.mark(2, 2);  game.mark(0, 0)
game.mark(0, 1);  game.mark(2, 1)
game.mark(1, 2);  game.mark(1, 0)
game.mark(2, 0)

print(game)
winner = game.winner()
if winner is None:
    print('Tie')
else:
    print(winner, 'wins!')

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 210)

notes.html:
Recursion Fundamentals & Examples

Definitions & Properties

Recursion is a technique in which a function calls itself during its execution. A recursive algorithm requires one or more base cases (conditions evaluated nonrecursively) and one or more recursive cases (steps that reduce progress toward a base case). An activation record (or frame) stores the function's namespace, local variables, and current instruction pointer during invocation.

1. The Factorial Function

The factorial function $n!$ represents the number of permutations of $n$ distinct elements. It is formally defined for any integer $n \ge 0$ as:

$$n! = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } n = 0 \\ n \cdot (n - 1)! & \text{if } n \ge 1 \end{cases}$$

Component Condition Behavior
Base Case $n = 0$ Returns $1$ directly without further recursive calls.
Recursive Case $n \ge 1$ Reduces the subproblem size to $n - 1$ and computes $n \cdot \text{factorial}(n - 1)$. 
def factorial(n):
    """Return the factorial of a nonnegative integer."""
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    else:
        return n * factorial(n - 1)
`factorial(5)`

Function Execution via the Call Stack

Each call creates an activation record in memory. Calling a nested invocation suspends the caller until the callee returns its value.

Stack Stage Active Activation Records Call Stack State
Descent (Unwinding) factorial(4) $\to$ factorial(3) $\to$ $\dots$ $\to$ factorial(0) Frames accumulate; each caller waits for its subproblem result.
Base Evaluation factorial(0) Returns $1$ without generating additional frames.
Ascent (Winding) Resolves arithmetic: $1 \cdot 1 = 1$, $2 \cdot 1 = 2$, $3 \cdot 2 = 6$, $4 \cdot 6 = 24$ Activation frames are popped in reverse order (LIFO).

2. Drawing an English Ruler

The markings of an English ruler exhibit a self-similar fractal structure. For each inch, a major tick line is drawn. Between whole inches, minor ticks are placed at intervals of $1/2$ inch, $1/4$ inch, and smaller powers of two.

Figure 4.2

Interval Decomposition Logic

An interval with a central tick length $L \ge 1$ decomposes into three consecutive steps:

  1. Draw top interval of central tick length $L - 1$.
  2. Draw single central tick line of length $L$.
  3. Draw bottom interval of central tick length $L - 1$.
def draw_line(tick_length, tick_label=''):
    """Draw one line with given tick length (followed by optional label)."""
    line = '-' * tick_length
    if tick_label:
        line += ' ' + tick_label
    print(line)

def draw_interval(center_length):
    """Draw tick interval based upon a central tick length."""
    if center_length > 0:                   # stop when length drops to 0
        draw_interval(center_length - 1)    # recursively draw top ticks
        draw_line(center_length)            # draw center tick
        draw_interval(center_length - 1)    # recursively draw bottom ticks

def draw_ruler(num_inches, major_length):
    """Draw English ruler with given number of inches, major tick length."""
    draw_line(major_length, '0')            # draw inch 0 line
    for j in range(1, 1 + num_inches):
        draw_interval(major_length - 1)     # draw interior ticks for inch
        draw_line(major_length, str(j))     # draw inch j line and label
`draw_interval(3)`

3. Binary Search

Binary search locates a target value within a sorted, indexable sequence of $n$ elements in $O(\log n)$ time, compared to $O(n)$ time for sequential search.

Figure 4.4

Candidate Interval Partitioning

The candidate range is defined by two indices, $\text{low}$ and $\text{high}$. The midpoint index is computed as:

$$\text{mid} = \lfloor (\text{low} + \text{high}) / 2 \rfloor$$

Case Condition Search Decision
Termination (Unsuccessful) $\text{low} > \text{high}$ Range is empty; returns False.
Termination (Successful) $\text{target} == \text{data}[\text{mid}]$ Value located; returns True.
Recur Left $\text{target} < \text{data}[\text{mid}]$ Restrict search interval to $[\text{low}, \text{mid} - 1]$.
Recur Right $\text{target} > \text{data}[\text{mid}]$ Restrict search interval to $[\text{mid} + 1, \text{high}]$. 
def binary_search(data, target, low, high):
    """Return True if target is found in indicated portion of a Python list.

    The search only considers the portion from data[low] to data[high] inclusive.
    """
    if low > high:
        return False                        # interval is empty; no match
    else:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if target == data[mid]:
            return True                     # found a match
        elif target < data[mid]:
            return binary_search(data, target, low, mid - 1)
        else:
            return binary_search(data, target, mid + 1, high)
Example of a binary search for target value 22

4. File Systems & Cumulative Disk Usage

File systems have a recursive hierarchy where directories can contain files and sub-directories nested to arbitrary depth.

Figure 4.7

Disk Space Calculation Rule

The cumulative disk space for entry $P$ equals its immediate disk usage plus the cumulative space of all nested child entries:

$$\text{cumulative\_space}(P) = \text{immediate\_space}(P) + \sum_{C \in \text{children}(P)} \text{cumulative\_space}(C)$$

Python os Module Methods

Method Return Type Description
os.path.getsize(path) int Returns the immediate disk usage of the file or directory in bytes.
os.path.isdir(path) bool Evaluates to True if the path designates a directory; False otherwise.
os.listdir(path) list[str] Returns entry names contained within the target directory.
os.path.join(path, filename) str Joins path components using the operating system directory separator. 
import os

def disk_usage(path):
    """Return the number of bytes used by a file/folder and any descendants."""
    total = os.path.getsize(path)                  # account for direct usage
    if os.path.isdir(path):                        # if this is a directory
        for filename in os.listdir(path):          # then for each child:
            childpath = os.path.join(path, filename)
            total += disk_usage(childpath)         # add child's usage to total

    print('{0:<7}'.format(total), path)            # descriptive output
    return total
Figure 4.8

References

Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 150)

notes.excerpt: --- Analyzing Recursive Algorithms [!info] Definitions & Properties To analyze the running time of a recursive algorithm, account for the primitive operations executed within each individual activatio
notes.html:
Analyzing Recursive Algorithms

Definitions & Properties

To analyze the running time of a recursive algorithm, account for the primitive operations executed within each individual activation frame. The overall running time is the sum of operations performed across all activations in the recursion trace.

1. Activation Accounting Framework

Analyzing a recursive function requires determining two quantities:

  1. The total number of recursive invocations (activation frames).
  2. The number of primitive operations performed within each activation frame (excluding subsequent recursive calls).

$$\text{Total Operations} = \sum_{\text{all activations } A} \text{Operations}(A)$$

2. Factorial Function Analysis

Computing factorial(n) (Section 4.1.1, Code Fragment 4.1) begins with parameter $n$ and decrements by 1 until reaching the base case $0$.

Metric Analysis Complexity
Total Activations $n + 1$ frames (factorial(n) down to factorial(0)) $O(n)$
Work per Activation Constant number of primitive operations (condition check, subtraction, multiplication) $O(1)$
Total Running Time $(n + 1) \cdot O(1)$ $O(n)$

3. English Ruler Output Analysis

Section 4.1.2 defines draw_interval(c), where $c$ denotes the central tick length. The overall work is proportional to the total number of lines drawn.

Proposition 4.1

For $c \ge 0$, a call to draw_interval(c) results in precisely $2^c - 1$ lines of output.

Proof by Induction (see Section 3.4.3)

  • Base Case ($c = 0$): draw_interval(0) executes no calls to draw_line. $$2^0 - 1 = 1 - 1 = 0 \text{ lines}$$

  • Inductive Step ($c > 0$): draw_interval(c) executes two calls to draw_interval(c - 1) and one call to draw_line(c). Assuming the claim holds for $c - 1$:

$$\text{Lines}(c) = 1 + 2 \cdot (2^{c-1} - 1) = 1 + 2^c - 2 = 2^c - 1$$

Recurrence Relation

The recurrence relation for the line count is $T(c) = 2T(c - 1) + 1$ with $T(0) = 0$. Solving this recurrence yields an exponential running time of $O(2^c)$ (see Section 12.2.4).

4. Binary Search Analysis

Binary search (Section 4.1.3, Code Fragment 4.3) searches a sorted sequence of $n$ elements by halving the candidate range at each invocation.

Proposition 4.2

The binary search algorithm runs in $O(\log n)$ time for a sorted sequence with $n$ elements.

Proof & Candidate Interval Bounds

Let the number of candidate entries be $\text{high} - \text{low} + 1$. With each recursive invocation, the midpoint index $\text{mid} = \lfloor (\text{low} + \text{high}) / 2 \rfloor$ reduces the search space:

$$\begin{aligned} (\text{mid} - 1) - \text{low} + 1 &= \left\lfloor \frac{\text{low} + \text{high}}{2} \right\rfloor - \text{low} \le \frac{\text{high} - \text{low} + 1}{2} \\ \text{high} - (\text{mid} + 1) + 1 &= \text{high} - \left\lfloor \frac{\text{low} + \text{high}}{2} \right\rfloor \le \frac{\text{high} - \text{low} + 1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Recursive Stage Maximum Remaining Candidates
Initial invocation ($j = 0$) $n$
After Call 1 ($j = 1$) $n / 2$
After Call 2 ($j = 2$) $n / 4$
After Call $j$ $n / 2^j$

In the worst-case (unsuccessful search), recursion terminates when candidate entries drop below 1:

$$\frac{n}{2^r} < 1 \implies 2^r > n \implies r > \log n$$

The maximum number of recursive calls is:

$$r = \lfloor \log n \rfloor + 1$$

Each call executes $O(1)$ operations, yielding an overall running time of $O(\log n)$.

5. File System Disk Usage Analysis

The disk_usage algorithm (Section 4.1.4, Code Fragment 4.5) computes cumulative disk usage for $n$ file-system entries.

Total Activation Invocations

Exactly $n$ recursive calls to disk_usage occur. Each entry $e$ is encountered exactly once inside the for loop of its unique parent directory.

Global Counting Argument (Amortized Analysis)

A superficial bound assumes each directory can contain up to $n - 1$ entries, leading to a loose estimate of $O(n)$ work per call $\times n$ calls = $O(n^2)$ time.

The tight upper bound is established by analyzing total loop iterations across the entire execution:

Operation Category Scope Across Entire Execution Aggregate Running Time
Outside Loop Executed once per activation frame ($n$ calls total, each doing $O(1)$ work) $O(n)$
Inside Loop Iterates over each directory child; exactly $n - 1$ total iterations across all frames $O(n)$
Total Running Time $\sum \text{Outside Loop} + \sum \text{Inside Loop}$ $O(n)$
Amortization and Tree Traversals

Evaluating the cumulative work of loop iterations across all recursive frames rather than assuming the worst case for each individual invocation is an amortized argument (see Section 5.3). The file-system hierarchy is a tree data structure, and disk_usage performs an $O(n)$ tree traversal (see Chapter 8, Section 8.4).

6. Algorithmic Complexity Comparison

Algorithm Input Parameter / Size Metric Total Recursive Activations Operations per Activation Frame Total Asymptotic Running Time
factorial(n) Integer $n$ $n + 1$ $O(1)$ $O(n)$
draw_interval(c) Tick length $c$ $2^{c+1} - 1$ $O(1)$ $O(2^c)$
binary_search Sequence length $n$ $\le \lfloor \log n \rfloor + 1$ $O(1)$ $O(\log n)$
disk_usage Total file-system entries $n$ $n$ Variable (amortized $O(1)$) $O(n)$

References

Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 161)

notes.html:
Recursion Run Amok

Definitions & Properties

Recursive algorithms become inefficient when subproblems overlap or when calls branch repeatedly without reducing problem size. Infinite recursion occurs when recursive calls fail to reach a base case, ultimately consuming system resources and exhausting available call-stack memory.

1. Exponential Call Branching

Poorly designed recursion can cause an explosion in the number of function calls, turning simple linear problems into exponential-time algorithms.

Element Uniqueness via Binary Branching

Section 3.3.3 introduced the element uniqueness problem. The implementation in Code Fragment 4.6 attempts to solve it by testing if the first $n - 1$ elements are unique, the last $n - 1$ elements are unique, and the first and last elements differ.

def unique3(S, start, stop):
    """Return True if there are no duplicate elements in slice S[start:stop]."""
    if stop - start <= 1:
        return True                             # at most one item
    elif not unique3(S, start, stop - 1):
        return False                            # first part has duplicate
    elif not unique3(S, start + 1, stop):
        return False                            # second part has duplicate
    else:
        return S[start] != S[stop - 1]          # do first and last differ?
Inefficiency of `unique3`

A problem of size $n$ triggers two subproblems of size $n - 1$, which trigger four subproblems of size $n - 2$, and so on. The total number of invocations follows a geometric progression (see Proposition 3.5): $$1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + 2^{n-1} = 2^n - 1$$

Since each call takes $O(1)$ nonrecursive work, the overall running time is $O(2^n)$.

Inefficient Fibonacci Numbers

The mathematical definition of the $n$-th Fibonacci number is:

$$\begin{aligned} F_0 &= 0 \\ F_1 &= 1 \\ F_n &= F_{n-2} + F_{n-1} \quad \text{for } n > 1 \end{aligned}$$

Directly translating this formula into a binary recursive function causes massive recalculation of identical subproblems (see Code Fragment 4.7).

def bad_fibonacci(n):
    """Return the nth Fibonacci number."""
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    else:
        return bad_fibonacci(n - 2) + bad_fibonacci(n - 1)

Let $c_n$ denote the total number of calls required to compute bad_fibonacci(n):

$n$ Recursive Expansion of Call Count $c_n$ Total Call Invocations ($c_n$)
0 Base case ($n = 0$) $1$
1 Base case ($n = 1$) $1$
2 $1 + c_0 + c_1 = 1 + 1 + 1$ $3$
3 $1 + c_1 + c_2 = 1 + 1 + 3$ $5$
4 $1 + c_2 + c_3 = 1 + 3 + 5$ $9$
5 $1 + c_3 + c_4 = 1 + 5 + 9$ $15$
6 $1 + c_4 + c_5 = 1 + 9 + 15$ $25$
7 $1 + c_5 + c_6 = 1 + 15 + 25$ $41$
8 $1 + c_6 + c_7 = 1 + 25 + 41$ $67$

The number of calls more than doubles every two indices ($c_4 > 2c_2$, $c_6 > 2c_4$). In general:

$$c_n > 2^{n/2}$$

The overall running time is exponential in $n$, making bad_fibonacci unusable even for moderate values like $n = 50$.

2. Linear Recursion Optimization

To compute Fibonacci numbers efficiently, avoid duplicating work by returning a pair of consecutive values $(F_n, F_{n-1})$, using the convention $F_{-1} = 0$.

def good_fibonacci(n):
    """Return pair of Fibonacci numbers, (F(n), F(n-1))."""
    if n <= 1:
        return (n, 0)
    else:
        (a, b) = good_fibonacci(n - 1)
        return (a + b, a)

print(good_fibonacci(8))
Metric bad_fibonacci(n) good_fibonacci(n)
Recursion Pattern Binary recursion (two recursive calls per non-base invocation) Linear recursion (one recursive call per invocation)
Total Invocations Exponential: $c_n > 2^{n/2}$ Linear: $n$ calls
Work per Call $O(1)$ $O(1)$
Time Complexity $O(2^n)$ $O(n)$
Space (Call Stack) $O(n)$ activation frames $O(n)$ activation frames

3. Maximum Recursive Depth in Python

Section 4.3.1 examines infinite recursion. An infinite recursion occurs when recursive calls fail to make progress toward a base case.

def fib(n):
    return fib(n)  # infinite recursion: no base case

Subtle bugs also cause infinite recursion. In binary search (see Section 4.1.3, Code Fragment 4.3), if the right-half recursive call is erroneously written as:

return binary_search(data, target, mid, high)  # incorrect: should use mid + 1

Searching a two-element range can result in a recursive call on the exact same interval, triggering infinite recursion.

Call Stack Limits and Reconfiguration

To prevent unbounded stack growth from exhausting system memory, Python sets an artificial limit on the number of simultaneous active activation records (typically 1000). Exceeding this limit causes the interpreter to raise an exception:

RuntimeError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
  • Logarithmic algorithms (e.g., binary_search) have a recursive depth of $O(\log n)$ and never hit this limit during practical use ($2^{1000}$ exceeds the number of atoms in the universe).
  • Linear recursive algorithms with depth proportional to $n$ will hit the 1000-call limit on modest inputs.

The recursion limit can be inspected and updated dynamically using the sys module:

import sys

old_limit = sys.getrecursionlimit()     # returns current limit (e.g., 1000)
sys.setrecursionlimit(1000000)          # reconfigures limit to 1,000,000 frames

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 165)

notes.excerpt: --- Recursion Patterns (Linear, Binary, Multiple) [!info] Definitions & Properties Recursive algorithms are classified by the maximum number of recursive invocations initiated from a single execution
notes.html:
Recursion Patterns (Linear, Binary, Multiple)

Definitions & Properties

Recursive algorithms are classified by the maximum number of recursive invocations initiated from a single execution frame:

  • Linear Recursion: Each invocation makes at most one recursive call.
  • Binary Recursion: An invocation makes two recursive calls.
  • Multiple Recursion: An invocation may make three or more recursive calls.

1. Linear Recursion

In linear recursion, each execution step initiates at most one recursive subproblem. The recursion trace forms a single sequential chain of activation records.

Structural vs. Asymptotic Terminology

The term "linear" describes the linear chain structure of the recursion trace, not the algorithm's asymptotic complexity. For example, binary search (see Section 4.1.3) is an instance of linear recursion that executes in $O(\log n)$ time.

Summing Elements Recursively

To sum an array $S$ of $n$ numbers, define the sum of $n = 0$ elements as $0$, and for $n > 0$, add the last element $S[n - 1]$ to the recursive sum of the first $n - 1$ elements.

Figure 4.9
def linear_sum(S, n):
    """Return the sum of the first n numbers of sequence S."""
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    else:
        return linear_sum(S, n - 1) + S[n - 1]
Figure 4.10

Computing linear_sum(S, n) requires $n + 1$ function calls. With $O(1)$ operations per activation, the algorithm executes in $O(n)$ time and requires $O(n)$ auxiliary space to maintain $n + 1$ simultaneous stack frames.

Reversing a Sequence

A sequence $S$ of length $n$ is reversed by swapping its first and last elements, then recursively reversing the remaining inner slice $S[\text{start} + 1 : \text{stop} - 1]$.

def reverse(S, start, stop):
    """Reverse elements in implicit slice S[start:stop]."""
    if start < stop - 1:                                # at least 2 elements
        S[start], S[stop - 1] = S[stop - 1], S[start]  # swap first and last
        reverse(S, start + 1, stop - 1)                 # recur on rest
Figure 4.11

The recursion terminates under two implicit base cases:

  • $\text{start} == \text{stop}$: Implicit slice is empty ($n$ is even).
  • $\text{start} == \text{stop} - 1$: Implicit slice contains one element ($n$ is odd).

The interval $\text{stop} - \text{start}$ decreases by $2$ at each step. The function terminates after $1 + \lfloor n / 2 \rfloor$ invocations, yielding $O(n)$ running time and $O(n)$ call-stack space.

Computing Powers

The power function $x^n$ for an integer $n \ge 0$ can be computed using two distinct recursive formulations:

1. Trivial Linear Formulation

$$x^n = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } n = 0 \\ x \cdot x^{n-1} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

def power(x, n):
    """Compute the value x**n for integer n."""
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    else:
        return x * power(x, n - 1)

This implementation decrements $n$ by $1$ per call, running in $O(n)$ time and using $O(n)$ stack space across $n + 1$ activation records.

2. Repeated Squaring Formulation

Using integer division $k = \lfloor n / 2 \rfloor$:

$$x^n = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } n = 0 \\ \left(x^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}\right)^2 & \text{if } n > 0 \text{ is even} \\ x \cdot \left(x^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}\right)^2 & \text{if } n > 0 \text{ is odd} \end{cases}$$

def power(x, n):
    """Compute the value x**n for integer n."""
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    else:
        partial = power(x, n // 2)          # rely on truncated division
        result = partial * partial
        if n % 2 == 1:                      # if n is odd, include factor of x
            result *= x
        return result
Figure 4.12
Avoiding Redundant Branching

Computing power(x, n // 2) * power(x, n // 2) without caching intermediate results creates two identical recursive branches, degrading performance back to $O(n)$ time.

Each recursive call halves the exponent $n$, limiting the total number of activations to $1 + \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. The running time drops to $O(\log n)$, and maximum call-stack depth drops to $O(\log n)$.

2. Binary Recursion

In binary recursion, an execution frame initiates two recursive subproblems. Examples include draw_interval (see Section 4.1.2) and bad_fibonacci (see Section 4.3).

Binary Summation

To sum elements in $S[\text{start}:\text{stop}]$, partition the range into two equal sub-intervals at $\text{mid} = \lfloor (\text{start} + \text{stop}) / 2 \rfloor$, recursively sum both halves, and return their addition.

def binary_sum(S, start, stop):
    """Return the sum of the numbers in implicit slice S[start:stop]."""
    if start >= stop:                                   # zero elements in slice
        return 0
    elif start == stop - 1:                             # one element in slice
        return S[start]
    else:                                               # two or more elements
        mid = (start + stop) // 2
        return binary_sum(S, start, mid) + binary_sum(S, mid, stop)
Figure 4.13

Linear Sum vs. Binary Sum

Property linear_sum (Code Fragment 4.9) binary_sum (Code Fragment 4.13)
Recursion Structure Linear (1 call per frame) Binary (2 calls per internal frame)
Total Invocations $n + 1$ calls $2n - 1$ calls (for $n$ a power of 2)
Time Complexity $O(n)$ $O(n)$
Maximum Stack Depth $n + 1$ activation frames $1 + \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ activation frames
Space Complexity $O(n)$ $O(\log n)$

3. Multiple Recursion

Multiple recursion generalizes binary recursion: a single activation frame may spawn three or more recursive calls. The file-system traversal algorithm disk_usage (see Section 4.1.4) uses multiple recursion, generating calls equal to the number of directory children.

Combinatorial Summation Puzzles

Summation puzzles require assigning unique digits ($0, 1, \dots, 9$) to letters such that an arithmetic identity holds:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{pot} + \text{pan} &= \text{bib} \\ \text{dog} + \text{cat} &= \text{pig} \\ \text{boy} + \text{girl} &= \text{baby} \end{aligned}$$

To solve puzzles by exhaustive enumeration, generate all $k$-length ordered subsets from a universe $U$ without repetition.

def PuzzleSolve(k, S, U):
    """Enumerate all k-length extensions to sequence S using elements of set U."""
    for e in list(U):
        S.append(e)
        U.remove(e)                                     # e is now being used
        if k == 1:
            # test whether S solves the puzzle
            if "S solves puzzle":
                print("Solution found:", S)
        else:
            PuzzleSolve(k - 1, S, U)                    # recursive call
        S.pop()                                         # remove e from end of S
        U.add(e)                                        # add e back to unused set U
Figure 4.14

Complexity Analysis

For a universe $U$ of size $m = \vert{}U\vert{}$, an initial call PuzzleSolve(k, S, U) generates a tree where:

  • Level 0 branches $m$ times.
  • Level 1 branches $m - 1$ times.
  • Level $k - 1$ terminates the recursion.

The total number of candidate sequences evaluated is the permutation count:

$$P(m, k) = \frac{m!}{(m - k)!} = m \cdot (m - 1) \cdots (m - k + 1)$$

4. Pattern Summary Matrix

Algorithm Recursion Type Recursive Calls per Step Time Complexity Auxiliary Space (Stack Depth)
linear_sum Linear $1$ $O(n)$ $O(n)$
reverse Linear $1$ $O(n)$ $O(n)$
power (trivial) Linear $1$ $O(n)$ $O(n)$
power (squaring) Linear $1$ $O(\log n)$ $O(\log n)$
binary_search Linear $1$ (from 2 choices) $O(\log n)$ $O(\log n)$
binary_sum Binary $2$ $O(n)$ $O(\log n)$
PuzzleSolve Multiple Up to $\vert{}U\vert{}$ $O(P(\vert{}U\vert{}, k))$ $O(k)$

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 169)

notes.excerpt: --- Recursive Design and Eliminating Tail Recursion [!info] Definitions & Properties Recursive design structures an algorithm into base cases and self-similar subproblems. Tail recursion occurs when t
notes.html:
Recursive Design and Eliminating Tail Recursion

Definitions & Properties

Recursive design structures an algorithm into base cases and self-similar subproblems. Tail recursion occurs when the recursive call is the final operation performed within a function, allowing execution without accumulating activation records after the call returns.

1. Designing Recursive Algorithms

A standard recursive algorithm consists of two mandatory components:

  • Test for base cases: Evaluate one or more stopping conditions that execute nonrecursively. Every execution path must eventually terminate at a base case.
  • Recur: If a base case is not met, perform one or more recursive calls that make strict progress toward a base case.

Parameterizing Recursion

Subproblems often require different boundaries than the original caller specifies. Reparameterizing the function signature allows tracking subproblem state without copying data.

Function Public Interface Recursive Signature Reparameterization Purpose
Binary Search binary_search(data, target) binary_search(data, target, low, high) Demarcates sublists by index boundaries; avoids $O(n)$ list slicing copies.
Sequence Reversal reverse(S) reverse(S, start, stop) Bounds the active slice between start and stop - 1.
Linear Sum linear_sum(S) linear_sum(S, n) Tracks the prefix length $n$ to sum.
Binary Sum binary_sum(S) binary_sum(S, start, stop) Defines interval boundaries for divide-and-conquer splitting.
Fibonacci fibonacci(n) good_fibonacci(n) Strengthens return type to a pair $(F_n, F_{n-1})$ to prevent duplicate calls.
Interface Encapsulation

Exposing low-level index parameters (such as low and high) clutters the public interface. A clean design exposes a user-friendly public function that delegates execution to a nonpublic recursive utility function containing the required parameters.

2. Eliminating Tail Recursion

Definitions & Properties

A recursive call is tail recursive if it is the very last operation executed by the enclosing function, and its return value is immediately returned to the caller. Tail recursion must be linear recursion.

General recursion can be made iterative by explicitly managing a stack data structure (see Section 6.1). However, tail recursion can be eliminated entirely without auxiliary memory.

Tail Recursive vs. Non-Tail Linear Recursion

Function Final Operation Tail Recursive? Reason
binary_search return binary_search(...) Yes Result is returned directly without further computation.
reverse reverse(...) Yes Final statement executes the recursive call; no pending operations.
factorial return n * factorial(n - 1) No Pending multiplication operation after the recursive call returns.
linear_sum return linear_sum(S, n - 1) + S[n - 1] No Pending addition operation after the recursive call returns.
good_fibonacci (a, b) = good_fibonacci(n - 1) No Constructs and returns new tuple (a + b, a) after the call returns.

Mechanical Conversion Pattern

To eliminate tail recursion mechanically:

  1. Enclose the function body in a while loop.
  2. Replace the base-case termination condition with its logical inverse as the loop condition.
  3. Replace each recursive call by reassigning local loop variables to the arguments of that call.

3. Iterative Implementations

Iterative Binary Search

Converting recursive binary_search (Section 4.1.3, Code Fragment 4.3) replaces the base case low > high with the loop condition while low <= high:. Parameter updates replace recursive function invocations.

def binary_search_iterative(data, target):
    """Return True if target is found in the given Python list."""
    low = 0
    high = len(data) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if target == data[mid]:
            return True                         # found a match
        elif target < data[mid]:
            high = mid - 1                      # only consider values left of mid
        else:
            low = mid + 1                       # only consider values right of mid
    return False                                # loop ended without success

Iterative Sequence Reversal

Converting recursive reverse (Section 4.4.1, Code Fragment 4.10) updates start and stop iteratively within a loop until fewer than two elements remain.

def reverse_iterative(S):
    """Reverse elements in sequence S."""
    start, stop = 0, len(S)
    while start < stop - 1:
        S[start], S[stop - 1] = S[stop - 1], S[start]  # swap first and last
        start, stop = start + 1, stop - 1              # narrow the range

Complexity: Recursive vs. Iterative Comparison

Converting tail-recursive algorithms to iterative loops preserves time complexity while eliminating call-stack memory overhead.

Algorithm Implementation Time Complexity Auxiliary Space (Call Stack)
Binary Search Recursive (Code Fragment 4.3) $O(\log n)$ $O(\log n)$ activation records
Iterative (Code Fragment 4.15) $O(\log n)$ $O(1)$ memory
Sequence Reversal Recursive (Code Fragment 4.10) $O(n)$ $O(n)$ activation records
Iterative (Code Fragment 4.16) $O(n)$ $O(1)$ memory
Non-Tail Recursion Iteration

Non-tail linear recursions can also be implemented iteratively with minimal state. For example, computing factorials, summing arrays, or calculating Fibonacci numbers via generators (see Section 1.8) runs in $O(n)$ time using only $O(1)$ auxiliary space.

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 177)

notes.html:
Double-Ended Queues (Deques)

Definitions & Properties

A double-ended queue, or deque (pronounced "deck"), is a linear sequence that supports element insertion and deletion at both endpoints (front and back). The deque ADT is a generalization of both the FIFO queue and LIFO stack abstractions.

1. The Deque Abstract Data Type (ADT)

The deque ADT defines symmetric update operations and accessors for both ends of the sequence.

Method Behavior
D.add_first(e) Inserts element e at the front of deque D.
D.add_last(e) Inserts element e at the back of deque D.
D.delete_first() Removes and returns the first element of D; raises an error if empty.
D.delete_last() Removes and returns the last element of D; raises an error if empty.
D.first() Returns the first element of D without removing it; raises an error if empty.
D.last() Returns the last element of D without removing it; raises an error if empty.
D.is_empty() Returns True if deque D contains no elements, False otherwise.
len(D) Returns the number of elements currently stored in deque D.

Deque Operation Trace (Example 6.5)

Operation Return Value Deque Contents (front↔back)
D.add_last(5) — [5]
D.add_first(3) — [3, 5]
D.add_first(7) — [7, 3, 5]
D.first() 7 [7, 3, 5]
D.delete_last() 5 [7, 3]
len(D) 2 [7, 3]
D.delete_last() 3 [7]
D.delete_last() 7 []
D.add_first(6) — [6]
D.last() 6 [6]
D.add_first(8) — [8, 6]
D.is_empty() False [8, 6]
D.last() 6 [8, 6]

2. Implementing a Deque with a Circular Array

An array-based deque maintains the same three internal state variables as ArrayQueue: _data, _size, and _front.

Modular Index Arithmetic

Given array capacity $N = \text{len}(\text{\_data})$

  • Last Element Index (last):
    $$\text{back} = (\text{\_front} + \text{\_size} - 1) \pmod N$$

  • Prepend Operation (add_first): To insert at the front, shift the front index cyclically to the left: $$\text{\_front}_{\text{new}} = (\text{\_front} - 1) \pmod N$$

  • Append Operation (add_last): Computes the next open slot at the rear:

    $$\text{avail} = (\text{\_front} + \text{\_size}) \pmod N$$

  • Delete Front (delete_first): Advances _front cyclically to the right:

$$\text{\_front}_{\text{new}} = (\text{\_front} + 1) \pmod N$$

class ArrayDeque:
    """Double-ended queue implementation using a circular array."""
    DEFAULT_CAPACITY = 10

    def __init__(self):
        self._data = [None] * ArrayDeque.DEFAULT_CAPACITY
        self._size = 0
        self._front = 0

    def __len__(self):
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self):
        return self._size == 0

    def first(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise Empty('Deque is empty')
        return self._data[self._front]

    def last(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise Empty('Deque is empty')
        back = (self._front + self._size - 1) % len(self._data)
        return self._data[back]

    def add_first(self, e):
        if self._size == len(self._data):
            self._resize(2 * len(self._data))
        self._front = (self._front - 1) % len(self._data)
        self._data[self._front] = e
        self._size += 1

    def add_last(self, e):
        if self._size == len(self._data):
            self._resize(2 * len(self._data))
        avail = (self._front + self._size) % len(self._data)
        self._data[avail] = e
        self._size += 1

    def delete_first(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise Empty('Deque is empty')
        answer = self._data[self._front]
        self._data[self._front] = None
        self._front = (self._front + 1) % len(self._data)
        self._size -= 1
        return answer

    def delete_last(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise Empty('Deque is empty')
        back = (self._front + self._size - 1) % len(self._data)
        answer = self._data[back]
        self._data[back] = None
        self._size -= 1
        return answer

    def _resize(self, cap):
        old = self._data
        self._data = [None] * cap
        walk = self._front
        for k in range(self._size):
            self._data[k] = old[walk]
            walk = (1 + walk) % len(old)
        self._front = 0
Complexity

All core accessors (first, last, is_empty, len) run in $O(1)$ worst-case time. The mutating operations (add_first, add_last, delete_first, delete_last) execute in $O(1)$ amortized time, subject to geometric array resizing.

3. Python's collections.deque

The Python standard library provides an optimized deque implementation via collections.deque.

Table 6.4: Comparison of Deque ADT vs. collections.deque

Our Deque ADT collections.deque Description
len(D) len(D) Number of elements.
D.add_first(e) D.appendleft(e) Add element to beginning.
D.add_last(e) D.append(e) Add element to end.
D.delete_first() D.popleft() Remove and return from beginning.
D.delete_last() D.pop() Remove and return from end.
D.first() D[0] Access first element.
D.last() D[-1] Access last element.
— D[j] Access arbitrary entry by index.
— D[j] = val Modify arbitrary entry by index.
— D.clear() Clear all contents.
— D.rotate(k) Circularly shift elements rightward $k$ steps.
— D.remove(e) Remove first matching element.
— D.count(e) Count occurrences of element e.

Implementation Characteristics

  • Underlying Architecture: collections.deque uses a hybrid data structure composed of a doubly linked list of fixed-length blocks (circular arrays).

  • Performance Profile: Guarantees strict $O(1)$ worst-case time for insertions and deletions at either end (append, appendleft, pop, popleft). Random access near the middle (D[j]) degrades to $O(n)$ time because the underlying linked nodes must be traversed.

  • Bounded Capacity (maxlen): Supports an optional maxlen parameter. When a bounded deque is full, adding an item to one end silently evicts an item from the opposing end without raising an overflow error.

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 247)

notes.excerpt: --- [!info] Definitions & Properties A queue is a linear collection of elements managed under the first-in, first-out (FIFO) principle. Elements enter at the back (rear) and are removed from the front
notes.html:
Definitions & Properties

A queue is a linear collection of elements managed under the first-in, first-out (FIFO) principle. Elements enter at the back (rear) and are removed from the front; the element residing in the queue the longest is always processed first. Common applications include operating system print buffers, web server request pools, customer support call centers, and breadth-first search traversals.

Figure 6.4

1. The Queue Abstract Data Type (ADT)

The queue ADT specifies two fundamental update operations and three auxiliary accessor methods:

Method Behavior
Q.enqueue(e) Inserts element e at the back of queue Q.
Q.dequeue() Removes and returns the element at the front of queue Q; raises an error if Q is empty.
Q.first() Returns a reference to the front element of queue Q without removing it; raises an error if Q is empty.
Q.is_empty() Returns True if queue Q contains no elements, False otherwise.
len(Q) Returns the number of elements currently stored in queue Q.

Queue Operation Trace (Example 6.4)

Operation Return Value Queue Contents ($\text{front} \leftarrow Q \leftarrow \text{back}$)
Q.enqueue(5) — [5]
Q.enqueue(3) — [5, 3]
len(Q) 2 [5, 3]
Q.dequeue() 5 [3]
Q.is_empty() False [3]
Q.dequeue() 3 []
Q.is_empty() True []
Q.dequeue() "error" []
Q.enqueue(7) — [7]
Q.enqueue(9) — [7, 9]
Q.first() 7 [7, 9]
Q.enqueue(4) — [7, 9, 4]
len(Q) 3 [7, 9, 4]
Q.dequeue() 7 [9, 4]

2. Array-Based Implementations & Flawed Approaches

Adapting a Python list to implement a queue naively introduces severe performance bottlenecks:

Flaw 1: The Linear Shift Trap

  • Using L.append(e) for enqueue and L.pop(0) for dequeue causes pop(0) to shift all remaining $n - 1$ elements one cell to the left.

  • Results in an unacceptable worst-case running time of $\Theta(n)$ per dequeue operation.

Flaw 2: The Rightward Drift Memory Leak

  • Setting the dequeued slot to None and advancing an explicit front pointer f achieves $O(1)$ time per dequeue.

  • However, the underlying array continues to expand indefinitely to the right, consuming $O(m)$ memory space where $m$ is the total historical number of enqueued items, even if the queue currently contains only a few active elements.

Figure 6.5

3. Circular Array Representation

To maintain both $O(1)$ time and $O(n)$ proportional memory, the queue is modeled as a circular buffer of fixed capacity $N$, where the indices wrap around to 0 upon reaching the array boundary.

Figure 6.6

Circular Pointer Arithmetic

Given current front index $f$, current element count $\text{size}$, and total buffer capacity $N = \text{len}(\text{data})$:

$$\text{Next Front Index (Dequeue):} \quad f_{\text{new}} = (f + 1) \pmod N$$

$$\text{Next Available Index (Enqueue):} \quad \text{avail} = (f + \text{size}) \pmod N$$

4. Python Implementation (ArrayQueue)

The ArrayQueue class tracks three instance variables:

  • _data: An underlying fixed-length list instance.

  • _size: The current number of elements in the queue.

  • _front: The array index of the current front element.

class Empty(Exception):
    """Error attempting to access an element from an empty container."""
    pass


class ArrayQueue:
    """FIFO queue implementation using a Python list as underlying storage."""
    DEFAULT_CAPACITY = 10          # moderate capacity for all new queues

    def __init__(self):
        """Create an empty queue."""
        self._data = [None] * ArrayQueue.DEFAULT_CAPACITY
        self._size = 0
        self._front = 0

    def __len__(self):
        """Return the number of elements in the queue."""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self):
        """Return True if the queue is empty."""
        return self._size == 0

    def first(self):
        """Return (but do not remove) the element at the front of the queue.

        Raise Empty exception if the queue is empty.
        """
        if self.is_empty():
            raise Empty('Queue is empty')
        return self._data[self._front]

    def dequeue(self):
        """Remove and return the first element of the queue (i.e., FIFO).

        Raise Empty exception if the queue is empty.
        """
        if self.is_empty():
            raise Empty('Queue is empty')
        answer = self._data[self._front]
        self._data[self._front] = None               # help garbage collection
        self._front = (self._front + 1) % len(self._data)
        self._size -= 1
        
        # shrink the underlying array if occupancy falls below 25%
        if 0 < self._size < len(self._data) // 4:
            self._resize(len(self._data) // 2)
            
        return answer

    def enqueue(self, e):
        """Add an element to the back of queue."""
        if self._size == len(self._data):
            self._resize(2 * len(self._data))        # double the array size
        avail = (self._front + self._size) % len(self._data)
        self._data[avail] = e
        self._size += 1

    def _resize(self, cap):                          # cap >= len(self)
        """Resize to a new list of capacity >= len(self)."""
        old = self._data                             # keep track of existing list
        self._data = [None] * cap                    # allocate list with new capacity
        walk = self._front
        for k in range(self._size):                  # only consider existing elements
            self._data[k] = old[walk]                # intentionally shift indices
            walk = (1 + walk) % len(old)             # use old size as modulus
        self._front = 0                              # front has been realigned

5. Resizing and Realignment Mechanics

When expanding the buffer via _resize(2 * len(self._data)), elements cannot simply be copied to their existing indices because circular modulo arithmetic depends directly on array length.

Figure 6.7

Realignment Rule

  • The elements are copied sequentially into the new array starting from destination index 0 up to $\text{size} - 1$.

  • The source pointer advances using the modulus of the old list length: walk = (1 + walk) % len(old).

  • self._front is reset to 0 in the expanded array.

Memory Shrinking Policy

To prevent an inactive queue that previously handled large traffic from holding excess memory, the array halves its capacity when 0 < _size < len(_data) // 4. Shrinking at one-fourth capacity prevents thrashing (rapid oscillation between doubling and halving) and maintains an amortized $O(1)$ bound.

6. Algorithmic Complexity

Table 6.3: Performance of Array-Based Queue Implementation

(Asterisk $*$ indicates an amortized running time bound. Total space usage is strictly bounded by $O(n)$.)

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 239)
