notes.html:
Definitions & Properties

A stack is a collection of objects inserted and removed according to the last-in, first-out (LIFO) principle. Access is restricted exclusively to the most recently inserted element residing at the top of the stack. Common applications include web browser page history (back-button stack), text editor undo buffers, and execution call stacks in programming runtimes.

Figure 6.1

1. The Stack Abstract Data Type (ADT)

The stack abstract data type specifies two fundamental update operations and three auxiliary accessor methods:

Stack Operation Trace (Example 6.3)

Operation Return Value Stack Contents (Top on Right)
S.push(5) — [5]
S.push(3) — [5, 3]
len(S) 2 [5, 3]
S.pop() 3 [5]
S.is_empty() False [5]
S.pop() 5 []
S.is_empty() True []
S.pop() "error" []
S.push(7) — [7]
S.push(9) — [7, 9]
S.top() 9 [7, 9]
S.push(4) — [7, 9, 4]
len(S) 3 [7, 9, 4]
S.pop() 4 [7, 9]
S.push(6) — [7, 9, 6]
S.push(8) — [7, 9, 6, 8]
S.pop() 8 [7, 9, 6]

2. Array-Based Implementation

Storing stack elements internally within a standard Python list aligns the top of the stack with the end of the list. Appending to and popping from the end of a dynamic array execute in $O(1)$ amortized time.

Figure 6.2

The Adapter Pattern

The Adapter design pattern customizes an existing class to match the interface of a different abstract data type by wrapping the adaptee class inside a hidden instance field.

Stack Method Realization with Python List L
S.push(e) L.append(e)
S.pop() L.pop()
S.top() L[-1]
S.is_empty() len(L) == 0
len(S) len(L)

Python Implementation (ArrayStack)

class Empty(Exception):
    """Error attempting to access an element from an empty container."""
    pass


class ArrayStack:
    """LIFO Stack implementation using a Python list as underlying storage."""

    def __init__(self):
        """Create an empty stack."""
        self._data = []                    # nonpublic list instance

    def __len__(self):
        """Return the number of elements in the stack."""
        return len(self._data)

    def is_empty(self):
        """Return True if the stack is empty."""
        return len(self._data) == 0

    def push(self, e):
        """Add element e to the top of the stack."""
        self._data.append(e)               # new item stored at end of list

    def top(self):
        """Return (but do not remove) the element at the top of the stack.

        Raise Empty exception if the stack is empty.
        """
        if self.is_empty():
            raise Empty('Stack is empty')
        return self._data[-1]              # the last item in the list

    def pop(self):
        """Remove and return the element from the top of the stack (i.e., LIFO).

        Raise Empty exception if the stack is empty.
        """
        if self.is_empty():
            raise Empty('Stack is empty')
        return self._data.pop()            # remove last item from list

3. Algorithmic Complexity

(Asterisk $*$ denotes an amortized time bound; worst-case execution is $O(n)$ during underlying array reallocation.)

Space Usage & Preallocation

The overall space complexity for an ArrayStack containing $n$ elements is $O(n)$. When the maximum capacity is known in advance, amortized resize penalties can be avoided by preallocating a fixed-length list (e.g., [None] * max_capacity) and maintaining an explicit integer pointer to track the current top index.

4. Reversing Data Using a Stack

Because the LIFO order reverses insertion order, a stack can invert sequences, such as lines in a file.

def reverse_file(filename):
    """Overwrite given file with its contents line-by-line reversed."""
    S = ArrayStack()
    original = open(filename)
    for line in original:
        S.push(line.rstrip('\n'))          # strip and push line
    original.close()

    # overwrite with contents in LIFO order
    output = open(filename, 'w')
    while not S.is_empty():
        output.write(S.pop() + '\n')       # re-insert newline characters
        output.close()

5. Delimiter & Markup Matching

Delimiter Matching Algorithm

Arithmetic expressions require opening delimiters ((, [, {) to match their corresponding closing symbols (), ], }) in nested order.

  • When an opening delimiter is read, push it onto the stack.

  • When a closing delimiter is read, pop from the stack and verify that the popped symbol matches the closing delimiter.

  • A syntax failure occurs if:

  1. A closing delimiter appears while the stack is empty.

  2. The popped opening delimiter does not match the closing delimiter type.

  3. The expression ends while opening delimiters remain on the stack.

def is_matched(expr):
    """Return True if all delimiters are properly matched; False otherwise."""
    lefty = '({['                               # opening delimiters
    righty = ')}]'                              # respective closing delims
    S = ArrayStack()
    for c in expr:
        if c in lefty:
            S.push(c)                           # push left delimiter on stack
        elif c in righty:
            if S.is_empty():
                return False                    # nothing to match with
            if righty.index(c) != lefty.index(S.pop()):
                return False                    # mismatched delimiter
    return S.is_empty()                         # were all symbols matched?
Complexity

For an expression of length $n$, the algorithm executes at most $n$ push and $n$ pop operations. Delimiter lookup runs in $O(1)$ time, yielding an overall running time of $O(n)$ and auxiliary stack space of $O(n)$.

Matching Tags in Markup Languages (HTML/XML)

HTML documents require opening tags (such as <body>, <h1>) to balance matching closing tags (</body>, </h1>).

Figure 6.3
def is_matched_html(raw):
    """Return True if all HTML tags are properly matched; False otherwise."""
    S = ArrayStack()
    j = raw.find('<')                           # find first '<' character (if any)
    while j != -1:
        k = raw.find('>', j + 1)                # find next '>' character
        if k == -1:
            return False                        # invalid tag syntax
        tag = raw[j + 1:k]                      # strip away < >
        if not tag.startswith('/'):
            S.push(tag)                         # opening tag: push onto stack
        else:
            if S.is_empty():
                return False                    # closing tag with no match
            if tag[1:] != S.pop():
                return False                    # mismatched tag label
        j = raw.find('<', k + 1)                # find next '<' character (if any)
    return S.is_empty()                         # were all opening tags matched?
Complexity

Scanning through $n$ characters of raw HTML performs at most $O(n)$ string slice and stack operations, resulting in an overall running time of $O(n)$.

References

  • Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 230)

notes.html:
Notes

1. Perceptual Blindness

Definition: The brain's tendency to filter out information it deems "irrelevant" while focusing on a specific task.

  • In Programming: When focusing on a specific complex part of code (e.g., a loop structure), you may become "blind" to obvious errors in simpler parts (e.g., print statements or variable logic).

  • The Danger: You fixate on where you think the error is, ignoring where it actually is.

  • Mitigation:

    • Practice: Experience helps distinguish essential from non-essential info.

    • Breaks: Step away to reset your focus; this requires starting work early.

    • Tools: Use comments, proper naming, and print debugging.

2. Readability: Comments vs. Naming

The goal of source code is to be Self-Documenting.

Code Comments

  • Purpose: To explain how code works to yourself or others.

  • Pitfall: Elaborate comments often compensate for bad code structure. They can become outdated or clutter the screen.

Self-Documenting Code

Instead of writing a comment explaining what a loop does, encapsulate that loop in a descriptive method.

Example: Evolution of Readability

Level 1: Heavily Commented (Cluttered)

// Iterate while value is greater than zero
while (value > 0) {
    System.out.println(value); 
    value = value - 1; // decrement
}

Level 2: Descriptive Method Naming (Preferred)

public static void printValuesFromTenToOne() {
    int value = 10;
    while (value > 0) {
        System.out.println(value);
        value = value - 1;
    }
}

Note: The functionality should be evident from the names of classes, methods, and variables.

3. Print Debugging

One of the most essential skills for finding errors is tracing the execution flow by printing values to the console.

Technique:

  1. Add System.out.println() statements at key points.

  2. Print the state (variable values).

  3. Print the flow (entry/exit of loops or conditionals).

Example: Debugging a Loop

System.out.println("-- Loop started, sum: " + sum); // Debug print

while (true) {
    // ... input logic ...
    
    if (value < 0) {
        System.out.println("-- Negative value found, breaking loop"); // Trace flow
        break;
    }
    
    values = values + 1;
    sum = sum + value;
    System.out.println("-- Updated sum: " + sum); // Trace state change
}

4. Testing & Corner Cases

Errors often hide in "exceptional" circumstances. You must test beyond standard inputs.

Corner Cases to Test:

  • Zeros: What if the input is 0? (Risk of division by zero).

  • Empty Input: What if the user enters nothing?

  • Extremes: Very large numbers or negative numbers.

  • Boundary Conditions: If logic changes at 1000, test 999, 1000, and 1001.

Example: Logic Ordering Bug

From the "Burger Chain" scenario: If you have overlapping conditions (e.g., every 25th customer vs. every 2000th customer), the order of if/else if statements matters.

  • Rule: Always check the most specific/strict condition before the general condition

References

https://java-programming.mooc.fi/part-3/1-discovering-errors

notes.excerpt: --- Object-Oriented Design Goals, Principles, and Patterns Core Concepts of Object-Oriented Programming In the object-oriented paradigm, the main "actors" are objects. Object: An instance of a class.
notes.html:
Object-Oriented Design Goals, Principles, and Patterns

Core Concepts of Object-Oriented Programming

In the object-oriented paradigm, the main "actors" are objects.

  • Object: An instance of a class.
  • Class: A blueprint that defines the view of objects, specifying what data they hold and what actions they can perform.
  • Instance Variables (Data Members): The data contained within an object.
  • Methods (Member Functions): The actions or behaviors an object can execute.

2.1.1 Object-Oriented Design Goals

Software design aims to achieve three primary goals.

1. Robustness

Software must be correct and capable of handling errors.

  • Correctness: Produces the right output for anticipated inputs.
  • Error Handling: Recovers gracefully from unexpected inputs (e.g., negative prices).
  • Safety: Critical in life-critical applications (e.g., medical devices like the Therac-25).

2. Adaptability

Software must evolve over time to meet changing conditions.

  • Evolvability: The ability to modify the software easily.
  • Portability: The ability to run on different hardware or operating systems with minimal changes.

3. Reusability

Code should be usable as a component in different systems.

  • Cost Efficiency: High-quality software is expensive; reusing it offsets costs.
  • Caution: Reuse must be done carefully to avoid introducing errors from previous contexts (e.g., Therac-20 software reused in Therac-25).

2.1.2 Object-Oriented Design Principles

Three chief principles facilitate the goals above.

1. Modularity

Organizing a system into separate, well-defined functional units.

  • Analogy: A house is organized into electrical, plumbing, and structural modules, not a jumble of wires and pipes.
  • Benefit: Easier to test, debug, and reuse individual components.

2. Abstraction

Distilling a complicated system down to its fundamental parts.

  • Abstract Data Types (ADTs): A mathematical model specifying what operations a data structure supports, but not how it implements them.
  • Public Interface: The collective set of behaviors supported by an ADT.
Duck Typing in Python

Python uses "duck typing" to handle abstractions. It does not check data types at compile time. Instead, it assumes an object supports a behavior. If the object "walks like a duck and quacks like a duck," Python treats it as a duck. If the assumption fails, a run-time error occurs.

Abstract Base Classes (ABC)

Python supports formal abstractions via Abstract Base Classes. An ABC cannot be instantiated directly but defines methods that concrete subclasses must implement.

3. Encapsulation

Hiding the internal details of a component from the outside world.

  • Freedom: Programmers can change internal implementation without breaking code that depends on the component, as long as the public interface remains the same.
  • Convention: In Python, names starting with a single underscore (e.g., _secret) are assumed to be nonpublic and should not be relied upon by external code.

2.1.3 Design Patterns

A design pattern is a general template for solving a typical software design problem. It describes a solution that can be applied in many different situations.

Components of a Pattern

  1. Name: Identifies the pattern.
  2. Context: Describes scenarios where the pattern applies.
  3. Template: Describes how to apply the pattern.
  4. Result: Analyzes what the pattern produces.

Categories of Patterns

The book categorizes patterns into two groups: Algorithm Design Patterns and Software Engineering Design Patterns.

Category Pattern Name Description / Context
Algorithm Design Recursion Solving problems by solving smaller instances of the same problem (Chapter 4).
Amortization Analyzing the average cost of operations over a sequence (Sections 5.3, 11.4).
Divide-and-Conquer Breaking a problem into subproblems, solving them, and combining results (Section 12.2.1).
Prune-and-Search Also known as decrease-and-conquer; eliminating parts of the search space (Section 12.7.1).
Brute Force Trying all possible solutions (Section 13.2.1).
Dynamic Programming Solving complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems (Section 13.3).
Greedy Method Making the locally optimal choice at each stage (Sections 13.4.2, 14.6.2, 14.7).
Software Engineering Iterator Accessing elements of a collection sequentially (Sections 1.8, 2.3.4).
Adapter Converting the interface of a class into another interface clients expect (Section 6.1.2).
Position Abstracting the location of an element in a container (Sections 7.4, 8.1.2).
Composition Building complex objects from simpler ones (Sections 7.6.1, 9.2.1, 10.1.4).
Template Method Defining the skeleton of an algorithm in a superclass (Sections 2.4.3, 8.4.6, etc.).
Locator Storing the location of an element (Section 9.5.1).
Factory Method Defining an interface for creating an object (Section 11.2.1).

References

Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 57)

notes.excerpt: --- 1. Organisation de la Mémoire : Stack vs Heap [!info] Définition : Pile (Stack) et Tas (Heap) - Stack (pile) : zone mémoire réservée automatiquement pour les variables locales et les appels de fon
notes.html:
1. Organisation de la Mémoire : Stack vs Heap

Définition : Pile (Stack) et Tas (Heap)
  • Stack (pile) : zone mémoire réservée automatiquement pour les variables locales et les appels de fonctions. Taille fixée à la compilation, gestion automatique (LIFO).
  • Heap (tas) : réserve (« storage pool ») dans laquelle les fonctions d'allocation dynamique (malloc, calloc, realloc) prélèvent des blocs à l'exécution. Gestion entièrement manuelle via free.

Appeler trop souvent ces fonctions — ou demander des blocs trop volumineux — peut épuiser le tas, auquel cas elles renvoient un pointeur nul.

📦 Statique 🔄 Dynamique
Déclaration int t[100]; int *t = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
Taille fixée à la compilation choisie à l'exécution
Zone mémoire pile (stack) tas (heap)
Gestion automatique, simple mais rigide manuelle (free), flexible
*(Description précise de l'illustration : organisation de la mémoire d'un processus C — segments de code, données, pile (stack) et tas (heap) avec blocs alloués/libérés)*

2. Pointeurs : Fondements

Définition / Théorème : Pointeur et opérateurs `&` / `*`

Un pointeur est une variable contenant l'adresse d'une autre variable.

  • &x : adresse de $x$ ;
  • *p : déréférencement, valeur située à l'adresse contenue dans $p$ ;
  • Passage d'un pointeur en argument : permet à la fonction de modifier la variable d'origine (passage par adresse).
Définition / Théorème : Pointeur générique `void*` et pointeur NULL (King §17.1)

Les fonctions d'allocation ignorent le type des données stockées : elles renvoient un void*, pointeur « générique » (une simple adresse), convertible vers tout type de pointeur sans cast explicite. En cas d'échec (bloc introuvable), elles renvoient un pointeur NULL (« pointer to nothing »), représenté par la macro NULL (définie dans <locale.h>, <stddef.h>, <stdio.h>, <stdlib.h>, <string.h>, <time.h>). $$ > p = \texttt{malloc}(10000); \quad \text{si } p == \texttt{NULL} \Rightarrow \text{échec d'allocation} > $$ Tester la valeur de retour est la responsabilité du programmeur. Déréférencer un pointeur NULL est un comportement indéfini (crash ou comportement erratique).

Vérité booléenne des pointeurs (King) : tous les pointeurs non nuls sont vrais, seul le pointeur nul est faux.

if (p == NULL) ...   /* comparaison explicite — style préféré par King */
if (!p) ...          /* équivalent */
if (p) ...           /* équivalent à p != NULL */
Piège / Cas Particulier

Ne jamais déréférencer un pointeur non initialisé ou NULL. Toujours vérifier le retour de toute fonction d'allocation avant utilisation.

3. Tableaux : Opérations de Base et Limites

3.1 Opérations élémentaires

Échanger deux cases (nécessite une variable temporaire) :

int tmp = t[i];
t[i] = t[j];
t[j] = tmp;
Définition / Théorème : Rôle de `tmp`

Sans variable temporaire, la première affectation écrase une valeur avant qu'elle ne soit copiée : t[i] = t[j]; t[j] = t[i]; produit deux copies identiques de t[j].

Recherche séquentielle (coût pire cas : parcours complet, $O(n)$) :

for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (t[i] == val)
        return i;      /* trouvé */
}
return -1;             /* non trouvé */

Maximum (initialiser → parcourir → mettre à jour) :

int max = t[0];
for (i = 1; i < n; i++) {
    if (t[i] > max)
        max = t[i];
}

Insérer (décalage des éléments suivants vers la droite) :

Exemple d'Application : Insertion dans un tableau

Tableau initial $[10, 20, 30, 40]$ ; insérer $15$ à l'indice $1$ : $$ > [10, 20, 30, 40] \xrightarrow{\text{décalage}} [10, \underline{15}, 20, 30, 40] > $$

for (i = n; i > pos; i--) {
    t[i] = t[i - 1];
}
t[pos] = valeur;      /* nouvelle taille : n + 1 */

Supprimer (décalage des éléments suivants vers la gauche pour combler le « trou ») :

Exemple d'Application : Suppression dans un tableau

Tableau initial $[10, 20, 30, 40]$ ; supprimer l'indice $1$ : $$ > [10, \cancel{20}, 30, 40] \xrightarrow{\text{décalage}} [10, 30, 40] > $$

for (i = pos; i < n - 1; i++) {
    t[i] = t[i + 1];
}
/* nouvelle taille : n - 1 */

3.2 Limites des tableaux classiques

Piège / Cas Particulier : Limites des tableaux statiques
  1. Taille fixe : définie à la compilation ; trop petit → débordement, trop grand → gaspillage.
  2. Insertion/suppression coûteuses : tout accès au milieu exige des décalages en $O(n)$.
  3. Zone contiguë obligatoire : le système doit trouver un bloc contigu suffisant, ce qui peut être difficile.

$\Rightarrow$ C'est l'allocation dynamique (tas) qui dépasse ces limites.

4. Relation Tableaux – Pointeurs (Decay)

Définition / Théorème : Propriété fondamentale et decay

Pour int t[5];, le nom t est équivalent à &t[0] : $$ > t == \&t[0] \quad (\text{vrai}) > $$ t n'est pas un pointeur constant : c'est un tableau qui, dans la plupart des expressions, se convertit automatiquement (decay) en pointeur vers son premier élément. Exceptions : la conversion n'a pas lieu dans sizeof(t) (taille totale du tableau) ni avec l'opérateur &t. Conséquence : t++ est interdit ; pour parcourir, déclarer un pointeur séparé int *p = t;.

Parcours par pointeur vs par indice (formes identiques en mémoire ; t[i] est compilé en *(t + i)) :

int *p;
for (p = t; p < t + n; p++) {
    printf("%d", *p);
}
/* équivalent à */
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    printf("%d", t[i]);
}

Passage d'un tableau à une fonction (deux écritures équivalentes) :

void afficher(int t[], int n);
/* équivalent à */
void afficher(int *t, int n);
Définition / Théorème : Sémantique du passage de tableau

En C, tous les arguments sont passés par valeur. Le paramètre int t[] est ajusté en int *t : la fonction reçoit une copie du pointeur vers le premier élément. Ce n'est pas un vrai passage par référence, mais le pointeur copié pointe vers le tableau original : toute modification de t[i] dans la fonction modifie le tableau original.

4.1 Tableaux 2D et ordre ligne par ligne (row-major)

int mat[3][4];      /* 3 lignes, 4 colonnes */
mat[i][j];          /* ligne i, colonne j */
Définition / Théorème : Stockage row-major

Une matrice mat[3][4] est stockée en mémoire linéaire ligne par ligne : toute la ligne 0, puis la ligne 1, puis la ligne 2 (12 cellules contiguës).

*(Description précise de l'illustration : matrice 3×4 indexée 0–2 projetée sur une rangée continue de 12 cellules en ordre row-major)*

Matrice dynamique avec int** :

Exemple d'Application : Allocation et libération d'une matrice dynamique
/* 1. Allouer le tableau de pointeurs (lignes) */
int **tab = malloc(n * sizeof(int *));
/* 2. Allouer chaque ligne */
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    tab[i] = malloc(m * sizeof(int));
}
/* ... utilisation tab[i][j] ... */
/* 3. Libérer ligne par ligne, puis le tableau de pointeurs */
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    free(tab[i]);
}
free(tab);

4.2 Chaînes de caractères et pointeurs

Définition / Théorème : Chaîne en C

Une chaîne est un tableau de char terminé par le caractère nul '\0'.

char s[] = "ENSAM";
char *p = s;          /* pointeur séparé ; s++ est interdit */
while (*p != '\0') { p++; }
Exemple d'Application : `longueur` (comme `strlen`) et `copier` (comme `strcpy`)
int longueur(char *s) {
    int n = 0;
    while (*s != '\0') {   /* s pointe le 1er caractère, *s = caractère courant */
        n++;               /* s++ avance au caractère suivant */
        s++;
    }
    return n;              /* arrêt quand *s == '\0' */
}

void copier(char *dest, char *src) {
while (*src != '\0') {
*dest = *src;
dest++;
src++;
}
dest = '\0';          / ne pas oublier le terminateur */
}


/* Version compacte (idiome C classique) : copie le caractère ET avance /
/ les deux pointeurs ; s'arrête quand '\0' est copié (valeur fausse).   */
while (*dest++ = *src++)
;

5. Allocation Dynamique : malloc, calloc, realloc

Définition / Théorème : `malloc` (King §17.1–17.3)
void *malloc(size_t size);

Alloue un bloc de size octets (non initialisé) et renvoie un pointeur vers celui-ci, ou NULL en cas d'échec. size_t est un type entier non signé. Toujours utiliser sizeof pour calculer la place nécessaire (portabilité 32/64 bits) :

int *a;
a = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
Piège / Cas Particulier : Sous-allocation
a = malloc(n * 2);   /* FAUX si sizeof(int) > 2 (quasi toutes les machines) */

Le bloc est trop petit : les accès ultérieurs provoquent crash ou comportement erratique. Échec d'allocation suffisant $\Rightarrow$ conséquences sévères.

Définition / Théorème : `calloc` (King §17.3)
void *calloc(size_t nmemb, size_t size);

Alloue un tableau de nmemb éléments de size octets et initialise tous les bits à 0 (plus lent mais plus sûr). Utilisable pour tout type de donnée :

struct point { int x, y; } *p;
p = calloc(1, sizeof(struct point));   /* x et y garantis à 0 */
Définition / Théorème : `realloc` et règles du standard C (King §17.3)
void *realloc(void *ptr, size_t size);

Redimensionne un bloc obtenu par un malloc/calloc/realloc antérieur (agrandir ou réduire), en préservant les données. Règles du standard :

  1. En extension, les octets ajoutés ne sont pas initialisés ;
  2. Si l'agrandissement est impossible : renvoie NULL, l'ancien bloc est inchangé ;
  3. realloc(NULL, size) se comporte comme malloc(size) ;
  4. realloc(ptr, 0) libère le bloc ;
  5. Réduction « in place » sans déplacement ; extension « in place » si possible, sinon nouveau bloc + copie du contenu $\Rightarrow$ mettre à jour tous les pointeurs après realloc.
Piège / Cas Particulier : `realloc` exige un pointeur temporaire
int *temp;
temp = realloc(tab, new_size);
if (temp == NULL) {
    /* tab est encore valide : ne surtout pas l'écraser */
    return;
}
tab = temp;

Écrire directement tab = realloc(tab, ...) perd l'ancien bloc si realloc échoue (fuite + pointeur NULL). De plus, le pointeur passé à realloc doit impérativement provenir d'un malloc/calloc/realloc antérieur (sinon comportement indéfini).

Vérification systématique du retour (code sûr) :

int *p;
p = malloc(sizeof(int));
if (p == NULL) {
    printf("Erreur allocation");
    return 1;
}
/* utiliser p ici */
Fonction Rôle Initialise ? Syntaxe type
malloc(t) allouer $t$ octets non (valeurs aléatoires) int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
calloc(n, t) allouer $n \times t$ octets oui (tout à zéro) int *p = calloc(n, sizeof(int));
realloc(p, t) redimensionner le bloc p non (préserve les données) p = realloc(p, nouvelle_taille);
free(p) libérer le bloc p — free(p); p = NULL;

5.1 Chaînes allouées dynamiquement (King §17.2)

Définition / Théorème : `malloc` pour une chaîne

sizeof(char) == 1 : pour $n$ caractères, allouer $n + 1$ octets (place pour le caractère nul) :

char *p = malloc(n + 1);      /* cast inutile : void* converti automatiquement */
strcpy(p, "abc");             /* mémoire non initialisée : initialiser explicitement */
Piège / Cas Particulier

Oublier le +1 pour '\0' provoque un débordement d'un octet lors de strcpy/strcat : corruption mémoire silencieuse.

Exemple d'Application : Fonction `concat` renvoyant une « nouvelle » chaîne (King §17.2)

La bibliothèque standard n'offre pas de concaténation sans modifier ses entrées (strcat modifie l'une des deux). On l'écrit soi-même :

char *concat(const char *s1, const char *s2) {
    char *result;
    result = malloc(strlen(s1) + strlen(s2) + 1);
    if (result == NULL) {
        printf("Error: malloc failed in concat\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    strcpy(result, s1);
    strcat(result, s2);
    return result;
}

Appel : p = concat("abc", "def"); $\Rightarrow$ p pointe vers "abcdef" (7 caractères, '\0' inclus), stocké dans un tableau dynamique. Obligation : appeler free sur la chaîne retournée dès qu'elle n'est plus utile, sinon fuite mémoire.

Exemple d'Application : Tableau de chaînes dynamiques — `remind2.c` (King §17.2)

Remplacer un tableau 2D char reminders[MAX_REMIND][MSG_LEN+1] par un tableau de pointeurs vers chaînes dynamiques apporte deux avantages : (i) allocation du nombre exact de caractères ; (ii) insertion sans strcpy de décalage — on ne déplace que des pointeurs.

char *reminders[MAX_REMIND];
char day_str[3], msg_str[MSG_LEN + 1];
int day, i, j, num_remind = 0;

for (;;) {
if (num_remind == MAX_REMIND) { printf("-- No space left--\n"); break; }
printf("Enter day and reminder:");
scanf("%2d", &day);
if (day == 0) break;
sprintf(day_str, "%2d", day);
read_line(msg_str, MSG_LEN);


for (i = 0; i < num_remind; i++)
    if (strcmp(day_str, reminders[i]) < 0) break;
for (j = num_remind; j > i; j--)
    reminders[j] = reminders[j - 1];      /* décalage de pointeurs only */

reminders[i] = malloc(2 + strlen(msg_str) + 1);
if (reminders[i] == NULL) { printf("-- No space left--\n"); break; }
strcpy(reminders[i], day_str);
strcat(reminders[i], msg_str);
num_remind++;



}

6. Libération : free, Fuites et Pointeurs Pendants

Définition / Théorème : `free` (King §17.4)
void free(void *ptr);

Rend au système le bloc pointé par ptr, disponible pour de futures allocations. Contraintes : l'argument doit être un pointeur préalablement renvoyé par une fonction d'allocation (ou NULL, auquel cas free n'a aucun effet). Passer tout autre pointeur (variable locale, élément de tableau…) est un comportement indéfini.

Piège / Cas Particulier : Fuite mémoire (memory leak / garbage)

Un bloc alloué puis perdu de vue devient du « garbage » : C n'a pas de ramasse-miettes, chaque programme recycle lui-même sa mémoire.

/* Cas 1 : oubli simple de free */
void fonction(void) {
    int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *p = 42;
    /* free(p) oublié : p (variable locale) est détruit, le bloc reste alloué */
}

/* Cas 2 : perte de la référence (le plus dangereux) */
int p = malloc(100 * sizeof(int));
p = malloc(200 * sizeof(int));   / le 1er bloc (100 ints) est PERDU à jamais */


/* Version King : p = q rend le 1er bloc inaccessible /
p = malloc(...);
q = malloc(...);
p = q;                            / plus aucun pointeur vers le 1er bloc */

Dans un programme long (serveur, boucle infinie), les fuites s'accumulent jusqu'à consommer toute la mémoire $\Rightarrow$ crash du programme ou du système.

*(Description précise de l'illustration : deux blocs alloués pointés par p et q ; après p = q, le premier bloc (grisé) n'a plus aucun pointeur : garbage)*
Piège / Cas Particulier : Pointeur pendant (dangling pointer)

free(p) libère le bloc mais ne modifie pas p :

char *p = malloc(4);
...
free(p);
...
strcpy(p, "abc");   /* *** WRONG *** : mémoire déjà rendue au système */

Accéder ou modifier un bloc libéré = comportement indéfini, crash probable. Aggravant : plusieurs pointeurs peuvent viser le même bloc ; après free, tous pendent.

Piège / Cas Particulier : Double free

Appeler free(p) deux fois sur le même pointeur $\Rightarrow$ crash ou corruption mémoire. Règle d'or : free(p); p = NULL; toujours ensemble — NULL neutralise dangling et double free (car free(NULL) est inoffensif).

*(Description précise de l'illustration : avant free — bloc alloué pointé par p ; après free — mémoire rendue au système, p non modifié pointe vers un bloc invalide)*
Modélisation : Cycle de vie d'un tableau dynamique
  1. Lire $n$ (taille désirée) ;
  2. Allouer : tab = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
  3. Vérifier : if (tab == NULL) ...
  4. Utiliser : tab[i] ;
  5. Libérer : free(tab); tab = NULL;
Bonnes Pratiques (Checklist Mémoire)
  1. Toujours vérifier le retour != NULL après chaque allocation ;
  2. Toujours utiliser sizeof pour la taille (portabilité) ;
  3. Libérer toute mémoire allouée dès qu'elle n'est plus nécessaire ;
  4. p = NULL après free ;
  5. Pointeur temporaire avec realloc — jamais p = realloc(p, ...) ;
  6. Jamais de double free, jamais d'accès après free ;
  7. Préférer calloc pour les tableaux nécessitant une initialisation à zéro.

7. Structures et Pointeurs vers Structures

Définition / Théorème : `struct` et `typedef`

Une structure regroupe des champs de types différents sous un même nom (nouveau type composé) :

struct Etudiant {
    int id;
    float moyenne;
    char nom[50];
};

typedef struct {
int id;
float moyenne;
} Etudiant;                 /* alias de type : s'utilise comme int ou float */


Etudiant e;
e.id = 1;                   /* opérateur point (.) sur variable structure */
e.moyenne = 15.5;

Définition / Théorème : Opérateur `->`

Avec un pointeur vers structure :

Etudiant e;
Etudiant *p = &e;
p->moyenne = 16;        /* équivalent à (*p).moyenne = 16; */

-> contracte (*p). : déréférence et accès au champ en une opération. C'est la notation standard.

8. Vers les Listes Chaînées (Aperçu)

Définition / Théorème : Nœud et liste chaînée (King §17.5)

Une liste chaînée est une chaîne de structures (nœuds), chaque nœud contenant un pointeur vers le nœud suivant ; le dernier contient un pointeur NULL.

typedef struct Node {
    int data;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

Alternative aux tableaux : insertion/suppression faciles, croissance libre ; en contrepartie, perte de l'accès aléatoire (tout élément d'un tableau s'accède en temps constant, pas celui d'une liste).

📦 Tableau 🔗 Liste chaînée
Stockage contigu (zone unique) dispersé, relié par pointeurs
Taille fixe (ou realloc) flexible (croît/diminue librement)
Accès au $i$-ème $O(1)$ $O(n)$
Insertion en tête $O(n)$ (décalages) $O(1)$
Insertion après nœud connu $O(n)$ (décalages) $O(1)$
Recherche du nœud précédent — peut coûter $O(n)$
*(Description précise de l'illustration : chaîne de nœuds (data + next) dont le dernier pointe vers NULL, comparée à un bloc contigu de tableau)*

9. Synthèse du Chapitre

Ce que ce chapitre établit
  • Mémoire : stack vs heap, segments, épuisement du tas ;
  • Pointeurs : déclaration, &, *, void*, NULL, passage par adresse, arithmétique, decay (t == &t[0], exceptions sizeof(t) et &t) ;
  • Tableaux : contiguïté, opérations de base (swap, recherche, min/max, insertion/suppression en $O(n)$), passage à une fonction, row-major 2D, matrice dynamique int** ;
  • Allocation dynamique : malloc / calloc / realloc / free, règles du standard pour realloc, erreurs classiques (fuite, dangling, double free) et checklist de bonnes pratiques ;
  • Structures : struct, typedef, opérateurs . et ->, pointeurs vers struct ;
  • Transition : les tableaux exigent une zone contiguë et des décalages coûteux ; les listes chaînées dispersent les éléments reliés par pointeurs — tous les outils nécessaires à leur implémentation sont désormais acquis.

References

  • Chapitre 1 — Rappels : mémoire, pointeurs et tableaux — ENSAM Casablanca
  • C Programming: A Modern Approach (2nd ed.), K. N. King — Ch. 17 « Advanced Uses of Pointers » (p. 413–424)

notes.html:
Date: 2026-09-26 Tags: C_Programming, Pointers, Array, Memory_Management

1. Pointer Arithmetic

When a pointer points to an array element, C allows you to perform pointer arithmetic (also called address arithmetic) to access other elements of the same array. C supports exactly three forms of pointer arithmetic.

Adding an Integer to a Pointer

If a pointer $p$ points to the array element $a[i]$, then adding an integer $j$ yields a pointer $p + j$ that points to the element $a[i+j]$.

int a[10], *p, *q;
p = &a[2];
q = p + 3; // q now points to a[5]
p += 6;    // p now points to a[8]

Subtracting an Integer from a Pointer

Similarly, if $p$ points to $a[i]$, subtracting an integer $j$ yields $p - j$, which points to $a[i-j]$.

p = &a[8];
q = p - 3; // q now points to a[5]

Subtracting One Pointer from Another

When one pointer is subtracted from another, the result is the distance (measured in array elements, not bytes) between the two pointers. If $p$ points to $a[i]$ and $q$ points to $a[j]$, then $p - q$ is equal to $i - j$.

p = &a[5];
q = &a[1];
int i = p - q; // i is 4
int j = q - p; // j is -4
Undefined Behavior in Arithmetic

Performing arithmetic on a pointer that does not point to an array element causes undefined behavior. Furthermore, subtracting one pointer from another is undefined unless both pointers point to elements of the same array.

Comparing Pointers

Pointers can be compared using relational operators (<, <=, >, >=) and equality operators (==, !=). This is only meaningful if both pointers point to elements of the same array; the outcome depends on their relative positions. If $p = \&a[5]$ and $q = \&a[1]$, then $p \le q$ is 0 (false), and $p \ge q$ is 1 (true).

2. Using Pointers for Array Processing

Pointer arithmetic allows us to visit the elements of an array by repeatedly incrementing a pointer variable.

The Pointer Loop Idiom

Instead of using a standard for loop with an integer index i, we can use a pointer p to step through the array memory directly:

#define N 10
int a[N], sum, *p;

sum = 0;
for (p = &a[0]; p < &a[N]; p++) {
    sum += *p;
}
Pointer Out-of-Bounds Exception

In the condition p < &a[N], the address &a[N] points to one element past the end of the array. Applying the address operator to a non-existent element in this specific loop-bound fashion is perfectly legal and safe in C, as the loop terminates before attempting to examine its value.

Combining the * and ++ Operators

C programmers heavily use the idiom *p++ (or *p++ = j) to process an array element and immediately advance to the next one.

Because the postfix ++ operator takes precedence over the indirection * operator, the expression *p++ means "return the value pointed to by $p$, then increment $p$ itself".

Expression Meaning
*p++ or *(p++) Value of expression is *p before increment; increment p later
(*p)++ Value of expression is *p before increment; increment *p later
*++p or *(++p) Increment p first; value of expression is *p after increment
++*p or ++(*p) Increment *p first; value of expression is *p after increment

3. Using an Array Name as a Pointer

The name of an array can be used as a pointer to the first element in the array. If we declare int a[10];, then a is completely equivalent to &a[0].

The Pointer-Array Equivalence Formula

For any array a and index i, the expression a + i is equivalent to &a[i]. Consequently, applying indirection yields the fundamental C equivalence:

$$*(a + i) \equiv a[i]$$

This simplifies pointer loops:

for (p = a; p < a + N; p++) {
    sum += *p;
}
Array Names are NOT Variables

While an array name can be used as a pointer, it is not possible to assign it a new value. a = p; or a++; will cause a compiler error.

Array Arguments (Revisited)

When an array name is passed to a function, C always treats it as a pointer. The array itself is never copied; only the address of the first element is copied. This has two major consequences:

  1. A function can modify the elements of the original array passed to it.

  2. The time required to pass an array to a function is constant and does not depend on the size of the array.

Because of this, an array parameter can be declared directly as a pointer:

// These two prototypes are identical to the compiler:
int find_largest(int a[], int n);
int find_largest(int *a, int n);

This also allows us to pass "slices" of arrays to functions. To process elements 5 through 14, we pass &b[5] as the start pointer and 10 as the length: find_largest(&b[5], 10);.

4. Pointers and Multidimensional Arrays

Just as pointers can iterate through one-dimensional arrays, they can process multidimensional arrays.

Row-Major Layout

C stores two-dimensional arrays in row-major order (elements of row 0 come first, followed immediately by elements of row 1, etc.).

int a[NUM_ROWS][NUM_COLS];
int *p;

Because of this continuous memory layout, we can view the entire 2D matrix as a flat 1D array and initialize it with a single loop:

for (p = &a[0][0]; p <= &a[NUM_ROWS-1][NUM_COLS-1]; p++) {
    *p = 0;
}

Processing Single Rows and Columns

  • Rows: The expression a[i] is a pointer to the first element in row i. To clear row i:
for (p = a[i]; p < a[i] + NUM_COLS; p++) *p = 0;
  • Columns: Processing a column requires stepping forward by the length of an entire row (NUM_COLS):
for (p = &a[0][i]; p < &a[NUM_ROWS][i]; p += NUM_COLS) *p = 0;

(Note: (*p)[i] requires parenthesis because [] has higher precedence than *).

References

C Programming: A Modern Approach (Chapter 12) (p. 257-271)

notes.html:
1. Pointer Fundamentals

At the machine level, main memory is divided into bytes (8 bits of information). Every byte has a unique numerical address. An executable C program consists of code (instructions) and data (variables), where each variable occupies one or more bytes of memory. The address of the first byte occupied by a variable is considered the address of that variable.

Definition: Pointer Variable

While ordinary variables store data values, a pointer variable is a special variable that stores a memory address. When a pointer variable $p$ stores the address of a variable $i$, we say that "$p$ points to $i$".

Declaring Pointers

To declare a pointer, the variable name is preceded by an asterisk (*):

int *p;    /* points only to integers */
double *q; /* points only to doubles */
char *r;   /* points only to characters */

C requires that every pointer point only to objects of a particular, declared type (the referenced type).

2. The Address (&) and Indirection (*) Operators

C uses a specific pair of operators to handle pointers.

The Address Operator (&)

To find the memory address of a variable, use the & operator. If x is a variable, &x is the address of x in memory.

int i, *p;
p = &i;  // p now holds the address of i

The Indirection Operator (*)

Once a pointer points to an object, the * (indirection or dereference) operator is used to access the actual data stored at that memory address.

int i = 1;
int *p = &i;
printf("%d", *p); // Prints 1, not the address of i
Mathematical Relationship

The * operator acts as the mathematical inverse of the & operator. Applying & to a variable produces a pointer to it; applying * to that pointer takes you back to the original variable: j = *&i; is equivalent to j = i;.

Uninitialized Pointer Pitfall

Never apply the indirection operator * to an uninitialized pointer variable. If p is uninitialized, executing *p = 1; will attempt to write data to a random memory address, which causes undefined behavior and will likely crash the program (Segmentation Fault).

3. Pointer Assignment

C allows the assignment operator to copy pointers, provided they have the same referenced type.

int i, j, *p, *q;
p = &i; // p points to i
q = p;  // q now ALSO points to i

In this scenario, p, q, and &i all hold the exact same memory address. Modifying the data through one pointer affects the original object:

*p = 1; // i is now 1
*q = 2; // i is now 2

4. Pointers as Function Arguments

In C, arguments are passed to functions by value (a copy is made). Therefore, a function cannot modify the original variable passed to it. Pointers solve this problem: instead of passing the variable x, we pass a pointer to x (&x).

When the function receives the address, it can use the * operator to create an alias for x and modify the original data directly.

Example: Finding Min and Max in an Array

This function uses pointers to return multiple values (both the largest and smallest elements) from a single function call.

#include 

void max_min(int a[], int n, int *max, int *min) {
    int i;
    *max = *min = a[0];
    for (i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (a[i] > *max)
            *max = a[i];
        else if (a[i] < *min)
            *min = a[i];
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int b[10] = {34, 82, 49, 102, 7, 94, 23, 11, 50, 31};
    int big, small;
    
    // We pass the ADDRESSES of big and small
    max_min(b, 10, &big, &small);
    
    printf("Largest: %d\n", big);
    printf("Smallest: %d\n", small);
    return 0;
}
Using `const` to Protect Arguments

If you pass a pointer to a function merely for efficiency (avoiding copying a large object) and do not want the function to alter it, use the const keyword: void f(const int *p) The compiler will now throw an error if the function attempts to modify *p.

5. Pointers as Return Values

Functions can also return pointers.

int *max(int *a, int *b) {
    if (*a > *b)
        return a;
    else
        return b;
}
// Usage: int *p = max(&i, &j);
Dangling Pointer Pitfall

Never return a pointer to an automatic local variable.

int *f(void) {
    int i = 5;
    return &i; /* WRONG */
}

The variable i only exists inside the stack frame of function f. Once f returns, its memory is destroyed. The returned pointer will point to invalid, garbage memory.

References

C Programming: A Modern Approach (Chapter 11) (p. 241-252)

notes.html:
Notes

JFC is a set of classes and interfaces that provide ready-made data structures to store and multiplate groups of objects efficiently.

  • Java provides built-in collection classes like Lis, Set, Map and Queue so developers don't need to write their own data management algorithms.
  • it helps with making the code more reusable and faster and also more optimized which is something that we dont see a lot nowadays.

Core Interfaces

The foundation of the Collections Framework is built on interfaces like Collection, List, Set, Queue, Deque and Map. They define the behavior of different collection types and serve as a blueprint for implementations.

  • Collection Interface
  • List Interface
  • Set Interface
  • Map Interface
  • Queue Interface
  • Deque Interface

Which implementation to choose

Interface Implementation Ordering Access/Search Add/Remove Best Use Case
List ArrayList Insertion Fast $O(1)$ Slow $O(n)$ Default choice. Fast reading and access by index, good for fixed/growing lists.
List LinkedList Insertion Slow $O(n)$ Fast $O(1)$ Specific scenarios only. Frequent inserts/deletes at ends (Queue/Stack).
Set HashSet Random Fast $O(1)$ Fast $O(1)$ Default Set. Fastest for checking uniqueness. No order guarantee.
Set TreeSet Sorted Medium $O(\log n)$ Medium $O(\log n)$ When you need unique items sorted (e.g., A-Z, 1-100).
Set LinkedHashSet Insertion Fast $O(1)$ Fast $O(1)$ Unique items, but keep them in the order they were added.
Map HashMap Random Fast $O(1)$ Fast $O(1)$ Default Map. Key-Value pairs. Fastest lookup.
Map TreeMap Sorted Keys Medium $O(\log n)$ Medium $O(\log n)$ When you need Keys sorted (e.g., Dictionary).
Map LinkedHashMap Insertion Fast $O(1)$ Fast $O(1)$ Keys + Values, but keep insertion order (e.g., Caching).
Queue PriorityQueue Priority Top is $O(1)$ Medium $O(\log n)$ Process tasks by importance, not arrival time.
Deque ArrayDeque Insertion Fast $O(1)$ Fast $O(1)$ Modern Stack/Queue. Faster than LinkedList for stacks/queues.
The "Pro" Cheat Sheet for Imports

Before Starting to code make sure to import java.util for each interface for example the interface ArrayList needs the package java.util.ArrayList;

// 1. Interfaces (The contracts)
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Queue;
import java.util.Deque;

// 2. Implementations (The actual objects)
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedList; // or java.util.ArrayDeque (preferred)
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.TreeMap;     // If sorting needed
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

// 3. Utilities (Helper methods like sort, shuffle)
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Objects;     // For hash() and equals() logic
import java.util.Arrays;      // For Arrays.asList()

OR you can just use- * - which covers 95% of the standard Collections framework:

import java.util.*; // Imports List, ArrayList, Map, HashMap, Collections, etc.

To not break the code always @Override ~={green}equals(), hashCode() and toString()=~

import java.util.Objects;

public class YourClassName {

    // Your fields (e.g., id, email, username)
    private String significantField1;
    private int significantField2;

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        // 1. Optimization: Check if they are the exact same object in memory
        if (this == o) return true;
        
        // 2. Null & Type Check: Ensure the other object is not null and is the same Class
        if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
        
        // 3. Casting: Convert the generic 'Object' to 'YourClassName'
        YourClassName that = (YourClassName) o;
        
        // 4. Comparison: Check actual data values
        // Use Objects.equals() for objects (Strings, Lists) to handle nulls safely
        // Use == for primitives (int, double, boolean)
        return significantField2 == that.significantField2 &&
               Objects.equals(significantField1, that.significantField1);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        // 5. Hash: Must use the EXACT SAME fields as equals()
        return Objects.hash(significantField1, significantField2);
    }
	    
    @Override
	public String toString() {
	    return "User{username='" + significantField1 + "', score=" + significantField2 + "}";
	}
}

Comparable and Comparator

These interfaces are strictly required for any collection that promises to keep things Sorted or organized by Priority. and if you want to use the method Collections.sort() it's must to redefine it in the class first. you can ignore these interfaces in the HASHED groupe (hashSet, hashMap) since they only need equals() and hashCode()

Collection Type How it uses Comparator/Comparable
List (ArrayList) Optional. Used only when you explicitly call .sort(). It rearranges the existing list.
TreeSet MANDATORY. It sorts items automatically as you .add() them. It uses the comparison logic to decide where the item sits in the tree.
TreeMap MANDATORY. Similar to TreeSet, but it sorts the Keys.
PriorityQueue MANDATORY. Uses it to decide which item is "VIP" and should be at the front of the line.

Comparator vs Comparable

Feature Comparable (Internal) Comparator (External)
Who implements it? The class itself (class Product implements Comparable). A separate class (class PriceJudge implements Comparator).
Method compareTo(Object other) compare(Object a, Object b)
Use case The "Natural" default order (e.g., Dates, Numbers). "Custom" order (e.g., Sort by Price, then by Rating).
Flexibility Rigid. You only get one implementation per class. Flexible. You can make 10 different comparators for 10 different scenarios.

Template for Comparator

Collections.sort(shop, new Comparator<Product>() {
    @Override
    public int compare(Product p1, Product p2) {
        // Use String's built-in compareTo method
        return p1.name.compareTo(p2.name);
    }
});
    //OR
public interface Comparator<T> {
		int compare(T o1, T o2);
}

Template for Integers (Sorting by ID, Score, Age)

astuce : do not use subtraction (e.g., this.id - other.id). If the numbers are large negative/positive, this causes an "Integer Overflow" error. Always use the helper Integer.compare().

public class Student implements Comparable<Student> {
    private int id; 
    private String name;

    public Student(int id, String name) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }
    // --- COMPARE TO (INTEGERS) ---
    @Override
    public int compareTo(Student other) {
        // "Natural Order": Low IDs first (1, 2, 3...)
        return Integer.compare(this.id, other.id);

        // If you want REVERSE order (High IDs first):
        return Integer.compare(other.id, this.id);
    }
}

Template for Strings (Sorting by Name, Email, City)

You don't need to write the alphabet logic yourself! The Java String class already knows how to sort itself. You just "delegate" the work to the string field.

public class Member implements Comparable<Member> {
    private String username;
    private int points;

    public Member(String username, int points) {
        this.username = username;
        this.points = points;
    }

    // --- COMPARE TO (STRINGS) ---
    @Override
    public int compareTo(Member other) {
        // "Natural Order": Alphabetical (A -> Z)
	    // We simply ask our username string to compare itself to the other                   username
        return this.username.compareTo(other.username);
        
        // If you want REVERSE Alphabetical (Z -> A):
        return other.username.compareTo(this.username);
    }
}

A Combo template

if you want to sort with both integers and Strings if you got for example the same name then you sort by age.

@Override
public int compareTo(User other) {
    // 1. Primary Sort: Compare Strings
    int nameCheck = this.username.compareTo(other.username);
    
    // 2. If names are NOT equal, return that result immediately
    if (nameCheck != 0) {
        return nameCheck;
    }
    
    // 3. If names ARE equal (result was 0), fall back to ID
    return Integer.compare(this.id, other.id);
}

Summary of the Rules

  1. Class Header: Must include implements Comparable<YourClassName>.
  2. Integer Fields: Use Integer.compare(this.val, other.val).
  3. String Fields: Use this.str.compareTo(other.str).
  4. Double Fields: Use Double.compare(this.val, other.val).

Collection Interface

En Java, une collection est une structure de données qui permet de stocker et de manipuler un groupe d'objets. Les collections en java sont un ensemble de classes et d'interfaces qui aident à manipuler les données efficacement.

Il existe de nombreuses implémentations de collections :

  • Certaines collections acceptent les doublons, d'autres pas.
  • Certaines sont ordonnées, d'autres pas.
  • Certaines collections émettent quelques restrictions, comme le type ou l'interdiction de la valeur null.

Collection vs Array (Tableau)

Arrays Limitations:

  1. Arrays are fixed in size.
  2. Can store only homogenous data elements.
Student[] student = new Student[10];
student[0] = new Student();
student[1] = new Student();
student[2] = new Book(); //will generate an error because arrays cant store different elements

//you can get around this by using the Object class, since Object is the super class of all objects
Object[] objects = new Object[10];
objects[0] = new Student();
objects[1] = new Student();
objects[2] = new Book(); // no error will be generated but its not an optimal way
  1. ready made APIs support is not available in array.

  • Use an Array when:

    • You know the exact number of elements ahead of time.

    • You are working with small, fixed-size data sets.

    • Maximum execution speed and memory efficiency are critical (e.g., low-level systems programming or image processing).

  • Use Collections when:

    • You do not know how much data you will have.

    • You need to frequently add or remove items.

    • You need complex data structures (like Maps or Sets) or advanced manipulation (sorting/searching) without writing code from scratch

Methods of Collection Interface

Method Description
add(E e) Adds an element to the collection (optional).
addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) Adds all elements from another collection.
clear() Removes all elements.
contains(Object o) Checks if an element exists.
containsAll(Collection<?> c) Checks if all elements exist.
remove(Object o) Removes a single instance of the specified element.
removeAll(Collection<?> c) Removes all elements present in another collection.
retainAll(Collection<?> c) Retains only elements present in another collection.
removeIf(Predicate<? super E> filter) Removes elements satisfying a predicate.
size() Returns the number of elements.
isEmpty() Checks if the collection is empty.
iterator() Returns an iterator over the elements.
stream() Returns a sequential stream.
parallelStream() Returns a parallel stream.
toArray() Converts the collection to an array.
equals(Object o) Compares this collection with another object.
hashCode() Returns hash code of the collection.
spliterator() Returns a Spliterator for elements.
Example 
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collection;

public class CollectionDemo {

	public static void main(String[] args) {
		
		//Initiliazing a Collection with ArrayList
		Collection<String> namesCollection = new ArrayList<>();
		
		//Adding element to collection
		namesCollection.add("Rayan");
		namesCollection.add("Fatine");
		namesCollection.add("Akioud");
		
		//printing COllection
		System.out.println(namesCollection);
		
		//remove an element from collection
		namesCollection.remove("Akioud");
		System.out.println(namesCollection);
		
		//checking if an element exists
		boolean e = namesCollection.contains("Fatine");
		System.out.println("does Fatine exist in list? " +e);
		
		//Checking if the list is empty
		boolean f = namesCollection.isEmpty();
		System.out.println("is the List empty? " +f);
		
		
		namesCollection.add("Riyad");
		
		//printing each element one by one
		namesCollection.forEach((element)->{
			System.out.println(element);
		});
		
		int size = namesCollection.size();
		System.out.println("the Size of the list is : " +size);
		
		//Clear the list from all elements
		namesCollection.clear();
		System.out.println("is the list Empty: "+ namesCollection.isEmpty());
		
	}
}

Output

[Rayan, Fatine, Akioud]

[Rayan, Fatine]

does Fatine exist in list? true

is the List empty? false

Rayan
Fatine
Riyad

the Size of the list is : 3

is the list Empty: true

What will you lose by using only Collection Interface

Collection is the parent interface of List, Set, Queue so a variable of type Collection can hold any of those implementations.

// All of these are valid!
Collection<String> c1 = new ArrayList<>();
Collection<String> c2 = new LinkedList<>();
Collection<String> c3 = new HashSet<>();
Collection<String> c4 = new PriorityQueue<>();

and they can all use the Methods of Collection since its the parent of all the children interfaces.

BUT doing this will prevent the access to the specific method of each child types. for example the get() method -a very handy method to get a specific item and bring it up- can't be used since it's specified for ArrayList and not generalized for all of Collection interfaces.

If you declare variable as... You can hold... But you can ONLY call methods like...
ArrayList<String> list Only ArrayList Everything! (get, add, remove, trimToSize...)
List<String> list ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector, Stack List stuff (get, set, indexOf..) + Collection stuff
Collection<String> col ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, TreeSet, Queue... Only basic stuff (add, remove, size, clear...)

References

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/java-collection-tutorial/ https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GdAon80-0KA

notes.excerpt: {red} Notes {green}Overview The List interface is one of the most commonly used interfaces in the Java Collections Framework. It extends the Collection interface and represents an {pink}ordered sequen
notes.html:
Notes

Overview

The List interface is one of the most commonly used interfaces in the Java Collections Framework. It extends the Collection interface and represents an ordered sequence of elements where Duplicates are allowed and elements can accessed by their index. Key characteristics

  • Maintain insertion order, If you insert "A" then "B", iterating through the list will always yield "A" then "B".
  • Allows duplicate elements, (e.g., [10, 20, 10] or [Fatine, Rayan, Rayan, Fatine] are valid).
  • Supports null elements. list.add(null);
  • access elements by index (like list.get(0)) , starts with 0.
  • Supports bidirectional traversal using ListIteratore.
  • Since Every class has Object as a superclass, if its the chosen type of the list every element can be inserted in the list.

Example

List<Object> myList = new ArrayList<>();
		myList.add("1");
		myList.add("4");
		myList.add("3");
		myList.add(2);
		myList.add("3");
		myList.add(9.77);
		myList.add(null);
		System.out.println(myList);

Output

[1, 4, 3, 2, 3, 9.77, null]
//we can also obvserve the maintenance of insertion and allowance of duplicates and null

Packages

the following packages must be imported before starting to code

// 1. Interfaces (The contracts)
import java.util.List;
// 2. Implementations (The actual objects)
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedList;

or just use

import java.util.*;

Hierarchy of Java List interface

The common implementation classes of the List interface are

ArrayList (The Default Choice)

  • Under the hood: A resizable dynamic array.
  • Best for: Random access. If you need to frequently call .get(index).
  • Worst for: Inserting or removing items at the start or middle (because it has to shift all other items in memory).

LinkedList

  • Under the hood: A chain of nodes (doubly linked).
  • Best for: Adding/removing items frequently, especially at the beginning or middle.
  • Worst for: Random access (.get(index)), because it has to traverse the chain from the start to find the item.

Vector (Legacy)

  • Under the hood: Like ArrayList, but Synchronized (Thread-Safe).
  • Usage: Rarely used in modern Java. If you need thread safety, programmers now prefer CopyOnWriteArrayList or Collections.synchronizedList().

Stack (Legacy)

  • Under the hood: Extends Vector. Represents Last-In-First-Out (LIFO).
  • Usage: Generally replaced by the Deque interface (using ArrayDeque).

Java List - Operations

we will use ArrayList in these examples as its the most common

CRUD Operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete)

Declaration of Java List Interface

to use List an implementation class must be initiated with it for example ArrayList or LinkedList

// 1. Create (Initialize)
List<String> myList = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> maList = new LinkedList<>();

✦ Adding Elements

using add(Object o)

//Append to the end of the list.
myList.add("Mercury"); 
myList.add("Earth"); 
myList.add("Mars");

✦ Insert Elements

using add(int index, Object o)

//Insert -Add at a specific index.
    // This shifts "Earth" and "Mars" to the right.
    myList.add(1, "Venus");

✦ Accessing Elements

using get(int index) which return element at the specified index.

//Read (Get by index)
    String secondPlanet = myList.get(1); 
    System.out.println("Planet at index 1: " + secondPlanet); 
        // Output: Planet at index 1: Venus

✦ Updating Elements

using set(int index, Object o)

// Update (Set/Replace)
    // Replaces "Mars" (index 3) with "Jupiter". Returns the OLD value.
    myList.set(3, "Jupiter");

✦ Removing Elements

using either:

  • remove(Object o) to remove the first occurred specified object from the list
  • remove(int index) to remove a specific element at an index (placement) in list
// Delete (Remove)
    // You can remove by Index OR by Object
    myList.remove(0);         // Removes "Mercury"
	myList.remove("Earth");   // Removes the first occurrence of "Earth"

Search and Status Operations

✦ Check if list is empty

using isEmpty()

//returns a boolean type if the list is empty its true if it got any elems then return fals
boolean check = myList.isEmpty();
System.out.println(check); 
// Output: false, since list is full of planets

✦ Size

using size() you can know how many elements are in the list by returning an integer

int size = myList.size();
System.out.println("the size of the list is :"+ size);

✦ Check if element is present or not

using contains(Object o) to check existence and return a boolean type either true if the element exits or false if it doesn't

boolean isIt = programming.contains("Earth");
System.out.println("is Earth in list? " +isIt);
//Output : is Earth in list? false

✦ Searching elements

either by using:

  • indexOf(Objec o) which return the index (Integer) of the first occurrence of the specified element in list or -1 if it dosent.
  • lastIndexOf(Object o) that return the index of the last occurrence of the specified element or -1 if the element isn't found so basically either check from start till it find it or checking from the end going backwards till it find it.
int firstIndex = myList.indexOf("Venus"); // Output: 0
int lastIndex = myList.lastIndexOf("Jupiter"); // Output: 1
int missingIndex = myList.indexOf("Earth");  // Output: -1 (Not found)

Slicing and Bulk Operations

These methods allow you to work with groups of elements or sections of the list.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays; // Helper to create lists quickly
import java.util.List;

public class ListBulkExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
        numbers.add(10);
        numbers.add(20);
        numbers.add(30);
        numbers.add(40);
        numbers.add(50);
        
        // 1. subList (Create a "View" of a range)
        // Syntax: subList(start, end) -> includes Start, excludes End
        List<Integer> middle = numbers.subList(1, 4); 
        System.out.println(middle); // Output: [20, 30, 40]
        
        // WARNING: subList is a "Window". 
        // Modifying 'middle' modifies 'numbers'!
        middle.set(0, 999); 
        System.out.println(numbers); // Output: [10, 999, 30, 40, 50]
        
        // 2. addAll (Merge lists)
        List<Integer> moreNumbers = Arrays.asList(60, 70);
        numbers.addAll(moreNumbers); 
        
        // 3. removeAll (Bulk delete)
        // Removes anything found in the provided list
        numbers.removeAll(Arrays.asList(999, 50));
    }
}

Sorting and Converting

makes life easier to find methods that sorts lists for you instead of creating your algorithm

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Comparator;

public class ListSortExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
        names.add("Charlie");
        names.add("Alice");
        names.add("Bob");

        // 1. Sort Naturally (A-Z)
        names.sort(null); 
        Collections.sort(names);
        System.out.println(names); // [Alice, Bob, Charlie]

        // 2. Sort Custom (Reverse Z-A)
        names.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());
        System.out.println(names); // [Charlie, Bob, Alice]

        // 3. Convert List to Array
        // We pass 'new String[0]' to tell Java the type of array we want.
        String[] nameArray = names.toArray(new String[0]);
    }
}

ArrayList

Hierarchy of ArrayList

It implements List Interface which is a sub-interface of Collection Interface.

ArrayList Constructors in Java

Java provides multiple constructors to create an ArrayList based on different requirements:

1. ArrayList()

Creates an empty ArrayList with default initial capacity.

ArrayList<Integer> arr = new ArrayList<>();

2. ArrayList(Collection<? extends E> c)

Creates an ArrayList initialized with elements from the specified collection.

ArrayList<String> arr = new ArrayList<>(collection);

3. ArrayList(int initialCapacity)

This constructor is used to build an array list with the initial capacity being specified.

ArrayList<Double> arr = new ArrayList<>(20);

Specific ArrayList Methods

Method Purpose Unique to ArrayList? Best Use Case
ensureCapacity(int) Pre-allocates memory Yes Before adding massive amounts of data.
trimToSize() Releases unused memory Yes After deleting many items to save RAM.
removeIf(Predicate) Conditional removal No (but optimized) Removing items based on logic (e.g., "remove all nulls").
replaceAll(Operator) In-place modification No (but optimized) Applying a math operation or formatting to every item.

Time and Space Complexity

Operation Time Complexity Space Complexity
Inserting Element in ArrayList O(1) O(N)
Removing Element from ArrayList O(N) O(1)
Traversing Elements in ArrayList O(N) O(N)
Replacing Elements in ArrayList O(1) O(1)

LinkedList

LinkedList nodes cannot be accessed directly by index; elements must be accessed by traversing from the head.

  • Dynamic Size: LinkedList grows or shrinks dynamically at runtime.
  • Efficient Insertion/Deletion: Adding or removing elements at the beginning or middle is faster compared to ArrayList.

Hierarchy of ArrayList

It implements the List and Deque interfaces, both of which are sub-interfaces of the Collection Interface.

Constructors of LinkedList

1. LinkedList()

This constructor is used to create an empty linked list. If we wish to create an empty LinkedList with the name list, then it can be created as:

LinkedList<Object> list = new LinkedList<>();  

2. LinkedList(Collection C)

This constructor is used to create an ordered list that contains all the elements of a specified collection, as returned by the collection's iterator. If we wish to create a LinkedList with the name list, then, it can be created as:

LinkedList<Object> list = new LinkedList<>(C);

Specific ArrayList Methods

Method Type Method Name Description Safety Note
Adding addFirst(E e) Adds element to index 0.
addLast(E e) Adds element to the very end. Same as add()
push(E e) Pushes an element onto the stack (adds to front). Stack terminology
Retrieving getFirst() Gets the first element. Throws Exception if empty
getLast() Gets the last element. Throws Exception if empty
peekFirst() Gets the first element. Returns null if empty (Safe)
peekLast() Gets the last element. Returns null if empty (Safe)
Removing removeFirst() Removes and returns the first element. Throws Exception if empty
removeLast() Removes and returns the last element. Throws Exception if empty
pollFirst() Removes and returns the first element. Returns null if empty (Safe)
pollLast() Removes and returns the last element. Returns null if empty (Safe)
pop() Removes the first element (Stack pop). Throws Exception if empty
Iterating descendingIterator() Returns an iterator that walks backwards (Tail $\rightarrow$ Head). Unique to LinkedList

ArrayList vs LinkedList

## Time and Space Complexity #### Time Complexity
Operation LinkedList ArrayList Why?
Get by Index get(i) O(n) (Slow) O(1) (Fast) LinkedList must walk from the start to find index 1000. ArrayList jumps instantly.
Add/Remove at Start O(1) (Fast) O(n) (Slow) LinkedList just updates a pointer. ArrayList must shift every element to the right.
Add/Remove at End O(1) O(1) Both are efficient here.
Add/Remove in Middle O(n) O(n) LinkedList takes O(n) to find the spot. ArrayList takes O(n) to shift elements.
Search contains() O(n) O(n) Both must check every item one by one.

Space Complexity

Structure Complexity Memory Overhead Detail
LinkedList High Heavy. Every single item is wrapped in a "Node" object. Each node stores:

1. The Data

2. Reference to Next

3. Reference to Previous

Result: Uses ~4x more memory per item than ArrayList.
ArrayList Low Light. Stores data in a compact array. The only wasted memory is the "buffer" space at the end (capacity minus size).

References

notes.html:
Notes

Overview

A Map is an object that maps keys to values. It is part of the Java Collections Framework (java.util), but unlike List or Set, it does not extend the Collection interface. Key Characteristics

  • Key-Value Pairs: Data is stored as an Entry<Key, Value>.
  • Unique Keys: A Map cannot contain duplicate keys. If you add a key that already exists, the old value is overwritten.
  • One Value per Key: Each key maps to at most one value.

Declaration of the Map interface

public interface Map<K, V>

  • K -> Type of keys maintained by the map
  • V -> Type of mapped values

Example

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class SimpleHashMapExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Create a HashMap (Key: Fruit Name, Value: Price)
        Map<String, Double> fruitPrices = new HashMap<>();

        // 2. Add items using put()
        fruitPrices.put("Apple", 0.99);
        fruitPrices.put("Banana", 0.50);
        fruitPrices.put("Cherry", 2.50);

        System.out.println("1. Initial Map: " + fruitPrices);

        // 3. Access a value using get()
        double bananaPrice = fruitPrices.get("Banana");
        System.out.println("2. Price of Banana: " + bananaPrice);

        // 4. Overwrite a value (Duplicate keys are NOT allowed)
        // We put "Apple" again with a new price. The old 0.99 is replaced.
        fruitPrices.put("Apple", 1.20); 
        System.out.println("3. After updating Apple: " + fruitPrices);

        // 5. Remove an item
        fruitPrices.remove("Cherry");
        System.out.println("4. After removing Cherry: " + fruitPrices);

        // 6. Check size
        System.out.println("5. Total items: " + fruitPrices.size());
    }
}

Output

1. Initial Map: {Apple=0.99, Cherry=2.50, Banana=0.5}
2. Price of Banana: 0.5
3. After updating Apple: {Apple=1.2, Cherry=2.50, Banana=0.5}
4. After removing Cherry: {Apple=1.2, Banana=0.5}
5. Total items: 2

Packages

the following packages must be imported before starting to code

// 1. Interfaces (The contracts)
import java.util.Map;
// 2. Implementations (The actual objects)
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.TreeMap;

or just use

import java.util.*;

Hierarchy of Map

### The common implementation classes of the Set interface are

A. HashMap (The Default Choice)

  • Structure: Uses a Hash Table.
  • Order: No guarantee. The order can change over time.
  • Nulls: Allows one null key and multiple null values.
  • Performance: Extremely fast ($O(1)$) for basic operations like get and put.
  • Use case: When you don't care about the order of items, just speed.

B. LinkedHashMap (The "Ordered" One)

  • Structure: Hash Table + Linked List.
  • Order: Maintains Insertion Order (the order you added them).
  • Nulls: Allows one null key and multiple null values.
  • Performance: Slightly slower than HashMap (because it has to maintain the links), but still $O(1)$.
  • Use case: When you need a cache or need to display items in the order they were added.

C. TreeMap (The "Sorted" One)

  • Structure: Red-Black Tree (a self-balancing binary search tree).
  • Order: Sorted according to the "natural ordering" of its keys (e.g., A-Z, 1-10) or a custom Comparator.
  • Nulls: Does NOT allow null keys (will throw exception), but allows null values.
  • Performance: Slower ($O(\log n)$) because it sorts every time you insert.
  • Use case: When you need a dictionary or a phone book sorted alphabetically.

Java Map - Operations

Using a Student Gradebook (Map<String, Integer>) for all examples to easily follow the logic.

CRUD Operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete)

These are the fundamental methods every Map supports.

//Declare
Map<String, Integer> grades = new HashMap<>();

// CREATE: put(Key, Value)
grades.put("Alice", 85);
grades.put("Bob", 90);

// UPDATE: put(Key, Value) 
// If the key exists, the old value is overwritten.
grades.put("Alice", 95); 

// READ: get(Key)
Integer aliceScore = grades.get("Alice"); 
Integer daveScore = grades.get("Dave"); // Returns null if missing

// DELETE: remove(Key)
grades.remove("Bob"); 

System.out.println("Alice's Score: " + aliceScore); // Prints 95
System.out.println("Dave's Score: " + daveScore);   // Prints null
System.out.println("Map: " + grades);               // Prints {Alice=95}

"Safe" Operations (Defensive Coding)

to avoid fucking up and overwriting some important elements

Map<String, Integer> grades = new HashMap<>();
grades.put("Alice", 85);

// SAFE READ: getOrDefault(Key, DefaultValue)
// Used when you aren't sure if the key exists.
Integer score = grades.getOrDefault("Charlie", 0); 
System.out.println("Charlie's Score: " + score); // Prints 0 (not null!)

// SAFE INSERT: putIfAbsent(Key, Value)
// Only puts the value if the key is NOT in the map.
grades.putIfAbsent("Alice", 100); // Alice exists, so this is IGNORED
grades.putIfAbsent("Bob", 70);    // Bob is new, so this is ADDED

System.out.println(grades); 
// Output: {Alice=85, Bob=70} (Alice kept her old score)

The "Views" (Iteration & Loops)

Maps cannot be iterated directly (you can't do for (x : map)). You must convert them into a View (Set or Collection) first.

Map<String, Integer> grades = new HashMap<>();
grades.put("Alice", 85);
grades.put("Bob", 90);

// OPTION A: Iterating Keys (keySet)
// Use when you only need names, or want to look up values manually.
System.out.print("Students: ");
for (String name : grades.keySet()) {
    System.out.print(name + " ");
}
// Output: Students: Alice Bob 

// OPTION B: Iterating Values (values)
// Use when you want to calculate an average and don't care who got what score.
int sum = 0;
for (Integer s : grades.values()) {
    sum += s;
}
System.out.println("\nTotal Sum: " + sum); // Output: 175

//## OPTION C: Iterating Entries (entrySet) - **MOST IMPORTANT** ##
// Use when you need BOTH the name and the score. most efficient.
for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> entry : grades.entrySet()) {
    String k = entry.getKey();
    Integer v = entry.getValue();
    System.out.println(k + " scored " + v);
}
entrySet(), the most powerful part of the Map interface.

getKey() and getValue() are absolutely necessary when you use entrySet(). What entrySet() actually returns When you call map.entrySet(), Java does not give you the keys or the values directly. Instead, it gives you a Set of Entry objects. Think of a Map like a wall of P.O. Boxes.

  • keySet() gives you a list of just the box numbers (101, 102, 103...).
  • values() gives you a pile of the mail found inside the boxes.
  • entrySet() gives you the actual drawers themselves. Each drawer is a single object that physically holds both the number (Key) and the mail (Value) welded together. In Java, this "drawer" is called Map.Entry.

Bulk Operations

These operations affect the entire map at once.

Map<String, Integer> classA = new HashMap<>();
classA.put("Alice", 85);

Map<String, Integer> classB = new HashMap<>();
classB.put("Bob", 90);
classB.put("Charlie", 88);

// MERGE: putAll(Map)
// Copies all mappings from classB into classA
classA.putAll(classB); 

System.out.println("Merged Class: " + classA);
// Output: {Alice=85, Bob=90, Charlie=88}

// CLEAR: clear()
// Removes everything.
classA.clear();

// CHECK EMPTY: isEmpty()
System.out.println("Is empty? " + classA.isEmpty()); // true

Checking for Existence

Simple boolean checks. like contains in List

Map<String, Integer> grades = new HashMap<>();
grades.put("Alice", 85);

// CONTAINS KEY: O(1) - Very Fast
if (grades.containsKey("Alice")) {
    System.out.println("Alice is present.");
}

// CONTAINS VALUE: O(n) - Slower (Must check every student)
if (grades.containsValue(100)) {
    System.out.println("Someone got a perfect score.");
} else {
    System.out.println("No perfect scores.");
}

Most common Operations for Map

Category Method Return Type Description
CRUD put(K, V) V (old value) Adds pair. Overwrites if key exists.
CRUD get(K) V Returns value or null.
CRUD remove(K) V (removed value) Deletes the pair.
Safety getOrDefault(K, D) V Returns D if key is missing.
Safety putIfAbsent(K, V) V Adds pair only if key is missing.
Views keySet() Set<K> Returns all keys (unique).
Views values() Collection<V> Returns all values (can repeat).
Views entrySet() Set<Entry<K,V>> Returns all pairs.

References
