notes.html:
Java Overview

Quick Facts
  • First released: 1995
  • Creator: James Gosling (Sun Microsystems, now Oracle)
  • Paradigm: Object-oriented, imperative, structured
  • Typing: Static, strong, safe, nominative
  • Memory management: Automatic (Garbage Collection)
  • Key principle: "Write Once, Run Anywhere" (WORA)
## Introduction

Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed to have as few implementation dependencies as possible. It is:

  • Platform-independent (via Java Virtual Machine)
  • Memory-safe (automatic garbage collection)
  • Multi-threaded (built-in concurrency support)
  • Secure (sandboxed execution environment)

Current Status

  • Rank: Consistently top 3-5 in popularity indices (TIOBE, GitHub, Stack Overflow)
  • Active version: Java 23 (as of 2025)
  • Primary maintainer: Oracle Corporation (with community via OpenJDK)

The Java Mascot: Duke

*Duke, Java's official mascot, was created by Joe Palrang*

Core Java Architecture

graph TD
    A[Java Source Code .java] --> B[Java Compiler javac]
    B --> C[Bytecode .class]
    C --> D[Java Virtual Machine JVM]
    D --> E[Platform-Specific Execution]

Three Pillars of Java Platform

  1. JDK (Java Development Kit)

    • Tools for developing Java applications
    • Includes compiler, debugger, documentation tools
    • Contains JRE + development tools

  2. JRE (Java Runtime Environment)

    • Libraries and JVM to run Java applications
    • End-user focused (no development tools)

  3. JVM (Java Virtual Machine)

    • Executes Java bytecode
    • Provides platform independence
    • Manages memory (garbage collection)

First Java Program

// A Java program to print Hello World!
public class HelloWorld {          // Class declaration
    public static void main(String[] args) {  // Main method - entry point
        System.out.println("Hello World!");   // Output statement
    }
}

Output:

Hello World!

Key Syntax Elements

Element Purpose Required?
public class Class declaration (must match filename) Yes
main() Application entry point Yes for executable apps
System.out.println() Output to console No (but commonly used)
Semicolons ; Statement terminator Yes (except blocks)

Java Syntax Fundamentals

Comments


// Single-line comment

/*
 * Multi-line comment
 * (Good practice: use javadoc style for documentation)
 */

/**
 * Javadoc comment
 * @param args command-line arguments
 * @return void
 */

Basic Structure


// File: MyProgram.java
package com.example.myapp;  // Optional package declaration

import java.util.Scanner;   // Import statements

// Class declaration (public class name must match filename)
public class MyProgram {
    
    // Main method - program entry point
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Program logic here
    }
    
    // Other methods
    public void myMethod() {
        // Method implementation
    }
}

Why Java? Key Features

1. Platform Independence

  • "Write Once, Run Anywhere" (WORA)
  • Bytecode runs on any JVM implementation
  • No need to recompile for different platforms

2. Object-Oriented

  • Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, Abstraction
  • Everything (except primitives) is an object

3. Automatic Memory Management

  • Garbage Collector automatically reclaims unused memory
  • Reduces memory leaks and segmentation faults

4. Rich Standard Library

  • Collections Framework
  • I/O, Networking, Concurrency utilities
  • Security, Database connectivity (JDBC)

5. Strong Community & Ecosystem

  • Mature frameworks (Spring, Jakarta EE, etc.)
  • Extensive tooling (Maven, Gradle, IDEs)
  • Large talent pool and learning resources

Java Applications & Use Cases

Enterprise Systems

  • Banking & Finance: Transaction processing, trading platforms
  • E-commerce: Backend systems, payment processing
  • Healthcare: EHR systems, medical record management

Web Development

Framework Purpose Popularity
Spring Boot Microservices, REST APIs ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Jakarta EE Enterprise applications ⭐⭐⭐⭐
Struts MVC web applications ⭐⭐
Play Framework Reactive web apps ⭐⭐⭐

Mobile Development

  • Android Apps (primary language for native Android development)
  • Cross-platform frameworks (Kotlin interoperable)

Game Development

  • Minecraft (most famous Java game)
  • LibGDX, jMonkeyEngine frameworks
  • Android mobile games

Cloud & Big Data

  • Hadoop (big data processing)
  • Apache Kafka (stream processing)
  • Apache Spark (data analytics)
  • Major cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) have extensive Java SDKs

Desktop Applications

  • JavaFX (modern UI framework)
  • Swing (legacy but still used)
  • IntelliJ IDEA (IDE built with Java)

Scientific Computing

  • Data analysis tools
  • Mathematical modeling
  • Research applications

Major Companies Using Java

Company Use Case
Google Android OS, backend services
Amazon E-commerce platform, AWS services
Netflix Content delivery, recommendation engine
Spotify Music streaming backend
Uber Ride-hailing backend, surge pricing
LinkedIn Professional networking platform
Twitter Backend services (migrating but still uses Java)
NASA World Wind project, data analysis

Learning Path & Prerequisites

Before Learning Java

  • Basic programming concepts (variables, loops, conditionals)
  • Understanding of object-oriented principles (helpful but not required)
  • No specific language prerequisite (Java can be a first language)

Core Concepts to Master

  1. Basics: Variables, Data Types, Operators
  2. Control Flow: Conditionals, Loops
  3. OOP: Classes, Objects, Inheritance, Polymorphism
  4. Advanced: Exception Handling, Collections, Multithreading
  5. Tools: Build tools (Maven/Gradle), Testing (JUnit)

Next Steps After Java Basics

graph LR
    A[Java Basics] --> B[Spring Framework]
    A --> C[Android Development]
    A --> D[Microservices]
    B --> E[Cloud Deployment]
    C --> F[Mobile App Publishing]
    D --> G[Containerization]

Common Criticisms & Alternatives

Criticisms

  • Verbose syntax (compared to Kotlin, Python)
  • Memory consumption (JVM overhead)
  • Slower startup time (improved with AOT compilation)
  • Less flexible than dynamically-typed languages

Modern Alternatives

Language Best For Java Comparison
Kotlin Android, modern JVM apps More concise, interoperable
Python Data science, scripting Dynamic typing, faster development
Go Cloud services, CLI tools Better performance, simpler concurrency
C# Windows apps, game dev Similar syntax, Microsoft ecosystem

Quick Reference

Compile & Run


# Compile
javac HelloWorld.java

# Run
java HelloWorld

# Create JAR file
jar cf myapp.jar *.class

Popular IDEs

  1. IntelliJ IDEA (most popular for Java)
  2. Eclipse (free, extensive plugins)
  3. VS Code (lightweight with Java extensions)
  4. NetBeans (official Oracle IDE)

Useful Links

  • Oracle Java Documentation
  • OpenJDK
  • Java on GitHub
  • Stack Overflow Java Tag
Learning Strategy

  1. Master core Java concepts thoroughly

  2. Build small projects (calculator, to-do app)

  3. Learn Spring Framework for enterprise development

  4. Contribute to open-source Java projects

  5. Stay updated with new Java versions (6-month release cycle)

Quote

"Java is to JavaScript what car is to carpet." — Chris Heilmann

notes.html:
Notes

A Constructor is a special method that initializes an object. Constructors in java are what give you the access to assign variables / parameters to a certain object of a class when its created. it can be done by using the new keyword:

Stduent stu = new Student();

//Student: Class name
//stu: Object name
  • Constructors should have the same name as the class name.
  • Constructors doesn't have a return type, not even void.
  • Constructors can have arguments (paramètres).
  • this keyword should be used to make the code more readable.

Types of Constructors

Default Constructors (Constructeur par défaut)

Also called No-Argument Contractor

public Personne() {
	nom= "Inconnu";  //Argumet type String 
	age = 0; //Argument type int
	//Or
	this("Inconnu",0);
}

Output:

Inconnu, 0

These arguments can't be changed when creating a new object and when running the code through the main function it will keep showing Inconnu, 0 unless you use Getters and Setters.

When there is no Constructor created in the class, JAVAC ( java's compiler) will create a default one automatically.

Parameterized Constructor (Constructeur surchargé)

public Personne(String nom, int age) {
	this.nom=nom;
	this.age=age;
}

You can initialize an Object using parameters and change with whatever info you'd like instead of a fixed one like the default constructor

We cant create 2 Constructors with the same amount and types of parameters

Utilization

In this example we can see also a Constructor overloading where there is both a default constructor and and parameterized one. It allows for creating either default or specified values.

public static void main(String[] args){

	//Default Constructors
	Personne p1 = new Personne(); 
	//Parameterized Constructors
	Personne p2 = new Personne("Fatine", 21);
	
	//Default
	System.out.println("p1-> Name: "+p1.name+", Age: "+p1.age);
	//Parameterized
	System.out.println("p2-> Name: "+p2.name+", Age: "+p12.age);
}

Output:

'This' keyword

in Java, this is a reference variable that refers to the current object or field. Used to:

  • Call curent class methods and fields.
  • Differentiate between the local and instance variables.
  • Reduce naming conflicts.
  • Pass an instance of current class as a parameter.
  • It can be useful for Getters and Setters.
  • it's not that big of a deal but it's better to be used just for clarity
public class Person{
	 String name;
     int age;
    
	Person(String name, int age)
    {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }
    //Getter for name
    public String get_name() { 
	    return name; 
    }
    // Setter for name
    public void change_name(String name)
    {
        this.name = name;
    }
    
	public void printDetails()
    {
        System.out.println("Name: " + this.name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + this.age);
        System.out.println();
    }
    // main function
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        // Objects Declared
        Person first = new Person("ABC", 18);
        Person second = new Person("XYZ", 22);
		//Details outpot
        first.printDetails();
        second.printDetails();
}

Output:

Name: ABC
Age: 18

Name: XYZ
Age: 22

notes.html:
Notes

Overview

An exception is an event that occurs during the execution of a program (Runtime) that disrupts the normal flow of instructions. It is Java's way of saying, "Something unexpected happened, and i don't know how to proceed" Intuition :

Java Exception Hierarchy

In Java, all exceptions and errors are subclasses of the `Throwable` class. They are organized into a strict family tree. Understanding this tree is the key to knowing _what_ to catch and _what_ to fix. It has two main branches: - **Error** - **Exception**

A. The Fatal Branch: Error

  • Definition: Severe problems related to the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) or system resources.
  • Examples: OutOfMemoryError (RAM full), StackOverflowError (infinite recursion).
  • Rule: Never catch these. They indicate the application is in an unstable state and should crash . Example
// DON'T DO THIS
public void recursiveDoom() {
    recursiveDoom(); // Calls itself forever
}
// Result: Exception in thread "main" java.lang.StackOverflowError

B. The Recoverable Branch: Exception

The "Bug" Branch: RuntimeException (~={red}Unchecked)=~

These exceptions are checked at runtime and do not require explicit handling at compile time.

  • Concept: These represent programming errors. They are your fault.
  • Rule: Do not fix these with try-catch. Fix the code logic instead. These are "Unchecked" because the compiler does not force you to handle them. Example:
int result = 10 / 0; // CRASH! ArithmeticException
  • The Wrong Fix: Using try-catch to hide the crash.
  • The Right Fix: validating the input: if (divisor != 0) ...
The "External" Branch: ~={red}Checked Exceptions=~

These exceptions are checked at compile time, forcing the programmer to handle them explicitly.

  • Concept: These represent valid, anticipated problems that happen outside your program's control (e.g., File not found, Network timeout).
  • Rule: You MUST handle these. The compiler will give you an error if you ignore them (Unhandled exception type...) .
  • Example: Trying to read a file that might not exist.
Summary
Category Unchecked Exceptions (exceptions non vérifiées ) Checked Exceptions (exceptions vérifiées)
Class Subclasses of RuntimeException. All other subclasses of Exception.
Cause Programming Logic Errors (Bugs). External Factors (Environment).
Examples NullPointerException, ArithmeticException. IOException, SQLException.
Rule Fix the code. Do not use try-catch. Must Handle. The compiler forces you to use try-catch or throws.

The Defense Mechanism: try, catch, finally

This trio allows you to handle errors gracefully without crashing the program.

  • The try block contains code that might throw an exception,
  • The catch block handles the exception if it occurs.

try-catch

Example

class Artithmetic{
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        
        int n = 10;
        int m = 0;

        try {
            int ans = n / m;
            System.out.println("Answer: " + ans);
        } catch (ArithmeticException e){
            System.out.println("Error: Division by 0!");
        } 
    }
}

Output

Error: Division by 0!

On peut déclarer plusieurs blocs catch, mais ils doivent être organisés du cas le plus spécifique au cas le plus général.

public class TestException{
	public static void main(String[] args) {
		try{
			int[] numbers = { 1, 2, 3 }; 
			System.out.println(numbers[3]);
		}catch(Exception ex){
			System.err.println(ex.getMessage());
		}catch(ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e){ //jamais appelé
			System.err.println(e.getMessage()); } } }

finally

Le bloc finally est utilisé pour contenir du code qui sera exécuté quel que soit le résultat de la tentative (try) et de la gestion d'exception (catch). Seul l'appel de System.exit() An Example with finally

public class InputExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String userInput = "ABC"; // Bad input
        
        try {
            // THE DANGER ZONE
            // We attempt code that might fail.
            int number = Integer.parseInt(userInput); 
            System.out.println("Converted number: " + number); // Skipped if error
            
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            // THE SAFETY NET
            // This runs ONLY if the specific exception occurs.
            System.out.println("Error: '" + userInput + "' is not a valid number.");
            
            // Helpful debugging tools mentioned in the course [cite: 1475-1476]:
            // e.getMessage(); // Returns "For input string: \"ABC\""
            // e.printStackTrace(); // Prints the full error trace to console
            
        } finally {
            // THE CLEANUP CREW
            // This runs ALWAYS (Success or Failure).
            // Used for closing files, databases, or saying goodbye.
            System.out.println("End of operation."); 
        }
    }
}

The Active Control: throw vs throws

  • throw (Verb): You explicitly cause an error. You are holding the grenade and pulling the pin.
class Demo {
    static void checkAge(int age) {
        
        if (age < 18) {
            throw new ArithmeticException("Age must be 18 or above");
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        checkAge(15);
    }
}
  • throws (Declaration): You warn others. You put a sign on your method saying "Danger: Calling this might cause an explosion." Le mot-clé throws est utilisé dans la déclaration d'une méthode pour indiquer que la méthode peut lancer certaines exceptions.
import java.io.*;
class Demo {
    static void readFile(String fileName) throws IOException {
        FileReader file = new FileReader(fileName);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args){
        try {
            readFile("test.txt");
        } catch (IOException e){
            
            System.out.println("File not found: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Example We will create a method checkAge that validates if a user can enter a club. The Exception:

// A simple custom checked exception
class UnderAgeException extends Exception {
    public UnderAgeException(String msg) { 
    super(msg);
    }
}

The Logic (throw and throws):

class Club {
    // 1. 'throws': The Warning Sign.
    // We tell the compiler: "This method MIGHT fail with UnderAgeException"
    public void enterClub(int age) throws UnderAgeException {
        
        if (age < 18) {
            // 2. 'throw': The Action.
            // The condition is met, so we stop everything and trigger the error.
            throw new UnderAgeException("Sorry, you must be 18+.");
        }
        
        System.out.println("Welcome to the club!");
    }
}

The Usage (Handling the Warning):

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Club myClub = new Club();
        
        try {
            // Because 'enterClub' has 'throws', we are FORCED to use try-catch
            myClub.enterClub(16); 
        } catch (UnderAgeException e) {
	        //e.getMessage() retrieves the string passed to the constructor: 
	        //"Sorry, you must be 18".
            System.out.println("Access Denied: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output

Access Denied: Sorry, you must be 18+.
Keyword Role Analogy Course Context
try Defines the block of code to monitor for errors. The "Danger Zone". "Bloc d'instructions à protéger" 5.
catch Defines the block that handles a specific exception type. The "Safety Net". "Traitement de l'exception" 6.
finally Code that runs always, regardless of success or failure. The "Cleanup Crew". "Exécuté systématiquement" 7.
throw Manually triggers an exception instance. Pulling the "Fire Alarm". "Lever une exception" 8.
throws Declares that a method might fail. The "Warning Sign". "Propager une exception" 9.

Methods to Print the Exception Information

  • printStackTrace(): Prints the full stack trace of the exception, including the name, message and location of the error.
  • toString(): Prints exception information in the format of the Name of the exception.
  • getMessage() : Prints the description of the exception

Nested try-catch

In Java, you can place one try-catch block inside another to handle exceptions at multiple levels.

public class NestedTryExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            System.out.println("Outer try block");
            try {
                int a = 10 / 0; // This causes ArithmeticException
            } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
                System.out.println("Inner catch: " + e);
            }
            String str = null;
            System.out.println(str.length()); // This causes NullPointerException
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("Outer catch: " + e);
        }
    }
}

In depth Example

package com.exception.exo5;
import java.util.Scanner;

public class Calculatrice {
    public double division(int a, int b){
        if (b == 0) {
            // On lance manuellement l'exception car Java ne le fait pas pour les doubles
            throw new ArithmeticException("Division par zéro impossible");
        }
        return (double)a/b;
    }
    public double racineCaree(double x){
        if(x<0){
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Impossible de claculer racine carre d'un nombre negatife");
        }
        return Math.sqrt(x);
    }
}

public class TestCalcuatrice {
    public static void main(String[] args){
        Scanner scan = new Scanner(System.in);
        Calculatrice calc = new Calculatrice();

        try{
            System.out.println("Donner deux nombre");
            int a = scan.nextInt();
            int b = scan.nextInt();
            try{
                double resultDiv = calc.division(a, b);
                System.out.println("Reuslta de division est: "+resultDiv);

            }catch(ArithmeticException e){
                System.out.println(e.getMessage());
            }

            try{
                double resultRacine = calc.racineCaree(a);
                System.out.println("RAcine carre de "+a+" est : "+resultRacine);
            }catch(IllegalArgumentException e){
                System.out.println(e.getMessage());
            }
            scan.close();
        }catch(Exception e){
            System.out.println("Valeur saisie invalide");
        }finally{
            System.out.println("thank you for your participation");
        }
    }
}

Output

Donner deux nombre
-9
0
Division par zéro impossible
Impossible de claculer racine carre d'un nombre negatife
thank you for your participation

Difference Between Exception and Error

Feature Exception Error
Definition An event that occurs during program execution, disrupting normal flow, which can be handled using try-catch. A serious problem that occurs in the JVM, generally cannot be handled by the application.
Package java.lang.Exception java.lang.Error
Recoverable Yes, can be caught and handled. No, usually not recoverable.
Examples IOException, SQLException, ArithmeticException OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError

notes.html:
Notes

In Java, Getter and Setter are methods used to protect your data and make your code more secure. Getter and Setter make the programmer convenient in setting and getting the value for a particular data type.

Getter in Java: Getter returns the value (accessors), it returns the value of data type int, String, double, float, etc. For the program's convenience, the getter starts with the word "get" followed by the variable name.

Setter in Java: While Setter sets or updates the value (mutators). It sets the value for any variable used in a class's programs. and starts with the word "set" followed by the variable name.

Syntax

class ABC{
    private variable;
    
    public void setVariable(int x){
        this.variable=x;
    }
    
    public int getVariable{
        return variable;
    }
}

Note: In both getter and setter, the first letter of the variable should be capital.

Examples of Getter and Setter in Java

Example 1:

// Java Program to Illustrate Getter and Setter

// Importing input output classes
import java.io.*;

// Class 1
// Helper class
class GetSet {

    // Member variable of this class
    private String name;

    // Method 1 - Getter
    public String getName() { 
	    return name; 
	}

    // Method 2 - Setter
    public void setName(String N)
    {
        // This keyword refers to current instance itself
        this.name = N;
    }
}

// Class 2
// Main class
class GFG {

    // Main driver method
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        // Creating an object of class 1 in main() method
        GetSet obj = new GetSet();

        // Setting the name by calling setter method
        obj.setName("Geeks for Geeks");
        // Getting the name by calling getter method
        System.out.println(obj.getName());
    }
}

Output:

Geeks for Geeks

Getter and Setter give you the convenience of entering the value of the variables of any data type by the requirement of the code. Getters and setters let you manage how crucial variables in your code are accessed and altered. It can be seen in the program discussed below as follows:

Example 2

// Java Program to Illustrate Getter and Setter

// Importing input output classes
import java.io.*;

class GetSet {
    // Member variable of this class
    private int num;

    // Method 1 - Setter
    public void setNumber(int number)
    {
        // Checking if number is between 1 to 10 exclusive
        if (number < 1 || number > 10) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        }
        num = number;
    }

    // Method 2 - Getter
    public int getNumber() { 
	    return num; 
	}
}

// Class 2
// Main class
class GFG {
    // Main driver method
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        GetSet obj = new GetSet();

        // Calling method 1 inside main() method
        obj.setNumber(5);

        // Printing the number as setter above
        System.out.println(obj.getNumber());
    }
}

Output

5

Explanation of the above program:

Here we can see that if we take a value greater than 10 then it shows an error, By using the setNumber() method, one can be sure the value of a number is always between 1 and 10. This is much better than updating the number variable directly.

References

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/getter-and-setter-in-java/

notes.html:
Notes

Overview

An interface in Java is a collection of abstract methods (methods without a body) and constants.

  • It functions as a contract: Any class implementing the interface guarantees it will provide the functionality defined by the interface.
  • It specifies what must be done, without defining how it is done.
## Syntax and "Invisible" Modifiers

When declaring an interface, Java implicitly applies specific modifiers to members even if you do not type them.

  • Attributes: Are always public, static, and final (constants).
  • Methods: Always public and abstract by nature (unless declared static or default)

Example

interface MyInterface {
    // Implicitly: public static final float PI = 3.14f;
    float PI = 3.14f; 
    // Implicitly: public abstract void meth1();
    void meth1(); 
}

Implementation Rules

A class uses the implements keyword to use an interface.

  1. Concrete Class: Must provide an implementation (body) for all methods defined in the interface.
  2. Abstract Class: If a class does not implement all methods of the interface, it must be declared abstract.

Inheritance and Polymorphism

  • Multiple Inheritance: Java classes cannot extend multiple classes, but they can implement multiple interfaces.
  • Interface Inheritance: An interface can inherit from one or more other interfaces using the extends keyword Example
class MyClass implements Math1, Math2 {
    // Must implement methods from both Math1 and Math2
}

Abstract Class vs. Interface

Feature Abstract Class Interface
Visibility No restrictions (can use private, protected, etc.). All constants and methods are public.
Constructors Can have constructors. Cannot have constructors.
Methods Can have concrete methods. Can have default or static methods.
Inheritance Single inheritance (extends). Multiple implementation (implements).

Example

import java.io.*;

// Interface Declared
interface testInterface {
  
    // public, static and final
    final int a = 10;

    // public and abstract
    void display();
}

// Class implementing interface
class TestClass implements testInterface {
  
    // Implementing the capabilities of Interface
    public void display(){ 
      System.out.println("Geek"); 
    }
}
class Geeks{ 
    public static void main(String[] args){
        
        TestClass t = new TestClass();
        t.display();
        System.out.println(t.a);
    }
}

Output

Geek
10

References

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/interfaces-in-java/

notes.html:
Notes

Overview

Definition : Polymorphism Derived from Greek -many forms-. in Java it allows a single variable (Reference) to point to Objects of different types at different ties, modifying the program's behavior based on the actual object in memory, not reference type. Key Mechanism : it is primarily realized through Inheritance (extends) and Interfaces (implements). The Golden Rule of Executions :

  • Compile Time : the compiler checks if the method exists in the Reference Type (e.g. Animal)
  • Runtime : The JVM executes the method version found in the Actual Object Type (e.g. Dog)

Features of polymorphism:

  • Multiple Behaviors: The same method can behave differently depending on the object that calls this method.
  • Method Overriding: A child class can redefine a method of its parent class.
  • Method Overloading: We can define multiple methods with the same name but different parameters.
  • Runtime Decision: At runtime, Java determines which method to call depending on the object's actual class.

Example

// Base class Person
class Person {
    // Method that displays the 
    // role of a person
    void role() {
        System.out.println("I am a person.");
    }
}

// Derived class Father that 
// overrides the role method
class Father extends Person {
  
    // Overridden method to show 
    // the role of a father
    @Override
    void role() {
        System.out.println("I am a father.");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Creating a reference of type Person 
        // but initializing it with Father class object
        Person p = new Father();
        
        // Calling the role method. It calls the 
        // overridden version in Father class
        p.role();  
    }
}

Output

I am a father.

Why Use Polymorphism

  • Code Reusability: Polymorphism allows the same method or class to be used with different types of Objects, which makes the code more reusable.
  • Flexibility: Polymorphism enables object of different classes to be treated as objects of a common superclass, which provides flexibility in method execution and object interaction.
  • Abstraction: it allows the use of abstract classes or interfaces, enabling you to work with general types (like a superclass or interface) instead of concrete types (like specific subclasses), thus simplifying the interaction with objects.

Method Overriding

Method Overriding in Java means when a subclass provides a specific implementation of a method that is already defined in its superclass. Example

// Class 1
class Parent {
    // Method of parent class
    void print() { 
        System.out.println("parent class");
    }
}

// Class 2
class Subclass1 extends Parent {
    // Improvement: @Override 
    @Override
    void print() { 
        System.out.println("subclass1"); 
    }
}

// Class 3
class Subclass2 extends Parent {
    // Improvement: @Override annotation added
    @Override
    void print() {
        System.out.println("subclass2");
    }
}

// Class 4
class Geeks {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Creating reference of type Parent
        Parent a;

        // 1. Upcasting to Subclass1
        a = new Subclass1();
        a.print(); // Output: subclass1

        // 2. Upcasting to Subclass2
        a = new Subclass2();
        a.print(); // Output: subclass2
    }
}

Output

subclass1
subclass2

What is @Override?

It ensures you are actually overriding a method and not accidentally creating a new one. It is optional but highly recommended as a best practice. Example The Parent Class:

class Animal {
    public void talk() {
        System.out.println("Je suis un animal!");
    }
}

The Child Class (Correct Usage):

class Cat extends Animal {
    // We explicitly state we are overriding the 'talk' method from Animal
    @Override 
    public void talk() {
        System.out.println("Meow!");
    }
}

What happens here:

  1. The compiler looks at Cat.
  2. It sees @Override on talk().
  3. It checks Animal: "Does Animal have a method called talk() with no parameters?"
  4. Yes: Compilation succeeds.

Countre-Example Imagine you make a small typo or get the parameters wrong. Without @Override, Java treats it as a new method, breaking polymorphism.

The "Silent Failure" Scenario (Without @Override):

class Dog extends Animal {
    // TYPO: 'talks' instead of 'talk'
    public void talks() { 
        System.out.println("Woof!");
    }
}
// Usage
Animal myDog = new Dog();
myDog.talk(); 
// OUTPUT: "Je suis un animal!" (The parent method runs, NOT "Woof!")
  • Result: The bug is hard to find because the code compiles perfectly, but the dog doesn't bark.

The Safety Scenario (With @Override):

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public void talks() { // Compiler Error Here! (talks type instead of talk)
        System.out.println("Woof!");
    }
}
  • Result: The compiler stops you: "Error: Method talks() of type Dog does not override or implement a method from a supertype." You fix the typo immediately.

Type Casting (Transtypage) Hierarchy

In Java, Objects are manipulated via references. Changing the type of this reference is called (Transtypage.)

Upcasting

  • Definition: Assigning an object of a Subclass to a reference of a Superclass.
  • Safety: Always safe and done implicitly.
  • Logic: A Dog is an Animal.
  • Constraint: You lose access to methods specific to the subclass (e.g., bark()) unless you cast back down Example
// Parent Class
class Animal {
    void talk() {
        System.out.println("Animal sound");
    }
}

// Child Class
class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void talk() {
        System.out.println("Woof!");
    }
    // Unique method: Only Dogs can do this
    void bark() {
        System.out.println("BARK BARK!");
    }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // UPCAST: We create a Dog, but the reference 'a' is type Animal
        Animal chien = new Dog(); 
        // 1. Polymorphism works:
        // The compiler sees talk() in Animal. The JVM runs talk() in Dog.
        chien.talk(); // Output: "Woof!"
        // 2. Upcast Limitation (The Error):
        // The compiler checks the reference type 'Animal'.
        // Does 'Animal' have a method called 'bark'? NO.
        chien.bark(); // COMPILER ERROR: "Cannot find symbol method bark()"
    }
}
How to fix errors of the constraint

As the previous example shows its not possible to access the bark() method but there is fix, to access the bark() method, you must tell the compiler to treat the reference as a Dog again. This is Downcasting.

// Solution: Explicit Downcast
if (a instanceof Dog) {     // Safety check first!
    Dog d = (Dog) a;        // Swap the 'Animal' remote for a 'Dog' remote
    d.bark();               // Now it works! Output: "BARK BARK!"
}

Upcast is always implicit, even though you can do it explicitly but it is rarely used and cause redundancy.

Downcasting

  • Definition: Assigning a reference of a Superclass to a variable of a Subclass.
  • Safety: Risky. Must be done explicitly.
  • Logic: An Animal might be a Dog, but it might also be a Cat.
  • Risk: If the object in memory is not actually that subclass, the program crashes with a ClassCastException. Example
// 1. Parent Class
class Animal {
    void talk() {
        System.out.println("Animal sound");
    }
}

// 2. Subclass
class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void talk() {
        System.out.println("Woof!");
    }

    // Specific method: Only Dogs can attack
    void attack() {
        System.out.println("The dog attacks!");
    }
}

public class DowncastingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // --- STEP 1: UPCAST (Implicit) ---
        // We create a Dog, but view it as a generic Animal.
        // Useful for lists: List<Animal> zoo = ...
        Animal myPet = new Dog(); 

        // Polymorphism works fine for shared methods:
        myPet.talk(); // Output: "Woof!" (Dynamic Binding)

        // --- STEP 2: THE LIMITATION ---
        // Compiler Error! The 'Animal' reference doesn't know about 'attack'.
        // myPet.attack(); // UNCOMMENTING THIS CAUSES A COMPILE ERROR

        // --- STEP 3: DOWNCAST (Explicit) ---
        // We assume responsibility and tell the compiler: 
        // "I know this is a Dog. Convert the reference."
        if (myPet instanceof Dog) {
           /***/ Dog myDog = (Dog) myPet; // <--- THE DOWNCAST /***/
            myDog.attack(); // Success! Output: "The dog attacks!"
        }
        
        // --- STEP 4: REAL WORLD USE CASE (Looping) ---
        // Imagine a mixed list of animals
        Animal[] zoo = { new Dog(), new Animal() }; 
        for (Animal a : zoo) {
            if (a instanceof Dog) {
                // Safe Downcast
                Dog d = (Dog) a;
                d.attack();
            } else {
                System.out.println("This animal cannot attack.");
            }
        }
    }
}

Why do we need it? When you store a Dog in an Animal variable, you lose access to Dog-specific methods like attack() because the Animal class doesn't know them. You must Downcast to regain access. Implicit Downcasting is Forbidden and cause compilation error it should always be done explicitly.

The Safety Guard: instanceof

Concept: To prevent your program from crashing during a Downcast, you must check the object's true identity first using the instanceof operator Example

class Animal {
    void makeSound() { System.out.println("Generic sound"); }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void makeSound() { System.out.println("Bark"); }
    void chaseTail() { System.out.println("Chasing tail!"); }
}

class Cat extends Animal {
    @Override
    void makeSound() { System.out.println("Meow"); }
    void scratch() { System.out.println("Scratching!"); }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Upcasting (Polymorphism in action)
        Animal[] zoo = { new Dog(), new Cat() };

        for (Animal a : zoo) {
            // Polymorphic call: "a" is type Animal, but runs Dog/Cat method
            a.makeSound(); 

            // 2. instanceof Check
            if (a instanceof Dog) {
                // 3. Safe Downcast
                Dog d = (Dog) a; 
                d.chaseTail();
            } 
            else if (a instanceof Cat) {
                // Java 16+ Pattern Matching (Simplified Downcast) [cite: 2700]
                ((Cat) a).scratch();
            }
        }
    }
}

Common Pitfall (The Static Trap): Static methods do not follow polymorphism. They are bound at compile time based on the Reference type, not the Object type. This is called "Hiding," not "Overriding".

  • If Animal has static void run() and Dog has static void run():
    • Animal a = new Dog();
    • a.run(); -> Runs Animal's method.

References

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/polymorphism-in-java/ polymorphisme exceptions interfaces.pdf

notes.excerpt: NumPy — Numerical Python [!info] Overview NumPy (Numerical Python) is the foundational open-source library for scientific computing in Python. It provides a high-performance multidimensional array obj
notes.html:
NumPy — Numerical Python

Overview

NumPy (Numerical Python) is the foundational open-source library for scientific computing in Python. It provides a high-performance multidimensional array object (ndarray) and a comprehensive collection of tools for working with arrays, linear algebra, Fourier transforms, random number generation, and matrices.

NumPy arrays are:

  • Homogeneous — every element must be of the same data type.
  • Fixed-size at creation — changing the size creates a new array and deletes the original.
  • Stored in contiguous memory — enabling cache-efficient, vectorized operations.
  • 10–100× faster than standard Python lists for numerical operations due to pre-compiled C code under the hood.
- Why use NumPy over Python lists?
Feature Python List NumPy Array
Data types Heterogeneous (mixed) Homogeneous (single type)
Speed Slow (interpreted loops) Fast (vectorized C loops)
Memory Higher overhead per element Compact, contiguous memory
Broadcasting Not supported Fully supported
Linear algebra Manual implementation Built-in (np.dot, np.linalg)
Element-wise ops Requires loops Native operator overloading 
import sys
print(sys.version)

1. Importing NumPy

import numpy as np
Convention

NumPy is always imported with the alias np. This is a universal convention across the entire data science ecosystem (Pandas, Matplotlib, Scikit-Learn, etc.).

Asking for Help

np.info(np.ndarray.dtype)   # Get help on a specific NumPy function or attribute
np.lookfor('create array')  # Search the NumPy docstrings for a keyword
help(np.array)              # Standard Python help

2. Creating Arrays

2.1 From Python Sequences

# 1D array from a list
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])

# 2D array from a nested list (each inner list = one row)
b = np.array([(1.5, 2, 3), 
			  (4, 5, 6)], dtype=float)

# 3D array
c = np.array([[(1.5, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6)],
              [(3, 2, 1), (4, 5, 6)]], dtype=float)
print(a)

2.2 Initial Placeholders (Built-in Constructors)

These functions create arrays pre-filled with specific values — essential for initializing weight matrices, accumulators, and buffers.

np.zeros((3, 4))                    # 3×4 array of zeros (float64 by default)
np.ones((2, 3, 4), dtype=np.int16)  # 2×3×4 array of ones (int16)
np.full((2, 2), 7)                  # 2×2 array filled with the constant 7
np.eye(2)                           # 2×2 identity matrix (1s on diagonal)
np.empty((3, 2))                    # 3×2 uninitialized array (garbage values — faster)
`np.empty` does **not** initialize values

The values are whatever happens to be in that memory location. Never assume they are zero. Use np.zeros when you need guaranteed initialization.

2.3 Sequences and Ranges

# Evenly spaced values with a STEP size
d = np.arange(10, 25, 5)        # array([10, 15, 20])  — excludes stop value

# Evenly spaced values with a specified NUMBER of samples
np.linspace(0, 2, 9)            # 9 evenly spaced values from 0 to 2 (inclusive)

# Logarithmically spaced values
np.logspace(0, 3, 4)            # array([1, 10, 100, 1000]) — 10^0 to 10<span class="block-ref" id="3"></span>
`np.linspace` for Plotting
```python x = np.linspace(-2 * np.pi, 2 * np.pi, num=100) y = np.sin(x) # 'x' and 'y' are now ready to be passed to matplotlib ```

2.4 Random Arrays

np.random.random((2, 2))        # Uniform distribution over [0, 1)
np.random.rand(3, 3)            # Same — uniform [0, 1), shape as positional args
np.random.randn(3, 3)           # Standard normal distribution (mean=0, std=1)
np.random.randint(0, 10, (3,3)) # Random integers in [0, 10)
np.random.seed(42)              # Set seed for reproducibility

3. Data Types (dtype)

Every NumPy array has a single, fixed data type for all elements. This is how NumPy achieves its memory efficiency and speed.

dtype Description Typical Size
np.int64 Signed 64-bit integer 8 bytes
np.int32 Signed 32-bit integer 4 bytes
np.float32 Single-precision float 4 bytes
np.float64 Double-precision float (default) 8 bytes
np.complex128 Complex number (two 64-bit floats) 16 bytes
np.bool_ Boolean (True / False) 1 byte
np.object_ Python object type varies
np.string_ Fixed-length byte string varies
np.unicode_ Fixed-length unicode string varies 
# Specifying dtype at creation
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32)

# Checking dtype
a.dtype        # dtype('float32')
a.dtype.name   # 'float32'

# Converting (casting) to a different type — returns a NEW array
b = a.astype(int)
Memory Optimization

For large datasets, using float32 instead of the default float64 halves memory usage with minimal precision loss — critical in Deep Learning and Machine Learning pipelines.

4. Inspecting Arrays

Understanding the structure of your array before performing operations prevents bugs and shape mismatches.

a = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])

print("shape: ",a.shape)       # (2, 3) — 2 rows, 3 columns
print("dimension: ", a.ndim)        # 2 — number of dimensions (axes)
print("size: ",a.size)        # 6 — total number of elements
print("type: ", a.dtype)       # dtype('int64') — data type of elements
print("type name:", a.dtype.name)  # 'int64' — string name of the data type
print('item size: ', a.itemsize)    # 8 — size in bytes of each element
print("total bytes consumed: ",a.nbytes)      # 48 — total memory consumed (size × itemsize)
print('number of rows: ', len(a))        # 2 — length of the first axis (number of rows)
Attribute Summary
Attribute Returns Example (2×3 array)
.shape Tuple of dimension sizes (2, 3)
.ndim Number of dimensions 2
.size Total element count 6
.dtype Element data type int64
.itemsize Bytes per element 8
.nbytes Total bytes 48

5. Indexing, Slicing, and Selecting

5.1 Basic Indexing (1D)

NumPy uses 0-based indexing. Negative indices count from the end.

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

a[0]     # 1 — first element
a[-1]    # 5 — last element
a[2]     # 3 — third element
a[0] = 100  # Reassign the first element

5.2 Basic Indexing (2D)

b = np.array([[1.5, 2, 3],
              [4,   5, 6]])

b[1, 2]   # 6.0 — row 1, column 2 (preferred NumPy syntax)
b[1][2]   # 6.0 — equivalent but less efficient (creates intermediate array)

5.3 Slicing [start:stop:step]

Slicing extracts a view (not a copy) of the array — modifications to the slice affect the original array.

1D Slicing

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])

a[0:2]     # array([1, 2]) — index 0 and 1
a[1:5:2]   # array([2, 4]) — index 1 to 4, step 2
a[4:]      # array([5, 6, 7]) — index 4 to end
a[:4]      # array([1, 2, 3, 4]) — start to index 3
a[::-1]    # array([7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]) — reversed array

2D Slicing

b = np.array([[1.5, 2, 3],
              [4,   5, 6]])

b[0:2, 1]    # array([2., 5.]) — rows 0–1, column 1
b[:1]        # array(<a class="wikilink wikilink-unresolved" href="/garden/note/15-2-3" data-target="1.5, 2., 3.">1.5, 2., 3.</a>) — all of row 0 (equiv. to b[0:1, :])
b[0, 0:2]   # array([1.5, 2.]) — row 0, columns 0–1
b[0:2, 0:2] # 2×2 block from top-left corner
Slices are Views, Not Copies!
original = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
sliced = original[1:4]
sliced[0] = 999
print(original)  # array([1, 999, 3, 4, 5]) — original is modified!

Use .copy() when you need an independent copy: safe = original[1:4].copy()

5.4 Boolean Indexing

Select elements based on a condition. Returns a copy (not a view).

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

a[a < 3]       # array([1, 2]) — elements where condition is True
a[a > 2]       # array([3, 4, 5])
a[a % 2 == 0]  # array([2, 4]) — even numbers only

# The condition creates a boolean mask:
mask = a < 3   # array([True, True, False, False, False])
a[mask]        # array([1, 2])

5.5 Fancy Indexing

Use arrays of indices to select specific elements in an arbitrary order. Returns a copy.

a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
indices = [0, 3, 4]
a[indices]  # array([10, 40, 50])

# 2D fancy indexing
b = np.array([[1.5, 2, 3],
              [4,   5, 6]])

b[[1, 0, 1, 0], [0, 1, 2, 0]]  # Elements at (1,0), (0,1), (1,2), (0,0)
                                 # array([4., 2., 6., 1.5])

# Select a subset of rows and columns
b<a class="wikilink wikilink-unresolved" href="/garden/note/1-0-1-0" data-target="1, 0, 1, 0">1, 0, 1, 0</a>[:, [0, 1, 2, 0]]  # Reordered rows and columns

5.6 Assigning Values with Indices

a = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])

# Single assignment
a[0] = 100

# Multiple assignment with a list of indices
select = [0, 2, 3]
a[select] = 999  # Elements at indices 0, 2, 3 all become 999

# Conditional assignment
a[a < 500] = 0   # All elements less than 500 become 0

6. Arithmetic Operations (Element-wise)

Standard arithmetic operators are element-wise (not matrix algebra) and require arrays of compatible shapes.

6.1 Basic Arithmetic

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([1.5, 2, 3])

# Subtraction
g = a - b               # array([-0.5, 0., 0.])
g = np.subtract(a, b)   # Equivalent

# Addition
z = b + a               # array([2.5, 4., 6.])
z = np.add(b, a)        # Equivalent

# Multiplication (element-wise, NOT matrix multiplication)
z = a * b               # array([1.5, 4., 9.])
z = np.multiply(a, b)   # Equivalent

# Division
z = a / b               # array([0.667, 1., 1.])
z = np.divide(a, b)     # Equivalent

6.2 Scalar Operations (Broadcasting)

When operating on an array and a scalar, NumPy broadcasts the scalar to every element.

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, -1])

a + 1    # array([2, 3, 4, 0])
a * 2    # array([2, 4, 6, -2])
a ** 2   # array([1, 4, 9, 1])
a / 2    # array([0.5, 1.0, 1.5, -0.5])

6.3 Hadamard Product vs. Matrix Multiplication

Critical Distinction
  • * operator → Element-wise (Hadamard) product
  • np.dot() or @ operator → True linear algebra matrix multiplication
X = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])
Y = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])

# Hadamard Product (element-wise)
Z = X * Y    # array([[2, 0], [0, 2]])

# Matrix Multiplication (dot product)
Z = np.dot(X, Y)  # array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
Z = X @ Y         # Equivalent (Python 3.5+)

6.4 Dot Product (Vectors)

For 1D arrays, np.dot computes the inner product (sum of element-wise products).

x = np.array([1, 2])
y = np.array([3, 2])

np.dot(x, y)  # (1×3) + (2×2) = 7

7. Universal Mathematical Functions (ufuncs)

NumPy provides universal functions that operate element-wise on arrays, executing optimized C-level loops.

7.1 Trigonometric and Transcendental

a = np.array([0, np.pi/2, np.pi])

np.sin(a)     # array([0., 1., 0.])     — sine
np.cos(a)     # array([1., 0., -1.])    — cosine
np.tan(a)     # tangent
np.arcsin(a)  # inverse sine

7.2 Exponential and Logarithmic

b = np.array([1, 2, 3])

np.exp(b)      # e^x for each element → array([2.718, 7.389, 20.086])
np.log(b)      # Natural logarithm (ln)
np.log2(b)     # Base-2 logarithm
np.log10(b)    # Base-10 logarithm
np.sqrt(b)     # Square root → array([1., 1.414, 1.732])
np.power(b, 3) # Element-wise power → array([1, 8, 27])

7.3 Rounding

a = np.array([1.7, 2.3, 3.5])

np.floor(a)    # array([1., 2., 3.])  — round down
np.ceil(a)     # array([2., 3., 4.])  — round up
np.round(a)    # array([2., 2., 4.])  — round to nearest even
np.abs(a)      # Absolute value

7.4 Constants

np.pi       # 3.141592653589793
np.e        # 2.718281828459045
np.inf      # Infinity
np.nan      # Not a Number
np.newaxis  # Used to increase array dimensions (broadcasting trick)

8. Aggregate / Statistical Functions

These functions reduce an array (or an axis) to a single summary value.

a = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])

# Global aggregates (entire array)
a.sum()         # 21 — sum of all elements
a.min()         # 1
a.max()         # 6
a.mean()        # 3.5
np.median(a)    # 3.5
a.std()         # Standard deviation
a.var()         # Variance
a.cumsum()      # Cumulative sum → array([1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21])
a.cumprod()     # Cumulative product
np.corrcoef(a)  # Correlation coefficient matrix

# Aggregates along an axis
a.sum(axis=0)   # array([5, 7, 9]) — sum down each column
a.sum(axis=1)   # array([6, 15])   — sum across each row
a.max(axis=0)   # array([4, 5, 6]) — max of each column
a.min(axis=1)   # array([1, 4])    — min of each row
Axis Reference
axis 0 → rows    (operates DOWN ↓ each column)
axis 1 → columns (operates ACROSS → each row)

Think of it as: the axis that gets collapsed/reduced.

Function Description
a.sum() Sum of all elements
a.min() Minimum value
a.max() Maximum value
a.mean() Arithmetic mean
np.median(a) Median value
a.std() Standard deviation
a.var() Variance
a.cumsum() Cumulative sum
a.cumprod() Cumulative product
np.corrcoef(a) Correlation coefficient matrix
np.argmax(a) Index of maximum value
np.argmin(a) Index of minimum value

9. Comparison Operators

Comparisons on NumPy arrays return boolean arrays, enabling powerful filtering.

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([3, 2, 1])

# Element-wise comparison
a == b                  # array([False, True, False])
a < 2                   # array([True, False, False])
a > b                   # array([False, False, True])
a != b                  # array([True, False, True])

# Array-wise comparison (single boolean result)
np.array_equal(a, b)    # False — checks if ALL elements are identical

10. Broadcasting

Broadcasting Rules

Broadcasting allows NumPy to perform operations on arrays of different shapes by automatically expanding the smaller array. The rules are:

  1. If arrays differ in number of dimensions, the shape of the smaller is padded with 1s on the left.
  2. Arrays with size 1 along a particular dimension act as if they had the size of the array with the largest shape along that dimension.
  3. If sizes disagree and neither is 1 → error.
# Scalar broadcast
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])
a + 10  # Adds 10 to every element

# Column vector broadcast
col = np.array([[100], [200]])  # Shape (2, 1)
a + col  # array([[101, 102, 103],
         #        [204, 205, 206]])

# Row vector broadcast
row = np.array([10, 20, 30])    # Shape (3,) → treated as (1, 3)
a + row  # array([[11, 22, 33],
         #        [14, 25, 36]])

11. Array Manipulation

11.1 Changing Shape

b = np.array([[1.5, 2, 3],
              [4,   5, 6]])

b.ravel()          # Flatten to 1D → array([1.5, 2., 3., 4., 5., 6.])
b.flatten()        # Flatten to 1D (returns a COPY, unlike ravel which returns a view)
b.reshape(3, 2)    # Reshape to 3×2 (total elements must remain the same)
b.reshape(6, -1)   # -1 lets NumPy auto-calculate that dimension
b.reshape(-1)      # Flatten (equivalent to ravel)

# Resize modifies the array IN-PLACE (can change total size)
b.resize((2, 6))   # Pads with zeros if new size is larger
`reshape` vs `resize`
  • reshape returns a new view with the same data; total size must stay the same.
  • resize modifies the array in place and can change the total number of elements (padding with zeros or truncating).

11.2 Transposing

Swaps rows and columns. For a matrix with shape (m, n), the transpose has shape (n, m).

C = np.array([[1, 1],
              [2, 2],
              [3, 3]])  # Shape (3, 2)

C.T                     # Shape (2, 3)
np.transpose(C)         # Equivalent

11.3 Adding and Removing Elements

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])

np.append(a, [7, 8])        # array([1, 2, 3, 7, 8]) — returns NEW array
np.insert(a, 1, 5)          # array([1, 5, 2, 3]) — insert 5 at index 1
np.delete(a, [1])            # array([1, 3]) — delete element at index 1
Performance Note

np.append, np.insert, and np.delete all return new arrays (they do not modify in place). Calling them repeatedly in a loop is very slow — build a Python list first, then convert to an array.

11.4 Combining Arrays

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
d = np.array([10, 15, 20])

# Concatenate along an existing axis
np.concatenate((a, d), axis=0)    # array([1, 2, 3, 10, 15, 20])

# Vertical stack (row-wise — adds rows)
e = np.array([[7, 7], [7, 7]])
f = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])
np.vstack((a.reshape(1,-1), d.reshape(1,-1)))  # Stack as rows
np.r_[e, f]                                     # Shorthand for vstack

# Horizontal stack (column-wise — adds columns)
np.hstack((e, f))
# array([[7, 7, 1, 0],
#        [7, 7, 0, 1]])

# Column stack
np.column_stack((a, d))
# array([[ 1, 10],
#        [ 2, 15],
#        [ 3, 20]])
np.c_[a, d]  # Shorthand equivalent

11.5 Splitting Arrays

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
c = np.array([[(1.5, 2, 1), (4, 5, 6)],
              [(3, 2, 3),   (4, 5, 6)]])

np.hsplit(a, 3)    # Split horizontally into 3 equal parts
                   # [array([1]), array([2]), array([3])]

np.vsplit(c, 2)    # Split vertically into 2 equal parts

np.array_split(a, 2)  # Split into 2 parts (handles uneven splits)

12. Copying Arrays

Understanding Views vs. Copies

This is one of the most common sources of bugs in NumPy code.

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

# VIEW — shares the same data buffer (changes propagate!)
h = a.view()
h[0] = 999
print(a[0])       # 999 — original is affected!

# SHALLOW COPY — same behavior as view for simple arrays
j = a

# DEEP COPY — completely independent array
k = a.copy()      # Equivalent: np.copy(a)
k[0] = 0
print(a[0])       # 999 — original is NOT affected
Method Same Data? Changes Propagate?
b = a Yes (same object) ✅ Yes
b = a.view() Yes (shared buffer) ✅ Yes
b = a[1:4] Yes (slice = view) ✅ Yes
b = a.copy() No (independent) ❌ No
b = a<a class="wikilink wikilink-unresolved" href="/garden/note/012" data-target="0,1,2">0,1,2</a> No (fancy = copy) ❌ No

13. Sorting

a = np.array([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9])

np.sort(a)            # Returns a sorted COPY → array([1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 9])
a.sort()              # Sorts IN-PLACE (modifies a)

# 2D sorting
c = np.array([[3, 1], [2, 4]])
c.sort(axis=0)        # Sort along columns (down each column)
c.sort(axis=1)        # Sort along rows (across each row)

# Argsort — returns INDICES that would sort the array
np.argsort(a)         # Useful for sorting one array based on another

14. I/O — Saving and Loading

14.1 Binary Format (.npy / .npz)

# Save single array
np.save('my_array', a)            # Saves as my_array.npy
np.load('my_array.npy')           # Load it back

# Save multiple arrays
np.savez('arrays.npz', a=a, b=b)  # Named arrays in a single file
data = np.load('arrays.npz')
data['a']                          # Access by name

# Compressed save
np.savez_compressed('arrays.npz', a=a, b=b)

14.2 Text Format (.txt / .csv)

np.savetxt("myarray.txt", a, delimiter=" ")
np.savetxt("myarray.csv", a, delimiter=",")

np.loadtxt("myfile.txt")
np.genfromtxt("my_file.csv", delimiter=',')  # Handles missing values

15. Linear Algebra (np.linalg)

NumPy includes a dedicated linear algebra submodule for common matrix operations.

A = np.array([[1, 2],
              [3, 4]])

np.linalg.inv(A)         # Matrix inverse
np.linalg.det(A)         # Determinant → -2.0
np.linalg.eig(A)         # Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
np.linalg.norm(A)        # Frobenius norm (default)
np.linalg.matrix_rank(A) # Rank of the matrix
np.linalg.solve(A, b)    # Solve Ax = b for x
np.trace(A)              # Sum of diagonal elements → 5

16. 2D Arrays — Complete Workflow

Overview

While 1D arrays represent vectors, 2D arrays represent matrices or tabular data with rows and columns. They are foundational for data manipulation, image processing, and linear algebra.

16.1 Creation and Attributes

a = [[11, 12, 13],
     [21, 22, 23],
     [31, 32, 33]]

A = np.array(a)

A.ndim    # 2
A.shape   # (3, 3)
A.size    # 9

16.2 Matrix Arithmetic Summary

X = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])
Y = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])

Z = X + Y       # Element-wise addition
Z = X - Y       # Element-wise subtraction
Z = 2 * Y       # Scalar multiplication (broadcasting)
Z = X * Y       # Hadamard product (element-wise multiplication)
Z = np.dot(X, Y) # Matrix multiplication
Z = X @ Y        # Matrix multiplication (Python 3.5+)

16.3 Applying Universal Functions to 2D Arrays

Z = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])

np.sin(Z)    # Sine of every element
np.exp(Z)    # e^x for every element
np.sqrt(Z)   # Square root of every element

17. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

Most Used Operations
import numpy as np

# ── CREATION ──
np.array([1,2,3])           # From list
np.zeros((r,c))             # Zeros
np.ones((r,c))              # Ones
np.eye(n)                   # Identity
np.arange(start,stop,step)  # Range
np.linspace(start,stop,num) # Evenly spaced
np.random.rand(r,c)         # Random uniform

# ── INSPECTION ──
a.shape, a.ndim, a.size, a.dtype

# ── INDEXING ──
a[i]          # 1D
a[r, c]       # 2D
a[start:stop] # Slice
a[a > 5]      # Boolean
a<a class="wikilink wikilink-unresolved" href="/garden/note/135" data-target="1,3,5">1,3,5</a>    # Fancy

# ── MATH ──
a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b  # Element-wise
np.dot(a, b)  # Dot product / matrix mult
a @ b         # Matrix mult (3.5+)

# ── STATS ──
a.sum(), a.mean(), a.std(), a.min(), a.max()

# ── SHAPE ──
a.reshape(r,c), a.ravel(), a.T

# ── COMBINE / SPLIT ──
np.concatenate, np.vstack, np.hstack
np.hsplit, np.vsplit

# ── COPY ──
a.copy()  # Deep copy (safe)

Using () vs [] in NumPy

As your professor, I need to give you a nuanced answer: It depends entirely on where you are using them.

1. Creating Arrays: YES (But lists are standard)

When you call np.array(), you are passing a "sequence-like" object. Python accepts both Lists [] and Tuples () as sequences.

Both of these result in the exact same NumPy array:

import numpy as np

# OPTION A: Using a List (Standard Convention)
# Most data scientists use this because data is often mutable before becoming an array.
a = np.array([1, 2, 3]) 

# OPTION B: Using a Tuple (Perfectly Valid)
# This works fine. 
b = np.array((1, 2, 3))
Professor's Advice

While np.array((1, 2, 3)) works, I recommend using brackets (lists) for defining the data inside the array. It is the visual standard in the industry. It makes it easier to read nested arrays (matrices) like [[1,2], [3,4]] rather than ((1,2), (3,4)).

2. Defining Shapes: YES (Tuples are actually preferred)

When you use functions like np.zeros, np.ones, or reshape, you need to tell NumPy the dimensions (shape).

  • Tuples () are the standard for shapes because shapes are immutable (they shouldn't change).
  • Lists [] are accepted but less "Pythonic" for this specific use case.
# PREFERRED: Using a Tuple for shape
z = np.zeros((3, 4)) 

# ACCEPTABLE: Using a List for shape
z = np.zeros([3, 4])
Common Beginner Mistake

You cannot forget the inner container!

  • ❌ Wrong: np.zeros(3, 4) -> NumPy thinks '3' is the shape and '4' is the data type.
  • ✅ Right: np.zeros((3, 4)) -> The tuple (3, 4) is the single argument for shape.

3. Indexing / Slicing: NO (Strictly Forbidden)

This is where you cannot use parentheses. In Python, parentheses () are used to call functions. Square brackets [] are used to access elements.

If you try to access an array element using (), Python thinks you are trying to "execute" the array like a function, and it will crash.

a = np.array([10, 20, 30])

# ✅ CORRECT: Accessing via Index
val = a[0] 

# ❌ WRONG: Raises 'TypeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object is not callable'
val = a(0)

Summary Cheat Sheet

Operation Syntax Allowed? Best Practice
Input Data np.array((1, 2)) ✅ Yes Use [] (Lists)
Shape Args np.zeros((2, 2)) ✅ Yes Use () (Tuples)
Indexing a(0) ❌ NO Must use []
Slicing a(0:5) ❌ NO Must use []

References

  • NumPy Cheat Sheet — DataQuest
  • NumPy Cheat Sheet — DataCamp (PDF)
  • Official NumPy Documentation
Quote

"NumPy is the foundation upon which nearly all of the power of Python's data science toolkit is built." — Jake VanderPlas, Python Data Science Handbook

notes.html:
Class Definitions

A class serves as the primary mechanism for abstraction in object-oriented programming. Every piece of data in Python is an instance of a class. A class acts as a blueprint for instances, defining behaviors through methods and state through attributes.

Definitions & Properties

A class defines the structure and behavior of objects. Methods represent member functions common to all instances. Attributes represent fields, instance variables, or data members that store state for individual instances. The self identifier references the specific instance executing a method.

1. Class Implementation & Encapsulation

Instance variables maintain state across method calls. Syntactically, self identifies the specific instance upon which a method is invoked. Python binds the target instance automatically to the parameter self during invocation.

Encapsulation Convention

A single leading underscore prefix signals that an attribute or method is nonpublic. External code should not access nonpublic members directly. Accessors retrieve values, while mutators modify state safely.

Member Type Purpose Method Example
Constructor Initializes instance variables upon creation __init__(self, ...)
Accessor (Getter) Retrieves instance state without modification get_balance(self)
Mutator (Setter) Modifies instance state with validation logic charge(self, price) 
class CreditCard:
    """A consumer credit card."""

    def __init__(self, customer, bank, acnt, limit):
        """Create a new credit card instance.

        The initial balance is zero.

        customer  the name of the customer (e.g., 'John Bowman')
        bank      the name of the bank (e.g., 'California Savings')
        acnt      the account identifier (e.g., '5391 0375 9387 5309')
        limit     credit limit (measured in dollars)
        """
        self._customer = customer
        self._bank = bank
        self._account = acnt
        self._limit = limit
        self._balance = 0

    def get_customer(self):
        """Return name of the customer."""
        return self._customer

    def get_bank(self):
        """Return the bank's name."""
        return self._bank

    def get_account(self):
        """Return the card identifying number (stored as a string)."""
        return self._account

    def get_limit(self):
        """Return current credit limit."""
        return self._limit

    def get_balance(self):
        """Return current balance."""
        return self._balance

    def charge(self, price):
        """Charge given price to the card, assuming sufficient credit limit.

        Return True if charge was processed; False if charge was denied.
        """
        if price + self._balance > self._limit:
            return False
        else:
            self._balance += price
            return True

    def make_payment(self, amount):
        """Process customer payment that reduces balance."""
        self._balance -= amount


if __name__ == '__main__':
    wallet = []
    wallet.append(CreditCard('John Bowman', 'California Savings', '5391 0375 9387 5309', 2500))
    wallet.append(CreditCard('John Bowman', 'California Federal', '3485 0399 3395 1954', 3500))
    wallet.append(CreditCard('John Bowman', 'California Finance', '5391 0375 9387 5309', 5000))

    for val in range(1, 17):
        wallet[0].charge(val)
        wallet[1].charge(2 * val)
        wallet[2].charge(3 * val)

    for c in range(3):
        print('Customer =', wallet[c].get_customer())
        print('Bank =', wallet[c].get_bank())
        print('Account =', wallet[c].get_account())
        print('Limit =', wallet[c].get_limit())
        print('Balance =', wallet[c].get_balance())
        while wallet[c].get_balance() > 100:
            wallet[c].make_payment(100)
            print('New balance =', wallet[c].get_balance())
        print()

2. Operator Overloading & Special Methods

Python built-in operators execute through special dunder methods. Defining special methods allows custom classes to utilize standard operator syntax, comparison expressions, and top-level functions (see Table 2.1).

Operator Binding Mechanics

Evaluating $a + b$ invokes the method a.__add__(b). If the left operand does not support the operation, Python attempts the right-hand reverse variant b.__radd__(a).

Operation Category Common Syntax Primary Special Method Reverse / Alternate Form
Binary Arithmetic $a + b$ a.__add__(b) b.__radd__(a)
$a - b$ a.__sub__(b) b.__rsub__(a)
$a \cdot b$ a.__mul__(b) b.__rmul__(a)
$a / b$ a.__truediv__(b) b.__rtruediv__(a)
$a // b$ a.__floordiv__(b) b.__rfloordiv__(a)
$a \% b$ a.__mod__(b) b.__rmod__(a)
$a ** b$ a.__pow__(b) b.__rpow__(a)
Augmented Assignment $a += b$ a.__iadd__(b) —
Unary Arithmetic $+a$, $-a$, $\sim a$ a.__pos__(), a.__neg__(), a.__invert__() —
Absolute Value $\text{abs}(a)$ a.__abs__() —
Comparisons $a < b$, $a \le b$ a.__lt__(b), a.__le__(b) —
$a > b$, $a \ge b$ a.__gt__(b), a.__ge__(b) —
$a == b$, $a \neq b$ a.__eq__(b), a.__ne__(b) —
Container Operations $v \in a$ a.__contains__(v) —
Element Access $a[k]$, $a[k] = v$, $\text{del } a[k]$ a.__getitem__(k), a.__setitem__(k, v), a.__delitem__(k) —
Invocation $a(\text{arg1}, \dots)$ a.__call__(arg1, ...) —
Utility Functions $\text{len}(a)$, $\text{hash}(a)$ a.__len__(), a.__hash__() —
Iteration $\text{iter}(a)$, $\text{next}(a)$ a.__iter__(), a.__next__() —
Conversions $\text{bool}(a)$, $\text{str}(a)$, $\text{repr}(a)$ a.__bool__(), a.__str__(), a.__repr__() —
Implied Default Behaviors

Python provides fallbacks when special methods are omitted. Evaluating truth value falls back to checking length if boolean conversion is missing. Iteration falls back to zero-based indexing using element access methods. Equivalence checks default to object identity.

3. Multidimensional Vector Class

A custom spatial vector illustrates operator overloading and sequence methods. Vector addition requires element-wise summation across equal dimensions:

$$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \langle u_0 + v_0, \, u_1 + v_1, \, \dots, \, u_{d-1} + v_{d-1} \rangle$$

Polymorphism

Polymorphism allows a method to process any argument type that adheres to the expected interface. Element addition executes successfully provided the right-hand operand supports length and index access protocols.

class Vector:
    """Represent a vector in a multidimensional space."""

    def __init__(self, d):
        """Create d-dimensional vector of zeros."""
        self._coords = [0] * d

    def __len__(self):
        """Return the dimension of the vector."""
        return len(self._coords)

    def __getitem__(self, j):
        """Return jth coordinate of vector."""
        return self._coords[j]

    def __setitem__(self, j, val):
        """Set jth coordinate of vector to given value."""
        self._coords[j] = val

    def __add__(self, other):
        """Return sum of two vectors."""
        if len(self) != len(other):
            raise ValueError('dimensions must agree')
        result = Vector(len(self))
        for j in range(len(self)):
            result[j] = self[j] + other[j]
        return result

    def __eq__(self, other):
        """Return True if vector has same coordinates as other."""
        return self._coords == other._coords

    def __ne__(self, other):
        """Return True if vector differs from other."""
        return not self == other

    def __str__(self):
        """Produce string representation of vector."""
        return '<' + str(self._coords)[1:-1] + '>'

4. Iterators

An iterator tracks state during collection traversal. It implements method __next__ to return sequential elements and raises StopIteration upon sequence exhaustion.

class SequenceIterator:
    """An iterator for any of Python's sequence types."""

    def __init__(self, sequence):
        """Create an iterator for the given sequence."""
        self._seq = sequence
        self._k = -1

    def __next__(self):
        """Return the next element, or else raise StopIteration error."""
        self._k += 1
        if self._k < len(self._seq):
            return self._seq[self._k]
        else:
            raise StopIteration()

    def __iter__(self):
        """By convention, an iterator must return itself as an iterator."""
        return self

5. Lazy Evaluation & Custom Range Class

The range type uses lazy evaluation. It calculates values on demand instead of allocating memory for entire number sequences.

Definitions & Properties

Lazy evaluation defers value computation until explicitly requested. Memory usage remains constant regardless of sequence magnitude $n$.

The total entry count $n$ for range parameters $(\text{start}, \text{stop}, \text{step})$ is calculated as:

$$n = \max\left(0, \, \left\lfloor \frac{\text{stop} - \text{start} + \text{step} - 1}{\text{step}} \right\rfloor\right)$$

class Range:
    """A class that mimics the built-in range class."""

    def __init__(self, start, stop=None, step=1):
        """Initialize a Range instance.

        Semantics is similar to built-in range class.
        """
        if step == 0:
            raise ValueError('step cannot be 0')

        if stop is None:
            start, stop = 0, start

        self._length = max(0, (stop - start + step - 1) // step)
        self._start = start
        self._step = step

    def __len__(self):
        """Return number of entries in the range."""
        return self._length

    def __getitem__(self, k):
        """Return entry at index k (using standard interpretation if negative)."""
        if k < 0:
            k += len(self)

        if not 0 <= k < self._length:
            raise IndexError('index out of range')

        return self._start + k * self._step

References

Data_Structures_and_Algorithms_in_Python_Michael_T_Goodrich_z_library.pdf(p, 69)
