Étapes détaillées

Étape Description
1. Spécification Forme générale du modèle qui explique le phénomène
2. Transformation Si nécessaire, transformer en modèle linéaire
3. Estimation Estimer les paramètres $\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_p$
4. Analyse variance Décomposer la variance totale de $Y$ en variance expliquée + résiduelle
5. Tests Test global (Fisher) et marginal (Student)
6. Validation Vérification des hypothèses fondamentales

Validation — Hypothèses à vérifier

  • ✅ Normalité des résidus
  • ✅ Non-autocorrélation des résidus
  • ✅ Qualité du modèle

3) Spécification du Modèle

Modèle général

$$Y = f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p) + \varepsilon$$

$$\boxed{Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p + \varepsilon}$$

$$\varepsilon = \underbrace{Y}_{\text{réel}} - \underbrace{(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p)}_{\text{estimation}}$$

Tableau des types de modèles

Type Forme Variation Caractéristique
Linéaire $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X$ $\Delta Y = \beta_1 \Delta X$ Proportion marginale constante $\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X} = \beta_1$
Log-linéaire $Y = \beta_0 \cdot X^{\beta_1}$ $\frac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \beta_1 \frac{\Delta X}{X}$ Élasticité constante $\beta_1 = \frac{\Delta Y/Y}{\Delta X/X}$
Exponentielle $Y = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X}$ $\frac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \beta_1 \Delta X$ Taux de croissance de $Y$, $\beta_1$ proportionnel à la variation de $X$
Logarithmique $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(X)$ $\Delta Y = \beta_1$ $\beta_1$ proportionnel à la variation de $Y$ et $\beta_1$ par taux de croissance de $X$

4) Régression Linéaire Simple

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon$$

Forme matricielle

$$\begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{pmatrix} = \beta_0 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \beta_1 \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon_n \end{pmatrix}$$

$$\boxed{Y = X\beta + \varepsilon}$$

$$\begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_1 \\ 1 & x_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon_n \end{pmatrix}$$

5) Régression Linéaire Multiple

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p + \varepsilon$$

$$\boxed{Y = X\beta + \varepsilon}$$

$$\begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1p} \\ 1 & x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2p} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{np} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_p \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon_n \end{pmatrix}$$

6) Hypothèses de la Régression Linéaire

N° Hypothèse
H1 Bonne spécification du modèle
H2 $E(\varepsilon_i) = 0,\quad i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$
H3 Homoscédasticité : $V(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2 = \text{cte},\quad i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$
H4 Non-autocorrélation des résidus : $\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j) = 0$
H5 $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),\quad i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$
H6 Les variables $X_1, \ldots, X_p$ sont linéairement indépendantes

7) Estimation des Paramètres — Moindres Carrés

Principe : On cherche $\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1$ qui minimisent la somme des carrés des résidus $S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \varepsilon_i^2$

Cas Régression Linéaire Simple

Étape 1 — Définir la fonction à minimiser

$$S(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \varepsilon_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)\right)^2$$

Étape 2 — Conditions du premier ordre (dérivées partielles = 0)

Dérivée par rapport à $\beta_0$ :

$$\frac{\partial S}{\partial \beta_0} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2 = -2\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0$$

$$\Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i - n\beta_0 - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = 0 \quad \cdots (1)$$

Dérivée par rapport à $\beta_1$ :

$$\frac{\partial S}{\partial \beta_1} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2 = -2\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0$$

$$\Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - \beta_0\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 = 0 \quad \cdots (2)$$

Étape 3 — Système des équations normales

$$\begin{cases} \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i - n\beta_0 - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = 0 \\[8pt] \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - \beta_0\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 = 0 \end{cases}$$

On réarrange :

$$\begin{cases} \beta_1\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i - n\beta_0 \\[8pt] \beta_0\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 \end{cases}$$

Étape 4 — Résolution par la Règle de Cramer

On écrit le système sous forme matricielle :

$$\begin{pmatrix} n & \displaystyle\sum x_i \\[4pt] \displaystyle\sum x_i & \displaystyle\sum x_i^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \displaystyle\sum y_i \\[4pt] \displaystyle\sum x_i y_i \end{pmatrix}$$

Le déterminant du système :

$$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} n & \displaystyle\sum x_i \\[4pt] \displaystyle\sum x_i & \displaystyle\sum x_i^2 \end{vmatrix} = n\sum x_i^2 - \left(\sum x_i\right)^2$$

Pour $\hat{\beta}_0$ — on remplace la 1ère colonne :

$$\hat{\beta}_0 = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} \displaystyle\sum y_i & \displaystyle\sum x_i \\[4pt] \displaystyle\sum x_i y_i & \displaystyle\sum x_i^2 \end{vmatrix}}{\Delta} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum y_i \cdot \sum x_i^2 - \sum x_i \cdot \sum x_i y_i}{n\displaystyle\sum x_i^2 - \left(\sum x_i\right)^2}$$

Pour $\hat{\beta}_1$ — on remplace la 2ème colonne :

$$\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} n & \displaystyle\sum y_i \\[4pt] \displaystyle\sum x_i & \displaystyle\sum x_i y_i \end{vmatrix}}{\Delta} = \frac{n\displaystyle\sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \cdot \sum y_i}{n\displaystyle\sum x_i^2 - \left(\sum x_i\right)^2}$$

Étape 5 — Simplification en divisant par $n$

$$\boxed{\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - \frac{\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\right)\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i\right)}{n}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 - \frac{\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\right)^2}{n}} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{V(X)}}$$

Étape 6 — Déduire $\hat{\beta}_0$

De l'équation $(1)$ : $\sum y_i = n\beta_0 + \beta_1 \sum x_i$

En divisant par $n$ :

$$\bar{Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \bar{X}$$

$$\boxed{\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}}$$

Interprétation géométrique : La droite de régression passe toujours par le point $(\bar{X}, \bar{Y})$

Cas Régression Multiple — Estimateur OLS

Étape 1 — Rappel des propositions matricielles

Ces propositions sont indispensables pour dériver la fonction de coût matricielle.

Proposition 1 : Soit $V \in \mathbb{R}^k$ et $a \in \mathbb{R}^k$ :

$$\frac{\partial V^T a}{\partial V} = \frac{\partial a^T V}{\partial V} = a$$

Intuition : c'est l'équivalent matriciel de $\frac{\partial (ax)}{\partial x} = a$

Proposition 2 : Soit $V \in \mathbb{R}^k$ et $M \in \mathbb{R}^{k\times k}$ :

$$\frac{\partial V^T M V}{\partial V} = (M + M^T)V$$

En particulier, si $M$ est symétrique ($M^T = M$) :

$$\frac{\partial V^T M V}{\partial V} = 2MV$$

Intuition : c'est l'équivalent matriciel de $\frac{\partial (ax^2)}{\partial x} = 2ax$

Étape 2 — Définir la fonction à minimiser

$$S(\beta) = \varepsilon^T\varepsilon = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \varepsilon_i^2$$

avec $\varepsilon = Y - X\beta$, donc :

$$\varepsilon^T = (Y - X\beta)^T = Y^T - \beta^T X^T$$

Étape 3 — Développer $\varepsilon^T\varepsilon$

$$\varepsilon^T\varepsilon = (Y - X\beta)^T(Y - X\beta)$$

$$= (Y^T - \beta^T X^T)(Y - X\beta)$$

$$= Y^T Y - Y^T X\beta - \beta^T X^T Y + \beta^T X^T X\beta$$

Remarque : $Y^T X\beta$ est un scalaire, donc $Y^T X\beta = (Y^T X\beta)^T = \beta^T X^T Y$

$$\boxed{\varepsilon^T\varepsilon = Y^TY - 2\beta^T X^T Y + \beta^T X^T X\beta}$$

où l'on identifie :

  • $Y^TY$ : scalaire constant (ne dépend pas de $\beta$)
  • $-2\beta^T X^T Y$ : terme linéaire en $\beta$ (forme $V^T a$ avec $a = X^TY$)
  • $\beta^T X^T X\beta$ : terme quadratique en $\beta$ (forme $V^T M V$ avec $M = X^TX$)

Étape 4 — Dériver par rapport à $\beta$

En appliquant les Propositions 1 et 2 :

$$\frac{\partial \varepsilon^T\varepsilon}{\partial \beta} = \frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\left[Y^TY\right] - \frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\left[2\beta^T X^T Y\right] + \frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\left[\beta^T X^T X\beta\right]$$

$$= 0 - 2X^TY + 2(X^TX)\beta$$

Note : $X^TX$ est symétrique car $(X^TX)^T = X^TX$, donc on applique la Prop. 2 avec $M = X^TX$ : $\frac{\partial \beta^T(X^TX)\beta}{\partial \beta} = 2(X^TX)\beta$

Étape 5 — Égaliser à zéro et résoudre

$$\frac{\partial \varepsilon^T\varepsilon}{\partial \beta} = -2X^TY + 2(X^TX)\beta = 0$$

$$\Rightarrow 2(X^TX)\beta = 2X^TY$$

$$\Rightarrow (X^TX)\beta = X^TY \quad \text{(équations normales)}$$

Si $\det(X^TX) \neq 0$ (colonnes de $X$ linéairement indépendantes — Hypothèse H6), on peut inverser :

$$\boxed{\hat{\beta} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^TY}$$

Résumé visuel de la dérivation

$$S(\beta) = \varepsilon^T\varepsilon$$ $$\downarrow \text{ développer}$$ $$Y^TY - 2\beta^TX^TY + \beta^TX^TX\beta$$ $$\downarrow \frac{\partial}{\partial\beta} = 0$$ $$-2X^TY + 2(X^TX)\beta = 0$$ $$\downarrow \text{ résoudre}$$ $$\hat{\beta} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^TY$$

8) Exemple de Transformation (Log-linéaire)

Modèle : $Y = \beta_0 \cdot X_1^{\beta_1}$

$$\ln Y = \ln(\beta_0) + \beta_1 \ln(X_1)$$

On pose $Y' = \ln(Y)$, $\beta_0' = \ln(\beta_0)$, $X_1' = \ln(X_1)$

$$\Rightarrow Y' = \beta_0' + \beta_1 X_1'$$

⚠️ Condition : $Y > 0$, $\beta_0 > 0$, $X_1 > 0$

9. Analyse de la Variance (ANOVA)

$$\boxed{SCT = SCReg + SCRes}$$

Terme Désignation Formule
$SCT$ Somme des Carrés Totale $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2$
$SCReg$ Somme des Carrés de Régression $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2$
$SCRes$ Somme des Carrés Résiduelle $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$
Note

Interprétation fondamentale La variance totale de $Y$ est la somme d'une variance expliquée par le modèle ($SCReg$) et d'une variance inexpliquée ou résiduelle ($SCRes$).

Coefficient de Détermination $R^2$

$$R^2 = \frac{SCReg}{SCT} = 1 - \frac{SCRes}{SCT} \qquad R^2 \in [0,,1]$$

Plus $R^2$ est proche de $1$, meilleur est l'ajustement du modèle aux données.

$R^2$ Ajusté

$$R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{n-1}{n-p-1}\quad,\quad(1 - R^2) = 1 - \frac{SCRes,/,(n-p-1)}{SCT,/,(n-1)}$$

Important

Utilité du $R^2$ ajusté En régression multiple, le $R^2$ ordinaire augmente mécaniquement à chaque ajout de variable, même non significative. Le $R^2$ ajusté corrige ce biais en pénalisant la complexité du modèle (nombre de variables $p$). Il est donc préférable pour comparer des modèles de tailles différentes.

Tableau des Risques de Décision

$H_0$ vraie $H_1$ vraie
$H_0$ acceptée Bonne décision — probabilité $1-\alpha$ Erreur de 2ème espèce — $\beta = P(\text{Rej};H_1 \mid H_0;\text{vraie})$
$H_1$ acceptée Erreur de 1ère espèce — $\alpha$ Bonne décision (puissance) — $1-\beta$

10. Tests Statistiques

Test Global de Fisher

Ce test détermine s'il existe une liaison significative globale entre $Y$ et l'ensemble des régresseurs $(X_1, \ldots, X_p)$.

$$H_0 : \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \cdots = \beta_p = 0 \qquad \text{vs} \qquad H_1 : \exists, i \in {1,\ldots,p},; \beta_i \neq 0$$

$$F_{\text{cal}} = \frac{SCReg / p}{SCRes / (n-p-1)} \qquad F_{theo} = F_{p,(n-p-1),(1-\alpha)}$$

Règle de décision : $$F_{\text{cal}} > F_{theo} \implies \text{rejet de } H_0 \implies \text{le modèle est globalement significatif}$$

Si on ne rejette pas $H_0$, cela ne signifie pas que tous les $\beta_i$ sont nuls, mais qu'on ne peut pas le prouver au seuil $\alpha$.

Test Marginal de Student

Ce test évalue la significativité individuelle de chaque coefficient $\beta_i$.

$$H_0 : \beta_i = 0 \qquad \text{vs} \qquad H_1 : \beta_i \neq 0$$

$$t_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_i}{\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\beta}_i}} \qquad t_{\text{théo}} = t_{n-p-1;1-\alpha/2}$$

Règle de décision : $$|t_{\text{cal}}| > t_{\text{théo}} \implies \text{rejet de } H_0 \implies \beta_i \text{ est individuellement significatif}$$

Écarts-Types des Estimateurs

Régression simple :

$$\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\beta}_0} = \sqrt{\frac{SCRes}{n-2}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})^2}} \qquad \hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\beta}_1} = \frac{\sqrt{SCRes/(n-2)}}{\sqrt{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})^2}}$$

Régression multiple :

$$\hat{\Omega}_{\hat{\beta}} = \hat{\sigma}^2_\varepsilon \cdot (X'X)^{-1} \qquad \text{avec} \quad \hat{\sigma}^2_\varepsilon = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n-p-1}$$

La matrice $\hat{\Omega}_{\hat{\beta}}$ est la matrice de variance-covariance des estimateurs :

$$\hat{\Omega}_{\hat{\beta}} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\beta}_0) & \mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_0,\hat{\beta}_1) & \cdots & \mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_0,\hat{\beta}_p) \\ & \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) & \cdots & \vdots \\ & & \ddots & \vdots \\ & & & \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\beta}_p) \end{pmatrix}$$

Les écarts-types $\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\beta}_i}$ sont les racines carrées des éléments diagonaux.

11. Diagnostic des Hypothèses du Modèle

(1) Hypothèse de Spécification (Linéarité)

Diagnostic graphique : Le nuage de points $(\hat{y}_i,; \hat{\varepsilon}_i)$ doit avoir une forme ronde, symétrique et horizontale. Toute structure systématique (courbe, entonnoir, pattern) indique une mauvaise spécification.

Remèdes :

  • Si $R^2 \approx 0$ : problème de spécification avéré
  • Transformer les variables (logarithme, différences, puissances)
  • Ajouter des variables explicatives manquantes
  • Reconsidérer la forme fonctionnelle du modèle

(2) Hypothèse d'Homoscédasticité

L'hypothèse stipule que $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2$ (constante pour tout $i$). Sa violation entraîne de l'hétéroscédasticité.

Diagnostic graphique : Le nuage $(\hat{y}_i,; \hat{\varepsilon}_i)$ présente une dispersion variable (évasée ou rétrécie), non uniforme.

Tests formels :

Test Principe
Goldfeld-Quandt Comparaison des variances sur deux sous-échantillons
Breusch-Pagan Régression auxiliaire des résidus au carré
White Version plus générale de Breusch-Pagan, sans hypothèse sur la forme
ARCH-LM Détection d'hétéroscédasticité conditionnelle (séries temporelles)

Remède : Estimer un modèle de type ARCH (Autorégressif Conditionnel Hétéroscédastique) qui modélise explicitement la variance conditionnelle.

(3) Hypothèse de Non-Autocorrélation

L'hypothèse stipule que $\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j) = 0$ pour $i \neq j$.

Diagnostic graphique : Le tracé chronologique des résidus $(i,;\hat{\varepsilon}_i)$ ne doit présenter aucune structure systématique — il doit ressembler à un bruit blanc (aléatoire, centré, sans tendance).

Test formel : Durbin-Watson

$$dw = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=2}^n (\hat{\varepsilon}_i - \hat{\varepsilon}_{i-1})^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{\varepsilon}_i^2}$$

Avec $d_L$ = borne inférieure et $d_U$ = borne supérieure (issues des tables de Durbin-Watson) :

Intervalle de $dw$ Décision
$[0,; d_L)$ Autocorrélation positive — $\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i \varepsilon_{i-1}) > 0$
$[d_L,; d_U)$ Zone de doute
$[d_U,; 4-d_U]$ Pas d'autocorrélation
$(4-d_U,; 4-d_L]$ Zone de doute
$(4-d_L,; 4]$ Autocorrélation négative — $\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i \varepsilon_{i-1}) < 0$

Remède : Enrichir le modèle pour capturer l'information restée dans les résidus : ajouter des variables retardées, intégrer un terme autorégressif, ou transformer la variable dépendante.

(4) Hypothèse de Normalité des Résidus

L'hypothèse stipule que $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.

Diagnostic graphique :

Outil Interprétation
Histogramme des résidus Doit approcher la forme d'une cloche symétrique
QQ-plot des résidus Les points doivent s'aligner sur la droite diagonale

Tests statistiques — Skewness et Kurtosis :

Pour une loi normale, les valeurs de référence sont :

Statistique Valeur de référence Interprétation si écart
Skewness (asymétrie) $0$ Distribution asymétrique
Kurtosis (aplatissement) $3$ Distribution trop plate ou trop pointue
Conséquence sur les tests La normalité des résidus est indispensable pour que les tests $F$ et $t$ soient valides en **petit échantillon**. En grand échantillon, le théorème central limite garantit la validité asymptotique même sans normalité stricte.
Récapitulatif des Hypothèses à Vérifier
Hypothèse Outil graphique Test(s) formel(s) Remède principal
Spécification Nuage $(\hat{y}_i, \hat{\varepsilon}_i)$ $R^2 \approx 0$ Transformation, changement de modèle
Homoscédasticité Nuage $(\hat{y}_i, \hat{\varepsilon}_i)$ White, Breusch-Pagan, ARCH-LM, GQ Modèle ARCH, MCG
Non-autocorrélation Tracé chronologique des résidus Durbin-Watson Variables retardées, modèle AR
Normalité Histogramme, QQ-plot Skewness $= 0$, Kurtosis $= 3$ Grand échantillon, transformation

11) Exercice Complet — Modèle Log-linéaire

Modèle : $M = \alpha \cdot PIB^{\beta}$

$$\log(M) = \log(\alpha) + \beta\log(PIB)$$

On pose : $Y = \log(M)$, $\beta_0 = \log(\alpha)$, $\beta_1 = \beta$, $X = \log(PIB)$

Estimation

$$\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum x_i y_i - \frac{(\sum x_i)(\sum y_i)}{n}}{\sum x_i^2 - \frac{(\sum x_i)^2}{n}} = 1{,}168$$

$$\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{X} = -3{,}584$$

Test de Fisher

$$F_{\text{calculé}} = \frac{SCReg/1}{SCRes/(n-2)} = \frac{59{,}39}{5{,}987} \approx 59{,}39 \quad > \quad F_{\alpha=5\%} = 5{,}99$$

✅ On rejette $H_0$ → le modèle est significatif au seuil 5%

Test de Student

$$|t_{\text{calculé}}| > t_{n-2;\,1-\alpha/2} = t_{6;\,0{,}975} = 2{,}447$$

Pour $\hat{\beta}_0$ : $|-2{,}503| > 2{,}447$ → ❌ On ne rejette pas $H_0$ → $\beta_0$ n'est pas significatif

Test de Durbin-Watson

$$d_L = 0{,}763 \qquad d_U = 1{,}332$$

Interprétation économique

$$\frac{\Delta M}{M} = \hat{\beta}_1 \frac{\Delta PIB}{PIB}$$

Si le PIB augmente de 1%, alors le taux de variation des importations sera $\hat{\beta}_1 \times 1\% = 1{,}168\%$

Prévision

$$\frac{M_{2013} - M_{2012}}{M_{2012}} = \hat{\beta}_1 \frac{\Delta PIB}{PIB}$$

$$\frac{M_{2013} - 8028}{8028} = 1{,}168 \times 4{,}5\%$$

$$M_{2013} = 8028(1{,}168 \times 4{,}5\%) + 8028$$

Résumé — Formules Clés

Concept Formule
Modèle général $Y = X\beta + \varepsilon$
Estimateur OLS $\hat{\beta} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^TY$
$\hat{\beta}_1$ simple $\dfrac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{V(X)}$
$\hat{\beta}_0$ simple $\bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}$
Décomposition variance $SCT = SCReg + SCRes$
Test Fisher $F = \dfrac{SCReg/p}{SCRes/(n-p-1)}$
Test Student $\|t\| > t_{n-p-1;\,1-\alpha/2}$

⚠️ Rappel clé : $\det(X^TX) \neq 0$ est nécessaire pour que $\hat{\beta} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^TY$ existe — cela implique que les colonnes de $X$ sont linéairement indépendantes (H6).

1. Introduction

Les SVM (Support Vector Machines, ou Séparateur à Vaste Marge) sont une classe d'algorithmes d'apprentissage supervisé initialement développés pour la discrimination binaire, puis généralisés à la régression et au multiclasse.

Idée clé : parmi tous les hyperplans séparateurs possibles, choisir celui qui maximise la marge entre les deux classes → meilleure généralisation.

Deux idées fondamentales :

  1. Marge optimale : hyperplan le plus éloigné possible de toutes les observations.
  2. Noyaux (kernels) : transformation implicite vers un espace de grande dimension pour traiter les cas non linéaires.

2. Notations et Définitions

Symbole Signification
$\mathcal{D}_n = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n$ Ensemble d'apprentissage
$x_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$ Vecteur de features de l'observation $i$
$y_i \in {-1, +1}$ Étiquette de classe
$w \in \mathbb{R}^p$ Vecteur normal à l'hyperplan
$b \in \mathbb{R}$ Biais (décalage par rapport à l'origine)
$\langle w, x \rangle = w^T x$ Produit scalaire usuel dans $\mathbb{R}^p$
$\|w\|$ Norme euclidienne de $w$
$\alpha_i \geq 0$ Multiplicateurs de Lagrange (variables duales)
$\gamma$ Marge maximale
$\xi_i \geq 0$ Variables d'écart (slack variables, cas non séparable)
$C > 0$ Paramètre de régularisation/pénalisation

3. SVM Linéaire — Cas Séparable

### 3.1 Données linéairement séparables

Définition. Les données $\mathcal{D}_n = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n$ sont dites linéairement séparables s'il existe $(w, b) \in \mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}$ tel que :

$$\forall, i = 1, \ldots, n \quad y_i \cdot (\langle w, x_i \rangle + b) > 0$$

Ce qui équivaut à :

$$\begin{cases} y_i = +1 & \text{si } \langle w, x_i \rangle + b > 0 \ y_i = -1 & \text{si } \langle w, x_i \rangle + b < 0 \end{cases}$$

Problèmes intrinsèques :

  • Il existe une infinité d'hyperplans séparateurs.
  • Les paramètres $(w, b)$ ne sont pas uniques : $(kw, kb)$ donne la même surface pour tout $k > 0$.

3.2 Hyperplan séparateur et marge

La fonction de décision est :

$$f(x) = \langle w, x \rangle + b$$

L'hyperplan central $H$ et les hyperplans marginaux $H^+, H^-$ :

$$H : \langle w, x \rangle + b = 0 \qquad H^+ : \langle w, x \rangle + b = +1 \qquad H^- : \langle w, x \rangle + b = -1$$

La distance d'un point $x_i$ à l'hyperplan $H$ est :

$$d(x_i, H) = \frac{|\langle w, x_i \rangle + b|}{|w|}$$

La marge géométrique est donc :

$$m = \min_{i \in {1,\ldots,n}} d(x_i, H) = \min_{i \in {1,\ldots,n}} \frac{|w^T x_i + b|}{|w|}$$

La marge totale (entre $H^+$ et $H^-$) vaut $\dfrac{2}{|w|}$.

Problème d'optimisation initial :

$$\max_{w,, b}; m = \max_{w,, b}; \min_{i \in {1,\ldots,n}} \frac{|w^T x_i + b|}{|w|}$$

sous les contraintes que les observations au-dessus de $H^+$ ont $y_i = +1$ et celles en-dessous de $H^-$ ont $y_i = -1$.

3.3 Normalisation et reformulation

Ce problème est mal posé : si $(w, b)$ est solution, $(kw, kb)$ l'est aussi $\forall k > 0$.

Changement de variables : on fixe la normalisation canonique :

$$\min_{i \in {1,\ldots,n}} y_i(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b) = 1$$

Ceci revient à poser $w' = \dfrac{w}{m|w|}$ et $b' = \dfrac{b}{m|w|}$, ce qui donne :

$$|w'| = \frac{1}{m} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad m = \frac{1}{|w'|}$$

Les contraintes deviennent alors :

$$\begin{cases} y_i = +1 & \Rightarrow \langle w, x_i \rangle + b \geq +1 \ y_i = -1 & \Rightarrow \langle w, x_i \rangle + b \leq -1 \end{cases} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \forall, i,; y_i(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b) \geq 1$$

Conséquence : Au lieu de maximiser $m = \dfrac{1}{|w|}$, on minimise $|w|$, ou de façon équivalente :

$$\min_{w, b}; \frac{1}{2}|w|^2$$

(le facteur $\frac{1}{2}$ facilite les calculs de dérivées)

3.4 Formulation Primale (SVM à marge rigide)

$$\boxed{\min_{w,, b}; \frac{1}{2}|w|^2 \quad \text{s.c.} \quad y_i(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b) \geq 1, \quad \forall, i = 1,\ldots,n}$$

Propriétés :

  • Programme quadratique convexe ($\frac{1}{2}|w|^2$ est quadratique, les contraintes sont linéaires).
  • Solution unique.
  • Complexité en $p + 1$ dimensions (dimension de $w$ + biais).

4. Dualité de Lagrange — Rappel Général

Problème Primal général :

$$\min_{u \in \mathbb{R}^p}; h(u) \quad \text{s.c.} \quad g_i(u) \leq 0, \quad \forall, i \in {1, \ldots, m}$$

Définition : Lagrangien. La fonction de Lagrange est définie sur $\mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}^m$ par :

$$\mathcal{L}(u, \alpha) = h(u) + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \alpha_i, g_i(u)$$

Les $\alpha_i$ sont appelés multiplicateurs de Lagrange ou variables duales.

Construction de la fonction duale :

Pour $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^m_+$ :

$$u_\alpha = \arg\min_{u \in \mathbb{R}^p} \mathcal{L}(u, \alpha)$$

$$\theta(\alpha) = \mathcal{L}(u_\alpha, \alpha) = \min_{u \in \mathbb{R}^p} \mathcal{L}(u, \alpha) \quad \longrightarrow \text{fonction duale}$$

Problème Dual :

$$\alpha^* = \arg\max_{\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^m} \theta(\alpha) \quad \text{s.c.} \quad \alpha_i \geq 0, \quad \forall, i \in {1,\ldots,m}$$

Théorème (dualité forte, conditions de Slater). Si le problème primal est convexe et satisfait les conditions de qualification de contraintes (Slater), alors la solution du problème dual $\alpha^{-}$ donne la solution primale via $u^- = u_{\alpha^*}$.

5. Formulation Duale — Dérivation Complète

5.1 Construction du Lagrangien SVM

Les contraintes du primal s'écrivent $g_i(w,b) = 1 - y_i(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b) \leq 0$.

Le Lagrangien associé au problème primal est :

$$\mathcal{L}(w, b, \alpha) = \frac{1}{2}|w|^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i \Big(y_i\big(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b\big) - 1\Big)$$

avec $\alpha_i \geq 0$.

5.2 Conditions de stationnarité (conditions nécessaires)

On annule les dérivées partielles par rapport à $w$ et $b$ :

Dérivée par rapport à $b$ :

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b}(w, b, \alpha) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \boxed{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i = 0}$$

Dérivée par rapport à $w$ :

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w}(w, b, \alpha) = w - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i x_i = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \boxed{w = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i x_i}$$

5.3 Développement de la fonction duale θ(α)

On substitue $w^* = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i x_i$ et la condition $\sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0$ dans le Lagrangien :

Terme $\frac{1}{2}|w|^2$ :

$$\frac{1}{2}|w|^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left\langle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i x_i,; \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j y_j x_j \right\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j \rangle$$

Terme $-\sum_i \alpha_i y_i \langle w, x_i \rangle$ :

$$-\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i \langle w, x_i \rangle = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i \left\langle \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j y_j x_j, x_i \right\rangle = -\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j \rangle$$

Terme $-b\sum_i \alpha_i y_i$ :

$$-b\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i = 0 \quad \text{(car } \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0 \text{)}$$

Terme $+\sum_i \alpha_i$ : reste tel quel.

Assemblage :

$$\theta(\alpha) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j \rangle - \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j \rangle + \sum_{i} \alpha_i$$

$$\boxed{\theta(\alpha) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j \rangle}$$

5.4 Problème Dual (SVM à marge rigide)

$$\boxed{\alpha^* = \arg\max_{\alpha}; \theta(\alpha) = \arg\max_{\alpha}; \left[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j \rangle\right]}$$

$$\text{s.c.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i = 0 \quad \text{et} \quad \alpha_i \geq 0,; \forall, i \in [![1, n]!]$$

Avantages de la formulation duale :

  • Problème quadratique en $n$ dimensions (nombre d'observations) vs $p+1$ dimensions pour le primal.
  • Si peu de données et beaucoup de variables → préférer le dual.
  • Fait apparaître la matrice de Gram $K_{ij} = \langle x_i, x_j \rangle$ → extension aux noyaux.

5.5 Conditions KKT (Karush-Kuhn-Tucker)

Les conditions KKT sont nécessaires et suffisantes (problème convexe, qualifié) :

Condition Expression Nom
Primal $y_i(\langle w^_, x_i \rangle + b^_) \geq 1,; \forall i$ Admissibilité primale
Dual $\alpha_i^* \geq 0,; \forall i$ Admissibilité duale
Complémentarité $\alpha_i^_\big(y_i(\langle w^_, x_i \rangle + b^*) - 1\big) = 0,; \forall i$ Complémentarité
Stationnarité $w^* = \sum_i \alpha_i^* y_i x_i$ et $\sum_i \alpha_i^* y_i = 0$ Stationnarité

Conséquence de la complémentarité :

$$\alpha_i^* > 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad y_i(\langle w^_, x_i \rangle + b^_) = 1 \quad \text{(point sur la frontière de marge)}$$

$$y_i(\langle w^_, x_i \rangle + b^_) > 1 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \alpha_i^* = 0 \quad \text{(point hors marge → n'influence pas $w^*$)}$$

5.6 Vecteurs Supports

Définition. Les vecteurs supports sont les observations $x_i$ telles que $\alpha_i^* > 0$, c'est-à-dire les points situés exactement sur les hyperplans marginaux $H^+$ ou $H^-$.

$$\text{V.S.} = {x_i \mid \alpha_i^* > 0} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad y_i(\langle w^_, x_i \rangle + b^_) = 1$$

Le nombre de vecteurs supports peut être faible → $w^*$ ne dépend que d'eux.

6. Règle de Décision (Cas Séparable)

Solution primale reconstruite à partir du dual :

$$w^* = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i^* y_i x_i = \sum_{x_i \in \text{V.S.}} \alpha_i^* y_i x_i$$

$$b^* : \text{résoudre pour } i \text{ t.q. } 0 < \alpha_i^* \leq C, \quad y_i(\langle w^_, x_i \rangle + b^_) = 1$$

Marge maximale :

$$\gamma^* = \frac{1}{|w^*|}$$

Classifieur (règle de décision) :

$$\phi_{w^_, b^_}(x) = \mathbb{1}_{\langle w^_, x \rangle + b^_ \geq 0} - \mathbb{1}_{\langle w^_, x \rangle + b^_ < 0}$$

$$\text{ou équivalemment :} \quad \phi(x) = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{si } \displaystyle\sum_{x_i \in \text{V.S.}} \alpha_i^* y_i \langle x_i, x \rangle + b^* \geq 0 \ -1 & \text{si } \displaystyle\sum_{x_i \in \text{V.S.}} \alpha_i^* y_i \langle x_i, x \rangle + b^* < 0 \end{cases}$$

7. SVM Linéaire — Cas Non Séparable (Marge Souple)

Quand les données ne sont pas linéairement séparables, on introduit des variables d'écart $\xi_i \geq 0$ (slack variables / variables ressort) pour tolérer des erreurs de classification.

Interprétation géométrique de $\xi_i$ :

Condition Valeur de $\xi_i$ Situation
$y_i(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b) \geq 1$ $\xi_i = 0$ Bien classé, dans la marge ou au-delà
$0 < y_i(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b) < 1$ $\xi_i \in (0,1)$ Bien classé mais dans la marge
$y_i(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b) \leq 0$ $\xi_i \geq 1$ Mal classé

On a toujours : $\xi_i = \max\big(0,; 1 - y_i(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b)\big)$

7.1 Formulation Primale (Marge Souple)

$$\boxed{\min_{w,, b,, \xi}; \frac{1}{2}|w|^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^{n} \xi_i}$$

$$\text{s.c.} \quad \begin{cases} y_i(\langle w, x_i \rangle + b) \geq 1 - \xi_i, & \forall, i = 1,\ldots,n \ \xi_i \geq 0, & \forall, i = 1,\ldots,n \end{cases}$$

  • $C > 0$ est le paramètre de régularisation (compromis marge large ↔ peu d'erreurs).
  • $C$ grand → peu d'erreurs tolérées → risque de sur-apprentissage.
  • $C$ petit → grande marge tolérée → risque de sous-apprentissage.

Solution du problème primal :

$$w^* = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i^* y_i x_i, \qquad b^* \text{ t.q. } y_i(\langle w^_, x_i \rangle + b^_) = 1 - \xi_i,; \forall, x_i \text{ avec } 0 < \alpha_i^* < C$$

7.2 Problème Dual (Marge Souple)

$$\max_{\alpha}; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j \rangle$$

$$\text{s.c.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i = 0 \quad \text{et} \quad 0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C, \quad \forall, i \in [![1, n]!]$$

Différence avec le cas séparable : les $\alpha_i$ sont bornés supérieurement par $C$.

7.3 Conditions KKT (Marge Souple)

$$0 \leq \alpha_i^* \leq C, \quad \forall, i \in [![1, n]!] \qquad \text{(admissibilité duale)}$$

$$y_i(\langle w^_, x_i \rangle + b^_) \geq 1 - \xi_i^*, \quad \forall, i \in [![1, n]!] \qquad \text{(admissibilité primale)}$$

$$\alpha_i^_\big(y_i(\langle w^_, x_i \rangle + b^_) + \xi_i^_ - 1\big) = 0, \quad \forall, i \in [![1, n]!] \qquad \text{(complémentarité 1)}$$

$$\xi_i^_(\alpha_i^_ - C) = 0, \quad \forall, i \in [![1, n]!] \qquad \text{(complémentarité 2)}$$

7.4 Classification des observations (3 cas)

Condition sur $\alpha_i^*$ Condition sur $\xi_i^*$ Type de point
$\alpha_i^* = 0$ $\xi_i^* = 0$ Bien classé, hors marge (non vecteur support)
$0 < \alpha_i^* < C$ $\xi_i^* = 0$ Sur la frontière de marge (Vecteur Support)
$\alpha_i^* = C$ $\xi_i^* > 0$ Dans la marge ou mal classé

Fonction de décision :

$$f(x) = \sum_{x_i \in \text{V.S.}} \alpha_i^* y_i \langle x_i, x \rangle + b^*$$

8. SVM Non Linéaire — Noyaux (Kernels)

Idée : transformer les données vers un espace de grande dimension où elles sont linéairement séparables, sans calculer explicitement la transformation.

8.1 Astuce du noyau (Kernel Trick)

Soit $\varphi : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{H}$ une fonction de redescription vers un espace de Hilbert $\mathcal{H}$.

La formulation duale ne dépend de $\varphi$ qu'au travers des produits scalaires :

$$\langle \varphi(x_i), \varphi(x_j) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \quad \text{et} \quad \langle \varphi(x_i), \varphi(x) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}}$$

Définition. Une fonction $k : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ telle que $$k(x, x') = \langle \varphi(x), \varphi(x') \rangle_{\mathcal{H}}$$ pour une fonction $\varphi : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{H}$ est appelée un noyau.

Remarque : un noyau est souvent bien plus simple à calculer que $\varphi$ elle-même.

8.2 Problème Dual Non Linéaire

On remplace $\langle x_i, x_j \rangle$ par $k(x_i, x_j)$ :

$$\max_{\alpha}; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j, k(x_i, x_j)$$

$$\text{s.c.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i = 0 \quad \text{et} \quad 0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C$$

Règle de décision non linéaire :

$$\phi(x) = \mathbb{1}_{\sum_i y_i \alpha_i^* k(x_i,, x) + b^* ,\geq, 0} - \mathbb{1}_{\sum_i y_i \alpha_i^* k(x_i,, x) + b^* ,<, 0}$$

8.3 Exemples de noyaux courants

Type Nom $k(s, t)$
Radial Gaussien (RBF) $\exp!\left(-\dfrac{\|s-t\|^2}{\sigma}\right)$
Radial Laplacien $\exp(-\|s-t\|/\sigma)$
Radial Rationnel $1 - \dfrac{\|s-t\|^2}{\|s-t\|^2 + \sigma}$
Projectif Polynomial $(s^\top t)^p$
Projectif Polynomial affine $(s^\top t + \sigma)^p$
Projectif Cosinus $\dfrac{s^\top t}{\|s\|t\|}$

Condition de Mercer : un noyau $k$ est valide si et seulement si la matrice de Gram $K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)$ est symétrique semi-définie positive.

9. SVM Multiclasses

L'approche SVM est formellement définie pour $y \in {-1, +1}$. Deux stratégies d'extension :

9.1 One-Against-Rest (OAR)

  • Construire $K$ classifieurs SVM : classe $k$ contre toutes les autres.
  • Classifieur $k$ : $y_k = +1$ vs $y_{j \neq k} = -1$ → $K$ fonctions $f_k(x)$.
  • Règle de décision :

$$\hat{y} = \arg\max_{k}; f_k(x)$$

9.2 One-Against-One (OAO / Pairwise)

  • Construire $\dfrac{K(K-1)}{2}$ classifieurs SVM pour chaque paire de classes.
  • Classifieur $(k, j)$ : $y_k = +1$ vs $y_j = -1$ → fonctions $f_{k,j}(x)$.
  • Règle de décision : vote majoritaire (classe avec le plus grand nombre de victoires).

10. Avantages et Inconvénients

✅ Avantages

  • Efficace en grande dimension ($p \gg n$ possible).
  • Robuste car seuls les vecteurs supports influencent le classifieur.
  • Traitement des problèmes non linéaires via les noyaux.
  • Non paramétrique (pas d'hypothèse sur la distribution des données).
  • Robuste aux points aberrants (contrôlé par $C$).
  • Souvent très performant en comparaison avec d'autres méthodes.

❌ Inconvénients

  • Sélection des hyperparamètres difficile ($C$, $\sigma$ pour le RBF, etc.) → validation croisée.
  • Difficile avec grandes bases ($n$ très élevé) → matrice de Gram $n \times n$ coûteuse en mémoire.
  • Problèmes si classes bruitées (multiplication des vecteurs supports).
  • Pas de modèle explicite pour les noyaux non linéaires.
  • Difficulté d'interprétation (pertinence des variables).
  • Extension multiclasses reste une question ouverte.

🔑 Récapitulatif — Formules Clés pour l'Examen

$$\boxed{m = \frac{2}{|w|} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{maximiser la marge} \equiv \min_{w,b}; \frac{1}{2}|w|^2}$$

$$\boxed{w^* = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i^* y_i x_i \qquad \text{(combinaison linéaire des vecteurs supports)}}$$

$$\boxed{\theta(\alpha) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j \rangle}$$

$$\boxed{\text{KKT}: \alpha_i^_\big(y_i(\langle w^_, x_i\rangle + b^_) - 1\big) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \alpha_i^_ > 0 \Leftrightarrow x_i \in \text{V.S.}}$$

$$\boxed{k(x, x') = \langle \varphi(x), \varphi(x') \rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \quad \text{(kernel trick : remplace } \langle x_i, x_j\rangle \text{ dans le dual)}}$$

$$\boxed{\gamma^* = \frac{1}{|w^_|} \qquad b^_ : y_i(\langle w^_, x_i\rangle + b^_) = 1 \text{ pour tout V.S. avec } 0 < \alpha_i^* < C}$$

notes.html:
Notes

Definition

Linear regression is a type of supervised machine-learning algorithm that learns from the labelled datasets and maps the data points with most optimized linear functions which can be used for prediction on new datasets. It assumes that there is a linear relationship between the input and output, meaning the output changes at a constant rate as the input changes. This relationship is represented by a straight line.

1. Terminology & Notation

To better understand linear regression we can take a closer look at the example of a model that predicts house prices. Let’s say you were given a dataset with size and prices. You can build a model based on linear regression — this model fits a line through the data.

If we look at the figure below, we can see the data points and the line that was fitted. Given that, we can see that for new house size 1250, the model will predict something like $250K.

This regression model predicts numbers and it is a form of supervised learning.

Some key terminology to understand:

  • Training set: the data used to train the model
  • Input variable: represents the input variable/feature and is usually denoted as $x$
  • Target variable: represents the target variable and is usually denoted as $y$
  • $m$ is the number of training examples
  • $(x, y)$ is the a single training example
  • $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ represents the $i^{(th)}$ training example

where $x^{(1)} = 2104$ and $y^{(1)}=400$. Therefore, $(x^{(1)}, y^{(1)}) = (2104, 400)$.

2. The Model (Hypothesis)

When designing a linear regression model the following are the important components:

  • First, you have a training set which represents your features and target variables
  • You feed that through a learning algorithm which can include a model (represented by a function $f$)
  • $x$ data is fed through the model which outputs the prediction or estimated value $\hat y$
  • $f$ can be represented as a linear function: $f(x) = wx + b$ or $\hat y = θ_0​+θ_1​x$
  • $w$ and $b$ are called the parameters of the model
  • When you are dealing with one single feature $x$ in linear regression it is referred to as univariate linear regression

Cost Function Formula

Recall that for linear regression the model function is defined as follows: $$ f_{w, b}(x)=w x+b $$ where $w$ and $b$ are the parameters of the model. To demonstrate how the parameters determine the function $f$ we can take a look at some plots in a chart.

Example:

The function f is important because it gives us the prediction $\hat y$. We then take that prediction and compare with the original target to compute what’s referred to as the cost function. The purpose of the cost function is to allow the model to optimize for values of w and b that reduces the errors of the model. In other words, find w and b where $\hat y^{(i)}$ is close to $y^{(i)}$ for all $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$.

A widely used cost function in linear regression is known as squared error cost function and is defined as follows: $$ J(w, b)=\frac{1}{2 m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(f_{w, b}\left(x^{(i)}\right)-y^{(i)}\right)^{2} $$

The code below calculates cost by looping over each example. In each loop:

  • f_wb, a prediction is calculated
  • the difference between the target and the prediction is calculated and squared.
  • this is added to the total cost.
def compute_cost(x, y, w, b): 
    """
    Computes the cost function for linear regression.
    
    Args:
      x (ndarray (m,)): Data, m examples 
      y (ndarray (m,)): target values
      w,b (scalar)    : model parameters  
    
    Returns
        total_cost (float): The cost of using w,b as the parameters for linear regression
               to fit the data points in x and y
    """
    # number of training examples
    m = x.shape[0] 
    
    cost_sum = 0 
    for i in range(m): 
        f_wb = w * x[i] + b   
        cost = (f_wb - y[i]) ** 2  
        cost_sum = cost_sum + cost  
    total_cost = (1 / (2 * m)) * cost_sum  

    return total_cost

Cost Function Intuition

Recall that to measure how well the choice of the parameters $w$ and $b$ fits the training data, you define the cost function $J$. $J$ measures the difference between the model’s predictions and the actual true values for $y$. So the overall goal is to minimize $J$ as a function of $w$ and $b$. This is defined as: $$ \underset{w, b}{\operatorname{min}} J(w, b) $$ To get a better intuition of the cost function, let’s take a look at an example and plot it. To do this, we can simplify our prediction function $f$ to be: $$ f_{w}(x) = wx $$ We have set $b=0$. So this gives us the following cost function: $$ J(w)=\frac{1}{2 m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(f_{w}\left(x^{(i)}\right)-y^{(i)}\right)^{2} $$ Now we want to minimize the following: $$ \underset{w}{\operatorname{min}} J(w) $$

As an example, let’s plot what a minimal prediction function looks like when we plot examples on a chart and $w=1$:

With substitution we end up with: $$ J(w) =\frac{1}{2 m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(w x^{(i)}-y^{(i)}\right)^{2} $$ If you look at the example above, we plotted the following three data points representing value pairs of $x$ and $y$: [1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]

If we replace the values in the cost function $J$ we end up with: $$ J(w) =\frac{1}{2 m}\left(0^{2}+0^{2}+0^{2}\right) $$

Given those calculations we can now plot the function $J$ with respect to the $w$ parameter. Let’s try to use many different values of $w$ given the same data points as before. The plot will look something like what’s shown below:

Use the code below to plot the function:

import torch
import numpy as np

def plot_cost_function(w, m, x, y):
    j_w = [ (1/(2*m)) * torch.sum(((w * x) - y)**2)  for w in w]
    plt.plot(w, j_w, '-', linewidth=6)

    plt.xlabel('w')
    plt.ylabel('J(w)')
    plt.show()
    return

w = torch.tensor([x for x in np.linspace(-0.5, 2.5, 25)], dtype=float) 
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=float)
y = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=float) 
m = 3.0

plot_cost_function(w, m, x, y)

One interesting observation you will note here is that when $w=1$ we saw a straight line through the data points in our previous chart, which means that a perfect line was fitted through the data points. In fact, when $w=1$ it produces $J(w) = 0$. So in this problem we want to choose $w$ that minimizes $J(w)$, which is this example turns out to be $w=1$.

So far, we have the following definitions:

Model:

$$ f_{w, b}(x)=w x+b $$

Parameters:

$$ w, b $$

Cost Function:

$$ J(w, b)=\frac{1}{2 m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(f_{w, b}\left(x^{(i)}\right)-y^{(i)}\right)^{2} $$

Learning objective:

$$ \underset{w, b}{\operatorname{minimize}} J(w, b) $$

You can also use this general form to visualize the cost function. However, it does require a bit more effort and different tools. The course has a great video explainer and visual examples of how the cost function looks. It uses counter plots which are a popular way to visualize the cost function.

2. Train the model with Gradient Descent

### **Gradient Descent Overview**

Gradient descent is one of the most important and widely used algorithms to train machine learning and deep learning models.

The gradient descent algorithm is a very simple concept. Let’s say we have some function $J(w, b)$ we want to minimize. We start with $w, b$, which you can initialize to zero. You then keep changing $w, b$ to reduce $J(w, b)$ until the algorithm settles as or gets near a minimum.

In the gradient descent algorithm, you can adjust the weight by using the following update formula:

$$ w=w-\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial w} J(w, b) $$

where $\alpha$ is the learning rate which controls how big of a step you take in the gradient descent procedure. $\frac{\partial}{\partial w} J(w, b)$ defines in which direction you want to take the step. You do the same assignment procedure on the $b$ parameter:

$$ b=b-\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial b} J(w, b) $$

So the algorithm updates those parameters until convergence where $w$ and $b$ don’t change much.

Gradient Descent Intuition

To get a better intuition about what the updates above do and how it helps the algorithm converge, we can take a look at the simplified version of the parameter update on $w$.

Given:

$$ w=w-\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial w} J(w) $$

If $\frac{\partial}{\partial w} J(w) > 0$, i.e., a positive number, then $w$ gets smaller as illustrated below:

$$ w=w-\alpha \cdot \text { (positive number) } $$

If $\frac{\partial}{\partial w} J(w) < 0$, i.e., a negative number then $w$ increases as illustrated below: $$ w=w-\alpha \cdot(\text { negative number }) $$

Choosing the right learning rate $\alpha$

Another important consideration when using the gradient descent algorithm is to choose the right value for the learning rate. A poor choice of $\alpha$ might make the algorithm inefficient. If $\alpha$ is too small, then the steps taken by the algorithm will also be small which makes the algorithm slow. If $\alpha$ is too large, the algorithm could be very close to the minimum and miss it entirely because of a big step taken. With too large learning rates the algorithms runs the risk of overshooting and never reach minimum.

The illustration below shows that if $\alpha$ is too small, gradient descent may be too slow.

On the other hand, if $\alpha$ is too large, gradient descent may overshoot, never reach minimum or fail to converge or even diverge:

Note that if you are already at a local minimum the parameters won’t change.

When $\frac{\partial}{\partial w} J(w) = 0$, $w$ remains unchanged.

As we approach a local minimum, the derivative value gets closer to zero. With the gradient descent algorithm, update steps become smaller until you reach that local minimum even with a fixed learning rate.

In Summary: Gradient descent iteratively updates the parameters $w$ and $b$ to minimize the cost function. The Update Rule: Repeat until convergence

$$ w = w - \alpha \frac{\partial J}{\partial w} $$ $$ b = b - \alpha \frac{\partial J}{\partial b} $$

Where:

  • $\alpha$ is the learning rate.
  • $\frac{\partial J}{\partial w}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial b}$ are the gradients (partial derivatives).

Gradient Definition

The gradient for the weight parameter $w$ is defined as:

$$ \frac{\partial J}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} (f_{w,b}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)})x^{(i)} $$ $$ \frac{\partial J}{\partial b} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} (f_{w,b}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}) $$

Simultaneous Update

Simultaneously means that you must calculate the partial derivatives for all parameters ($w$ and $b$) using the current values before updating any of them.

Correct:

  1. Calculate $tmp\_w = \frac{\partial J}{\partial w}$
  2. Calculate $tmp\_b = \frac{\partial J}{\partial b}$
  3. $w = w - \alpha \cdot tmp\_w$
  4. $b = b - \alpha \cdot tmp\_b$

Incorrect: Updating $w$ and then using the new $w$ to calculate the update for $b$.

Implementation and Python

You will need three functions:

  • compute_gradient implementing equation (4) and (5) above
  • compute_cost implementing equation (2) above (code from previous lab)
  • gradient_descent, utilizing compute_gradient and compute_cost

Conventions:

  • The naming of python variables containing partial derivatives follows this pattern,∂𝐽(𝑤,𝑏)∂𝑏 will be dj_db.
  • w.r.t is With Respect To, as in partial derivative of 𝐽(𝑤𝑏) With Respect To 𝑏.

Tools

In this lab, we will make use of:

  • NumPy, a popular library for scientific computing
  • Matplotlib, a popular library for plotting data
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Data

a house with 1000 square feet sold for $300,000 and a house with 2000 square feet sold for $500,000.

Size (1000 sqft) Price (1000s of dollars)
1 300
2 500 
x_train = np.array([1.0, 2.0])          
y_train = np.array([300.0, 500.0])

compute_cost

To calculate the error and see how close to zero the cost function $J$ is while searching for $w$ and $b$

def compute_cost(x, y, w, b): 
    m = x.shape[0] 
    cost_sum = 0 
    for i in range(m): 
        f_wb = w * x[i] + b   
        cost = (f_wb - y[i]) ** 2  
        cost_sum = cost_sum + cost  
    total_cost = (1 / (2 * m)) * cost_sum  
    return total_cost

Vectorizing the compute_cost function:

  • Instead of the loop, you can write the cost function in one line using NumPy. This is a great snippet to add to your note as a "Level Up":
def compute_cost_vectorized(x, y, w, b):
    m = len(x)
    f_wb = np.dot(x, w) + b  # Vectorized prediction
    cost = np.sum((f_wb - y)**2) / (2 * m)
    return cost

compute_gradient

Returns $\frac{\partial J}{\partial w}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial b}$.

def compute_gradient(x, y, w, b): 

    # Number of training examples
    m = x.shape[0]    
    dj_dw = 0
    dj_db = 0
    
    for i in range(m):  
        f_wb = w * x[i] + b 
        dj_dw_i = (f_wb - y[i]) * x[i] 
        dj_db_i = f_wb - y[i] 
        dj_db += dj_db_i
        dj_dw += dj_dw_i 
    dj_dw = dj_dw / m 
    dj_db = dj_db / m 
    return dj_dw, dj_db

Gradient Descent

you will utilize this function to find optimal values of 𝑤 and 𝑏 on the training data.

def gradient_descent(x, y, w_in, b_in, alpha, num_iters, gradient_function): 
    w = w_in
    b = b_in
    for i in range(num_iters):
        dj_dw, dj_db = gradient_function(x, y, w, b)
        w = w - alpha * dj_dw
        b = b - alpha * dj_db
    return w, b

Initialize parameters

initial_w = 0
initial_b = 0
iterations = 10000
alpha = 0.1 # Learning rate

Running and Plotting the Gradient Descent

We will be running the algorithm and plotting the linear regression function with prediction to a random value

# Run gradient descent
w_final, b_final = gradient_descent(x_train, y_train, initial_w, initial_b, alpha, iterations, compute_gradient)

print(f"w found by gradient descent: {w_final:.2f}")
print(f"b found by gradient descent: {b_final:.2f}")
print(f"cost function or error of this model: {compute_cost(x_train, y_train, w_final, b_final)}")

x_new = 1.5
y_prediction = w_final * x_new + b_final

print(f"Prediction for x={x_new}: ${y_prediction:.2f} (in thousands)")

# --- PLOTTING ---
plt.figure() # Create a new figure
plt.scatter(x_train, y_train, marker='x', c='r', label='Actual Values')
plt.plot(x_train, w_final * x_train + b_final, c='b', label='Prediction')
plt.title("Housing Prices")
plt.ylabel('Price (in 1000s of dollars)')
plt.xlabel('Size (1000 sqft)')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Python code using scikit-learn

Much easier with already built in functions for fitting the model and making predictions without the need to create any compute functions

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# 1. DATA PREPARATION
# Sklearn expects 'X' to be a 2D array (rows, columns). 
# .reshape(-1, 1) converts [1.0, 2.0] into [[1.0], [2.0]]
x_train = np.array([1.0, 2.0]).reshape(-1, 1) 
y_train = np.array([300.0, 500.0])

# 2. MODEL TRAINING
# This single line replaces the entire 'compute_cost' and 'gradient_descent' functions
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(x_train, y_train)

# 3. RESULTS
# Extract the learned parameters (w and b)
w = model.coef_[0]      # Slope
b = model.intercept_    # Y-intercept

print(f"w (Coefficient): {w}")
print(f"b (Intercept): {b}")

# 4. PREDICTION & PLOTTING
predictions = model.predict(x_train)

# 4. 1. Define the new value
x_new = 1.5

# 2. Reshape it to a 2D array: <a class="wikilink wikilink-unresolved" href="/garden/note/15" data-target="1.5">1.5</a>
# sklearn expects shape (n_samples, n_features)
x_new_reshaped = np.array(<a class="wikilink wikilink-unresolved" href="/garden/note/x_new" data-target="x_new">x_new</a>) 

# 3. Make the prediction
Y_prediction = model.predict(x_new_reshaped)

print(f"Prediction for x = {x_new}: {Y_prediction[0]}$")

plt.scatter(x_train, y_train, color='red', label='Actual')
plt.plot(x_train, predictions, color='blue', label='Prediction')
plt.xlabel('Size (1000 sqft)')
plt.ylabel('Price (1000s)')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

notes.html:
Notes

1. Introduction: What is Classification?

Classification (often called Clustering or Segmentation) is a descriptive, unsupervised method. Its primary goal is to group objects (individuals or variables) into classes (clusters) such that the structure of the data is revealed.

The Two Fundamental Principles

  1. Homogeneity (Intra-class): Two objects in the same group should resemble each other as much as possible.

  2. Heterogeneity (Inter-class): Two objects in distinct groups should differ as much as possible.

Key Concept

Unlike supervised learning, there is no privileged target variable (no $Y$). We are describing a complex reality by summarizing it into groups.

2. The CAH Algorithm (Bottom-Up)

The method is "Ascendant" (Agglomerative) because it starts from the bottom (leaves) and builds up to the root.

Step-by-Step Process

  1. Initialization: Every individual $x_i$ forms its own class. If you have $n$ individuals, you start with $n$ classes.

  2. Distance Calculation: Calculate the distance (dissimilarity) between every pair of classes.

  3. Agglomeration: Merge the two classes that are closest to each other (minimum distance).

  4. Update Distances: Calculate the distances between this new merged class and all remaining classes using an Aggregation Criterion.

  5. Iteration: Repeat steps 3 and 4 until all individuals are grouped into a single class (the root).

3. Mathematical Foundations

A. Data Preparation

Before calculating distances, it is crucial to standardize (centrer et réduire) variables if they are not measured in the same units or have different variances. This prevents variables with large scales from dominating the calculation.

B. Distances Between Individuals

To define similarity, we need a metric. Let $x_i$ and $x_j$ be two individuals defined by $p$ variables ($q=1 \dots p$).

  1. Euclidean Distance (Most Common):

    $$d(x_i, x_j) = \sqrt{\sum_{q=1}^{p} (x_i^q - x_j^q)^2}$$

  2. Manhattan Distance ($L_1$):

    $$l_{manh}(x_i, x_j) = \sum_{q=1}^{p} |x_i^q - x_j^q|$$

4. Aggregation Strategies (Linkage Criteria)

When we merge two individuals $x$ and $y$ into a new group $h = \{x, y\}$, how do we calculate the distance between this new group $h$ and another existing group $z$?

This choice defines the "shape" of your clusters.

  1. Simple Linkage (Saut Minimum)

We take the distance between the two closest elements.

$$d(z, h) = \min \{ d(z, x), d(z, y) \}$$

  • Effect: Can create the "chain effect" (long, stringy clusters).
  1. Complete Linkage (Saut Maximum)

We take the distance between the two farthest elements.

$$d(z, h) = \max \{ d(z, x), d(z, y) \}$$

  • Effect: Tends to produce compact, spherical clusters.
  1. Average Linkage (Moyen)

We take the average of the distances.

$$d(z, h) = \frac{d(z, x) + d(z, y)}{2}$$

4. Ward's Method (Critère de Ward)

This is the most statistically robust method. It is based on the concept of Inertia.

  • Goal: At each step, merge the two classes that result in the minimum loss of Inter-class Inertia (which is equivalent to the minimum increase in Intra-class Inertia).

  • Ward's Distance Formula:

    $$D(G_i, G_j) = \frac{n_i n_j}{n_i + n_j} d^2(g_i, g_j)$$

    • $n_i, n_j$: Number of individuals (effectif) in class $G_i$ and $G_j$.

    • $g_i, g_j$: Centers of gravity (barycentres) of class $G_i$ and $G_j$.

    • $d^2(g_i, g_j)$: Squared Euclidean distance between the centers.

  • Interpretation: It penalizes merging large groups ($n$ is large) and groups that are far apart. It groups objects of low weight and avoids the chain effect.

5. Inertia Decomposition (Huygens Theorem)

This theorem is the "engine" behind Ward's method and quality assessment.

$$\text{Inertia}_{\text{Total}} = \text{Inertia}_{\text{Inter}} + \text{Inertia}_{\text{Intra}}$$

Definitions:

  1. Total Inertia ($I_T$): Constant. It represents the total variability of the dataset. $$I_T = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} d^2(x_i, g)$$

    (Where $g$ is the global center of gravity)

  2. Intra-Class Inertia ($I_{Intra}$): The sum of inertias inside each cluster. Measures compactness.

    $$I_{Intra} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{J} \sum_{i \in G_k} d^2(x_i, g_k)$$

  3. Inter-Class Inertia ($I_{Inter}$): The inertia of the cluster centers weighted by their size. Measures separation.

    $$I_{Inter} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{J} n_k d^2(g_k, g)$$ avec: $$g_k = \frac{1}{n_k} \sum_{x \in G_k} x$$

The Trade-off

  • At the start ($n$ classes): $I_{Intra} = 0$, $I_{Inter} = I_{Total}$.

  • As we merge: $I_{Intra}$ increases, $I_{Inter}$ decreases.

  • Objective: We want to stop merging before $I_{Intra}$ becomes too large. We look for a partition that maximizes the ratio $\frac{I_{Inter}}{I_{Total}}$.

6. The Dendrogram & Choosing the Number of Classes ($k$)

The Dendrogram is the visual history of every merge performed by the algorithm.

How to cut the tree?

We need to choose a "Cutting Level" (Niveau de coupure) to define the final partition.

  1. Visual Heuristic: Cut the tree where the branches are long (vertical lines). A long branch indicates that the two groups being merged are very different (large distance).

  2. Inertia Gain (Saut d'inertie): Look at the loss of inter-class inertia at each step.

    • If merging two groups causes a small jump, they were similar (good merge).

    • If merging causes a huge jump (large loss of Inter-Inertia), we should stop before that merge.

    • Example from Course: In the cities example, passing from 2 classes to 1 class caused a massive loss (7.88), suggesting 2 classes is a natural partition.

7. Pros & Cons of CAH

Avantages (Pros) Limites (Cons)
No fixed $k$: It suggests the number of classes via the dendrogram. Computational Cost: Very heavy for large datasets ($n$ large).
Hierarchy: Reveals the structure of sub-groups within groups. Static: Once an individual is assigned to a group in an early step, it cannot be moved later (non-optimal structure).
Visual: The dendrogram is a powerful explanatory tool. Subjectivity: Choosing the cutting level can be difficult.

8. Implementation Code

R Implementation (Exam Standard)

Based on the specific commands found in slides 24-25 & 42.

# 1. Import and Prepare Data
# data(iris) # Using built-in dataset
# summary(iris)

# 2. Distance Matrix Calculation
# We use columns 1 to 4 (quantitative variables)
d_euc <- dist(iris[, 1:4], method = 'euclidean')

# 3. Hierarchical Clustering (Hclust)
# method = 'ward.D2' is the R standard for Ward's method. 
# Slide 25 uses 'ave' (Average Linkage) as an example.
hc <- hclust(d_euc, method = 'ave') 

# 4. Plot Dendrogram
plot(hc, main = "Dendrogramme CAH", xlab = "Individus", sub = "")

# 5. Cut the Tree (Partitioning)
# We choose k=3 based on the dendrogram analysis
class_cah <- cutree(hc, k = 3)

# 6. Analyze Results
# Compare our clusters with the real species
table(class_cah, iris$Species)

# Visualizing the clusters on a 2D plot (Sepal.Length vs Petal.Width)
plot(iris[, 3:4], col = c('red','blue','green')[class_cah], 
     main = "Projection des classes CAH")

Python Implementation (Bonus)

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage, fcluster
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

# 1. Load & Scale Data
iris = load_iris()
df = pd.DataFrame(iris.data, columns=iris.feature_names)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(df)

# 2. Hierarchical Clustering (Linkage Matrix)
# method='ward' corresponds to Ward's criterion
Z = linkage(X_scaled, method='ward', metric='euclidean')

# 3. Plot Dendrogram
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.title("Dendrogramme CAH (Ward)")
dendrogram(Z)
plt.axhline(y=10, c='k', ls='--', label='Cut Level') # Example cut line
plt.show()

# 4. Cut the Tree
# t=3 for 3 clusters
clusters = fcluster(Z, t=3, criterion='maxclust')

# 5. Visualization
plt.scatter(df.iloc[:, 2], df.iloc[:, 3], c=clusters, cmap='viridis')
plt.xlabel('Petal Length')
plt.ylabel('Petal Width')
plt.title('Partition CAH (k=3)')
plt.show()

notes.html:
Notes

1. Concept & The Partitioning Problem

Unlike hierarchical methods (CAH) that build a tree structure, partitioning methods aim to directly divide $N$ objects into $K$ distinct clusters.

The Objective

To find, among all possible partitions, the one that optimizes a predefined criterion (usually minimizing Intra-class Inertia).

The Combinatorial Problem:

It is impossible to test every single possible partition to find the "perfect" one. For $N$ objects and $K$ classes, the number of possible partitions is roughly $K^N / K!$.

  • Implication: We need heuristic algorithms (like K-Means) that find a "good" solution (local optimum) efficiently, even if it's not mathematically guaranteed to be the absolute best.

2. K-Means vs. Nuées Dynamiques

The course distinguishes between two very similar approaches 2:

  • K-Means (Centres Mobiles): Each class is represented by its barycentre (mean). The center is updated iteratively.

  • Nuées Dynamiques: Each class is represented by a kernel (noyau)—a subset of actual individuals (e.g., the most central ones), rather than an abstract geometric mean.

3. The K-Means Algorithm

The algorithm alternates between assigning points to clusters and moving the cluster centers.

The Steps:

  1. Initialization:

    • Fix the number of classes $k$ (a priori).

    • Choose $k$ individuals (or random points) as the initial centers.

  2. Assignment (Affectation):

    • Assign every individual $x_i$ to the class whose center is closest (usually Euclidean distance). $$x_i \in C_k \iff d(x_i, c_k) \le d(x_i, c_j), \forall j \neq k$$

  3. Update (Représentation):

    • Recalculate the barycentre (center of gravity) of each class based on the new members. $$c_k^{new} = \frac{1}{n_k} \sum_{x \in C_k} x$$

  4. Iteration:

    • Repeat steps 2 and 3.

    • Stopping Criterion: Stop when the centers no longer move (stability) or when a maximum number of iterations is reached.

Convergence

Convergence is usually fast (often around 10 iterations).

4. Concrete Example: Medicines

Based on the detailed walkthrough in slides.

Scenario: Classify 4 medicines (A, B, C, D) into $K=2$ classes based on "Concentration" and "Efficiency".

Medicine Concentration (X) Efficiency (Y)
A 1 1
B 2 1
C 4 3
D 5 4

Iteration 1

  1. Initialization: Randomly select A and B as centers. $c_1 = (1, 1)$

    $c_2 = (2, 1)$

  2. Assignment: Calculate distance of remaining points (C, D) to centers.

    • For D(5,4):

      • $d(D, c_1) = \sqrt{(5-1)^2 + (4-1)^2} = 5$ 6

      • $d(D, c_2) = \sqrt{(5-2)^2 + (4-1)^2} = 4.24$

      • $\rightarrow$ D is closer to $c_2$. Assign D to Class 2.

    • (Similarly, C is found to be closer to $c_2$).

    • Result: Class 1 = $\{A\}$, Class 2 = $\{B, C, D\}$.

  3. Update Centers:

    • $c_1^{new} = A = (1, 1)$

    • $c_2^{new} = \text{Mean}(B, C, D) = (\frac{2+4+5}{3}, \frac{1+3+4}{3}) = (3.67, 2.67)$.

### Iteration 2:

  1. Assignment: Re-measure distances of all points to new centers $(1,1)$ and $(3.67, 2.67)$.

    • Result: A and B are now closest to $c_1$. C and D are closest to $c_2$.

    • New Partition: Class 1 = $\{A, B\}$, Class 2 = $\{C, D\}$.

  2. Update Centers:

    • $c_1 = \text{Mean}(A, B) = (1.5, 1)$.

    • $c_2 = \text{Mean}(C, D) = (4.5, 3.5)$.

**Convergence:** If we run another iteration, the assignments won't change. The algorithm stops.

5. Pros & Cons (Avantages et Limites)

Essential for theoretical questions on the exam 11.

Avantages (Pros) Limites (Cons)
Speed: Low algorithmic complexity. Can handle large datasets efficiently. Fixed $k$: Number of classes must be chosen a priori.
Simplicity: Easy to implement and interpret. Initialization Bias: The final result depends on the initial centers (random seed). It can get stuck in local optima.
Sequential: Can process data as it arrives (streaming potential). Sensitivity: Sensitive to outliers (they pull the mean) and assumes spherical clusters.

6. The "Mixed" Approach

How to solve the problem of choosing $k$ and initialization? Combining methods is the best practice.

  1. Step 1: CAH: Run CAH on a sample or aggregated dataset.

  2. Step 2: Cut: Analyze the dendrogram to find the optimal number of classes $k$.

  3. Step 3: Centers: Use the barycenters of the CAH classes as the initial centers for K-Means.

  4. Step 4: K-Means: Run K-Means on the full dataset to refine the partition.

7. Implementation Code

R Implementation (Exam Standard)

Based on commands in Slide 42.

# 1. Load Data
data(iris)

# 2. Run K-Means
# We use only numerical columns (1 to 4)
# centers = 3 : We fix k=3
# nstart = 20 : Runs the algorithm 20 times with different random seeds 
# and keeps the best result (lowest Intra-class inertia). Crucial for stability!
km <- kmeans(iris[, 1:4], centers = 3, nstart = 20)

# 3. Analyze Results
print(km)

# View the coordinates of the final centroids
print(km$centers) 

# 4. Evaluation (Croisement)
# Compare the cluster results with the actual species
table(km$cluster, iris$Species)

# Compare K-Means results with CAH results (if 'class_cah' exists)
# table(class_cah, km$cluster) [cite: 610]

# 5. Visualization
# Plot variables (e.g., Sepal.Length vs Sepal.Width) colored by cluster
plot(iris[, 1:2], col = c('red','blue','green')[km$cluster], 
     main = "Résultats K-Means", pch = 19)

Python Implementation (Bonus)

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

# 1. Load Data
iris = load_iris()
X = iris.data

# 2. Run K-Means
# n_init=20 is equivalent to nstart=20 in R
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init='k-means++', n_init=20, random_state=42)
kmeans.fit(X)

# 3. Get Results
labels = kmeans.labels_
centroids = kmeans.cluster_centers_

# 4. Inertia (Elbow Method potential)
print(f"Intra-class Inertia: {kmeans.inertia_}")

# 5. Visualization
# Plotting first two dimensions
plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='viridis')
plt.scatter(centroids[:, 0], centroids[:, 1], s=200, c='red', marker='X', label='Centroids')
plt.xlabel('Sepal Length')
plt.ylabel('Sepal Width')
plt.title('K-Means Partition (k=3)')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Notes

Date: 2026-04-01 Tags: Mathematics, Machine Learning, Python, Neural Networks, Deep Learning, Theory

Neural Networks — Foundations

“Artificial” neural networks are inspired by the organic brain, translated to the computer. It’s not a perfect comparison, but there are neurons, activations, and lots of interconnectivity, even if the underlying processes are quite different

Definition

A neural network is a computational model inspired by the structure of the biological brain. It consists of a collection of interconnected nodes (neurons) organized into layers, where each connection transmits a weighted signal. Signals flow from an input layer through one or more hidden layers to an output layer, with each layer performing a nonlinear transformation on the data received from the previous layer.

Important

What makes neural networks powerful is that they automatically learn optimal internal representations from raw data, without requiring manual feature engineering. Each successive layer builds higher-level abstractions from the representations discovered by the layer before it.

The network begins with edges connecting every possible pair of neurons between adjacent layers. During training, the weights on these connections are adjusted so that the model learns the most predictive relationships in the data.

1. Terminology & Notation

The following conventions are used consistently throughout these notes.

  • $l$ — layer index, ranging from $0$ (input) to $L$ (output)
  • $n^{[l]}$ — number of neurons (units) in layer $l$
  • $j$ — neuron index within a layer
  • $\vec{x} = \vec{a}^{[0]}$ — the input vector (layer 0)
  • $\vec{a}^{[l]}$ — activation vector for layer $l$; its $j$-th element is $a_j^{[l]}$
  • $W^{[l]}$ — weight matrix for layer $l$, shape $(n^{[l-1]}, n^{[l]})$
  • $\vec{b}^{[l]}$ — bias vector for layer $l$, shape $(n^{[l]},)$
  • $z_j^{[l]}$ — pre-activation (linear combination) at neuron $j$ in layer $l$
  • $g(\cdot)$ — activation function
  • $\hat{y}$ — model prediction (output of the final layer)
  • $m$ — number of training examples
  • $\alpha$ — learning rate

The forward data flow through the network can be summarized as:

$$\vec{x}^{[0]} \;\longrightarrow\; \vec{a}^{[1]} \;\longrightarrow\; \cdots \;\longrightarrow\; \vec{a}^{[l-1]} \;\longrightarrow\; a^{[L]}$$

2. The Model (Hypothesis)

2.1 Single Neuron

Each neuron in layer $l$ computes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias, then applies a nonlinear activation function:

$$z_j^{[l]} = \vec{w}_j^{[l]} \cdot \vec{a}^{[l-1]} + b_j^{[l]}$$

$$a_j^{[l]} = g\!\left(z_j^{[l]}\right)$$

where $\vec{w}_j^{[l]}$ is the weight vector for neuron $j$ in layer $l$, and $\vec{a}^{[l-1]}$ is the activation output of the previous layer (equivalently, the input $\vec{x}$ when $l = 1$).

2.2 Layer Vector Form

Collecting all neurons in a layer into vector notation:

$$\vec{a}^{[l]} = g\!\left(W^{[l]\top} \vec{a}^{[l-1]} + \vec{b}^{[l]}\right)$$

2.3 Output Layer and Prediction

When the activation values reach the final layer $L$, the model produces a scalar (for binary tasks) or a vector (for multiclass tasks). For binary classification, a threshold is applied:

$$\hat{y} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } a^{[L]} \geq 0.5 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Since the output is a function of the original input, it is commonly written as $f(\vec{x})$. The entire model is also denoted $f_{\vec{w},\vec{b}}(\vec{x})$.

red X is considered 1 and blue O are 0

3. Neural Network Architecture

3.1 Layer Types

Dense (Fully Connected) Layer — Every neuron in the layer receives input from all neurons in the previous layer. This is the standard building block.

Convolutional Layer — Each neuron receives input from only a local region (receptive field) of the previous layer. Benefits include faster computation and reduced overfitting due to parameter sharing. Networks composed of multiple such layers are called Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and they excel at spatially structured data such as images and time-series.

3.2 Network Depth and Width

When a network has $s_{\text{in}}$ units in one layer and $s_{\text{out}}$ units in the next:

  • $W$ has shape $(s_{\text{in}}, s_{\text{out}})$
  • $b$ has shape $(s_{\text{out}},)$

A three-layer network for digit recognition (e.g., $400 \to 25 \to 15 \to 1$) has the following parameter count:

Layer W shape b shape Parameters
Layer 1 $(400, 25)$ $(25,)$ $10{,}025$
Layer 2 $(25, 15)$ $(15,)$ $390$
Layer 3 $(15, 1)$ $(1,)$ $16$
Total $10{,}431$

4. Activation Functions

Activation functions introduce nonlinearity into the network. Without them, a deep network collapses into a single linear transformation, no matter how many layers it has.

4.1 Common Activation Functions

Name Formula Output Range Typical Use
Linear $g(z) = z$ $(-\infty, +\infty)$ Regression output
Sigmoid $g(z) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$ $(0, 1)$ Binary classification output
ReLU $g(z) = \max(0, z)$ $[0, +\infty)$ Hidden layers (default)
Softmax $g(z_j) = \dfrac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_{k=1}^{N} e^{z_k}}$ $(0, 1)$, sums to $1$ Multiclass output

4.2 Choosing an Activation Function

Output layer:

  • Binary classification $\Rightarrow$ Sigmoid (or linear + from_logits)
  • Multiclass classification $\Rightarrow$ Softmax (or linear + from_logits)
  • Regression $\Rightarrow$ Linear
  • Non-negative regression $\Rightarrow$ ReLU

Hidden layers:

  • ReLU is the default and preferred choice in practice.
  • Sigmoid is rarely used in hidden layers due to the vanishing gradient problem: gradient descent slows dramatically on the flat regions of the sigmoid curve (near 0 and 1). ReLU has only one flat region ($z \leq 0$), making training faster.
Important

If all hidden layers use a linear activation function, the entire network is mathematically equivalent to linear regression, regardless of depth. Similarly, linear hidden layers with a sigmoid output reduce to logistic regression. Never use linear activations in hidden layers.

4.3 Softmax Regression

Softmax Regression generalizes logistic regression to the multiclass setting. For $N$ classes:

$$z_j = \vec{w}_j \cdot \vec{x} + b_j \qquad j = 1, \ldots, N$$

$$a_j = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_{k=1}^{N} e^{z_k}} = P(y = j \mid \vec{x})$$

The key property is that all outputs sum to one: $\sum_{j=1}^{N} a_j = 1$.

5. Multiclass Classification

5.1 Problem Setup

In binary classification, the model estimates $P(y = 1 \mid \vec{x})$. In multiclass classification with $N$ classes, the model simultaneously estimates:

$$P(y = 1 \mid \vec{x}), \quad P(y = 2 \mid \vec{x}), \quad \ldots, \quad P(y = N \mid \vec{x})$$

These $N$ probabilities form a probability distribution (they sum to 1) and are produced by a softmax output layer.

5.2 Decision Rule

The predicted class is the index of the largest output probability:

$$\hat{y} = \arg\max_{j} \; a_j = \arg\max_{j} \; P(y = j \mid \vec{x})$$

5.3 Comparison: Binary vs. Multiclass

Aspect Binary Classification Multiclass Classification
Output units 1 $N$
Output activation Sigmoid Softmax (or linear + from_logits)
Loss function BinaryCrossentropy SparseCategoricalCrossentropy
Decision Threshold at 0.5 argmax of outputs

See also: Neural Networks - Training · Neural Networks - Implementation

References

  • MIT Neural Networks Lecture Slides
  • NumPy Documentation
  • TensorFlow / Keras Documentation
  • PyTorch Documentation
  • MNIST Dataset
