12. The Formula to Remember

$$\boxed{\tilde{h}_j = \frac{r_j \cdot h_j}{1-p}, \quad r_j \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1-p)}$$

  • $h_j$ — the neuron's output before dropout
  • $r_j$ — random binary mask (1=keep, 0=drop)
  • $p$ — dropout rate (0.3 in your model)
  • $\tilde{h}_j$ — the neuron's output after dropout

At inference: $r_j = 1$ for all $j$, no scaling applied.

8. The 1D Convolution — What Kernel Size 3 Actually Sees

One sentence summary: A 1D convolution slides a small window of size 3 across the 64-frame sequence, at each position computing a weighted sum of 3 consecutive frames — learning to detect local temporal patterns like velocity, acceleration, and oscillation between adjacent frames.

1. Starting Point — What Enters the 1D-CNN

After the Linear Projection and LayerNorm, you have:

$$\mathbf{H}^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d_{\text{model}}} = \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 256}$$

  • $B = 64$ — batch size (64 sign sequences)
  • $T = 64$ — temporal frames
  • $d_{\text{model}} = 256$ — learned features per frame

Think of this as a sequence of 64 vectors, each of length 256. Each vector is one frame's learned representation — not raw coordinates anymore, but 256 abstract features learned by the projection.

Frame  1: [f₁, f₂, f₃, ..., f₂₅₆]  ← 256 features
Frame  2: [f₁, f₂, f₃, ..., f₂₅₆]
Frame  3: [f₁, f₂, f₃, ..., f₂₅₆]
...
Frame 64: [f₁, f₂, f₃, ..., f₂₅₆]

2. The Problem — Why We Need a CNN at All

The Transformer (Stage 4) will handle long-range relationships between frames — "what is happening at frame 5 compared to frame 60?"

But the Transformer is permutation-invariant. Without positional encoding, shuffling the frames would produce the same output. Even with positional encoding, the Transformer computes all pairwise frame relationships simultaneously — it does not naturally focus on what is happening between adjacent frames.

Local motion — the velocity and acceleration of hands between consecutive frames — is the most physically meaningful signal for sign recognition. A sign is defined by how the hand moves, not just where it is at each instant.

The 1D-CNN exists specifically to compute this local temporal structure before the Transformer handles global structure.

Analogy: Imagine reading a sentence:

"The cat sat on the mat"

A Transformer reads all words simultaneously and compares every word to every other word. But to understand grammar, you first need to notice that "cat" and "sat" are adjacent — that "cat" is the subject performing "sat." Local adjacency matters.

For sign language, the 1D-CNN notices that frame 20 and frame 21 show the hand moving upward — that local adjacency is velocity.

3. The PyTorch Convention — Why We Transpose

PyTorch's Conv1d expects input shape:

$$\text{(Batch, Channels, Length)}$$

But your data is:

$$\text{(Batch, Time, Features)} = (64, 64, 256)$$

So before the CNN you transpose:

x = x.transpose(1, 2)   # (64, 64, 256) → (64, 256, 64)
                         #  B   T   C       B   C    T

Now:

  • Channels = 256 (the learned features — treated like image channels)
  • Length = 64 (the time axis — treated like spatial width)

The convolution slides along the time axis (length=64), treating the 256 features as parallel channels.

After the CNN you transpose back:

x = x.transpose(1, 2)   # (64, 256, 64) → (64, 64, 256)

4. What One Convolutional Filter Does

A single convolutional filter of kernel size 3 is a weight matrix of shape:

$$\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}} \times 3} = \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256 \times 3}$$

Wait — that is enormous. Let us simplify to understand one output channel $k$ and one input channel $c$:

$$K_{k,c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 = [w_{-1},\ w_0,\ w_{+1}]$$

This tiny vector of 3 numbers is the kernel for output channel $k$, applied to input channel $c$.

At time position $t$, this kernel produces one output value:

$$\text{out}_{k,c}(t) = w_{-1} \cdot h_c(t-1) + w_0 \cdot h_c(t) + w_{+1} \cdot h_c(t+1)$$

Where $h_c(t)$ is the value of input channel $c$ at frame $t$.

The full output at channel $k$, time $t$ sums over all input channels:

$$\text{out}_k(t) = \sum_{c=1}^{256} \left[ w_{k,c,-1} \cdot h_c(t-1) + w_{k,c,0} \cdot h_c(t) + w_{k,c,+1} \cdot h_c(t+1) \right] + b_k$$

This is a weighted sum of three consecutive frames, across all 256 input channels, producing one output value at position $t$ for output channel $k$.

5. The Sliding Window — Frame by Frame

The kernel slides across all 64 time positions:

Input sequence (simplified to 1 channel, 6 frames):

Frame:  [  1    2    3    4    5    6  ]
Value:  [0.2  0.5  0.8  0.6  0.3  0.1]

Kernel: [w₋₁, w₀, w₊₁] = [-0.5, 1.0, 0.5]

At position t=2 (frame 2):

out(2) = w₋₁ × frame(1) + w₀ × frame(2) + w₊₁ × frame(3)
       = (-0.5)(0.2) + (1.0)(0.5) + (0.5)(0.8)
       = -0.10 + 0.50 + 0.40
       = 0.80

At position t=3 (frame 3):

out(3) = (-0.5)(0.5) + (1.0)(0.8) + (0.5)(0.6)
       = -0.25 + 0.80 + 0.30
       = 0.85

At position t=4 (frame 4):

out(4) = (-0.5)(0.8) + (1.0)(0.6) + (0.5)(0.3)
       = -0.40 + 0.60 + 0.15
       = 0.35

The kernel slides across all positions producing one output value per position. The output sequence has the same length as the input (because padding=1 adds one zero on each end).

6. What the Kernel Actually Learns — The Physics

Here is the deep part. The kernel weights $[w_{-1}, w_0, w_{+1}]$ are learned during training. What patterns do they converge to?

Kernel that detects velocity (1st derivative):

$$\mathbf{K}_{\text{velocity}} = [-1,\ 0,\ +1]$$

$$\text{out}(t) = (+1) \cdot h(t+1) + (0) \cdot h(t) + (-1) \cdot h(t-1) = h(t+1) - h(t-1)$$

This is the central difference approximation of the first derivative — the rate of change. If the hand moves from position 0.2 to 0.8 in two frames, this kernel outputs 0.6 — a strong positive velocity signal.

Kernel that detects acceleration (2nd derivative):

$$\mathbf{K}_{\text{accel}} = [+1,\ -2,\ +1]$$

$$\text{out}(t) = h(t+1) - 2h(t) + h(t-1)$$

This is the second difference — the rate of change of the rate of change. If the hand is decelerating (moving fast then slow), this kernel fires strongly.

Kernel that detects a local peak:

$$\mathbf{K}_{\text{peak}} = [-1,\ +2,\ -1]$$

Fires strongly when $h(t)$ is larger than both its neighbors — detecting the apex of a hand movement.

Kernel that detects static hold:

$$\mathbf{K}_{\text{hold}} = [+1,\ +1,\ +1]$$

Fires strongly when three consecutive frames have similar high values — detecting intentional stillness (a valid ASL phoneme).

The model does not know these templates in advance. It discovers them through training by learning which local temporal patterns are most useful for distinguishing between 250 ASL signs. The weights converge to something resembling these derivatives because that is genuinely what distinguishes signs at the local level.

Important: Convolution vs Cross-Correlation

In pure mathematics, convolution flips the kernel before sliding: $(f * k)(t) = \sum_i k(i) \cdot f(t-i)$. PyTorch Conv1d computes cross-correlation instead — no flip: $(f \star k)(t) = \sum_i k(i) \cdot f(t+i)$.

In practice this distinction is irrelevant because the kernels are learned during training. If the mathematically correct velocity kernel is $[-1, 0, +1]$, PyTorch will simply learn $[+1, 0, -1]$ instead — the two are equivalent up to a sign flip. Every deep learning framework uses cross-correlation and calls it convolution by convention.

7. Two Layers — Why Stack Two Convolutions?

Your model has two consecutive Conv1d layers:

self.cnn_block = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv1d(256, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
    nn.GELU(),
    nn.Dropout(0.3),
    nn.Conv1d(256, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
    nn.GELU(),
    nn.Dropout(0.3),
)

The Receptive Field Argument

The receptive field is how many original input frames one output unit depends on.

After Conv1 (kernel=3): Each output frame sees 3 input frames:

Output frame t depends on: input frames [t-1, t, t+1]
Receptive field = 3 frames

After Conv2 (kernel=3 applied to Conv1 output): Each Conv2 output depends on 3 Conv1 outputs. Each Conv1 output depends on 3 original inputs. Therefore:

Output frame t depends on: input frames [t-2, t-1, t, t+1, t+2]
Receptive field = 5 frames

Two stacked size-3 convolutions give an effective receptive field of 5 frames — without increasing kernel size.

The Hierarchy Argument

Layer 1 detects simple local patterns:

  • "Hand moved upward between frame $t-1$ and $t+1$"
  • "Hand is stationary at frame $t$"

Layer 2 detects patterns of patterns:

  • "Hand moved upward THEN decelerated"
  • "Hand was stationary THEN started moving"

This is the same principle as deep CNNs in image recognition: Layer 1 detects edges. Layer 2 detects corners (edges of edges). Layer 3 detects shapes (corners of edges of edges).

For your sign sequences: Layer 1 detects velocity Layer 2 detects acceleration and motion phase transitions

8. The Residual Connection — Why We Add the Input Back

After both conv layers, your code does:

residual = x            # save input before CNN
x = self.cnn_block(x)  # apply both conv layers
x = self.cnn_norm(x + residual)  # ADD INPUT BACK

The output is:

$$\mathbf{H}^{(1)} = \text{LayerNorm}(\text{Conv}_2(\text{Conv}_1(\mathbf{H}^{(0)})) + \mathbf{H}^{(0)})$$

Why Is This Critical?

The CNN block computes motion features (velocity, acceleration). These are useful but they are not the only useful information. The original projected features from Stage 1 encode positional information — where the hand is at each frame.

Without the residual connection:

Output = motion features only
→ model knows HOW the hand moves but not WHERE it is

With the residual connection:

Output = motion features + positional features
→ model knows BOTH where the hand is AND how it is moving

For sign recognition, both are essential:

  • "THINK": finger touches temple (position) with a tapping motion (velocity)
  • "FEEL": finger touches chest (position) with a circular motion (velocity)

Remove position → cannot distinguish temple from chest Remove velocity → cannot distinguish tap from circle

The residual connection ensures both signals survive.

The Gradient Flow Argument

During backpropagation, the gradient must flow backward through the CNN layers. If the CNN learns to suppress some features (output near zero), those features get zero gradient — the projection weights before them stop learning.

The residual connection creates a gradient highway:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{H}^{(0)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{H}^{(1)}} \cdot \underbrace{\left(1 + \frac{\partial \text{CNN}(\mathbf{H}^{(0)})}{\partial \mathbf{H}^{(0)}}\right)}_{\text{never zero due to the +1}}$$

The $+1$ term means the gradient can always flow directly backward through the residual connection, even if the CNN path is suppressed. The projection weights always receive some gradient signal.

9. Padding = 1 — Why the Sequence Length Does Not Change

Your conv layers use padding=1. This adds one zero on each side of the time axis before convolution:

Original: [f₁, f₂, f₃, ..., f₆₄]         length = 64

Padded:   [0, f₁, f₂, f₃, ..., f₆₄, 0]   length = 66

After conv (kernel=3): length = 66 - 3 + 1 = 64

Without padding, a kernel of size 3 would reduce the sequence: $64 - 3 + 1 = 62$ frames. Two layers would give $60$ frames. The residual connection would then fail because you cannot add a $(64, 64, 256)$ tensor to a $(64, 60, 256)$ tensor.

padding=1 preserves the $T=64$ dimension so that:

  1. The residual addition works dimensionally
  2. The positional encoding at Stage 3 works on the same $T$
  3. The Transformer at Stage 4 receives a consistent $T=64$

The padding zeros at the boundaries are a minor artefact — the kernel at $t=1$ sees one zero and two real frames. At $t=64$ it sees two real frames and one zero. This boundary effect is negligible in practice.

10. The Full Shape Flow Through the CNN Block

Input to CNN block:
  H⁰ shape: (B=64, T=64, C=256)

Transpose (PyTorch Conv1d requires B, C, T):
  (64, 64, 256) → (64, 256, 64)

Conv1d layer 1 (kernel=3, padding=1):
  Input:  (64, 256, 64)   ← 256 input channels, 64 time steps
  Kernel: (256, 256, 3)   ← 256 output channels, 256 input channels, size 3
  Output: (64, 256, 64)   ← same shape (padding preserves T)

GELU activation:
  (64, 256, 64) → (64, 256, 64)  ← same shape, values changed

Dropout:
  (64, 256, 64) → (64, 256, 64)  ← same shape, 30% zeroed

Conv1d layer 2 (kernel=3, padding=1):
  Input:  (64, 256, 64)
  Output: (64, 256, 64)

GELU + Dropout:
  (64, 256, 64) → (64, 256, 64)

Transpose back:
  (64, 256, 64) → (64, 64, 256)

Residual addition + LayerNorm:
  (64, 64, 256) + (64, 64, 256) = (64, 64, 256)

Output H¹: (B=64, T=64, C=256)  ← same shape as input

The entire CNN block is shape-preserving: $(B, T, 256)$ in, $(B, T, 256)$ out. Only the values change.

11. Parameter Count of the CNN Block

Each Conv1d(256, 256, kernel_size=3):

$$\text{parameters} = d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}} \times k + d_{\text{out}}$$ $$= 256 \times 256 \times 3 + 256 = 196{,}608 + 256 = 196{,}864$$

Two Conv1d layers plus LayerNorm:

$$2 \times 196{,}864 + 2 \times 256 = 394{,}240 \text{ parameters}$$

This matches the parameter count table in your report. These 394,240 parameters collectively learn to detect all the local temporal patterns (velocity, acceleration, holds, peaks) that are useful for distinguishing between your 250 ASL signs.

12. Why Not Just Use the Transformer for Everything?

A fair question. The Transformer already handles frame relationships via self-attention. Why add a CNN?

1D-CNN Transformer Self-Attention
Scope Local (3-5 adjacent frames) Global (all 64 frames)
Computation $O(T \times k)$ per layer $O(T^2)$ per layer
What it learns Velocity, acceleration, holds Which frames to compare
Inductive bias Temporal locality matters All relationships equal
Position-aware Yes (sliding window is local) Needs explicit PE

The CNN provides local inductive bias — it builds in the assumption that adjacent frames are more related than distant frames. This is physically true for sign language: the hand at frame $t$ is always most similar to the hand at frames $t-1$ and $t+1$.

By giving the Transformer pre-computed local motion features (instead of raw projected coordinates), you let the Transformer focus on what it is best at: deciding which parts of the sign are most informative and how they relate across the full temporal extent.

The combination is greater than either alone:

CNN:         "the hand is accelerating upward between frames 20-25"
Transformer: "this acceleration at frames 20-25 is the most
              important part of this sign — attend to it"
Classifier:  "this pattern of acceleration = AIRPLANE"

14. The Formula to Remember

For one output channel $k$ at time $t$:

$$\boxed{ \text{out}_k(t) = \sum_{c=1}^{256} \sum_{i \in \{-1,0,+1\}} w_{k,c,i} \cdot h_c(t+i) + b_k }$$

  • Outer sum: over all 256 input channels
  • Inner sum: over the 3 kernel positions ($t-1$, $t$, $t+1$)
  • $w_{k,c,i}$: weight for output channel $k$, input channel $c$, offset $i$
  • $h_c(t+i)$: value of input channel $c$ at frame $t+i$

This operation, repeated for all 256 output channels at all 64 time positions, is what transforms raw projected features into rich local motion representations ready for the Transformer.

We chose the architecture (256 kernels, size 3, 2 layers).
Backpropagation chose the weights (what each kernel actually detects).
The model discovered velocity and acceleration detectors because that is what the loss function rewarded — not because we told it to look for them.

9. Residual Connection — Why We Add the Input Back

One sentence summary: A residual connection adds the original input of a block directly to its output — creating a shortcut that allows gradients to flow freely backward and forces each layer to learn only what is missing from the previous representation, rather than relearning everything from scratch.

1. The Problem That Required a New Idea

The Degradation Problem (2015)

Before residual connections existed, a strange and counterintuitive thing happened when researchers tried to train very deep networks:

Shallow network (20 layers):  test accuracy = 91.25%
Deep network    (56 layers):  test accuracy = 90.67%

The deeper network performed worse — not because of overfitting (training accuracy was also worse), but because it simply could not learn effectively.

This was called the degradation problem and it seemed to violate common sense. Adding more layers should at minimum be able to replicate the shallower network — the extra layers could just learn identity functions (output = input) and ignore themselves.

But in practice, neural networks could not learn identity functions through standard backpropagation. The gradient signal was too weak by the time it reached the early layers. Adding depth made things worse, not better.

2. The Insight — Learn the Residual, Not the Mapping

In 2015, He et al. at Microsoft Research published the paper that introduced residual connections: "Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition." The key insight was deceptively simple.

The old way (standard layer):

A layer tries to learn a function $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x})$ that maps input $\mathbf{x}$ to the desired output.

Input x ──→ [Layer: learn H(x)] ──→ Output H(x)

The new way (residual layer):

Instead of learning $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x})$ directly, learn only the residual — what needs to be added to the input to produce the desired output:

$$\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{x}$$

Then the output is:

$$\text{output} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}$$

Input x ──────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                │ (shortcut)
         ↓                                │
    [Layer: learn F(x)]                   │
         │                                │
         ↓                                │
    F(x) ──────────────────(+)────────────┘
                            │
                            ↓
                    Output: F(x) + x

The $+$ is literally just addition. No parameters. No learned weights. Just element-wise addition of two tensors.

3. Why This Makes Learning Easier — The Identity Shortcut

Consider the extreme case where the layer is not needed at all. The optimal function is the identity: $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$.

Without residual connection: The layer must learn weights such that $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$. For a linear layer, this means the weight matrix must converge to the identity matrix $\mathbf{I}$ — every diagonal weight = 1, every off-diagonal weight = 0. This is a very specific target in a high-dimensional weight space. It is hard to hit.

With residual connection: The layer must learn $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) = 0$. Every weight just needs to go to zero. Zero is the default pull of weight decay (L2 regularisation). This is trivially easy.

Without residual: learn W = I   (hard — specific target)
With residual:    learn W = 0   (easy — weight decay does it naturally)

If a layer is not useful, the residual connection allows it to gracefully become a no-op by pushing its weights toward zero. Without the residual, a useless layer must instead learn a complex identity mapping.

4. The Gradient Highway — The Real Reason It Works

This is the deepest reason residual connections exist.

During backpropagation, the gradient flows backward through the network. At each layer, the gradient is multiplied by the layer's local gradient (via the chain rule):

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}$$

Without residual connection, if the layer learns to suppress certain features (weights near zero), $\frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}$ is near zero — and the gradient vanishes before reaching earlier layers.

With residual connection:

$$\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}$$

$$\frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \mathbf{x}} + 1$$

The $+1$ term is always present regardless of what the layer learned. It means:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{y}} \cdot \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{F}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} + 1\right)$$

Even if $\frac{\partial \mathcal{F}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = 0$ (the layer learned nothing useful), the gradient is still:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{y}} \cdot 1 = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{y}}$$

The gradient passes through unchanged. No vanishing. No matter how deep the network, the gradient always has a direct path backward through the residual shortcuts.

Think of it as a gradient highway:

Loss
  │
  ↓ gradient flows back
Layer N  ──(shortcut)──────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                    │
  ↓ gradient × (∂F/∂x + 1)                             │
Layer N-1 ──(shortcut)─────────────────────────────────┤
  │                                                    │
  ↓                                                    │
  ...                                                  │
  │                                                    │
Layer 1  ──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ↓ gradient still strong because of shortcuts
Input

Without shortcuts, the gradient must pass through every layer sequentially, getting multiplied by potentially small numbers each time. With shortcuts, the gradient has a direct path that bypasses the multiplicative chain.

5. A Physical Intuition — Renovating a Building

Imagine you are renovating a building (the model) to serve a new purpose (classify ASL signs).

Without residual connections (rebuilding from scratch):

Each floor (layer) must completely reconstruct its representation of the building from the floor below. Floor 3 cannot assume floor 2 preserved anything useful. Every floor must relearn everything.

This is enormously redundant. And if floor 2 makes a mistake, floor 3 has nothing to fall back on.

With residual connections (renovating, not rebuilding):

Each floor keeps the original structure (the residual $\mathbf{x}$) and only adds the new modifications ($\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})$). Floor 3 says:

"Floor 2 already gave me a decent representation. I just need to add what is missing — the motion features that floor 2 did not compute."

If floor 2's modification was not useful, it naturally becomes zero (weights shrink via gradient descent), and floor 3 simply inherits floor 2's input unchanged. The useful structure is always preserved.

6. Concretely in Your Model

Your CNN block does this:

residual = x                              # save input
x = self.cnn_block(x)                    # apply 2 conv layers
x = self.cnn_norm(x + residual)          # ADD INPUT BACK

Let us trace what this means for one specific frame.

Before the CNN block (frame $t=20$):

H⁰[20] = [0.8, -0.3, 1.2, ..., 0.6]   ← 256 projected features
          representing WHERE the hand is at frame 20

After the CNN block (without residual):

CNN_out[20] = [0.1, 0.7, -0.2, ..., 0.4]   ← 256 motion features
              representing HOW the hand is moving around frame 20
              (velocity, acceleration)

BUT the original position information is GONE.

After the CNN block (with residual):

H¹[20] = CNN_out[20] + H⁰[20]
       = [0.1+0.8, 0.7+(-0.3), -0.2+1.2, ..., 0.4+0.6]
       = [0.9,     0.4,         1.0,      ..., 1.0]
         ↑ position AND motion combined in one vector

Now frame 20's representation contains:

  • Where the hand is (from the residual $\mathbf{H}^{(0)}$)
  • How the hand is moving (from the CNN output $\mathcal{F}$)

Both signals are available to the Transformer in Stage 4. Without the residual, the Transformer would only see motion features and would not know where the hand is positioned.

7. Why This Matters for ASL Specifically

In ASL, location and motion are both phonemic features — both change the meaning of a sign:

THINK:  index finger taps temple (LOCATION: temple, MOTION: tap)
FEEL:   index finger circles chest (LOCATION: chest, MOTION: circle)
KNOW:   flat hand taps forehead (LOCATION: forehead, MOTION: tap)

Distinguishing THINK from FEEL:   location changes (temple vs chest)
Distinguishing THINK from KNOW:   handshape changes (index vs flat)
Distinguishing TAP from CIRCLE:   motion changes

If you remove the residual connection:

  • The CNN outputs only motion features
  • The Transformer sees motion but not location
  • THINK and FEEL both become "tap near face" — indistinguishable
  • Accuracy would likely drop 10-15%

The residual connection is not optional for your task. It is load-bearing.

8. Residual Connections in the Transformer Too

The residual connection is not only in your CNN block. It also appears inside every Transformer layer (Stage 4).

Each Transformer layer has two sub-layers:

  1. Multi-Head Self-Attention
  2. Feed-Forward Network

Both use residual connections:

$$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x} + \text{Attention}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{x}))$$ $$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x} + \text{FFN}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{x}))$$

Your model uses Pre-LN style (LayerNorm before the sub-layer, as shown above). This is why you specified norm_first=True in the TransformerEncoderLayer.

With 4 Transformer layers, there are 8 residual connections inside the Transformer alone, plus 1 in the CNN block = 9 total residual connections in your model.

Every single one of them is a gradient highway, ensuring that the gradient from the loss can reach every set of weights directly.

9. The Mathematical Beauty — Any Layer Can Be Skipped

Here is the most elegant property of residual networks.

In a network with residual connections at every layer:

$$\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + \mathcal{F}_1(\mathbf{x}) + \mathcal{F}_2(\mathbf{x} + \mathcal{F}_1(\mathbf{x})) + \ldots$$

Expanding this shows that the final output is an implicit ensemble of paths of different depths through the network:

Path 1: input → output directly (all F's = 0)
Path 2: input → Layer 1 → output
Path 3: input → Layer 2 → output
Path 4: input → Layer 1 → Layer 2 → output
...
Path 2^N: input → all N layers → output

A network with $N$ residual blocks implicitly computes $2^N$ different paths from input to output. The final prediction averages over all these paths.

This is another form of ensembling — similar to dropout — but operating at the architectural level rather than the neuron level.

10. Summary

Concept Definition
Residual connection $\text{output} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}$
What $\mathcal{F}$ learns Only the difference from the input — the "missing" information
Gradient highway The $+1$ in $\frac{\partial(\mathcal{F}+\mathbf{x})}{\partial\mathbf{x}}$ ensures gradient never vanishes

In your CNN block Combines position features (residual) with motion features (CNN output)

11. The Formula to Remember

$$\boxed{\text{output} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}}$$

  • $\mathbf{x}$ — the input (preserved via shortcut)
  • $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})$ — what the layer learned to add
  • The addition has no parameters — just $+$
  • Gradient of output w.r.t. input always contains $+1$ → gradient highway guaranteed

The entire idea is this: instead of learning to transform $\mathbf{x}$ into something new, learn what is missing from $\mathbf{x}$ and add only that. If nothing is missing, add nothing. The input is always preserved.

10. Positional Encoding — How Sine Waves Tell the Transformer Where You Are

One sentence summary: Positional encoding adds a unique mathematical fingerprint to each frame's representation so that the Transformer — which otherwise treats all frames as an unordered set — knows that frame 5 comes before frame 6 and after frame 4.

1. Your Intuition About Tokens — Partially Right

You asked if positional encoding is like tokenization in NLP. Let us clarify the relationship precisely.

In Natural Language Processing (NLP)

Sentence: "The cat sat on the mat"

Step 1 — Tokenization: convert words to integer IDs
  "The" → 2045
  "cat" → 8303
  "sat" → 6341
  "on"  → 319
  "the" → 2045
  "mat" → 12493

Step 2 — Embedding: convert IDs to vectors
  2045 → [0.2, -0.5, 0.8, ..., 0.3]  (512 numbers)
  8303 → [0.7,  0.1, -0.3, ..., 0.9]

Step 3 — Positional Encoding: add position information
  Position 1 → add [sin(1/1), cos(1/1), sin(1/100), ...]
  Position 2 → add [sin(2/1), cos(2/1), sin(2/100), ...]

Tokenization converts words into numbers. Embedding converts those numbers into rich vectors. Positional encoding tells the model WHERE each token sits.

In Your ASL Model

You skip the first two steps because you already have vectors. Your 345 landmark coordinates are already a rich representation of each frame — you do not need tokenization or embedding lookup.

Frame 20: [x_lm0, y_lm0, z_lm0, ..., z_lm114]  ← already a vector
              ↓ Linear Projection
          [f₁, f₂, ..., f₂₅₆]                   ← 256-dim vector

Then directly:
              ↓ Positional Encoding
          [f₁ + PE₁(20), f₂ + PE₂(20), ..., f₂₅₆ + PE₂₅₆(20)]

So positional encoding in your model is step 3 only — you do not need steps 1 and 2 because landmark vectors are already semantically rich.

The analogy to tokenization: tokens give words an identity. Positional encoding gives positions an identity. You already have frame identities (the landmark vectors). You just need position identities.

2. The Core Problem — Why the Transformer Is Blind to Order

Before understanding the solution, you must deeply understand the problem.

The Transformer Sees a Set, Not a Sequence

Self-attention computes:

$$\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)\mathbf{V}$$

Look at this formula carefully. The matrices $\mathbf{Q}$, $\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{V}$ are computed from the input sequence. But the formula itself involves no notion of order. It computes dot products between every pair of frames — but a dot product between frame 5 and frame 20 gives the same number regardless of whether they are 15 positions apart or adjacent.

The Transformer, as originally designed, is permutation invariant: if you shuffle the 64 frames into a random order, the output is also shuffled in the exact same way — the model cannot detect that anything changed.

Proof by Permutation

Take your 64 frames and shuffle them:

Original:  [frame_1,  frame_2,  frame_3,  ..., frame_64]
Shuffled:  [frame_42, frame_7,  frame_19, ..., frame_3 ]

Feed both to a Transformer without positional encoding. The attention scores between frame_42 and frame_7 are identical in both cases — the model does not know that in the original, frames 1 and 2 were adjacent.

For image classification, this does not matter much (a dog is a dog regardless of pixel order in some sense). For sign language recognition, this is catastrophic:

"DRINK": hand moves TO mouth (upward trajectory)
"GIVE":  hand moves AWAY from body (outward trajectory)

Without position: the model sees 64 frames of hand movement
                  but cannot tell which came first
→ DRINK and GIVE look identical (same frames, different order)
→ model cannot distinguish them

3. The Solution Space — Three Approaches

When researchers discovered this problem, they considered three solutions:

Option A: Learned Position Embeddings

Create a trainable embedding table:

$$\mathbf{E}_{\text{pos}} \in \mathbb{R}^{T_{\text{max}} \times d_{\text{model}}}$$

Position 1 gets a learned vector. Position 2 gets a different learned vector. These vectors are updated by backpropagation just like any other weight.

Problem: If you train on sequences up to length 64 and then try to run the model on a sequence of length 80, there is no embedding for positions 65-80. The model cannot extrapolate beyond its training length.

Option B: One-Hot Position Encoding

Assign each position a one-hot vector:

$$\text{pos}_1 = [1, 0, 0, ..., 0]$$ $$\text{pos}_2 = [0, 1, 0, ..., 0]$$ $$\text{pos}_{64} = [0, 0, 0, ..., 1]$$

Problem: These vectors are all orthogonal. The model learns that position 1 ≠ position 2, but it cannot learn that positions 1 and 2 are close while positions 1 and 64 are far. Relative distance between positions is invisible.

Option C: Sinusoidal Positional Encoding (What You Use)

Use mathematical functions — specifically sine and cosine — to generate position vectors. These are not learned. They are fixed mathematical formulas that produce unique, structured patterns for each position.

This is what Vaswani et al. chose in the original Transformer paper, and what your model uses.

4. Why Sine and Cosine — The Deep Reason

This is the part nobody explains well. Why sine and cosine specifically? Why not squares, or cubes, or random patterns?

The Binary Analogy — Building Intuition

Consider how integers are represented in binary:

Position  1: 0 0 0 0 0 1
Position  2: 0 0 0 0 1 0
Position  3: 0 0 0 0 1 1
Position  4: 0 0 0 1 0 0
Position  8: 0 0 1 0 0 0
Position 16: 0 1 0 0 0 0
Position 32: 1 0 0 0 0 0

Notice the pattern:

  • The rightmost bit alternates every 1 position
  • The next bit alternates every 2 positions
  • The next every 4 positions
  • The next every 8 positions
  • And so on (powers of 2)

Each bit oscillates at a different frequency. The combination of all bits gives a unique, structured representation of every integer.

Sinusoidal positional encoding is the continuous version of binary counting.

Instead of bits that flip between 0 and 1, you use sine and cosine waves that oscillate smoothly between -1 and +1. Instead of doubling the period (1, 2, 4, 8...), you use exponentially increasing periods.

Dimension 0:   sine wave, period = 2π (fastest)
Dimension 1:   cosine wave, period = 2π
Dimension 2:   sine wave, period = 2π × 100^(2/256)
Dimension 3:   cosine wave, same period
...
Dimension 254: sine wave, period = 2π × 10000 (slowest)
Dimension 255: cosine wave, period = 2π × 10000

Each pair of dimensions oscillates at a different frequency. The combination of all 256 values gives a unique fingerprint for every position.

5. The Formula — Every Symbol Explained

$$\text{PE}(t, 2i) = \sin\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)$$

$$\text{PE}(t, 2i+1) = \cos\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)$$

Where:

  • $t \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 63\}$ — frame index (which frame)
  • $i \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 127\}$ — dimension pair index
  • $d = d_{\text{model}} = 256$ — total model dimension
  • $2i$ — even dimensions get sine
  • $2i+1$ — odd dimensions get cosine

Breaking Down the Frequency Term

$$\frac{1}{10000^{2i/d}}$$

This is the angular frequency — how fast the wave oscillates.

  • When $i = 0$: frequency $= \frac{1}{10000^0} = 1.0$ (fastest)
  • When $i = 64$: frequency $= \frac{1}{10000^{0.5}} = \frac{1}{100} = 0.01$
  • When $i = 127$: frequency $= \frac{1}{10000^{0.992}} \approx \frac{1}{9752}$ (slowest)

The frequencies decrease exponentially from 1.0 to 1/10000 across the 128 dimension pairs. This is the continuous analogue of the binary pattern where periods go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16...

What Each Dimension Encodes

Dimensions 0-1 (fastest sine/cosine, period ≈ 6.28):
  These oscillate so fast that adjacent frames have
  very different values. They encode FINE-GRAINED
  position — distinguishing consecutive frames.

Dimensions 254-255 (slowest, period ≈ 62,832):
  These oscillate so slowly that across 64 frames
  the value barely changes. They encode COARSE position —
  distinguishing the first half from the second half.

Together, the 256 dimensions create a multi-resolution representation of position — like a clock with many hands running at different speeds.

6. A Concrete Worked Example

Let us compute $\text{PE}$ for three frames and two dimensions (simplified to $d=4$ for readability):

$$\text{PE}(t, 0) = \sin\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{0}}\right) = \sin(t)$$

$$\text{PE}(t, 1) = \cos\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{0}}\right) = \cos(t)$$

$$\text{PE}(t, 2) = \sin\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{0.5}}\right) = \sin\!\left(\frac{t}{100}\right)$$

$$\text{PE}(t, 3) = \cos\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{0.5}}\right) = \cos\!\left(\frac{t}{100}\right)$$

Computing for frames $t = 0, 1, 2$:

Frame $t$ $\sin(t)$ $\cos(t)$ $\sin(t/100)$ $\cos(t/100)$
0 0.000 1.000 0.000 1.000
1 0.841 0.540 0.010 1.000
2 0.909 -0.416 0.020 1.000

Each frame gets a unique 4-dimensional fingerprint. Frame 0: $[0.000, 1.000, 0.000, 1.000]$ Frame 1: $[0.841, 0.540, 0.010, 1.000]$ Frame 2: $[0.909, -0.416, 0.020, 1.000]$

No two frames have the same fingerprint.

7. The Key Properties — Why This Design Is Genius

Property 1: Every Position Is Unique

No two values of $t$ produce the same PE vector. This is guaranteed by the mathematics of sine and cosine — at any given frequency, no two integer positions within a reasonable range map to the same value.

Property 2: Relative Distance Is Encoded

This is the most important property. For any fixed offset $k$:

$$\text{PE}(t + k) \text{ can be expressed as a linear function of } \text{PE}(t)$$

Specifically, using the trigonometric addition formulas:

$$\sin(t + k) = \sin(t)\cos(k) + \cos(t)\sin(k)$$ $$\cos(t + k) = \cos(t)\cos(k) - \sin(t)\sin(k)$$

This means: knowing the PE at position $t$ and the offset $k$, you can compute the PE at position $t+k$ using a linear transformation (a rotation matrix in 2D).

The Transformer can therefore learn to attend to frames that are "exactly $k$ positions after frame $t$" by learning the appropriate linear transformation on the PE vectors. Relative distances are not just representable — they are computable.

For your ASL model: "attend to the frame 5 positions later" is a learnable operation. The model can discover that the end of a hand movement (frame $t+5$) is relevant to understanding the start of the movement (frame $t$).

Property 3: Bounded Values

All PE values lie in $[-1, +1]$. They never explode to large magnitudes regardless of position. When added to the projected frame vectors $\mathbf{H}^{(0)}$, they do not dominate the representation.

Property 4: Generalization Beyond Training Length

If your model trained on $T=64$ frames, it can still process a sequence of 80 frames — just compute $\text{PE}(65)$, $\text{PE}(66)$... using the same formula. No new weights needed. This is why sinusoidal PE generalises while learned embeddings cannot.

8. How It Is Added — The Operation

The positional encoding is added element-wise to the projected frame vectors:

$$\mathbf{H}^{(2)} = \mathbf{H}^{(1)} + \mathbf{PE}$$

Where:

  • $\mathbf{H}^{(1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 256}$ — output of CNN block
  • $\mathbf{PE} \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 256}$ — positional encoding matrix
  • $\mathbf{H}^{(2)} \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 256}$ — PE-enriched representation

The addition is the simplest possible operation. No weights. No parameters. Just $+$.

After addition, each frame's 256-dimensional vector contains:

  • The sign content (from the projected landmarks + CNN)
  • The temporal position fingerprint (from PE)

The Transformer can now ask: "how does the content of frame 5 relate to the content of frame 20, given that frame 5 is at the beginning of the sign and frame 20 is in the middle?"

9. Precomputed and Registered as a Buffer

In your code:

class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, max_len=128, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout)

        # Pre-compute the entire PE matrix ONCE
        pe = torch.zeros(max_len, d_model)
        position = torch.arange(0, max_len).unsqueeze(1).float()
        div_term = torch.exp(
            torch.arange(0, d_model, 2).float() *
            (-math.log(10000.0) / d_model)
        )
        pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(position * div_term)
        pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(position * div_term)
        pe = pe.unsqueeze(0)   # (1, max_len, d_model)

        # Register as BUFFER not as parameter
        self.register_buffer('pe', pe)

    def forward(self, x):
        # x: (B, T, d_model)
        # self.pe: (1, max_len, d_model) → slice to (1, T, d_model)
        x = x + self.pe[:, :x.size(1)]
        return self.dropout(x)

Why register_buffer and Not nn.Parameter?

nn.Parameter:  tracked by optimizer, updated by backpropagation
register_buffer: NOT tracked by optimizer, never updated

PE is mathematical constants. They should never change.
If backpropagation updated them, they would stop being
sinusoidal and lose all their mathematical properties.

register_buffer means:

  • PE moves to GPU with .to(device) automatically
  • PE is saved in the checkpoint with torch.save
  • PE is NOT updated by the optimizer
  • PE is invisible to model.parameters()

Why Pre-compute?

The PE matrix is computed once in __init__ and stored. During each forward pass, we just look up pre-computed values and slice to the right length:

self.pe[:, :x.size(1)]   # slice first T positions

Computing sine and cosine every forward pass would waste time. Pre-computing is a standard optimization.

10. Dropout After PE — Why?

return self.dropout(x)   # dropout rate = 0.1

After adding the positional encoding, a small dropout is applied. This prevents the model from relying too heavily on exact positional information.

For sign language this makes sense: the sign "DRINK" should be recognised whether it starts at frame 5 or frame 20 in the sliding window. By randomly dropping some positional information during training, the model learns to classify signs based on their content AND their general temporal structure — not their exact position in the window.

Learned? Yes (embedding table) Sometimes / No (sinusoidal) No (sinusoidal)

Your PE is equivalent to NLP positional encoding only. You skip tokenization entirely because landmark vectors are already semantically rich representations.

12. Connection to Your ASL Project — What PE Enables

Without PE, your Transformer would compute the same output for these two inputs:

Sign A: frame sequence [open_hand, moving_up, closed_fist]
Sign B: frame sequence [closed_fist, moving_up, open_hand]

Without PE: both produce identical Transformer output
            (same frames, different order)
→ model cannot distinguish them

With PE:
  Sign A: open_hand+PE(0), moving_up+PE(1), closed_fist+PE(2)
  Sign B: closed_fist+PE(0), moving_up+PE(1), open_hand+PE(2)
→ completely different inputs to the Transformer
→ model correctly learns these are different signs

For a real ASL pair: DRINK (hand moves TO mouth) vs GIVE (hand moves AWAY from body) — the frames are similar but the temporal order is reversed. PE makes these distinguishable.

14. The Formula to Remember

$$\boxed{ \text{PE}(t, 2i) = \sin\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \quad \text{PE}(t, 2i+1) = \cos\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2i/d}}\right) }$$

  • $t$ = frame index (0 to 63 in your model)
  • $i$ = dimension pair index (0 to 127)
  • $d$ = model dimension (256)
  • Even dimensions → sine (fast oscillations at small $i$)
  • Odd dimensions → cosine (same frequency as adjacent sine)
  • As $i$ increases → frequency decreases → slower oscillation

The combination of 128 sine/cosine pairs at exponentially decreasing frequencies creates a unique, structured fingerprint for every frame position — the continuous analogue of binary counting.

12. Multi-Head Attention

One sentence summary: Multi-head attention runs 8 independent self-attention operations in parallel — each learning to look for a different type of relationship between frames — then combines all 8 answers into a single rich representation.

1. The Problem With a Single Attention Head

In concept 11 you built one self-attention head. It worked. But it has a fundamental limitation.

A single softmax produces one distribution over the 64 frames. Frame 20 can only distribute its attention in one way across all other frames.

But sign language has multiple simultaneous structures:

Structure 1: Where is the hand relative to the face?
Structure 2: How fast is the hand moving?
Structure 3: What handshape is forming?
Structure 4: Are the eyebrows raised or furrowed?
Structure 5: When does the sign start and end?

A single attention head must try to capture all of these with one set of Q, K, V projections. It cannot. It will learn the most dominant pattern and ignore the rest.

Multi-head attention solves this by running 8 independent heads in parallel, each free to specialize on a different structure.

2. The Intuition — 8 Specialists Working Simultaneously

Think of 8 different experts analyzing the same sign video simultaneously:

Expert 1: "I will focus on hand location relative to body"
Expert 2: "I will focus on velocity and motion direction"  
Expert 3: "I will focus on handshape formation"
Expert 4: "I will focus on facial expression timing"
Expert 5: "I will focus on the boundary between preparation and core sign"
Expert 6: "I will focus on symmetry between left and right hand"
Expert 7: "I will focus on which frames to ignore (padding detection)"
Expert 8: "I will focus on overall temporal structure of the sign"

Each expert independently decides what to pay attention to.

Then you ask all 8 experts for their answer and concatenate their reports into one complete picture.

That is multi-head attention.

3. The Mechanics — How 8 Heads Work

Step 1: Split into 8 heads

Your model dimension is $d_{\text{model}} = 256$. You have $h = 8$ attention heads. Each head gets:

$$d_k = \frac{d_{\text{model}}}{h} = \frac{256}{8} = 32 \text{ dimensions}$$

Each head $i$ has its own learned weight matrices:

$$\mathbf{W}^i_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 32}, \quad \mathbf{W}^i_K \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 32}, \quad \mathbf{W}^i_V \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 32}$$

Step 2: Each head computes its own attention

For head $i$:

$$\mathbf{Q}^i = \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$$ $$\mathbf{K}^i = \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_K \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$$ $$\mathbf{V}^i = \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_V \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$$

$$\text{head}_i = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}^i (\mathbf{K}^i)^\top}{\sqrt{32}} + \mathbf{M}\right)\mathbf{V}^i \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$$

This is exactly the formula from concept 11 — but applied 8 times with 8 different weight matrices.

Step 3: Concatenate all 8 outputs

$$\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \text{head}_2, \ldots, \text{head}_8) \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 256}$$

Each head produced $(64 \times 32)$. Concatenating 8 of them along the last dimension gives $(64 \times 256)$.

Step 4: Final linear projection

$$\text{MultiHead}(\mathbf{H}^2) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_8)\, \mathbf{W}_O$$

Where $\mathbf{W}_O \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256}$ is a learned output projection matrix.

This final projection mixes information from all 8 heads together, allowing the model to combine the specialists' reports into one coherent representation.

4. The Complete Formula

$$\text{MultiHead}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\, \mathbf{W}_O$$

$$\text{where} \quad \text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(\mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_Q,\ \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_K,\ \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_V)$$

$$\text{and} \quad \text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \mathbf{M}\right)\mathbf{V}$$

5. Shape Transformations — The Complete Picture

Input: H² (64, 256)
              │
    ┌─────────┴─────────────────────────────┐
    │ Replicate H² to all 8 heads           │
    └─────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
              │
   ┌──────────┼──────────────────┐
   │          │          ...     │
 Head 1     Head 2           Head 8
(64,256)   (64,256)         (64,256)
   │ ×Wq,Wk,Wv               │ ×Wq,Wk,Wv
(64,32)   (64,32)           (64,32)
   │ attention                 │ attention
(64,32)   (64,32)           (64,32)
   │          │                 │

              │ Concatenate

              │

              │

The input and output shapes are identical: $(64, 256) \rightarrow (64, 256)$.

This is important. The Transformer layer does not change the shape of the data. It enriches the representation of each frame by incorporating information from all other frames.

6. A Concrete Worked Example

Let us trace one frame through two heads to see the difference.

Setup: Frame 20 (the core mouth motion in DRINK)

Frame 20 representation: h₂₀ ∈ ℝ²⁵⁶
(This is the 256-dimensional vector after the CNN block)

Head 1 — specialised for hand position:

K¹_j  = h_j × W¹_K  →  keys encode "what hand position does this frame have"

Attention weights for head 1:
  A¹[20, 5]  = 0.02   (Frame 5 has hand far from face — not relevant)
  A¹[20, 15] = 0.31   (Frame 15 has hand approaching face — highly relevant)
  A¹[20, 20] = 0.45   (Frame 20 itself — hand at face — most relevant)
  A¹[20, 35] = 0.18   (Frame 35 has hand leaving face — somewhat relevant)
  A¹[20, 55] = 0.00   (Padding — zeroed by mask)

K²_j  = h_j × W²_K  →  keys encode "what velocity profile does this frame have"

Attention weights for head 2:
  A²[20, 5]  = 0.28   (Frame 5 has fast upward motion — highly relevant for context)
  A²[20, 15] = 0.38   (Frame 15 has decelerating motion — very relevant)
  A²[20, 20] = 0.22   (Frame 20 itself)
  A²[20, 35] = 0.12   (Frame 35 has fast downward motion — somewhat relevant)

head₂[20] = weighted sum of V²_j vectors → rich "velocity context"

After concatenation:

[head₁[20] | head₂[20] | ... | head₈[20]]

└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Frame 20 now contains:
  - hand position context from head 1
  - velocity context from head 2
  - handshape context from head 3
  - facial expression context from head 4
  ... and so on for all 8 heads

After the output projection $\mathbf{W}_O$, these 8 perspectives are mixed into a single $(256)$-dimensional vector that is richer than any single head could produce.

7. Why Not Just Use One Big Head?

A natural question: why not just use $d_k = 256$ instead of 8 heads of $d_k = 32$?

This is a fair question. Here is the technical answer and the intuitive answer.

Technical answer:

With $d_k = 256$ (one big head), the softmax operates on scores across 256 dimensions. It can learn one complex attention pattern. With 8 heads of $d_k = 32$, you have 8 independent softmax operations. Each produces its own complete distribution over all 64 frames.

The key word is independent. Head 2 cannot interfere with head 1 because they have completely separate weight matrices. They are forced to specialise differently because they are optimised by the same loss but through different parameter paths.

Intuitive answer:

One attention distribution cannot simultaneously say "pay most attention to frame 15" and "pay most attention to frame 5" — softmax forces a single distribution. But:

  • Head 1 can say: "pay most attention to frame 15"
  • Head 2 can say: "pay most attention to frame 5"
  • Head 3 can say: "pay most attention to frame 30"

All simultaneously. One big head would have to compromise.

Parameter count comparison:

Approach Parameters
1 head, $d_k = 256$ $3 \times (256 \times 256) = 196{,}608$
8 heads, $d_k = 32$ $8 \times 3 \times (256 \times 32) + 256 \times 256 = 262{,}144$

Multi-head attention has slightly more parameters, mostly in $\mathbf{W}_O$. But the qualitative difference — forced specialisation — is worth it.

8. Parameter Count in Your Model

Your model uses $h = 8$ heads, $d_{\text{model}} = 256$, $d_k = 32$.

For one Transformer layer, the multi-head attention module contains:

Parameter Size Count
$\mathbf{W}^i_Q$ per head $256 \times 32$ 8 heads
$\mathbf{W}^i_K$ per head $256 \times 32$ 8 heads
$\mathbf{W}^i_V$ per head $256 \times 32$ 8 heads
$\mathbf{W}_O$ output $256 \times 256$ 1
Biases various small

Total per layer: $$3 \times 8 \times (256 \times 32) + (256 \times 256) = 196{,}608 + 65{,}536 = 262{,}144 \text{ parameters}$$

Your model has 4 Transformer layers (in the base configuration), so multi-head attention contributes:

$$4 \times 262{,}144 \approx 1{,}048{,}576 \text{ parameters}$$

That is about 27% of the 3.86M total parameters in the base model.

9. The Padding Mask — How It Works Across 8 Heads

The padding mask $\mathbf{M}$ is applied inside every head independently.

Before softmax in each head, any column corresponding to a padding frame is set to $-\infty$. This means:

For all 8 heads:
  If frame j is padding:
    score(i, j) = -∞ for all frames i
    → after softmax: A[i, j] = 0 for all frames i

Padding frames contribute zero value to every output,
regardless of which head is computing.

This is what src_key_padding_mask does in PyTorch's nn.MultiheadAttention. You pass a boolean tensor where True means "this frame is padding — ignore it".

10. What Specialisation Actually Looks Like

Nobody tells the heads what to specialise in. It emerges from training. But visualising attention weights from trained sign language models reveals consistent patterns:

Typically observed (not guaranteed):

Some heads learn to attend to:
  → The beginning and end of the sign (boundary detection)
  → Frames with similar handshape regardless of time position
  → The peak motion frame from all surrounding frames
  → The dominant hand versus the non-dominant hand

Some heads become "garbage collectors":
  → They learn to attend mostly to the current frame itself
     (diagonal attention matrix)
  → These seem to act as a passthrough, preserving the
     original representation when global context is not needed

The fact that some heads become near-diagonal (attending mostly to themselves) is actually useful — it means the model can choose, per-frame, whether to incorporate global context or just use local information.

11. Connection to Your Model Architecture

In your ASLTransformerV11, multi-head attention appears inside nn.TransformerEncoderLayer, called as:

encoder_layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(
    d_model   = 512,    # scaled config
    nhead     = 8,      # 8 attention heads → d_k = 64
    dim_feedforward = 2048,
    dropout   = 0.3,
    activation = 'gelu',
    batch_first = True,
    norm_first  = True,  # Pre-LN: LayerNorm BEFORE attention
)

With the scaled architecture ($d_{\text{model}} = 512$):

$$d_k = \frac{512}{8} = 64 \text{ dimensions per head}$$

Each head's Q, K, V matrices are $512 \times 64$. The output matrix $\mathbf{W}_O$ is $512 \times 512$.

12. Pre-LayerNorm vs Post-LayerNorm

Your model uses norm_first=True. This means LayerNorm is applied BEFORE the attention operation, not after. This is called Pre-LN or Pre-Norm.

Post-LN (original Transformer): $$\text{output} = \text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{H}^2 + \text{MultiHead}(\mathbf{H}^2))$$

Pre-LN (your model): $$\text{output} = \mathbf{H}^2 + \text{MultiHead}(\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{H}^2))$$

Pre-LN is more stable during training because the gradients flow through the residual connection without being modified by LayerNorm first. Research has shown Pre-LN converges faster and is less sensitive to learning rate choice. This is why almost all modern Transformers use it.

13. Summary

Concept Definition
Number of heads $h = 8$ — 8 independent attention operations
Dimension per head $d_k = d_{\text{model}} / h = 256/8 = 32$ (base) or $512/8 = 64$ (scaled)
Per-head Q, K, V $\mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_Q$, etc. — different projection for each head
Head output $(64, 32)$ — one head's attended representation
Concatenation $(64, 256)$ — 8 heads joined along the feature dimension
Output projection $\mathbf{W}_O$ mixes all heads' information

14. The Full Equation — Every Symbol Explained

$$\boxed{\text{MultiHead}(\mathbf{H}^2) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_8)\, \mathbf{W}_O}$$

$$\text{head}_i = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{H}^2\mathbf{W}^i_Q\,(\mathbf{H}^2\mathbf{W}^i_K)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \mathbf{M}\right)\mathbf{H}^2\mathbf{W}^i_V$$

Symbol Shape Meaning
$\mathbf{H}^2$ $(64, 256)$ Input: 64 frame representations after CNN
$\mathbf{W}^i_Q$ $(256, 32)$ Head $i$'s query projection
$\mathbf{W}^i_K$ $(256, 32)$ Head $i$'s key projection
$\mathbf{W}^i_V$ $(256, 32)$ Head $i$'s value projection
$d_k = 32$ scalar Dimension per head
$\sqrt{d_k}$ scalar Gradient stabilisation
$\mathbf{M}$ $(64, 64)$ Padding mask ($0$ or $-\infty$)

$\mathbf{W}_O$ $(256, 256)$ Output projection
Output $(64, 256)$ Enriched frame representations

15. What Comes Next

Multi-head attention produces $(64, 256)$ — the same shape as its input.

This output goes through:

  1. Residual connection — add the original input back
  2. LayerNorm — stabilise the values
  3. Feed-Forward Block — process each frame independently with a two-layer MLP (concept 13)
  4. Residual connection — add again
  5. LayerNorm — stabilise again

Together, attention + feed-forward + two residuals + two layer norms = one complete Transformer encoder layer.

Your model has 4 of these layers stacked (base config) or 6 (scaled config). Each layer refines the frame representations further, each time with access to the full global context of all 64 frames.

13. The Feed-Forward Block

One sentence summary: The feed-forward block takes each frame's representation after attention and runs it through a two-layer neural network independently — giving the model a chance to think deeply about each frame on its own, after it has already gathered information from all other frames.

1. Where We Are in the Pipeline

After multi-head attention, each frame has been enriched with global context. Frame 20 now knows what frame 5 and frame 40 are doing. The representation has changed shape from input to output of attention:

Input to attention:   H² (64, 256)   ← each frame is 256-dimensional
Output of attention:  Z  (64, 256)   ← same shape, richer content

But attention is fundamentally a mixing operation. It combines information from different frames. It does not deeply process any single frame's representation on its own.

The feed-forward block does the opposite: it takes each frame and thinks about it independently, with no communication between frames.

Attention:      every frame talks to every other frame
Feed-forward:   every frame thinks for itself

Together they are complementary. The Transformer alternates between these two operations in every layer.

2. The Intuition — A Two-Step Thought Process

Imagine you are a linguist watching a sign video.

Step 1 — Attention: You watch all 64 frames simultaneously and take notes about which frames are related. "Frame 5 is the preparation. Frame 20 is the core sign. Frame 40 is the retraction."

Step 2 — Feed-forward: You now sit down with your notes about frame 20 and think deeply: "Given everything I know about frame 20 and its relationship to the other frames, what does this actually MEAN? Is this consistent with the DRINK sign? Or could it be MILK? What non-linear features do I need to compute to answer this?"

The feed-forward block is the deep thinking step. Attention gathers information. Feed-forward processes it.

3. The Architecture — Two Linear Layers with GELU

The feed-forward block (also called the position-wise feed-forward network, or FFN) is a simple two-layer MLP:

$$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}_2 \cdot \text{GELU}(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2$$

Where:

Symbol Shape What it is
$\mathbf{x}$ $(256,)$ One frame's representation after attention
$\mathbf{W}_1$ $(256, 1024)$ First weight matrix — expands dimension
$\mathbf{b}_1$ $(1024,)$ First bias
$\text{GELU}(\cdot)$ $(1024,)$ Non-linearity applied element-wise
$\mathbf{W}_2$ $(1024, 256)$ Second weight matrix — compresses back
$\mathbf{b}_2$ $(256,)$ Second bias
$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{x})$ $(256,)$ Processed frame representation

Input dimension: 256 Hidden dimension: 1024 (4× expansion) Output dimension: 256 (back to original)

This is applied independently to each of the 64 frames. Not to the sequence as a whole. Not to all frames at once. Each frame goes through its own FFN computation with the same weights but its own input vector.

4. The $4\times$ Expansion — Why?

The hidden dimension is always $4 \times d_{\text{model}}$. In your base model:

$$d_{\text{ff}} = 4 \times d_{\text{model}} = 4 \times 256 = 1{,}024$$

In your scaled model (Experiment 10 and 11):

$$d_{\text{ff}} = 4 \times 512 = 2{,}048$$

Why $4\times$?

The first linear layer expands the representation from 256 dimensions to 1024 dimensions. In this higher-dimensional space the model has more room to compute complex non-linear transformations of the frame's features.

Think of it this way. You have a 256-dimensional description of what is happening at frame 20. You want to compute all the non-linear interactions between those 256 features — velocity cross-correlated with hand position, handshape interacting with facial expression, etc. Projecting to 1024 dimensions gives you 1024 neurons to detect all those combinations. Then you compress back to 256.

The $4\times$ ratio comes from the original Transformer paper (Vaswani et al. 2017) and has remained standard because it works well empirically across almost all Transformer applications.

5. Step-by-Step Computation

Let us trace one frame through the entire FFN.

Setup: Frame 20 after attention, $\mathbf{z}_{20} \in \mathbb{R}^{256}$

z₂₀ = [0.42, -0.18, 0.91, 0.03, ..., -0.55]   (256 values)

Step 1: First linear layer — expand to 1024

$$\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{z}_{20} + \mathbf{b}_1$$

$$\underbrace{(1024, 256)}_{\mathbf{W}_1} \times \underbrace{(256,)}_{\mathbf{z}_{20}} + \underbrace{(1024,)}_{\mathbf{b}_1} = \underbrace{(1024,)}_{\mathbf{h}}$$

Each of the 1024 output neurons computes a weighted sum of all 256 input features plus a bias. This is a linear combination:

$$h_j = \sum_{i=1}^{256} W_1[j, i] \cdot z_{20,i} + b_1[j] \quad \text{for } j = 1 \ldots 1024$$

At this point the computation is still linear. Nothing interesting has happened yet.

Step 2: GELU activation — introduce non-linearity

$$\mathbf{h}' = \text{GELU}(\mathbf{h})$$

Applied element-wise to each of the 1024 values.

Without this step the entire FFN would collapse to a single linear transformation — two linear layers in sequence are equivalent to one linear layer. The activation function is what gives the FFN its expressive power.

We will cover GELU in detail below (Section 6).

Step 3: Second linear layer — compress back to 256

$$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{z}_{20}) = \mathbf{W}_2 \mathbf{h}' + \mathbf{b}_2$$

$$\underbrace{(256, 1024)}_{\mathbf{W}_2} \times \underbrace{(1024,)}_{\mathbf{h}'} + \underbrace{(256,)}_{\mathbf{b}_2} = \underbrace{(256,)}_{\text{output}}$$

The 1024-dimensional activated representation is compressed back to 256. The model has selected which of the 1024 computed features are actually useful and mixed them back into the 256-dimensional space.

6. GELU — Why Not ReLU?

You learned about activation functions in concept 5. The FFN in your model uses GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) instead of the more common ReLU.

ReLU reminder

$$\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x)$$

If $x > 0$: pass through unchanged. If $x \leq 0$: set to zero.

GELU definition

$$\text{GELU}(x) = x \cdot \Phi(x)$$

Where $\Phi(x)$ is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution:

$$\Phi(x) = P(X \leq x) \quad \text{where } X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$$

In practice, a fast approximation is used:

$$\text{GELU}(x) \approx 0.5 \cdot x \cdot \left(1 + \tanh\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(x + 0.044715 x^3\right)\right)\right)$$

What GELU looks like

x:       -3    -2    -1     0    0.5    1     2     3
ReLU:     0     0     0     0    0.5    1     2     3
GELU:  -0.004 -0.046 -0.159 0  0.346  0.841  1.954  2.996

The critical difference

ReLU is binary: a neuron is either completely on (identity) or completely off (zero). There is a hard cliff at $x = 0$.

GELU is smooth: a neuron with value $x = -0.5$ is not completely zeroed out — it passes through about $-0.09$ (33% of its value). A neuron with $x = 0.5$ passes through about $0.35$ (69% of its value). The transition is smooth.

Why this matters for Transformers

The hard cutoff in ReLU creates dead neurons — neurons that get stuck at exactly zero and stop receiving gradient signal. This is more problematic in deep models.

The smooth gradient of GELU means every neuron always receives some gradient signal, even small negative values. This produces more stable training for deep Transformer architectures.

GELU was introduced by Hendrycks & Gimpel (2016) and has become the standard for Transformers. GPT, BERT, and your model all use GELU in the FFN.

7. Position-Wise — What This Actually Means

The FFN is described as position-wise in the original Transformer paper. This is a key word.

Position-wise means: the same function is applied to each position (each frame) independently, with the same weights.

Frame 1  → FFN(z₁)  using W₁, W₂
Frame 2  → FFN(z₂)  using W₁, W₂  ← same weights
Frame 20 → FFN(z₂₀) using W₁, W₂  ← same weights
Frame 64 → FFN(z₆₄) using W₁, W₂  ← same weights

All 64 frames use the same $\mathbf{W}_1$ and $\mathbf{W}_2$. The only difference is the input vector.

This is different from attention, which processes all 64 frames simultaneously as one matrix operation.

In terms of computation, the position-wise FFN applied to all 64 frames at once is:

$$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{Z}) = \text{GELU}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}_1 + \mathbf{b}_1)\mathbf{W}_2 + \mathbf{b}_2$$

$$\underbrace{(64, 256)}_{\mathbf{Z}} \times \underbrace{(256, 1024)}_{\mathbf{W}_1} = \underbrace{(64, 1024)}_{\text{hidden}}$$

$$\underbrace{(64, 1024)}_{\text{GELU applied}} \times \underbrace{(1024, 256)}_{\mathbf{W}_2} = \underbrace{(64, 256)}_{\text{output}}$$

Efficient. Parallelisable across all 64 frames simultaneously.

Let us use small dimensions to make this concrete. Suppose $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ and $d_{\text{ff}} = 8$ (2× for simplicity instead of 4×).

Input: $\mathbf{z}_{20} = [1.2, -0.5, 0.8, 0.3]$

W₁ = [[ 0.3,  0.1, -0.2,  0.5],

Step 2: Apply GELU element-wise

GELU(0.30)  ≈ 0.185   (positive, mostly passes through)
GELU(-0.84) ≈ -0.101  (negative, mostly suppressed)
GELU(0.76)  ≈ 0.576   (positive, passes through)

GELU(-0.51) ≈ -0.074  (negative, mostly suppressed)
