notes.html:
One sentence summary: Multi-head attention runs 8 independent self-attention operations in parallel — each learning to look for a different type of relationship between frames — then combines all 8 answers into a single rich representation.

1. The Problem With a Single Attention Head

In concept 11 you built one self-attention head. It worked. But it has a fundamental limitation.

A single softmax produces one distribution over the 64 frames. Frame 20 can only distribute its attention in one way across all other frames.

But sign language has multiple simultaneous structures:

Structure 1: Where is the hand relative to the face?
Structure 2: How fast is the hand moving?
Structure 3: What handshape is forming?
Structure 4: Are the eyebrows raised or furrowed?
Structure 5: When does the sign start and end?

A single attention head must try to capture all of these with one set of Q, K, V projections. It cannot. It will learn the most dominant pattern and ignore the rest.

Multi-head attention solves this by running 8 independent heads in parallel, each free to specialise on a different structure.

2. The Intuition — 8 Specialists Working Simultaneously

Think of 8 different experts analysing the same sign video simultaneously:

Expert 1: "I will focus on hand location relative to body"
Expert 2: "I will focus on velocity and motion direction"  
Expert 3: "I will focus on handshape formation"
Expert 4: "I will focus on facial expression timing"
Expert 5: "I will focus on the boundary between preparation and core sign"
Expert 6: "I will focus on symmetry between left and right hand"
Expert 7: "I will focus on which frames to ignore (padding detection)"
Expert 8: "I will focus on overall temporal structure of the sign"

Each expert independently decides what to pay attention to.

Then you ask all 8 experts for their answer and concatenate their reports into one complete picture.

That is multi-head attention.

3. The Mechanics — How 8 Heads Work

Step 1: Split into 8 heads

Your model dimension is $d_{\text{model}} = 256$. You have $h = 8$ attention heads. Each head gets:

$$d_k = \frac{d_{\text{model}}}{h} = \frac{256}{8} = 32 \text{ dimensions}$$

Each head $i$ has its own learned weight matrices:

$$\mathbf{W}^i_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 32}, \quad \mathbf{W}^i_K \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 32}, \quad \mathbf{W}^i_V \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 32}$$

Step 2: Each head computes its own attention

For head $i$:

$$\mathbf{Q}^i = \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$$ $$\mathbf{K}^i = \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_K \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$$ $$\mathbf{V}^i = \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_V \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$$

$$\text{head}_i = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}^i (\mathbf{K}^i)^\top}{\sqrt{32}} + \mathbf{M}\right)\mathbf{V}^i \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$$

This is exactly the formula from concept 11 — but applied 8 times with 8 different weight matrices.

Step 3: Concatenate all 8 outputs

$$\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \text{head}_2, \ldots, \text{head}_8) \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 256}$$

Each head produced $(64 \times 32)$. Concatenating 8 of them along the last dimension gives $(64 \times 256)$.

Step 4: Final linear projection

$$\text{MultiHead}(\mathbf{H}^2) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_8)\, \mathbf{W}_O$$

Where $\mathbf{W}_O \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256}$ is a learned output projection matrix.

This final projection mixes information from all 8 heads together, allowing the model to combine the specialists' reports into one coherent representation.

4. The Complete Formula

$$\text{MultiHead}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\, \mathbf{W}_O$$

$$\text{where} \quad \text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(\mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_Q,\ \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_K,\ \mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_V)$$

$$\text{and} \quad \text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \mathbf{M}\right)\mathbf{V}$$

5. Shape Transformations — The Complete Picture

Input: H² (64, 256)
              │
    ┌─────────┴─────────────────────────────┐
    │ Replicate H² to all 8 heads           │
    └─────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
              │
   ┌──────────┼──────────────────┐
   │          │          ...     │
 Head 1     Head 2           Head 8
(64,256)   (64,256)         (64,256)
   │ ×Wq,Wk,Wv               │ ×Wq,Wk,Wv
(64,32)   (64,32)           (64,32)
   │ attention                 │ attention
(64,32)   (64,32)           (64,32)
   │          │                 │
   └──────────┴─────────────────┘
              │ Concatenate
         (64, 256)   ← 8 × 32 = 256
              │
              │ × Wo (256×256)
              │
         (64, 256)
              │
           Output

The input and output shapes are identical: $(64, 256) \rightarrow (64, 256)$.

This is important. The Transformer layer does not change the shape of the data. It enriches the representation of each frame by incorporating information from all other frames.

6. A Concrete Worked Example

Let us trace one frame through two heads to see the difference.

Setup: Frame 20 (the core mouth motion in DRINK)

Frame 20 representation: h₂₀ ∈ ℝ²⁵⁶
(This is the 256-dimensional vector after the CNN block)

Head 1 — specialised for hand position:

Q¹₂₀ = h₂₀ × W¹_Q   →  q¹₂₀ encodes "looking for frames with hand near face"
K¹_j  = h_j × W¹_K  →  keys encode "what hand position does this frame have"

Attention weights for head 1:
  A¹[20, 5]  = 0.02   (Frame 5 has hand far from face — not relevant)
  A¹[20, 15] = 0.31   (Frame 15 has hand approaching face — highly relevant)
  A¹[20, 20] = 0.45   (Frame 20 itself — hand at face — most relevant)
  A¹[20, 35] = 0.18   (Frame 35 has hand leaving face — somewhat relevant)
  A¹[20, 55] = 0.00   (Padding — zeroed by mask)

head₁[20] = weighted sum of V¹_j vectors → rich "hand position context"

Head 2 — specialised for motion velocity:

Q²₂₀ = h₂₀ × W²_Q   →  q²₂₀ encodes "looking for frames with decelerating motion"
K²_j  = h_j × W²_K  →  keys encode "what velocity profile does this frame have"

Attention weights for head 2:
  A²[20, 5]  = 0.28   (Frame 5 has fast upward motion — highly relevant for context)
  A²[20, 15] = 0.38   (Frame 15 has decelerating motion — very relevant)
  A²[20, 20] = 0.22   (Frame 20 itself)
  A²[20, 35] = 0.12   (Frame 35 has fast downward motion — somewhat relevant)
  A²[20, 55] = 0.00   (Padding)

head₂[20] = weighted sum of V²_j vectors → rich "velocity context"

After concatenation:

[head₁[20] | head₂[20] | ... | head₈[20]]
 (32)         (32)               (32)
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
               (256)

Frame 20 now contains:
  - hand position context from head 1
  - velocity context from head 2
  - handshape context from head 3
  - facial expression context from head 4
  ... and so on for all 8 heads

After the output projection $\mathbf{W}_O$, these 8 perspectives are mixed into a single $(256)$-dimensional vector that is richer than any single head could produce.

7. Why Not Just Use One Big Head?

A natural question: why not just use $d_k = 256$ instead of 8 heads of $d_k = 32$?

This is a fair question. Here is the technical answer and the intuitive answer.

Technical answer:

With $d_k = 256$ (one big head), the softmax operates on scores across 256 dimensions. It can learn one complex attention pattern. With 8 heads of $d_k = 32$, you have 8 independent softmax operations. Each produces its own complete distribution over all 64 frames.

The key word is independent. Head 2 cannot interfere with head 1 because they have completely separate weight matrices. They are forced to specialise differently because they are optimised by the same loss but through different parameter paths.

Intuitive answer:

One attention distribution cannot simultaneously say "pay most attention to frame 15" and "pay most attention to frame 5" — softmax forces a single distribution. But:

  • Head 1 can say: "pay most attention to frame 15"
  • Head 2 can say: "pay most attention to frame 5"
  • Head 3 can say: "pay most attention to frame 30"

All simultaneously. One big head would have to compromise.

Parameter count comparison:

Approach Parameters
1 head, $d_k = 256$ $3 \times (256 \times 256) = 196{,}608$
8 heads, $d_k = 32$ $8 \times 3 \times (256 \times 32) + 256 \times 256 = 262{,}144$

Multi-head attention has slightly more parameters, mostly in $\mathbf{W}_O$. But the qualitative difference — forced specialisation — is worth it.

8. Parameter Count in Your Model

Your model uses $h = 8$ heads, $d_{\text{model}} = 256$, $d_k = 32$.

For one Transformer layer, the multi-head attention module contains:

Parameter Size Count
$\mathbf{W}^i_Q$ per head $256 \times 32$ 8 heads
$\mathbf{W}^i_K$ per head $256 \times 32$ 8 heads
$\mathbf{W}^i_V$ per head $256 \times 32$ 8 heads
$\mathbf{W}_O$ output $256 \times 256$ 1
Biases various small

Total per layer: $$3 \times 8 \times (256 \times 32) + (256 \times 256) = 196{,}608 + 65{,}536 = 262{,}144 \text{ parameters}$$

Your model has 4 Transformer layers (in the base configuration), so multi-head attention contributes:

$$4 \times 262{,}144 \approx 1{,}048{,}576 \text{ parameters}$$

That is about 27% of the 3.86M total parameters in the base model.

9. The Padding Mask — How It Works Across 8 Heads

The padding mask $\mathbf{M}$ is applied inside every head independently.

Before softmax in each head, any column corresponding to a padding frame is set to $-\infty$. This means:

For all 8 heads:
  If frame j is padding:
    score(i, j) = -∞ for all frames i
    → after softmax: A[i, j] = 0 for all frames i

Padding frames contribute zero value to every output,
regardless of which head is computing.

This is what src_key_padding_mask does in PyTorch's nn.MultiheadAttention. You pass a boolean tensor where True means "this frame is padding — ignore it".

10. What Specialisation Actually Looks Like

Nobody tells the heads what to specialise in. It emerges from training. But visualising attention weights from trained sign language models reveals consistent patterns:

Typically observed (not guaranteed):

Some heads learn to attend to:
  → The beginning and end of the sign (boundary detection)
  → Frames with similar handshape regardless of time position
  → The peak motion frame from all surrounding frames
  → The dominant hand versus the non-dominant hand

Some heads become "garbage collectors":
  → They learn to attend mostly to the current frame itself
     (diagonal attention matrix)
  → These seem to act as a passthrough, preserving the
     original representation when global context is not needed

The fact that some heads become near-diagonal (attending mostly to themselves) is actually useful — it means the model can choose, per-frame, whether to incorporate global context or just use local information.

11. Connection to Your Model Architecture

In your ASLTransformerV11, multi-head attention appears inside nn.TransformerEncoderLayer, called as:

encoder_layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(
    d_model   = 512,    # scaled config
    nhead     = 8,      # 8 attention heads → d_k = 64
    dim_feedforward = 2048,
    dropout   = 0.3,
    activation = 'gelu',
    batch_first = True,
    norm_first  = True,  # Pre-LN: LayerNorm BEFORE attention
)

With the scaled architecture ($d_{\text{model}} = 512$):

$$d_k = \frac{512}{8} = 64 \text{ dimensions per head}$$

Each head's Q, K, V matrices are $512 \times 64$. The output matrix $\mathbf{W}_O$ is $512 \times 512$.

12. Pre-LayerNorm vs Post-LayerNorm

Your model uses norm_first=True. This means LayerNorm is applied BEFORE the attention operation, not after. This is called Pre-LN or Pre-Norm.

Post-LN (original Transformer): $$\text{output} = \text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{H}^2 + \text{MultiHead}(\mathbf{H}^2))$$

Pre-LN (your model): $$\text{output} = \mathbf{H}^2 + \text{MultiHead}(\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{H}^2))$$

Pre-LN is more stable during training because the gradients flow through the residual connection without being modified by LayerNorm first. Research has shown Pre-LN converges faster and is less sensitive to learning rate choice. This is why almost all modern Transformers use it.

13. Summary

Concept Definition
Number of heads $h = 8$ — 8 independent attention operations
Dimension per head $d_k = d_{\text{model}} / h = 256/8 = 32$ (base) or $512/8 = 64$ (scaled)
Per-head Q, K, V $\mathbf{H}^2 \mathbf{W}^i_Q$, etc. — different projection for each head
Head output $(64, 32)$ — one head's attended representation
Concatenation $(64, 256)$ — 8 heads joined along the feature dimension
Output projection $\mathbf{W}_O$ mixes all heads' information
Specialisation Each head learns different relationships — not programmed, emerges
Padding mask Applied inside every head — padding columns receive zero attention

14. The Full Equation — Every Symbol Explained

$$\boxed{\text{MultiHead}(\mathbf{H}^2) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_8)\, \mathbf{W}_O}$$

$$\text{head}_i = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{H}^2\mathbf{W}^i_Q\,(\mathbf{H}^2\mathbf{W}^i_K)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \mathbf{M}\right)\mathbf{H}^2\mathbf{W}^i_V$$

Symbol Shape Meaning
$\mathbf{H}^2$ $(64, 256)$ Input: 64 frame representations after CNN
$\mathbf{W}^i_Q$ $(256, 32)$ Head $i$'s query projection
$\mathbf{W}^i_K$ $(256, 32)$ Head $i$'s key projection
$\mathbf{W}^i_V$ $(256, 32)$ Head $i$'s value projection
$d_k = 32$ scalar Dimension per head
$\sqrt{d_k}$ scalar Gradient stabilisation
$\mathbf{M}$ $(64, 64)$ Padding mask ($0$ or $-\infty$)
$\text{head}_i$ $(64, 32)$ One head's output
$\text{Concat}(\cdot)$ $(64, 256)$ 8 heads joined
$\mathbf{W}_O$ $(256, 256)$ Output projection
Output $(64, 256)$ Enriched frame representations

15. What Comes Next

Multi-head attention produces $(64, 256)$ — the same shape as its input.

This output goes through:

  1. Residual connection — add the original input back
  2. LayerNorm — stabilise the values
  3. Feed-Forward Block — process each frame independently with a two-layer MLP (concept 13)
  4. Residual connection — add again
  5. LayerNorm — stabilise again

Together, attention + feed-forward + two residuals + two layer norms = one complete Transformer encoder layer.

Your model has 4 of these layers stacked (base config) or 6 (scaled config). Each layer refines the frame representations further, each time with access to the full global context of all 64 frames.

References

  • Vaswani et al. (2017) — Attention Is All You Need — the original multi-head attention paper
  • Ba et al. (2016) — Layer Normalization
  • Your project: src/model.py → ASLTransformerV5 and ASLTransformerV11
  • Your project: notebooks/03_training.ipynb → Experiment results showing 4-layer vs 6-layer impact

notes.html:
One sentence summary: The feed-forward block takes each frame's representation after attention and runs it through a two-layer neural network independently — giving the model a chance to think deeply about each frame on its own, after it has already gathered information from all other frames.

1. Where We Are in the Pipeline

After multi-head attention, each frame has been enriched with global context. Frame 20 now knows what frame 5 and frame 40 are doing. The representation has changed shape from input to output of attention:

Input to attention:   H² (64, 256)   ← each frame is 256-dimensional
Output of attention:  Z  (64, 256)   ← same shape, richer content

But attention is fundamentally a mixing operation. It combines information from different frames. It does not deeply process any single frame's representation on its own.

The feed-forward block does the opposite: it takes each frame and thinks about it independently, with no communication between frames.

Attention:      every frame talks to every other frame
Feed-forward:   every frame thinks for itself

Together they are complementary. The Transformer alternates between these two operations in every layer.

2. The Intuition — A Two-Step Thought Process

Imagine you are a linguist watching a sign video.

Step 1 — Attention: You watch all 64 frames simultaneously and take notes about which frames are related. "Frame 5 is the preparation. Frame 20 is the core sign. Frame 40 is the retraction."

Step 2 — Feed-forward: You now sit down with your notes about frame 20 and think deeply: "Given everything I know about frame 20 and its relationship to the other frames, what does this actually MEAN? Is this consistent with the DRINK sign? Or could it be MILK? What non-linear features do I need to compute to answer this?"

The feed-forward block is the deep thinking step. Attention gathers information. Feed-forward processes it.

3. The Architecture — Two Linear Layers with GELU

The feed-forward block (also called the position-wise feed-forward network, or FFN) is a simple two-layer MLP:

$$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}_2 \cdot \text{GELU}(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2$$

Where:

Symbol Shape What it is
$\mathbf{x}$ $(256,)$ One frame's representation after attention
$\mathbf{W}_1$ $(256, 1024)$ First weight matrix — expands dimension
$\mathbf{b}_1$ $(1024,)$ First bias
$\text{GELU}(\cdot)$ $(1024,)$ Non-linearity applied element-wise
$\mathbf{W}_2$ $(1024, 256)$ Second weight matrix — compresses back
$\mathbf{b}_2$ $(256,)$ Second bias
$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{x})$ $(256,)$ Processed frame representation

Input dimension: 256 Hidden dimension: 1024 (4× expansion) Output dimension: 256 (back to original)

This is applied independently to each of the 64 frames. Not to the sequence as a whole. Not to all frames at once. Each frame goes through its own FFN computation with the same weights but its own input vector.

4. The $4\times$ Expansion — Why?

The hidden dimension is always $4 \times d_{\text{model}}$. In your base model:

$$d_{\text{ff}} = 4 \times d_{\text{model}} = 4 \times 256 = 1{,}024$$

In your scaled model (Experiment 10 and 11):

$$d_{\text{ff}} = 4 \times 512 = 2{,}048$$

Why $4\times$?

The first linear layer expands the representation from 256 dimensions to 1024 dimensions. In this higher-dimensional space the model has more room to compute complex non-linear transformations of the frame's features.

Think of it this way. You have a 256-dimensional description of what is happening at frame 20. You want to compute all the non-linear interactions between those 256 features — velocity cross-correlated with hand position, handshape interacting with facial expression, etc. Projecting to 1024 dimensions gives you 1024 neurons to detect all those combinations. Then you compress back to 256.

The $4\times$ ratio comes from the original Transformer paper (Vaswani et al. 2017) and has remained standard because it works well empirically across almost all Transformer applications.

5. Step-by-Step Computation

Let us trace one frame through the entire FFN.

Setup: Frame 20 after attention, $\mathbf{z}_{20} \in \mathbb{R}^{256}$

z₂₀ = [0.42, -0.18, 0.91, 0.03, ..., -0.55]   (256 values)

Step 1: First linear layer — expand to 1024

$$\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{z}_{20} + \mathbf{b}_1$$

$$\underbrace{(1024, 256)}_{\mathbf{W}_1} \times \underbrace{(256,)}_{\mathbf{z}_{20}} + \underbrace{(1024,)}_{\mathbf{b}_1} = \underbrace{(1024,)}_{\mathbf{h}}$$

Each of the 1024 output neurons computes a weighted sum of all 256 input features plus a bias. This is a linear combination:

$$h_j = \sum_{i=1}^{256} W_1[j, i] \cdot z_{20,i} + b_1[j] \quad \text{for } j = 1 \ldots 1024$$

At this point the computation is still linear. Nothing interesting has happened yet.

Step 2: GELU activation — introduce non-linearity

$$\mathbf{h}' = \text{GELU}(\mathbf{h})$$

Applied element-wise to each of the 1024 values.

Without this step the entire FFN would collapse to a single linear transformation — two linear layers in sequence are equivalent to one linear layer. The activation function is what gives the FFN its expressive power.

We will cover GELU in detail below (Section 6).

Step 3: Second linear layer — compress back to 256

$$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{z}_{20}) = \mathbf{W}_2 \mathbf{h}' + \mathbf{b}_2$$

$$\underbrace{(256, 1024)}_{\mathbf{W}_2} \times \underbrace{(1024,)}_{\mathbf{h}'} + \underbrace{(256,)}_{\mathbf{b}_2} = \underbrace{(256,)}_{\text{output}}$$

The 1024-dimensional activated representation is compressed back to 256. The model has selected which of the 1024 computed features are actually useful and mixed them back into the 256-dimensional space.

6. GELU — Why Not ReLU?

You learned about activation functions in concept 5. The FFN in your model uses GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) instead of the more common ReLU.

ReLU reminder

$$\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x)$$

If $x > 0$: pass through unchanged. If $x \leq 0$: set to zero.

GELU definition

$$\text{GELU}(x) = x \cdot \Phi(x)$$

Where $\Phi(x)$ is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution:

$$\Phi(x) = P(X \leq x) \quad \text{where } X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$$

In practice, a fast approximation is used:

$$\text{GELU}(x) \approx 0.5 \cdot x \cdot \left(1 + \tanh\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(x + 0.044715 x^3\right)\right)\right)$$

What GELU looks like

x:       -3    -2    -1     0    0.5    1     2     3
ReLU:     0     0     0     0    0.5    1     2     3
GELU:  -0.004 -0.046 -0.159 0  0.346  0.841  1.954  2.996

The critical difference

ReLU is binary: a neuron is either completely on (identity) or completely off (zero). There is a hard cliff at $x = 0$.

GELU is smooth: a neuron with value $x = -0.5$ is not completely zeroed out — it passes through about $-0.09$ (33% of its value). A neuron with $x = 0.5$ passes through about $0.35$ (69% of its value). The transition is smooth.

Why this matters for Transformers

The hard cutoff in ReLU creates dead neurons — neurons that get stuck at exactly zero and stop receiving gradient signal. This is more problematic in deep models.

The smooth gradient of GELU means every neuron always receives some gradient signal, even small negative values. This produces more stable training for deep Transformer architectures.

GELU was introduced by Hendrycks & Gimpel (2016) and has become the standard for Transformers. GPT, BERT, and your model all use GELU in the FFN.

7. Position-Wise — What This Actually Means

The FFN is described as position-wise in the original Transformer paper. This is a key word.

Position-wise means: the same function is applied to each position (each frame) independently, with the same weights.

Frame 1  → FFN(z₁)  using W₁, W₂
Frame 2  → FFN(z₂)  using W₁, W₂  ← same weights
Frame 20 → FFN(z₂₀) using W₁, W₂  ← same weights
Frame 64 → FFN(z₆₄) using W₁, W₂  ← same weights

All 64 frames use the same $\mathbf{W}_1$ and $\mathbf{W}_2$. The only difference is the input vector.

This is different from attention, which processes all 64 frames simultaneously as one matrix operation.

In terms of computation, the position-wise FFN applied to all 64 frames at once is:

$$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{Z}) = \text{GELU}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}_1 + \mathbf{b}_1)\mathbf{W}_2 + \mathbf{b}_2$$

$$\underbrace{(64, 256)}_{\mathbf{Z}} \times \underbrace{(256, 1024)}_{\mathbf{W}_1} = \underbrace{(64, 1024)}_{\text{hidden}}$$

$$\underbrace{(64, 1024)}_{\text{GELU applied}} \times \underbrace{(1024, 256)}_{\mathbf{W}_2} = \underbrace{(64, 256)}_{\text{output}}$$

Efficient. Parallelisable across all 64 frames simultaneously.

8. A Tiny Worked Example

Let us use small dimensions to make this concrete. Suppose $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ and $d_{\text{ff}} = 8$ (2× for simplicity instead of 4×).

Input: $\mathbf{z}_{20} = [1.2, -0.5, 0.8, 0.3]$

Weight matrix $\mathbf{W}_1$ (8×4):

W₁ = [[ 0.3,  0.1, -0.2,  0.5],
      [-0.4,  0.7,  0.1, -0.3],
      [ 0.2, -0.1,  0.6,  0.4],
      [ 0.8,  0.2, -0.5,  0.1],
      [-0.1,  0.4,  0.3, -0.6],
      [ 0.5, -0.3,  0.2,  0.7],
      [-0.2,  0.6, -0.4,  0.2],
      [ 0.4, -0.8,  0.5, -0.1]]

Step 1: $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{z}_{20}$ (ignoring bias for clarity)

h₁ = 0.3×1.2 + 0.1×(-0.5) + (-0.2)×0.8 + 0.5×0.3
   = 0.36 - 0.05 - 0.16 + 0.15 = 0.30

h₂ = (-0.4)×1.2 + 0.7×(-0.5) + 0.1×0.8 + (-0.3)×0.3
   = -0.48 - 0.35 + 0.08 - 0.09 = -0.84

... (computed for all 8 neurons)

h = [0.30, -0.84, 0.76, 0.69, -0.51, 0.89, -0.42, 0.23]

Step 2: Apply GELU element-wise

GELU(0.30)  ≈ 0.185   (positive, mostly passes through)
GELU(-0.84) ≈ -0.101  (negative, mostly suppressed)
GELU(0.76)  ≈ 0.576   (positive, passes through)
GELU(0.69)  ≈ 0.508   (positive, passes through)
GELU(-0.51) ≈ -0.074  (negative, mostly suppressed)
GELU(0.89)  ≈ 0.706   (positive, passes through)
GELU(-0.42) ≈ -0.059  (negative, mostly suppressed)
GELU(0.23)  ≈ 0.131   (positive, partly suppressed)

h' = [0.185, -0.101, 0.576, 0.508, -0.074, 0.706, -0.059, 0.131]

Step 3: $\mathbf{W}_2 \mathbf{h}'$ compresses back to 4 dimensions.

The negative values from GELU contribute small negative amounts. The positive values contribute larger amounts. The final 4-dimensional output is a non-linear transformation of the original input.

9. What Does the FFN Actually Learn?

The weight matrix $\mathbf{W}_1$ learns to detect patterns in the 256-dimensional frame representation. Each of the 1024 neurons in the hidden layer computes one specific linear combination of the 256 input features.

After GELU, only neurons that are strongly activated (large positive values) significantly influence the output. Neurons with large negative values are suppressed.

Concretely in your ASL project:

After training, certain neurons in $\mathbf{W}_1$ might specialise in detecting:

Neuron 42:  high activation when  (left wrist y-velocity > 0.3)
              AND (right hand x-position > 0.4)
              "hand moving upward and to the right simultaneously"

Neuron 187: high activation when  (eyebrow position < -0.2)
              AND (mouth is open)
              "furrowed brows + open mouth" (wh-question marker in ASL)

Neuron 613: high activation when  (velocity block entries ≈ 0)
              "the frame is nearly static"
              → likely padding or retraction phase

None of these were programmed. They emerge from 421 minutes of gradient descent on 212,000 training sequences.

10. The Residual Connection Around FFN

Just like after attention, the FFN is wrapped in a residual connection and LayerNorm.

In your model (Pre-LN style, norm_first=True):

$$\text{output} = \mathbf{z} + \text{FFN}(\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{z}))$$

Where $\mathbf{z}$ is the output of the attention block (already with its own residual connection applied).

Breaking this down:

z           (64, 256)   ← attention output with residual
LayerNorm(z)(64, 256)   ← normalise before FFN
FFN(...)    (64, 256)   ← two-layer MLP
z + FFN(...)(64, 256)   ← add residual

Why the residual connection matters here:

The FFN might not improve every frame's representation. For some frames the original attention output $\mathbf{z}$ is already good enough. The residual connection allows the FFN to output approximately zero (a small perturbation) for those frames, effectively being bypassed. Only frames that need deeper processing receive significant modification.

This is the same argument from concept 9 (Residual Connection) applied here.

11. One Complete Transformer Layer — The Full Picture

Now you have all the pieces. One Transformer encoder layer = attention + FFN, each with residual + LayerNorm.

In Pre-LN style (your model):

Input: x  (64, 256)
│
├── LayerNorm(x)                    normalise
│       ↓
├── MultiHeadAttention(...)          attend to all frames
│       ↓
├── x + attention_output            residual connection 1
│       ↓  (call this x')
├── LayerNorm(x')                   normalise again
│       ↓
├── FFN(...)                        process each frame independently
│       ↓
└── x' + ffn_output                 residual connection 2
        ↓
     Output: (64, 256)

Your base model has 4 of these layers stacked. Your scaled model (Experiments 10 and 11) has 6.

Each layer refines the frame representations:

  • Attention: global context (connect all frames)
  • FFN: local processing (think deeply about each frame)
  • Residual: preserve what was already good
  • LayerNorm: keep values in a stable range

12. Shape Transformations — Complete FFN View

After attention:
  z  (64, 256)

LayerNorm:
  (64, 256)   → values stabilised per frame

First linear layer (W₁: 256→1024):
  (64, 256) × (256, 1024) = (64, 1024)

GELU:
  (64, 1024)   → non-linearity applied element-wise

Second linear layer (W₂: 1024→256):
  (64, 1024) × (1024, 256) = (64, 256)

Residual:
  (64, 256) + (64, 256) = (64, 256)

Output: (64, 256)   ← same shape, richer representation

The FFN never changes the shape. Input and output are always $(64, 256)$ in the base model or $(64, 512)$ in the scaled model.

13. Parameter Count in Your Model

For the base configuration ($d_{\text{model}} = 256$, $d_{\text{ff}} = 1024$):

Component Size Parameters
$\mathbf{W}_1$ $256 \times 1024$ 262,144
$\mathbf{b}_1$ $1024$ 1,024
$\mathbf{W}_2$ $1024 \times 256$ 262,144
$\mathbf{b}_2$ $256$ 256
Total per layer 525,568
Total (4 layers) 2,102,272

For the scaled configuration ($d_{\text{model}} = 512$, $d_{\text{ff}} = 2048$):

Component Size Parameters
$\mathbf{W}_1$ $512 \times 2048$ 1,048,576
$\mathbf{W}_2$ $2048 \times 512$ 1,048,576
Biases 2,560
Total per layer 2,099,712
Total (6 layers) 12,598,272

The FFN accounts for the majority of parameters in a Transformer layer — more than multi-head attention. This is by design: the FFN is where the model stores most of its "knowledge" about what combinations of features matter.

14. Why Is the FFN So Important?

A common misconception is that attention is the most important part of the Transformer. Research suggests the FFN stores more learned knowledge.

Evidence from mechanistic interpretability studies:

  • When you ablate (remove) attention layers, performance drops but the model can still classify roughly
  • When you ablate FFN layers, performance collapses completely

One interpretation: attention decides where to look, the FFN decides what to do with what it saw.

In your ASL project:

  • Attention learns which frames are related to which other frames
  • FFN learns the feature detectors that map frame representations to sign class evidence

Both are essential. Neither alone is sufficient.

15. Summary

Concept Definition
FFN Two-layer MLP applied independently to each frame
$d_{\text{ff}}$ Hidden dimension = $4 \times d_{\text{model}}$
Expand $\mathbf{W}_1$: $256 \rightarrow 1024$ — more room for non-linear computation
GELU Smooth activation — avoids dead neurons, better gradients
Compress $\mathbf{W}_2$: $1024 \rightarrow 256$ — select useful features
Position-wise Same weights for every frame — applied independently
Residual Add input back — model can bypass FFN if not needed
Purpose Deep per-frame processing after global context from attention

16. The Full Equation — Every Symbol Explained

$$\boxed{\text{FFN}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}_2 \cdot \text{GELU}(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2}$$

Symbol Shape What it does
$\mathbf{x}$ $(256,)$ One frame's attended representation
$\mathbf{W}_1$ $(256, 1024)$ Expands to higher-dimensional space
$\mathbf{b}_1$ $(1024,)$ Bias for expansion
$\text{GELU}(\cdot)$ $(1024,)$ Smooth non-linearity
$\mathbf{W}_2$ $(1024, 256)$ Compresses back to model dimension
$\mathbf{b}_2$ $(256,)$ Bias for compression
$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{x})$ $(256,)$ Deeply processed frame representation

Applied to all 64 frames simultaneously via matrix multiplication:

$$\text{FFN}(\mathbf{Z}) = \text{GELU}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}_1 + \mathbf{b}_1)\mathbf{W}_2 + \mathbf{b}_2$$

$$\underbrace{(64, 256)}_{\mathbf{Z}} \rightarrow \underbrace{(64, 1024)}_{\text{expand}} \rightarrow \underbrace{(64, 1024)}_{\text{GELU}} \rightarrow \underbrace{(64, 256)}_{\text{compress}}$$

17. What Comes Next

After the FFN and its residual connection, you have completed one full Transformer encoder layer:

One encoder layer:
  Attention (global context)   → residual + LN
  FFN       (per-frame depth)  → residual + LN
  Output:   (64, 256)

Your model stacks 4 (base) or 6 (scaled) of these layers.

After all layers complete, the output is $(64, 256)$ — 64 frame representations, each enriched by:

  • 4 (or 6) rounds of global attention
  • 4 (or 6) rounds of deep per-frame processing
  • Residual connections preserving all previous information

The next step is to collapse these 64 frames into a single vector for classification.

That is concept 14: Global Average Pooling.

notes.html:
One sentence summary: Global Average Pooling collapses the entire 64-frame sequence into a single 256-dimensional vector by averaging across time — but only over real frames, not padding — giving the classifier one compact summary of the entire sign.

1. Where We Are

After passing through all Transformer encoder layers, you have:

Output of final Transformer layer:  Z^(L)  shape: (64, 256)

Where $L$ is the number of layers (4 in base config, 6 in scaled config).

Each of the 64 rows is a 256-dimensional vector representing one frame, enriched by:

  • Local motion patterns from the 1D-CNN
  • Global temporal context from multi-head attention (repeated $L$ times)
  • Deep non-linear processing from the feed-forward blocks (repeated $L$ times)

The problem: your classifier needs one fixed-size vector to make a prediction. It cannot accept a sequence of 64 vectors — it needs a single summary.

Global Average Pooling (GAP) collapses the $(64, 256)$ tensor into a single $(256,)$ vector.

2. The Naive Approach — And Why It Fails

The simplest collapse is to just average all 64 frames:

$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{naive}} = \frac{1}{64} \sum_{t=1}^{64} \mathbf{h}^{(L)}_t$$

This seems reasonable. But there is a critical flaw.

Your sequences are center-padded with zeros. A sign of median length 21 frames inside a 64-frame window looks like this:

Frame layout:
[0,0,...,0 | sign frame 1, 2, ..., 21 | 0,0,...,0]
 ←21 zeros→  ←────── real sign ──────→  ←22 zeros→

If you average over all 64 frames:

$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{naive}} = \frac{1}{64} \left( 21 \times \mathbf{h}_{\text{real}} + 43 \times \mathbf{0} \right) = \frac{21}{64} \mathbf{h}_{\text{real}}$$

The padding zeros dilute the signal by a factor of $\frac{21}{64} \approx 0.33$.

The classifier receives a vector that is roughly one third the magnitude it should be. For a short sign, the model effectively reads mostly silence.

This was Bug Fix 3 identified in Experiment 4. The fix is to average only over real frames.

3. Masked Global Average Pooling — The Correct Version

The production implementation computes the average exclusively over non-padding frames.

Step 1: Identify real frames

A frame is real if at least one of its 690 feature values is non-zero after standardisation:

$$m_t = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}_t\|_\infty > 0 \quad \text{(real frame)} \\ 0 & \text{if } \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{(padding)} \end{cases}$$

In practice, the padding mask is computed before the Transformer as:

padding_mask = (x == 0.0).all(dim=2)   # True = padding
real_mask    = ~padding_mask            # True = real

Shape of real_mask: $(B, 64)$ — one boolean per frame per sample.

Step 2: Count real frames per sample

$$n_{\text{real}} = \sum_{t=1}^{64} m_t \quad \in \{1, 2, \ldots, 64\}$$

Clipped to a minimum of 1 to avoid division by zero:

$$n_{\text{real}} = \max\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^{64} m_t,\ 1\right)$$

Step 3: Compute the masked average

$$\mathbf{z} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{64} m_t \cdot \mathbf{h}^{(L)}_t}{n_{\text{real}}} \in \mathbb{R}^{256}$$

In matrix form:

$$\mathbf{z} = \frac{\mathbf{m}^\top \mathbf{H}^{(L)}}{n_{\text{real}}}$$

Where $\mathbf{m} \in \{0,1\}^{64}$ and $\mathbf{H}^{(L)} \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 256}$.

4. A Concrete Worked Example

Sign: DRINK, 21 real frames, center-padded to 64.

Real frame mask:
m = [0,0,...,0, 1,1,...,1, 0,0,...,0]
    ←21 zeros→  ←21 ones→  ←22 zeros→

n_real = 21

Frame representations after final Transformer layer:

h₁  = [0, 0, ..., 0]         ← padding (zeros)
h₂  = [0, 0, ..., 0]         ← padding
...
h₂₂ = [0.42, -0.18, ..., 0.71]   ← first real frame (preparation)
h₂₃ = [0.38, -0.22, ..., 0.69]   ← second real frame
...
h₄₂ = [0.91, 0.03, ..., -0.44]   ← last real frame (retraction)
h₄₃ = [0, 0, ..., 0]         ← padding
...
h₆₄ = [0, 0, ..., 0]         ← padding

Masked average:

$$\mathbf{z} = \frac{1}{21} \sum_{t=22}^{42} \mathbf{h}^{(L)}_t$$

The padding frames contribute exactly zero to the sum (because $m_t = 0$ for them). The result is a faithful average of the 21 real sign frames only.

Comparison with naive average:

Method Sign magnitude What the classifier sees
Naive (all 64 frames) $\times \frac{21}{64} = \times 0.328$ Diluted signal
Masked (21 real frames) $\times 1.0$ Full signal

The masked version gives the classifier the correct-magnitude summary regardless of sign length.

5. Why Average Instead of Other Pooling Methods?

Several alternatives exist. Here is why average pooling was chosen:

Alternative 1: Take the last real frame

$$\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{t_{\text{last real}}}$$

Problem: The last real frame is the retraction phase (hand returning to rest). This is the least informative moment of the sign. The preparation and core motion would be ignored.

Alternative 2: Take the first real frame

Problem: The first frame is the preparation phase. Same issue — the most informative core sign motion is in the middle.

Alternative 3: Max pooling

$$z_d = \max_{t: m_t=1} h^{(L)}_{t,d} \quad \text{for each dimension } d$$

Problem: Takes the maximum value in each dimension independently. The maximum of dimension 42 might come from frame 15, while the maximum of dimension 87 comes from frame 31. The resulting vector is a chimera that never actually existed at any single point in time.

Why average pooling wins

Average pooling gives equal weight to every real frame. A sign is a process — the beginning, middle, and end all carry information. The model has already used attention to weight frames internally during the Transformer layers. GAP then takes an unweighted summary of those enriched representations.

The sign classification is a property of the entire sequence, not of any single moment. Average pooling respects this.

6. The Effect of the Attention Layers on GAP

Here is a subtle but important point.

Before the Transformer layers, the frame representations only contain local information. Global average pooling over those would just average 64 independent frames — not very informative.

After the Transformer layers, each frame representation has been enriched with information from all other frames via self-attention.

Frame 20 (core mouth motion for DRINK) now contains:

  • Its own local features
  • Information borrowed from frame 5 (preparation phase)
  • Information borrowed from frame 40 (retraction phase)
  • Context from frame 30 (mid-motion)

So when GAP averages over all real frames, it is averaging over 21 richly contextualised representations, each of which already "knows" about the entire sign.

This is why GAP after a Transformer is much more powerful than GAP after a plain CNN — the Transformer has pre-aggregated the temporal information within each frame's representation.

7. Shape Transformations

Output of final Transformer layer:
  H^(L)      (B, 64, 256)

Real frame mask (computed before Transformer, reused here):
  real_mask  (B, 64)       ← boolean, True = real frame

Zero out padding frames:
  H^(L) * real_mask[:, :, None]   (B, 64, 256)

Sum over time dimension:
  sum = (H^(L) * mask).sum(dim=1)   (B, 256)

Count real frames:
  counts = real_mask.sum(dim=1).clamp(min=1)   (B,)

Divide:
  z = sum / counts[:, None]   (B, 256)

Output:
  z   (B, 256)   ← one summary vector per sign in the batch

The temporal dimension (64) is gone. The batch dimension ($B$) and feature dimension (256) remain.

8. The Code in Your Model

In src/model.py, inside ASLTransformerV5.forward():

# Stage 5: Masked Global Average Pooling

real_mask   = ~padding_mask                    # (B, T) — True = real
real_counts = real_mask.sum(1, keepdim=True)   # (B, 1) — how many real frames
             .float().clamp(min=1.0)           # avoid division by zero

x = (x * real_mask.unsqueeze(2).float()        # zero out padding frames
    ).sum(1) / real_counts                     # sum then divide

# x: (B, 256)  ← ready for classifier

Line by line:

Line Operation Shape
real_mask = ~padding_mask Invert: True = real $(B, 64)$
real_counts = real_mask.sum(1, keepdim=True) Count real frames $(B, 1)$
.float().clamp(min=1.0) Ensure no division by zero $(B, 1)$
x * real_mask.unsqueeze(2).float() Zero out padding rows $(B, 64, 256)$
.sum(1) Sum over time $(B, 256)$
/ real_counts Divide by real frame count $(B, 256)$

9. What the Pooled Vector Represents

After masked GAP, $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{256}$ is the model's best single-vector summary of the entire sign.

Intuitively it captures:

  • The average hand position across the sign trajectory
  • The average velocity profile of the sign
  • The average facial expression throughout
  • The dominant motion pattern

But because each frame was enriched by attention before pooling, $\mathbf{z}$ also implicitly captures:

  • The relationship between the start and end of the sign
  • The co-occurrence of hand position and facial expression
  • The temporal rhythm of the sign

This vector then goes directly into the classification head.

10. Bug Fix 3 Revisited — The Quantitative Impact

Experiment 3 (v3) suffered from unmasked global average pooling.

For a median-length sign of 21 frames padded to 64:

$$\text{Dilution factor (naive)} = \frac{21}{64} \approx 0.328$$

The classification vector had magnitude about one-third of what it should be.

After fixing this in Experiment 4 (v4):

Metric v3 (unmasked) v4 (masked) Gain
Top-1 test 42.18% 46.14% +3.96%
Top-5 test 69.48% 71.24% +1.76%

Note: v4 fixed four bugs simultaneously so the gain cannot be attributed to GAP alone. But this was identified as the most impactful of the four.

The effect is largest for short signs (1-10 frames) because those had the worst dilution ratio. Error analysis in Notebook 04 confirmed that short sign accuracy improved the most from v3 to v4.

11. Masked GAP vs Attention Masking — Two Different Things

Both appear in your model and both use the same padding mask. They are different operations:

Attention masking Masked GAP
Where Inside each Transformer layer After all Transformer layers
What it does Prevents frames from attending to padding Prevents padding from contributing to the summary vector
Effect Real frames do not receive information from padding Padding frames do not dilute the final pooled representation
Without it Real frames get "noise" from attending to zeros Short signs get magnitude-diluted classification vectors

Both are necessary. Removing either one degrades performance.

12. Summary

Concept Definition
Global Average Pooling Collapse time dimension by averaging
Masked Only average over real (non-padding) frames
Input $(B, 64, 256)$ — 64 enriched frame representations
Output $(B, 256)$ — one summary vector per sign
Real frame mask Boolean $(B, 64)$ — True = real, False = padding
Why not naive average Padding zeros dilute the signal by up to 67% for short signs
Why not max pooling Mixes dimensions from different time steps incoherently
Why not last frame Retraction phase is least informative
Why average works Attention has already enriched each frame with global context — averaging is a faithful summary

13. The Full Equation — Every Symbol Explained

$$\boxed{\mathbf{z} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T} m_t \cdot \mathbf{h}^{(L)}_t}{\displaystyle\max\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T} m_t,\ 1\right)}}$$

Symbol Shape Meaning
$T = 64$ scalar Fixed sequence length
$\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_t$ $(256,)$ Frame $t$ after final Transformer layer
$m_t \in \{0,1\}$ scalar 1 if frame $t$ is real, 0 if padding
$\sum m_t$ scalar Number of real frames in this sign
$\max(\cdot, 1)$ scalar Prevents division by zero for all-padding edge case
$\mathbf{z}$ $(256,)$ Final summary vector — input to classifier

14. What Comes Next

$\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{256}$ (base) or $\mathbb{R}^{512}$ (scaled) is now passed to the classification head.

The classification head is a two-layer MLP:

$$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{W}_2 \cdot \text{GELU}(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{z} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{250}$$

This produces 250 raw scores — one per ASL sign class. The highest score is the model's prediction.

That is concept 15: CrossEntropyLoss — what the model is actually optimising, and how those 250 scores are turned into a probability distribution and compared to the true label.

References

  • Vaswani et al. (2017) — Attention Is All You Need — GAP used for sequence summarisation
  • Your project: src/model.py → ASLTransformerV5.forward() — Stage 5: Masked GAP
  • Your project: notebooks/03_training.ipynb → Experiment 4, Bug Fix 3
  • Your project: notebooks/04_error_analysis.ipynb → short sign accuracy improvement v3→v4

notes.html:
One sentence summary: CrossEntropyLoss measures how wrong the model's predicted probability distribution is compared to the true label — and gives the gradient signal that drives all 21 million parameters to improve.

1. Where We Are

After Masked Global Average Pooling, you have:

z  (256,)   ← one summary vector for the entire sign

The classification head transforms this into 250 raw scores:

ŷ = W₂ · GELU(W₁z + b₁) + b₂    shape: (250,)

Each of these 250 numbers is called a logit — a raw unnormalised score. The sign with the highest logit is the model's prediction.

But logits are not probabilities. They can be any real number — positive, negative, large, small. Before we can compare the model's output to the true label, we need to convert them to a proper probability distribution. That is what CrossEntropyLoss does internally.

2. The Two Steps Inside CrossEntropyLoss

CrossEntropyLoss combines two operations into one:

Step 1:  Softmax   → convert logits to probabilities
Step 2:  NLL Loss  → measure how wrong the probabilities are

PyTorch combines them for numerical stability. But understanding them separately makes the concept clear.

3. Step 1 — Softmax: Logits to Probabilities

The problem: The 250 logits are arbitrary real numbers. We need them to be:

  • All positive
  • Sum to exactly 1.0
  • Larger logit → larger probability

The solution: Softmax.

$$\hat{p}_c = \frac{e^{\hat{y}_c}}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{250} e^{\hat{y}_j}} \quad \text{for } c = 1, \ldots, 250$$

The exponential $e^x$ converts any real number to a positive number. Dividing by the sum normalises everything to sum to 1.

A tiny worked example

Suppose the model produces logits for 4 classes (simplified from 250):

Logits:
  DRINK:   ŷ₁ = 3.2
  MILK:    ŷ₂ = 1.8
  WATER:   ŷ₃ = 0.5
  HELLO:   ŷ₄ = -0.9

Step 1: Exponentiate each:

e^3.2  = 24.53
e^1.8  =  6.05
e^0.5  =  1.65
e^-0.9 =  0.41
Sum    = 32.64

Step 2: Divide by sum:

p̂(DRINK) = 24.53 / 32.64 = 0.752   (75.2%)
p̂(MILK)  =  6.05 / 32.64 = 0.185   (18.5%)
p̂(WATER) =  1.65 / 32.64 = 0.051   ( 5.1%)
p̂(HELLO) =  0.41 / 32.64 = 0.013   ( 1.3%)
Sum       = 1.000

The model is 75.2% confident the sign is DRINK. If the true label is DRINK, this is a good prediction. If the true label is WATER, this is a bad prediction.

But how do we measure how bad it is? That is the job of the loss.

4. Step 2 — Negative Log-Likelihood: Measuring How Wrong

Given the true label $c^*$ (the index of the correct sign), the loss is simply:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log \hat{p}_{c^*}$$

We take the negative log of the predicted probability for the correct class only.

Why the negative log?

The log function has a critical property:

log(1.0) = 0      ← perfect prediction, zero loss
log(0.5) = -0.69  ← somewhat wrong
log(0.1) = -2.30  ← very wrong
log(0.01) = -4.60 ← extremely wrong
log(0.001) = -6.91 ← catastrophically wrong

The negative log of the correct class probability:

-log(1.0) = 0      ← perfect, no loss
-log(0.5) = 0.69   ← somewhat wrong, some loss
-log(0.1) = 2.30   ← very wrong, large loss
-log(0.01) = 4.60  ← extremely wrong, huge loss

As the model's confidence in the correct class approaches 1.0, the loss approaches 0. As confidence approaches 0, the loss approaches infinity.

Back to the DRINK example

Case 1: True label is DRINK

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log \hat{p}(\text{DRINK}) = -\log(0.752) = 0.285$$

Small loss. The model is mostly right.

Case 2: True label is WATER

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log \hat{p}(\text{WATER}) = -\log(0.051) = 2.976$$

Large loss. The model was very confident about DRINK but the answer was WATER.

Case 3: True label is DRINK, but model was unsure

Suppose the logits were flatter and $\hat{p}(\text{DRINK}) = 0.30$:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log(0.30) = 1.204$$

Moderate loss. The model predicted the correct class but with low confidence.

5. The Full CrossEntropyLoss Formula

Combining softmax and negative log-likelihood:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} = -\log \hat{p}_{c^*} = -\log \frac{e^{\hat{y}_{c^*}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{250} e^{\hat{y}_j}}$$

Expanding the log:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} = -\hat{y}_{c^*} + \log \sum_{j=1}^{250} e^{\hat{y}_j}$$

This form is numerically more stable and is what PyTorch actually computes internally.

The two terms have clear interpretations:

Term Role
$-\hat{y}_{c^*}$ Reward: push up the logit of the correct class
$+\log \sum_j e^{\hat{y}_j}$ Penalty: push down all logits (to prevent them from growing to infinity)

The loss is minimised when the correct class logit $\hat{y}_{c^*}$ is much larger than all other logits — exactly what we want.

6. The Gradient — How the Loss Drives Learning

The whole point of the loss is to produce gradients that update the model parameters.

Taking the derivative of CrossEntropyLoss with respect to the logit $\hat{y}_c$:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}}{\partial \hat{y}_c} = \hat{p}_c - \mathbf{1}[c = c^*]$$

Where $\mathbf{1}[c = c^*]$ is 1 if $c$ is the correct class and 0 otherwise.

This is a remarkably clean result. For each class:

Class Gradient Effect
Correct class ($c = c^*$) $\hat{p}_{c^*} - 1$ Always negative → push logit UP
Wrong class ($c \neq c^*$) $\hat{p}_c$ Always positive → push logit DOWN

Intuition:

  • The correct class gradient is $\hat{p}_{c^*} - 1$. If the model predicts 75% confidence, gradient = $0.75 - 1 = -0.25$. This negative gradient tells the model to increase the DRINK logit.
  • Every wrong class gets a positive gradient proportional to how much probability it was assigned. If the model gave 18.5% to MILK when the answer was DRINK, the MILK logit gets pushed down by 0.185.

The gradients are larger when the model is more wrong. A prediction of 1% on the correct class produces a gradient of $0.01 - 1 = -0.99$ — a strong signal to correct itself. A prediction of 99% produces a gradient of $0.99 - 1 = -0.01$ — almost no update needed.

This is the self-calibrating property of CrossEntropyLoss. The stronger the error, the stronger the correction.

7. Over a Full Batch

In practice, you compute the loss over a batch of $B = 64$ samples and average:

$$\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\text{CE}} = -\frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \log \hat{p}^{(i)}_{c^*_i}$$

Where $c^*_i$ is the true label for sample $i$ in the batch.

In your training loop:

criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)
logits    = model(batch_X)          # (64, 250)
loss      = criterion(logits, batch_y)  # scalar
loss.backward()                     # compute gradients
optimizer.step()                    # update all parameters

nn.CrossEntropyLoss in PyTorch:

  • Accepts raw logits (not softmax outputs)
  • Applies log-softmax internally (numerically stable)
  • Averages over the batch automatically
  • Takes integer class indices as targets (not one-hot vectors)

8. Why Not Use Mean Squared Error?

A natural question: why not just use:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{250} \sum_{c=1}^{250} (p_c - \hat{p}_c)^2$$

Where $p_c = 1$ for the correct class and 0 for all others?

Three reasons CrossEntropy is better:

Reason 1: Gradient magnitude

MSE gradient for the correct class:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}}{\partial \hat{p}_{c^*}} = 2(\hat{p}_{c^*} - 1)$$

At $\hat{p}_{c^*} = 0.99$ (almost perfect): gradient = $2(0.99-1) = -0.02$ — very small, good. At $\hat{p}_{c^*} = 0.01$ (very wrong): gradient = $2(0.01-1) = -1.98$ — strong, good.

But MSE operates on probabilities which are squashed by softmax. The gradient through softmax is small for extreme values. CrossEntropy avoids this by operating on logits directly.

Reason 2: Probabilistic interpretation

CrossEntropyLoss has a direct probabilistic interpretation: it minimises the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true label distribution and the predicted distribution. This is the mathematically correct objective for classification.

MSE treats classification as a regression problem — it tries to minimise the squared distance to a target vector. This is mathematically incorrect for probability distributions.

Reason 3: Speed of learning

When the model is very wrong (predicts 1% on the correct class), CrossEntropy gradient is $0.01 - 1 = -0.99$ — very strong correction.

MSE gradient at the same point is approximately $-1.98$ through the probabilities but much smaller through the logits after the softmax Jacobian. In practice, CrossEntropy learns faster on classification problems.

9. Label Smoothing — The Version Your Model Actually Uses

Your model does not use pure CrossEntropyLoss. It uses label smoothing with $\epsilon = 0.1$.

The problem with hard labels

Standard CrossEntropyLoss trains toward:

$$\mathbf{p}_{\text{true}} = [0, 0, \ldots, 1, \ldots, 0]$$

All probability on one class, zero on all others. The model is incentivised to push the correct class logit toward $+\infty$ — which is impossible and leads to overconfident predictions that generalise poorly.

What label smoothing does

Instead of training toward the one-hot vector, label smoothing trains toward a softer distribution:

$$\tilde{p}_c = \begin{cases} 1 - \epsilon + \dfrac{\epsilon}{250} & \text{if } c = c^* \\ \dfrac{\epsilon}{250} & \text{if } c \neq c^* \end{cases}$$

With $\epsilon = 0.1$ and 250 classes:

$$\tilde{p}_{c^*} = 1 - 0.1 + \frac{0.1}{250} = 0.9004$$

$$\tilde{p}_{c \neq c^*} = \frac{0.1}{250} = 0.0004$$

Instead of training toward $[0, 0, \ldots, 1, \ldots, 0]$, the model trains toward $[0.0004, 0.0004, \ldots, 0.9004, \ldots, 0.0004]$.

The smoothed loss formula

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}} = -\sum_{c=1}^{250} \tilde{p}_c \log \hat{p}_c$$

Expanding:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}} = -\tilde{p}_{c^*} \log \hat{p}_{c^*} - \sum_{c \neq c^*} \tilde{p}_c \log \hat{p}_c$$

$$= -(1-\epsilon)\log \hat{p}_{c^*} - \frac{\epsilon}{250} \sum_{c=1}^{250} \log \hat{p}_c$$

The first term is the standard CrossEntropy. The second term is the entropy of the uniform distribution — it pulls all predicted probabilities toward $\frac{1}{250}$.

What this achieves in your model

Two concrete benefits for signer-independent evaluation:

Benefit 1: Prevents overconfident predictions

Without smoothing, the model might predict DRINK with 99.9% confidence on training signers. When it sees a new signer, the same hand position might look slightly different and the model still assigns 99.9% — incorrectly.

With smoothing, the model is never incentivised to go beyond 90% confidence. It stays in a regime where the 250-class probability distribution is informative.

Benefit 2: Better calibration

Error analysis on your production model confirmed ECE = 0.097 with no temperature scaling. When the model says 82%, it is correct 82.5% of the time. This calibration emerges naturally from label smoothing.

A worked example with smoothing

True label: DRINK ($c^* = $ index of DRINK in 250 classes)

Without smoothing, target distribution:
  DRINK: 1.0000
  all others: 0.0000

With label smoothing (ε=0.1, 250 classes):
  DRINK: 0.9004
  MILK:  0.0004
  WATER: 0.0004
  ... (all 249 other classes): 0.0004

The model now gets a small gradient signal to not completely ignore the other 249 classes. This prevents the model from confidently mapping "anything that looks like a wrist moving toward the mouth" to DRINK — it must preserve some uncertainty.

10. What the Loss Value Actually Means

After training converges, what does a loss of, say, 2.2 mean?

Random baseline: If the model predicts uniformly (1/250 = 0.004 for each class):

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{random}} = -\log\!\left(\frac{1}{250}\right) = \log(250) \approx 5.52$$

Perfect prediction: If the model always predicts 100% on the correct class:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{perfect}} = -\log(1.0) = 0$$

Your model's training loss (Experiment 11, best epoch 79):

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}} \approx 0.89$$

This means the model assigns an average of $e^{-0.89} \approx 41\%$ probability to the correct class on training data — reasonable given 250 classes and label smoothing capping the ceiling.

Your model's validation loss (Experiment 11, best epoch 79):

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}} \approx 2.37$$

This means the model assigns an average of $e^{-2.37} \approx 9.4\%$ probability to the correct class on validation data. With 250 classes, 9.4% is about 23× better than random (0.4%). The gap between training loss and validation loss reflects the generalisation challenge of signer-independent evaluation.

11. CrossEntropy and the 250-Class Problem

With 250 classes, CrossEntropyLoss has a specific challenge: the model must distinguish between signs that are linguistically very similar (awake/wake, cut/scissors, hear/listen).

The loss does not know about linguistic similarity. It treats every wrong class identically — predicting MILK when the answer is DRINK incurs exactly the same loss as predicting HELLO when the answer is DRINK.

This is both a strength and a weakness:

Strength: The model is forced to find discriminative features for every pair of signs, even similar ones.

Weakness: The model cannot communicate "I was almost right" — predicting MILK when the answer is DRINK is treated identically to a completely wrong prediction.

Label smoothing partially addresses this by softening the hard boundary — the model is never penalised infinitely for assigning a tiny probability to wrong classes.

12. The Training Loop — Complete Picture

Now you can see how all the pieces connect:

For each batch of 64 signs:

1. Forward pass:
   X (64, 64, 690)          ← batch of 64 sign sequences
       ↓ Linear projection
   H⁰ (64, 64, 256)
       ↓ CNN block
   H¹ (64, 64, 256)
       ↓ Positional encoding
   H² (64, 64, 256)
       ↓ 4 (or 6) Transformer layers
   H^L (64, 64, 256)
       ↓ Masked GAP
   z  (64, 256)
       ↓ Classification head
   ŷ  (64, 250)             ← 250 logits per sign

2. Loss computation:
   L = CrossEntropyLoss(ŷ, y_true)   ← scalar

3. Backward pass:
   ∂L/∂ŷ   → (64, 250) gradient of loss w.r.t. logits
   ∂L/∂z   → (64, 256) backprop through classifier
   ∂L/∂H^L → (64, 64, 256) backprop through Transformer
   ...all the way back to W_proj...

4. Update:
   θ ← θ - η · ∇_θ L    (AdamW handles this)

The CrossEntropyLoss is the single scalar at the centre of this entire operation. Everything before it is the forward pass producing the prediction. Everything after it is the backward pass propagating corrections.

13. Summary

Concept Definition
Logit Raw unnormalised score for one class — any real number
Softmax Converts 250 logits to a probability distribution summing to 1
NLL Loss $-\log \hat{p}_{c^*}$ — negative log probability of the correct class
CrossEntropyLoss Softmax + NLL combined — operates on logits directly
Loss = 0 Model predicts 100% confidence on the correct class
Loss = 5.52 Model predicts randomly (uniform over 250 classes)
Gradient $\hat{p}_c - \mathbf{1}[c = c^*]$ — push correct class up, wrong classes down
Label smoothing Replaces hard targets with soft distribution — prevents overconfidence
$\epsilon = 0.1$ 90.04% on correct class, 0.04% on each wrong class
ECE = 0.097 Your model's calibration — confidence tracks accuracy well

14. The Full Equation — Every Symbol Explained

Standard CrossEntropyLoss:

$$\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} = -\log \frac{e^{\hat{y}_{c^*}}}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{250} e^{\hat{y}_j}} = -\hat{y}_{c^*} + \log \sum_{j=1}^{250} e^{\hat{y}_j}}$$

With label smoothing (what your model uses):

$$\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}} = -(1-\epsilon)\log \hat{p}_{c^*} - \frac{\epsilon}{250}\sum_{c=1}^{250}\log \hat{p}_c}$$

Symbol Meaning
$\hat{y}_c$ Logit for class $c$ — raw output of classifier head
$c^*$ True class index (correct ASL sign)
$\hat{p}_c = \frac{e^{\hat{y}_c}}{\sum_j e^{\hat{y}_j}}$ Predicted probability for class $c$ after softmax
$\epsilon = 0.1$ Label smoothing parameter
$(1-\epsilon) = 0.9$ Weight on correct class
$\frac{\epsilon}{250} = 0.0004$ Small weight distributed to all wrong classes

15. What Comes Next

CrossEntropyLoss gives you a scalar $\mathcal{L}$ and its gradients $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{y}_c}$.

Those gradients flow backwards through the entire model — through the classifier, through GAP, through the Transformer layers, through the CNN, through the linear projection — updating all 21 million parameters.

The mechanism that uses those gradients to update the parameters is the optimiser.

That is concept 17: AdamW — how the weights actually update.

But before that, concept 16 covers label smoothing in more depth: why softening the targets makes the model more honest about what it does not know.

References

  • Vaswani et al. (2017) — Attention Is All You Need — CrossEntropyLoss for sequence classification
  • Müller et al. (2019) — When Does Label Smoothing Help? — empirical analysis of label smoothing
  • Your project: notebooks/03_training.ipynb → criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)
  • Your project: notebooks/04_error_analysis.ipynb → ECE = 0.097 on production model
  • PyTorch docs: torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss

MASTER CONTEXT PROMPT — ASL TRANSLATION PFE PROJECT (FINAL v3)

You are assisting with a final-year engineering thesis (Projet de Fin d'Études, PFE) titled:

"Bidirectional Sign Language Translation System"

Authors: Rayan Akioud, Debbab Boutaina Supervisor: Azouagh Nabil Institution: FSTM Academic Year: 2025–2026

ASSISTANT RULES

  • Move slowly. One step at a time. One concept at a time.
  • Never rush. Never give the entire solution at once.
  • Wait for confirmation before moving to the next step.
  • Never revisit frozen decisions.
  • Think like a research collaborator, not a code generator.
  • When in doubt, ask. Do not assume.

1. THE VISION

A real bidirectional conversation between a deaf person and a hearing person.

DEAF PERSON:
  Signs continuously in front of webcam
  → MediaPipe Holistic extracts 115 body landmarks
  → Position + velocity features (690 per frame)
  → Sliding window T=64 → ASLTransformerV5
  → State machine with IDLE/ACTIVE detection
  → Gloss stream accumulation
  → Sentence boundary detection (pause = end)
  → LM Studio (async) → Natural English
  → Display + TTS

HEARING PERSON:
  Types response in text box
  → Displayed for deaf person to read

2. PROJECT PHASES

Phase 1 (Current): Sign → Text

Status: Model trained. Flask app running. ASL Citizen finetuning in progress.

Phase 2 (Future): Text → Sign

Via video retrieval or skeletal animation. Not started.

3. HARDWARE AND ENVIRONMENT (CRITICAL)

AMD hardware. ROCm. NOT NVIDIA. NOT CUDA.

CPU:  AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (8 cores)
GPU:  AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT (RDNA3, gfx1100, 20GB VRAM)
RAM:  32GB DDR5
OS:   Windows 11 + WSL2 Ubuntu 22.04
WSL2 RAM allocation: 24GB

ML Stack:

Python:     3.10
PyTorch:    2.4.1+rocm6.0
ROCm:       6.0
MediaPipe:  0.10.9  (downgraded from 0.10.33 — solutions API)
OpenCV:     4.13.0
pose-format: installed (for ASL Citizen .pose files)

Two critical ROCm fixes permanently applied:

# Fix 1: deleted conflicting library
rm .../torch/lib/libhsa-runtime64.so

# Fix 2: environment variable
export HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=11.0.0

device = torch.device('cuda') is correct for ROCm.

4. DATASET — GOOGLE ISLR (PRIMARY)

Google ISLR (Kaggle 2023) — child-directed ASL vocabulary

Samples:    94,477
Classes:    250 ASL signs
Signers:    21 people
Format:     Parquet (long format)
Raw size:   ~56 GB
Nature:     Child-directed vocabulary

Signer-independent split (zero overlap verified):

Train: 16 signers → 74,841 samples
Val:    2 signers →  8,521 samples (signers 25571, 53618)
Test:   3 signers → 11,115 samples (signers 18796, 30680, 27610)

5. DATASET — ASL CITIZEN (FINETUNING — IN PROGRESS)

ASL Citizen poses — HuggingFace: SorensenAI/asl-citizen-poses

Total files:    104,450 .pose files
Format:         Binary .pose (pose-format library)
Signers:        52 diverse signers
Our subset:     2,335 files matching 67 conversational signs
Download size:  ~1.5 GB (subset only)
Output dir:     data/asl_citizen/
Processed dir:  data/processed_asl_citizen/

5 signs missing from ASL Citizen (ISLR only):

DAD, GRANDMA, LOOK, MOM, THANKYOU

ASL Citizen .pose file structure:

Component offsets (fixed for all files):
  POSE_LANDMARKS:       offset 0   (33 points)
  FACE_LANDMARKS:       offset 33  (468 points)
  LEFT_HAND_LANDMARKS:  offset 501 (21 points)
  RIGHT_HAND_LANDMARKS: offset 522 (21 points)
  POSE_WORLD_LANDMARKS: offset 543 (33 points) ← IGNORED

Coordinate system: pixel space (NOT normalised to [0,1])
After shoulder-relative normalisation: identical to ISLR ✓
Missing landmarks: 0.0 (masked array, not NaN)

Reading .pose files:

from pose_format import Pose
import numpy as np

with open(file_path, 'rb') as f:
    pose = Pose.read(f.read())

data = np.array(pose.body.data)   # (F, 1, 576, 3) float32
mask = np.ma.getmaskarray(pose.body.data)  # True = missing

6. LANDMARK SELECTION (FROZEN)

115 landmarks from 543 total:

Ordering in our 115-landmark array:
  Slots  0–39:  40 face landmarks (curated)
  Slots 40–72:  33 pose landmarks (all)
  Slots 73–93:  21 left hand landmarks (all)
  Slots 94–114: 21 right hand landmarks (all)

Selected face landmark indices (MediaPipe face mesh):

FACE_LANDMARKS = [
    107, 105, 66, 63, 70,        # Left eyebrow
    336, 334, 293, 296, 300,     # Right eyebrow
    33, 160, 158, 133, 153, 144, # Left eye
    362, 385, 387, 263, 373, 380,# Right eye
    61, 40, 0, 267, 291,         # Upper lip
    146, 17, 375,                # Lower lip
    78, 82, 13, 312, 308, 14,    # Inner lip
    1, 2, 98, 327,               # Nose
]

Shoulder indices within 115-landmark array:

Left shoulder:  slot 40 + 11 = 51
Right shoulder: slot 40 + 12 = 52

7. FEATURE ENGINEERING (FROZEN)

Normalisation (per frame, shoulder-relative)

anchor = (arr[IDX_LS] + arr[IDX_RS]) / 2.0
scale  = np.linalg.norm(arr[IDX_LS] - arr[IDX_RS])
scale  = max(scale, 1e-5)
normalised = (arr - anchor) / scale

Feature Vector Layout — GROUPED (690 per frame)

Position block (345):
  [x_0..x_114 | y_0..y_114 | z_0..z_114]   indices 0–344

Velocity block (345):
  [Δx_0..Δx_114 | Δy_0..Δy_114 | Δz_0..Δz_114]  indices 345–689

Velocity: Δt = pt − pt−1, computed BEFORE padding/cropping
First frame velocity = 0

Temporal Handling

T = 64 frames fixed
F < 64: center-pad with zeros
F ≥ 64: center-crop from middle

Standardisation (padding-aware, two-pass)

# Pass 1: mean (real frames only)
# Pass 2: std  (real frames only)
# Apply row-by-row (avoids 13GB broadcast spike)
for i in range(X.shape[0]):
    X[i] -= mean      # (690,)
    X[i] /= std       # (690,)
    X[i][~mask[i]] = 0.0   # restore padding
    np.clip(X[i], -10.0, 10.0, out=X[i])

# Saved stats (for inference):
logs/train_mean_v5.npy   (690,)
logs/train_std_v5.npy    (690,)

Mirror Augmentation Index Ranges (v5)

P_LH_X = (73, 94);   P_RH_X = (94, 115)
P_LH_Y = (188, 209); P_RH_Y = (209, 230)
P_LH_Z = (303, 324); P_RH_Z = (324, 345)
V_LH_X = (418, 439); V_RH_X = (439, 460)
V_LH_Y = (533, 554); V_RH_Y = (554, 575)
V_LH_Z = (648, 669); V_RH_Z = (669, 690)

8. MODEL ARCHITECTURE — ASLTransformerV5 (PRODUCTION)

Input: (B, 64, 690)

Stage 1: Linear(690→256) + LayerNorm        → (B, 64, 256)
Stage 2: 1D CNN (2 layers, kernel=3)
         + residual + LayerNorm             → (B, 64, 256)
Stage 3: Sinusoidal Positional Encoding     → (B, 64, 256)
Stage 4: Transformer Encoder
         4 layers, 8 heads, d_model=256
         d_ff=1024, dropout=0.3
         norm_first=True, activation=gelu
         src_key_padding_mask for padding   → (B, 64, 256)
Stage 5: Masked Global Average Pooling     → (B, 256)
Stage 6: LayerNorm → Linear(256→256)
         → GELU → Dropout → Linear(256→250) → (B, 250)

Stats:

Parameters: 3,861,242
Size:       ~15.4 MB
VRAM:       <0.5 GB
Checkpoint: checkpoints/best_model_v5.pt (epoch 41)

9. TRAINING CONFIGURATION (FROZEN)

Loss:      CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)
Optimizer: AdamW(lr=5e-4, weight_decay=1e-4, betas=(0.9,0.999))
Scheduler: CosineAnnealingLR(T_max=80, eta_min=1e-6)
Clipping:  max_norm=1.0
Stopping:  patience=15
Batch:     64
Epochs:    80 max

Augmentation (training only):

Gaussian noise:  σ=0.05, p=0.50
Temporal shift:  ±3 frames, p=0.30
Spatial scale:   ×0.9–1.1, p=0.30
Mirror flip:     p=0.50
  → Negate x_pos (0–114) and x_vel (345–459)
  → Swap left↔right hand blocks in position and velocity

10. COMPLETE EXPERIMENT HISTORY

Exp Val Test Top-1 Test Top-5 Params Key Change
v1 48.68% — — 3.77M Baseline
v2 54.64% 43.88% 68.39% 3.77M Dropout + augmentation
v3 47.38% 42.18% 69.48% 14.75M T=128, d=512 — proved data bottleneck
v4 55.93% 46.14% 71.24% 3.77M 4 bug fixes + mirror flip
v5 57.94% 47.47% 73.29% 3.86M Position + velocity (690 input)

7 TBD TBD TBD 3.86M ASL Citizen finetune (IN PROGRESS)

Production model: v5 + 6a filter

67-sign conversational subset: 68.66% top-1, 86.68% top-5
Full 250-class evaluation:     47.47% top-1, 73.29% top-5

Four confirmed scientific findings:

  1. Signer diversity is the dominant accuracy ceiling
  2. Implementation quality matters (+2.26% from bug fixes)
  3. Explicit motion features help (+1.33% from velocity)
  4. Vocabulary restriction is highly effective (+21.19% from subset filter)
